  re-ran the scan, and got the old arithmetic back out of the cache. The key
  carries the costing revision now, read once per scan. (The Claude index
  already held this rule; this was the half that did not, and its own signature
  is deliberately left alone so no store that is already correct is discarded.)
- **`.acwinw`'s block rule had been dead since X-196** — a bare class loses to
  `common.css`'s `span.af-tipw`, which nothing noticed while it was alone on its
  line. The second block landed beside it and the spend figure drew glued to the
  tail of the reset sentence.

## 3.503.0 - The account box keeps its own lane while a swap is pending (U-135) (2026-09-14)

- **A promised account swap no longer draws over the control beside it.**
  Picking another sign-in on a live session moves the conversation at the next
  message, and X-213 puts that promise on the box itself — an arrow in front of
  the value and the colour that means "not yet". The arrow went INSIDE the sized
  box while the value went on asking for the whole of it, so the account was
  pushed out the far side and lay over its neighbour. Measured on scene 11 of
  the console fixture: box 635..767, value 647..779, the next control starting
  at 773. Nothing was wrong with the markup, which is why the suite had been
  green over it since X-213 shipped.
- **The arrow is paid for by the row, not by the value.** Letting the value
  shrink for it cured the overlap and caused something worse: 132px draws
  `personal@gmail · 12%`, 120px draws `personal@gmail · 1`, and that is a
  different figure rather than a shorter one. The box grows by the width of the
  mark for as long as the swap is pending, and the spacer — which holds no
  information — gives up the room.
- **Held by a measurement, since no string test could ever have seen it.**
  `test_console_column_ruler.js` now measures every value on the composer row
  against the box it was given, refuses to pass unless a box carrying a mark was
  actually on the page, and fails on the old rule naming the overlap in pixels.
- **And the box's own hover no longer reads as "an account is never
  remembered anywhere"** (X-255). That sentence was true when nothing was
  remembered; it now says what is decided in this box is for this session, and
  points at the standing sign-in an agent carries on its own row in Farm
  Settings.

## 3.502.0 - The account card says who is on it and who is next (X-258) (2026-09-14)

- **A card now says who is ON this sign-in right now** (●). In a live rotation
  cockpit that is the first thing asked of a card and the page could not answer
  it at all. Two sources, neither guessed at: the Console seats this window
  hosts (each carrying the account it was resolved to at launch), and the
  ENGINE’S OWN registry inside that slot’s directory — one file per live
  process, so a record found there IS signed in as that account. What the
  registry cannot say is what those processes are, and the card does not
  pretend: a count with "not hosted here" beside it is the whole claim.
- **And who is NEXT** (🔁 `next` / `2nd` / …), which is the other half. ‼️ It is
  DRAWN, never recomputed: `accountOrder` is now the line and `pickAccount` is
  its HEAD rather than a second implementation beside it — the one arrangement
  in which the sentence on the page and the account the runner picks cannot
  come apart. The pool is that engine’s sign-ins at the standing ceiling, which
  is the rotation a walled run’s handover really takes; claiming a campaign’s
  order on a page that cannot know which campaign would be the invented answer.
- **A sign-in at the wall is OUT of the line, not last in it** — it gets no chip
  at all. Drawing it as last would offer the reader a turn the rotation is never
  going to give it.
- **‼️ And the single number on the card no longer belongs to a queue nobody
  asked about.** The yellow `1`/`2` is a place in the REFRESH READING queue
  (X-206); on a page that now also draws a rotation, a naked digit is read as
  whichever order the reader has in mind — it was read that way in the audit
  that opened this item. The digit now travels with the ⟳ the idle state
  already wears, so the badge always says which line it is counting, and its
  panel opens by naming that line and disclaiming the other (SHORTHAND).
- Photographed on the `enginespanel` fixture in both themes, in every arity that
  differs: a card with a hosted seat, one with only processes this window can
  see, one with nobody, the leader, a middle place, an unmeasured account behind
  every measured one, and one out of the line entirely. The leader’s chip is
  deliberately NOT filled with colour — the first draft filled it green and it
  was photographed two centimetres from the green "who is on it" line, one
  colour carrying a forecast and a live fact at once.
- `accounts.list` returns `onIt` and `line` with the rest, so an agent reads the
  same two answers the card draws.

## 3.501.0 - An agent can stand on a sign-in of its own (X-255) (2026-09-14)

- **Every agent now has a standing account, per engine, and it outranks the
  machine-wide one.** "developer always runs on this plan, youtuber on that
  one" is the first thing a person wants once they hold three sign-ins, and
  until now it had to be chosen by hand at every launch: the per-agent record
  held a model, an effort and a route, and the word `account` did not appear in
  it. The box is on the agent’s row in Farm Settings, beside the model and the
  effort, and it is drawn only where that engine has captured sign-ins.
- **The order is written once and lives in one place** (`accountStore.
  resolveAccount`): what the launch itself names → this agent’s standing
  sign-in → the machine-wide "use this next" (`agentFarm.activeAccounts`) →
  nothing at all, which is the main sign-in. The per-agent rung had to sit
  ABOVE the machine-wide one or it would be a control that stores what it is
  told and changes nothing: a standing choice is set on this machine
  essentially always.
- **Which is why both surfaces now say WHOSE answer they are (ONE SUBJECT).**
  The Engines page’s ⚡ chip is the MACHINE’s choice and its panel says so,
  naming how many agents name a sign-in of their own and will not follow it —
  drawn from the real count, so a machine with nobody pinned reads no warning
  at all. Each account card names the agents that stand on it (📌), so the
  reader deciding whether to spend this plan can see who is on it without
  changing page. Without those two the chip would have become a button that
  quietly does nothing — the failure Principle 1 exists to prevent.
- **It is a LAYER, not a per-door feature.** One resolver feeds every launch
  door (`withAccount` now carries the agent), the terminal and Console spawns,
  the launch manifest (so "whose plan paid" is recorded correctly), the task
  runner’s environment and its pre-spawn refusal, and the bridge.
- **And it holds at 3 a.m. too.** The headless service resolves the same order
  from a new `agentAccounts` table the extension writes into
  `service-config.json` beside the slot list, rewritten whenever the box moves.
  A rung added only in the window would mean the promise held by day and
  silently stopped holding at night, which is where it matters most and where
  nobody is watching. Only the account travels; the rest of the defaults store
  stays on this side.
- **A standing sign-in this machine no longer holds REFUSES the launch** rather
  than falling through to whoever is logged in — the same rule a named one has
  followed since X-169, and it matters more here because nobody typed it at
  this launch, so nobody is looking. The bridge refuses the WRITE for the same
  reason: `agents.defaults.set` takes `account` and rejects an id naming no
  stored slot of that engine, which would otherwise refuse every later launch
  of that agent from a setting the user cannot see. `agents.defaults` reports
  the resolution with its own vocabulary (`agent` / `machine` / `main`).
- Drawn and looked at in both themes on the `engines` and `enginespanel`
  fixtures, in both arities: the agent that stands on its own sign-in and the
  one beside it that falls through to `Default → <the machine’s>`.
- Fixed on the way past: `tools/parity_suggest.js` crashed with an ENOENT
  stack unless the gate’s output had been redirected into a file called
  `par.out` — it now runs the gate itself and takes capability names on the
  command line. And the Console page’s live permission strip had a stale
  assertion left from 3.500.0 (the suite was red at HEAD); the code was right,
  the test was pinning the line before it.

## 3.500.0 - Antigravity is not offered a permission mode it cannot keep (S-60) (2026-09-14)

- **The "ask me" rows are gone from Antigravity's pickers.** The engine has no
  approval protocol — nothing leaves the process asking "may I", so nothing
  outside it can answer — and a mode whose meaning is "ask me" (`manual`) or
  "stop rather than ask" (`dontAsk`) was a promise the box made and the engine
  could not keep (session 5768a908: the model wrote "do you approve?" into its
  own text and carried on, because that sentence was prose, not a gate). The
  rows an engine can keep are now ONE rule (`permissionChoicesFor`, off the
  engine's own `AGY_MODES_REFUSED`): the Console composer, the Tasks form and
  its schedule steps, the Missions member rows and profile tool, and both
  launcher QuickPicks draw from it; `validateLaunch` and the bridge's run
  dimensions refuse the same names at the door with the engine's own sentence —
  so a schedule written with `agy` + `manual` is refused when it is written,
  not at 3 a.m. Every other engine keeps the whole list, the same object.
- **`--sandbox` — the engine's one real restraint — is deliberately NOT wired,
  and the reason is a measurement, not a preference.** On this machine, agy
  print mode: without the flag, `echo WROTE > file` finished in 3.9 s with the
  file on disk; with `--sandbox`, the stream reached `run_command · ACTIVE` and
  never left it — 60 s and 180 s, no output, no file, and the same for a bare
  `echo hi`. A run wired to it would sit until `--print-timeout` (two hours)
  looking like a broken engine. The measurement is on the constant
  (`AGY_SANDBOX_HANGS_HERE`) and beside the plan row; the decision is back on
  Notices.
- Measured in the laid-out DOM (`measure_page`): the Antigravity composer's
  permission box is `|plan|acceptEdits|bypassPermissions`; every other
  composer's carries `manual` and `dontAsk`. New scene `console-agy`.

## 3.499.0 - the leader turn spends the pool or waits for it, and a half turn is never leadership (X-302) (2026-09-14)

- **The sentry's leader turn never leaves the pool.** When every account the
  campaign was given is at or past its ceiling, the turn used to resolve to
  `''` — and on the spawn seam `''` means no variable, and no variable means
  the machine's own sign-in: the exact plan the pool was drawn to protect.
  `leaderAccountFor` (the same `campaignPick` the round makes) now answers
  either an account or a HOLD, and a hold is what it says: the campaign
  sleeps to the earliest five-hour reset INSIDE the pool and runs the leader
  turn there. A named leader account with no room is waited for the same way,
  never swapped.
- **A held turn is taken up again, not forgotten.** The poll that fires after
  the sleep carries no finished task, and a tick with none judges nothing and
  opens the round on a template the leader never saw. The round that woke the
  leader is remembered on the record (`leaderHold`) and re-measured from its
  own transcript when the pool has room; until then no round opens at all.
- **‼️ The trap: an account at 95% opens the turn and hits its limit a few
  thousand tokens in.** That was one more failed turn on the mechanical path —
  the round opened on a template, the streak grew, and the night went on as if
  the leader had been consulted. Judged now on the engine's own limit sentence
  (`isLimitFailure`, the reader the task board already retries on): the turn is
  `held`, nothing it wrote counts, the slot's figure is re-read (the cached
  percentage is the one that lied) and the pool is asked once more WITHOUT it —
  room elsewhere is a clean turn now, none is the hold above. The money is
  counted (it was spent); the streak is not (a wall is not a broken setup).
- A stopped campaign drops its hold. Everything above is pure and measured in
  `test_sentry_run` and `test_sentry_leader`; the runtime seam is `sentryTick`.

## 3.498.0 - the terminal's command history is the fleet's, not the account's (X-277) (2026-09-14)

- **Not one Claude slot on this machine had a `history.jsonl` at all.** Every
  isolated REPL session has been typing into a history that dies with the
  account — the X-270 fault by another name, and the last open child of that
  family.
- **A shared FILE is not a shared folder.** The five `sharedPaths` are reached
  by junctions; a file the engine appends to has to be the same file under two
  names, or the copies diverge the moment either is written. So `sharedFiles`
  is its own axis with its own mechanism: a hard link, and sameness answered by
  inode rather than by resolving a path (a hard link has no target to resolve,
  and `lstat` reports it as an ordinary file).
- Measured before it was built: Claude Code opens the file with a locked
  APPEND, so the inode never changes and the link survives ordinary use; the
  one path that would replace it is the retention prune, gated behind an
  enterprise taint that is off here. `linkSync` needs no administrator on NTFS,
  two links report one inode and a separate file another.
- **The slot's own typing is never dropped.** A history that exists only in the
  slot is moved INTO the pool and then linked; where both exist and differ, the
  pool wins and the slot's copy is set aside as `.slot-copy` rather than
  deleted.
- Two refusals, both by name: a slot on a different drive is told that a hard
  link cannot cross one — never quietly given a copy, which is the answer this
  family exists to refuse — and a file system that cannot report an inode reads
  "cannot say" rather than turning every healthy slot into a permanent gap.

## 3.497.0 - the housekeeping run that breaks a slot is now the one that repairs it (X-301) (2026-09-14)

- **The sixth gate watched the fleet and never the slot.** Everything it heard
  travelled one way — the user edited `settings.json`, so the slots must follow
  — and it had nothing to say about a slot that was whole and then broke. Slots
  break on a schedule: the engine prunes its own scratch directories, and on a
  relocated config directory those are junctions, so a recursive remove unlinks
  them instead of walking into them.
- So the contract was only ever asked again when somebody opened a door, and
  between two doors a slot sat writing its records **inside the account**
  instead of into the pool — the one thing the shared links exist to prevent.
- Each slot's housekeeping stamp is now watched beside the fleet's files. The
  stamp is the engine announcing it has just been through that directory, so
  the event that breaks the slot is the event that repairs it. No loop is
  possible: the contract writes junctions and the files it names, never the
  engine's own stamp.
- An engine that stamps nothing contributes no watcher — the same refusal
  `keptAt` already makes — rather than being given an invented filename that
  would report "nothing ever changes" for ever.
- Correction to the previous entry: the `afterHousekeeping` reading was already
  surfaced — the Engines card draws a `↻N` badge whose panel names the cause and
  says *"every repeat followed this engine's own housekeeping"*. What was
  missing was never the telling; it was that nothing acted on it.

## 3.496.0 - a gate that may not fail a launch may not fail silently either (X-301) (2026-09-14)

- **Two slots sat with `link:todos` and `link:shell-snapshots` missing across a
  whole night of launches** — the junctions that keep a slot's records in the
  shared pool instead of piling up inside the account (X-271). The repair
  primitive works: called by hand it restored both, wrote them to disk and
  journalled them. The journal held **not one row** to say the launch gate had
  ever tried.
- All four contract gates — `start`, `watch`, `capture`, `launch` — caught
  everything and said nothing, each with a comment explaining why it must never
  fail the thing it runs beside. Every one of those comments is right; what
  none of them may do is leave no trace, because **a swallowed throw and a gate
  that never ran look identical from outside** — which is exactly where a
  person stands when the invariant is quietly gone.
- The promise is kept and the silence is not: the gate still cannot fail its
  caller, and the reason now lands in the instrument that already exists, as
  `clause: 'contract'` — a different fact from a clause whose own repair failed.
- **The engine's own housekeeping is what deletes them, and the product had
  already proved it without anyone reading the answer.** `accounts.repairs`
  reports `afterHousekeeping` against `compared`; on this machine it stands at
  **24 of 24** for those two clauses and **0** for every other clause in the
  contract. The correlation X-292 built to answer this question has been
  sitting at "the engine does it, every time" while the fleet re-repaired for
  ever. Surfacing that reading, and acting on it, is the rest of X-301.

## 3.495.0 - a session ran for as long as its turns ran, not for as long as it was open (S-53) (2026-09-14)

- **The Duration column is now the turns' own durations added up.** S-52 took
  the absences out of the wall clock and was right about them; everything
  shorter than the break limit was still inside the figure — somebody reading
  an answer, somebody typing the next prompt, twenty minutes of neither. On a
  conversation worked in bursts that was most of the number.
- **Three rungs, each one a refusal to invent**: the sum where the turns were
  measured, the wall clock less absences where they were not, and the raw wall
  clock for an embedding that has never heard of either. A transcript nobody
  could read (over the scan limit, an import) shows nothing rather than a
  borrowed figure — the host sends `busyMin` only where it exists.
- **The panel accounts for the difference** instead of letting the figure
  shrink unexplained: *ran for* · *between turns — thinking, typing, nothing* ·
  *away over N breaks* · *wall clock*. Cost per hour, minutes per turn, seconds
  per API call, the sort and the range filter all move onto the run time, and
  they move together because the page has one reader for it.
- Switching the absence rule off (`agentFarm.sessionBreakMin: 0`) no longer
  also forgets the turns: that setting is a statement about absences, and
  tying the two would make one figure depend on a decision that is not about it.

## 3.494.0 - the project's start buttons say which sign-in they would spend, in a panel that can hold it (X-296 / X-262) (2026-09-14)

- **X-262 was done on one of its two surfaces.** Agent Detail put the inherited
  setup — engine · model · effort · permission mode, the sign-in, and its live
  window figure — into an AFTip. The Projects page built the same four
  paragraphs and put them in a native `title`, which truncates, cannot scroll
  and cannot be entered with the pointer. The figure at the end of the sign-in
  line is the one part of that setup that goes stale on its own, and it is
  exactly the part a cut-off tooltip drops.
- Both start controls on the Work tab now carry it in the panel. The rule is by
  SHAPE, not by length: anything that is text is an AFTip.
- **The test never asked which surface** — every assertion was about the text,
  and the text was right on both pages. It asks now.
- Honest limit: this was not photographed. The Projects page is the one large
  surface with no render fixture, so `render_page` cannot be pointed at it —
  opened as its own item. The wrapper was checked against the layout instead
  (`.pj-worktop` has no direct-child rule, and the click handler selects the
  button itself rather than a parent).

## 3.493.0 - a sign-in that is not on this machine stops the run instead of quietly changing it (X-296 / X-260) (2026-09-14)

- **The same task spent a different plan depending on whether a window was
  open.** The headless service already refused a run whose account resolves to
  nothing — its own words: *"a name that resolves to nothing REFUSES the run
  rather than falling through to the main sign-in… at 3 a.m. with nobody
  watching it is worse, not better."* The extension's own runner fell straight
  through: `accountEnv` answers `{}` for a slot it cannot find, `{}` is no
  environment variable, and no variable is the machine's own sign-in.
- **So a schedule naming a forgotten account ran, succeeded, and spent whoever
  happened to be signed in** — off the rotation, unattributable, and with
  nothing anywhere saying so. Three ways in: the slot was deleted, the slot
  belongs to another engine, or the standing choice itself points at a slot
  that is gone (which a settings file carried from another machine can do on
  its own).
- **It is a HOLD here, not a skip**, and that is the only difference allowed
  between the two runners: the board can carry the sentence and release the
  work the moment the sign-in is captured again; the night cannot. The hold
  reads as waiting for a **hand** — the one wait in the table that no run
  finishing and no minute passing will ever clear — and names the door
  (`accounts.capture`).
- **Forgetting a sign-in now names everything that points at it.** The dialog
  listed the runs already on the board and said nothing about the runs that do
  not exist yet: schedules, templates, workflow steps, triggers and launch
  profiles all carry an account, and the nightly schedule saved on the slot
  being deleted was never mentioned.

## 3.492.0 - the record of an automated run is derived from the run (X-296 / X-251) (2026-09-14)

- **A task's launch manifest was assembled by hand from three fields** while
  the spawn a few lines below it read the whole task. Four dimensions were
  therefore recorded wrong on every headless, scheduled, triggered, workflow
  and mission run: the **account**, the **route** (`providerId`/`tier`), the
  **tier** in the requested half, and the **CLI**.
- **The account is X-251's own fault, at the one door X-251 never read.**
  Measured live: a run spending `claude-murvietnam` filed a manifest naming
  `claude-aicozums` — the engine's *active* sign-in — because the recorder
  resolved a slot from options that had no `account` in them, while the
  environment layer beside it took the task's real one. Two readers, two
  answers, and the manifest is the only witness a transcript cannot replace.
- **The route was resolved with nothing chosen**, on the strength of a comment
  saying a stored automation carries no provider selection. It does — the spawn
  passes `routeOf(task)` to the runtime — so a run served by one endpoint could
  be recorded against another.
- **The discipline was read off the agent, not the run**: a job that switched
  superpowers off, and every mission member (which never gets the default),
  was recorded as whatever the agent's own setting said.
- **The list is no longer written by hand anywhere.** `launchDimsOf(task)` is
  the task's launch dimensions in the shape the record takes them, and the
  guard is derived rather than declared: the suite reads `LaunchOptions` and
  `RunDimensions` out of their own sources and fails on a shared dimension that
  does not travel. The recorder's parameter type carried the same narrowing —
  three optional fields accept an object with eight — and now takes the shape.

## 3.491.0 - a 429 that says how long is believed, not out-guessed (S-63) (2026-09-14)

- **The usage endpoint's `Retry-After` was never read.** The comment over the
  backoff curve always said "a 429 with no Retry-After leaves one safe
  reading" — but the GET returned `{status, body}` and nothing else, so both
  readers (the dashboard's plan card and the fleet's per-account service)
  invented the 3 → 15 min curve on every 429: too long (a counter stale for no
  reason) or too short (one more request spent for nothing).
- **The endpoint's own figure is the hold now**, delay-seconds or HTTP-date,
  within a ceiling of an hour (a header that says "a day" is treated as no
  header). A hold the endpoint named does not feed the curve: the next
  unexplained 429 starts it afresh. Per account, as X-278 left it — the account
  that was told the figure holds for it and no other.
- **The card says which happened**: *"asked for 42 s"* against *"did not say
  how long — backing off"*.
- The reply also carries the `anthropic-ratelimit-*` headers verbatim
  (`limitHeaders`), so whether a 429 is about the token or the machine can be
  READ off the next one rather than inferred from a second account's refusal.

## 3.490.0 - a claude running for nobody is seen, and ended only where it is ours (S-59) (2026-09-14)

- **A survivor of a reload showed on no surface at all.** A window reload or a
  crash kills the extension host and not the `claude -p` under it: the child
  keeps its session in the CLI's registry, keeps working on a dead pipe, keeps
  spending — and the new host's seat map is empty, the task board's sweep has
  already re-queued its run, and the registry was read only when a resume
  happened to name that one id. X-266 reclaimed the Console survivors of a
  `resume:true` restart; the headless survivor and every ordinary reload's
  survivors were left where they were.
- **`farm.health` → `sessions.leftovers`** is the whole set, read the way every
  door now reads it (`leftoversOf`): program-owned (`sdk-cli`), not the
  daemon's spare, not hosted by this window, not read by another. `ours` names
  what started each one — a Console card, or a task run by the id the board
  wrote down — and only those may be ended by a door; a program-owned session
  this farm has no record of is somebody else's SDK and is reported, never
  touched. Empty is the only healthy answer.
- **The two unattended doors end a leftover of ours instead of waiting for it.**
  A person at the Console door is asked ("End it and continue here"); a queued
  task and a bridge caller have nobody to ask, and a survivor never lets go by
  itself. The S-19 gate parked a resumed run behind it for ever — which after
  a `resume:true` restart is the continuation of the very conversation the
  survivor holds, so the night shift stalled on its own leftover. The gate now
  ends it (once per pid, asynchronously, said on the row) and asks again on its
  next beat. `console.start resume=` used to start `--resume` against whatever
  held the id and leave the CLI to sort it out — measured as a card frozen in
  `starting` behind a lock it never got; it now reclaims a leftover of ours and
  waits it out, and refuses any other holder by name rather than doubling it.
- The Console door's own offer widened by the same reading: a headless run's
  survivor is ours too, which the old `consoleIds`-only test could not see.

## 3.489.0 - a card removed while it was live closes its own lane (X-300) (2026-09-14)

- **"End & Remove Session" on a running card left its swim lane open on the
  Live Timeline for ever.** The Console mirror says `SessionEnd` when the seat's
  status turns `ended` — but removing a LIVE card closes it silently and fires
  once with the seat already gone (S-29: one gesture, one repaint), so the pass
  that would have said it never ran. Measured 2026-09-13 on a Codex lane, the
  engine whose hook file declares no `SessionEnd` of its own, so the mirror was
  the only thing that could ever have closed it. `console.close forget=true`
  takes the same path.
- **The lane now remembers enough to close itself** — the session id, cwd and
  engine every payload was stamped with — and when the seat it mirrored is
  gone it closes any open tool span and says `SessionEnd` from that memory,
  still yielding to a wire that reports the end itself (X-297). A seat that
  never opened a lane closes nothing: no invented end.
- The after-end transcript sweep (X-271) sat behind the same early return and
  treats a vanished seat as ended too.
- Closing without `forget` was never affected: the ordinary close fires with
  the seat still there, and the status pass says the end as before.

## 3.488.0 - a 429 is about a token, until the machine says it twice (X-278) (2026-09-14)

- **One account running out of queries froze the counters of every other
  account.** The usage service held ONE backoff for the whole fleet, on the
  stated ground that "the limit being reported is about this caller" — and that
  premise was an assumption nobody had measured. The accounts hold different
  tokens with different allowances, so a 429 for one of them said nothing
  whatever about the other two, and blinded them for up to three minutes at a
  time.
- **Now the refused account backs off alone** — its own curve, 30 s doubling to
  3 min — and it is SKIPPED in the round robin rather than handed the fleet's
  one request per interval, which would have been the same blindness arriving
  by the other door. The accounts that were never refused keep being read.
- **The fleet backs off only once a SECOND account is refused while the first is
  still held**, which is the shape a limit about the machine actually has. So
  the policy is correct under either reading of what a 429 means here, and
  finding out which one is true costs exactly one extra request rather than N.
  A request the endpoint answers clears both holds: it is the plainest possible
  evidence that this machine is not the thing being limited.
- **And the card says which of the two happened** instead of one sentence for
  both: *"rate limited THIS account — it backs off for 3 min; the other accounts
  keep being read, because their allowance is their own"*, or *"…and another is
  held too — that is a limit on this machine, so every account backs off."*
- The politeness the old rule was protecting never lived in the backoff: it
  lives in the shared floor — at most one request per interval, whatever the
  number of accounts — and that is untouched.

## 3.487.0 - a sign-in says how long it has left, and why signing in elsewhere missed it (X-275) (2026-09-14)

- **An account's health was a verdict on the present tense and nothing else.** A
  slot read `🟢 ready` right up to the hour its refresh token died and
  `🟠 needs signing in` the hour after, with no warning in between. MEASURED on
  this machine 2026-09-14: a Claude refresh token is issued for ~30 days — the
  four credentials on disk had 18.5, 20.5, 21.3 and 27.4 days left — while the
  access token beside it lasts hours and is renewed over HTTP without anybody
  noticing. So the only clock that ever needs a person is the slow one, and it
  was the one nothing read: a month of notice reached nobody.
- **The card now says it, in the badge rather than a panel** — `🟡 3 days left`,
  keeping the WORKING colour on purpose, because it does work. Painting it the
  same amber as an expired sign-in would be two verdicts with one lie in them.
  The panel names the date it stops refreshing and which of the two clocks that
  is.
- **And the half the user actually hit: a slot's sign-in is its OWN credential.**
  Signing in through the browser or `/login` writes `~/.claude/.credentials.json`
  and leaves every slot exactly as dead as it was. That is not a fault — it is
  what keeping accounts apart MEANS — but it was invisible, so a person renewed
  the machine's sign-in, saw the row unchanged and read the fleet as broken.
  Where the machine's sign-in is THIS SAME account and this row is not working,
  the card says so and points at the cure that does reach it: the 🔑 beside it,
  which opens the flow in this account's own directory.
- **Copying the live credential across is refused out loud rather than silently
  not offered.** An OAuth refresh ROTATES the refresh token, so one grant in two
  directories is two copies invalidating each other: the row would work until
  the machine's own install refreshed, then die again saying no more than it
  does now.

## 3.486.0 - stop means stop, including the words already on their way (S-54) (2026-09-14)

- **Interrupt looked like it worked for a second and the agent carried on.**
  Measured against claude-cli 2.1.269 (haiku, test-driven): a message said into
  a running turn is QUEUED by the CLI; a plain `interrupt` ends the turn and one
  second later the CLI opens a NEW turn with the queued message, unprompted —
  its receipt had even said `still_queued: []`. The model, reading its own
  context, carries on with exactly what it was doing. The deny text the reader
  saw ("The user doesn't want to proceed with this tool use…") was never the
  cause: the turn did end; the queue started the next one.
- **The CLI advertises the cure on `system/init.capabilities`:**
  `interrupt_cancel_queued_v1` — the same request with `cancel_queued: true`
  withdraws every queued message alongside the abort and names them under
  `cancelled`. `ConsoleHost.interrupt` now sends it when advertised (measured:
  no new turn in the twelve seconds watched); an older CLI gets the plain
  request as before.
- **Every message the host says is stamped with a uuid**, the id the CLI's
  receipts speak in, and the ones said into the running turn are remembered by
  it — so the card can say which words were withdrawn: *"1 message you said into
  this turn was withdrawn with it and did NOT reach the model: «…» — say it
  again if you still mean it."* A CLI that cannot withdraw them is reported
  just as plainly: *"still queued and WILL start a new turn"*. An empty receipt
  says nothing — a silent stop is the right stop.

## 3.485.0 - a request is claimed before it runs, and a timeout says which of two things happened (X-268) (2026-09-13)

- **The bridge ran requests one behind the other, awaiting each handler.** An op
  that asks a person — `sessions.end` opens a confirmation dialog, by design —
  therefore held EVERY request behind it until the dialog was answered, and
  unrelated ops from other agents died at the client's 20 s. Measured 2026-09-09.
- **And the client called that a failure of the extension** ("timed out — ensure
  VS Code and Agent Farm are active") while the runner still had the file in its
  listing and ran it AFTER the caller had been told so: one `projects.log`
  reached the worklog under a "failure", and one `console.start` became two
  conversations once the caller repeated it.
- **Now the scan never waits.** Each request is read, TAKEN OFF THE DISK, given
  a `.pending.json` marker (op, when, which boot) and dispatched without being
  awaited — so a dialog holds nobody but its own caller, and a request runs at
  most once: a second scan, a second window on the same storage, or the same
  file dropped again all find it gone, and an id this host already answered is
  answered from memory rather than run again.
- **`af.js` reads the marker at its timeout and says the truth** — `detail.state`
  is `running` (the extension took the op and is still on it; NOT a failure, do
  not repeat a mutating op, the answer lands in `detail.response`, kept 24h) or
  `unclaimed` (nobody is listening; the request was withdrawn, nothing ran).
- **A marker left by a previous boot** is a request the host died under: it is
  closed on activation with an answer that says so, never re-run — a mutation
  it may have completed cannot be undone by running it twice.

## 3.484.0 - one live process per session id, made true before a resume (X-266) (2026-09-13)

- **A window reload kills the extension host and NOT the `claude -p` under it.**
  The survivor keeps the session in the CLI's registry and keeps working — files,
  commits, bridge calls — with its words on a dead pipe. Reviving the same id
  beside it was measured twice: as two agents editing one repo (2026-09-09), and
  as a card frozen in `starting` for twenty minutes behind a lock it never got
  (2026-09-13, claude-cli 2.1.269). Either way the process the reader was
  looking at was never the one doing the work.
- **So every revived row is RECLAIMED before it is started** (`ConsoleHost.reclaim`):
  the holder is ended and its registry record watched until it drops; only then
  is the id started, and its first line says the survivor was ended. A holder
  that will not go is reported as lost with its pid and never started beside.
  The reclaiming is phase one of the revive and the only part that waits; the
  index is read and subscribed to in one synchronous phase two, so the scan's
  completion cannot fall into a gap (the ordering test pins this).
- **‼️ The registry is per claude home, and a machine has several.** A session
  on an account slot writes `<slot>/sessions/<pid>.json` and `~/.claude/sessions/`
  stays empty — measured with the twin on disk: every reader that asked the
  machine's own home answered "nobody owns this", which is the answer that starts
  a second copy. All sixteen readers now ask every home at once (the machine's,
  the window's own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, every captured Claude slot), so ending a
  card, switching its account, refusing a held resume and hiding a spare worker
  all see slot sessions for the first time.
- **`farm.health` reports `sessions.twins`** — any session id the registry shows
  under more than one live pid, across every home. Empty is the only healthy
  answer; a check that reads the process list races the thing it watches.

## 3.483.0 - the fleet writes Codex's hook file, not only its trust (X-298) (2026-09-13)

- **X-295 taught this side to SIGN a Codex hook file and read it back; the file
  itself was still whatever somebody typed once.** On this machine that was
  2026-09-06, and it still carried `-m 3` — the timeout X-265 retired for cutting
  off the one listener worth waiting for. A machine with no such file had no
  Codex wire at all, and moving `agentFarm.livePort` repaired Claude's side while
  merely REPORTING Codex's.
- **So the fleet's `~/.codex/hooks.json` is now written by the same wire that
  signs it** — seven events, the current command, at every gate that already
  completes a slot. A hook is ours by the marker in its URL, exactly as on
  Claude: a hook the user wired themselves is never read, never re-pointed and
  never removed, and the first file they wrote is kept beside it as
  `.agentfarm-bak`.
- **The file is written in ONE place.** A slot receives it by carry and grows no
  `hooks.json` of its own, so the carry clause and the hooks clause cannot each
  undo the other's answer; the fleet's wire is signed before the slots are
  projected from it, so what a slot copies is already right.

## 3.482.0 - a declared hook that never arrives is not a wire (X-297) (2026-09-13)

- **3.481.0 believed the hook file, and the Live Timeline lost every Codex
  turn-end.** Verified live on that build: `hooks.json` declares a `Stop` hook,
  `config.toml` trusts it, `hooks/list` reports it trusted — and two Codex turns
  in a row produced no `stop` event at all. Suppressing the mirror on that
  declaration took away the only turn-end those lanes had ever had.
- **So the mirror now stands aside only for what has actually been HEARD.** Each
  real hook teaches its own name (`LiveMonitor.realHookKinds`), the proof is kept
  per engine in `globalState`, and the adapter's `liveWire.events` is only the
  upper bound — a payload from somewhere else cannot teach the mirror to go
  quiet. Keeping the proof is also what closes the race the previous build used
  the wire reading for: Codex names its thread eight seconds before its first
  hook fires, and a hook heard in an earlier session is one the next session's
  first event can already stand aside for.
- Same lesson as X-295, one layer up: **"trusted" is a file's claim, not a
  measurement.**

## 3.481.0 - the mirror says only what the engine will not (X-297) (2026-09-13)

- **A Codex Console session was telling the Live Timeline everything twice.**
  Measured 2026-09-13 in `live-events.jsonl`: session `01a09aa0…` logged `start`
  at 11:56:28 and again at 11:56:36, `prompt` at 11:56:30 and again at 11:56:36 —
  once from the Console mirror, once from the hook wire that started working in
  3.479.0. Every turn on the Codex strip was marked twice and the version counts
  were inflated.
- **X-265's stand-down was right about doubling and too wide about everything
  else.** It silenced the WHOLE mirror the moment one real hook arrived. But the
  reply the agent gave (U-78), the question a turn is parked on (A-18) and the
  END of a Codex lane come from the Console and from nowhere else — Codex's seven
  hooks are `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `SessionStart`,
  `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop`, with **no `SessionEnd` among them**,
  so a lane silenced wholesale would never have closed. Measured on the other
  side too: of 111 lanes in the last ten days, 68 hook-fed ones carried no `say`
  at all — the agent's own words had not reached the timeline of a Claude Console
  session since X-265.
- **Suppression is per EVENT now, against the wire's own list.** An adapter
  declares `liveWire.events`: Claude's is the hooks installer's list (one place,
  not two), Codex's is READ from `hooks.json` because that file is the user's and
  may name any subset, and an engine with no wire declares none and is mirrored
  in full as before. The rule is `mirrorOwns` in `core/live.ts` — a function a
  test pins, not a closure inside `activate()`.
- **And it is read when the lane OPENS, not on the first hook.** "Has a hook
  spoken for this id yet" answered eight seconds too late for Codex, which names
  its thread before its hooks fire; the fleet's own wire reading (X-295) answers
  before the first event.
- **A lane also opens where the conversation already is.** A resume — including
  the revive after a window reload — arrives with its whole transcript in the
  card, and replaying those turns would stamp an old conversation onto the live
  timeline at today's clock.
- The agent's replies are back on hosted lanes, on every engine. User's decision,
  2026-09-13.

## 3.480.0 - the reading you chose is where the Console opens (K-38) (2026-09-13)

- **"Show everything" could never be kept.** The Console's line filter is a
  multi-select whose `null` means *everything*, and the page rewrote a stored
  `null` back to Dialog on every load — a migration line that could not tell
  "nobody has chosen" from "the reader chose everything". So the one reading a
  person asks for most often was silently taken back, with nothing saying so
  (Principle 1). A mark on the stored state (`kindsSeeded`) settles the question
  once, on the load that reads it; from then on `null` is an answer and survives.
- **And the filter now survives the panel being closed at all.** `show` belongs
  to the CARD (K-21) and a card's answer lives in the webview's own state, which
  is emptied when the panel closes or the window reloads — and whose session ids
  do not survive either, so keying by them could not have helped. The last
  reading chosen is kept by the host instead (`agentfarm.consolePrefs` in
  `globalState`, beside `lastLaunch` and the slash catalog, for the same reason:
  a second reader of that store is a second answer). A page with **no state of
  its own** — a panel opening cold — starts its cards there; a page that has
  state keeps its own, so nothing on screen is ever rewritten behind the reader
  and K-21 is untouched.
- The picker says so on itself: *the last one you set is where a freshly opened
  Console starts*.

## 3.479.0 - a Codex wire is trusted where it lands (X-295) (2026-09-13)

- **Not one Codex event had reached the Live Timeline — from an account or from
  the main directory.** Codex runs no hook without a persisted trust record in
  `config.toml`, keyed by the hook file's path *as Codex resolves it* and holding
  a hash of the hook's normalized identity. Measured 2026-09-13 with
  `codex app-server` → `hooks/list`: every one of the seven hooks in
  `~/.codex/hooks.json` read **untrusted** — the fleet's own records named the
  `C:\Users\…` path Codex now resolves through the junction to `D:\…`, and held a
  hash an older Codex had computed. A captured account, holding a verbatim copy of
  both files since 3.477.0, trusted nothing either: its records named the fleet's
  file, not its own. Two silent failures, one symptom, no surface saying so.
- **The trust is now written by the contract, unasked** — the user's decision:
  the hook file is theirs, carried byte for byte, and a prompt at every account's
  first run was the thing they refused.
  - `core/codexHooks.ts` reproduces Codex's own hash (`hook_hash` /
    `version_for_toml`, rust-v0.149.0): the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of
    `{event_name, matcher?, hooks:[{type, command, timeout, async, …}]}`, with the
    engine's normalizations (default timeout 600, `stop` and `user_prompt_submit`
    drop their matcher, `session_end` clamps to 1–3 s, the default context limit
    is dropped, `commandWindows` wins on Windows). The seven values the real
    machine reported are pinned in `test/test_codex_hooks.js`.
  - **`config.toml` is projected, not carried verbatim.** A carried file may now
    declare a projection (`carryProject`): the fleet's bytes, plus every hook of
    the fleet's `hooks.json` trusted under the account's *resolved* path
    (`realpathSync.native`, which agrees with Codex on Windows). Nothing is parsed
    and nothing re-serialised — the user's model, MCP servers and plugins survive
    byte for byte — and an answer the account gave on its own (a project hook
    trusted at the TUI) is kept, X-291's rule applied to a trust record.
  - **The fleet's own `~/.codex` is signed the same way**, before the accounts
    are projected from it, at every gate — so what an account copies is already
    true, and a main-directory Codex session is heard too.
- **The `hooks` clause is the engine's own now.** It was derived from "does this
  adapter carry `settings.json`" — a Claude file name inside the engine-agnostic
  layer, the trap the handover named. An adapter declares its `liveWire`
  (read / repair, and whether the fleet's directory is its to sign); Claude's is
  the same `hooks` block on the live port it always was, Codex's reads the way
  `hooks/list` would: *7 hooks trusted for this directory, wire on :8377*, or
  *3 of 7 hooks untrusted — pre_tool_use, stop, …*, or *trusted but the wire names
  :8377 — the live port is :9000*. The Engines card, `accounts.list`,
  `migration.verify` and the repair journal all read it without a line changed;
  `accounts.list.engines[].wire` carries the fleet's own reading.
- **What is deliberately not done:** `hooks.json` is the user's file and is not
  installed or rewritten by Agent Farm — a wire on the wrong port is reported by
  name, not repaired. Installing it (and keeping its port current) is the open
  half of X-295 and is stated as such.

## 3.478.0 - the sixth gate: a change nobody made a move for (X-294) (2026-09-13)

- **A permission you granted at a terminal prompt in the main directory, or a key
  you typed into the settings file by hand, reached no account until something
  else happened to open a gate.** The account contract runs both ways now (X-291),
  but only at somebody's move: activation, capture, launch, a press on the card, a
  bridge call. Nothing was lost — the next gate carried it — but a session started
  in between ran on the old value, and the sentence for that is "I changed it and
  it did not work". The engine's own files are now watched, and a change opens the
  gate by itself.
  - **Which files is derived, never typed.** The set is exactly what the contract
    reads from the fleet — every carried behaviour file and every file with
    key-level ownership — so Codex's `config.toml` and `hooks.json`, which only
    existed as of the release before this one, are watched without anything here
    naming them.
  - **It calls the gate that already exists**, under its own name (`watch`), so a
    repair that happened because a file changed is told apart from one that
    happened because you pressed something — `accounts.repairs` says which.
- **‼️ And the hard part was not the watching, it was not hearing yourself.** The
  return leg writes these same files: a promotion puts an account's new answer
  into `~/.claude.json`, which is watched, which would open the gate, which would
  promote again. Convergence alone would end it — the second pass writes nothing —
  but a loop that stops only because the work happens to be idempotent is one
  non-idempotent write away from spinning for ever with nothing to say so. So this
  is **quiet by comparison, not by flag**, the rule the settings reproduction
  already lived by: every watched file's content is fingerprinted, an event whose
  file still says what we last saw never reaches the gate, and the gate
  re-fingerprints afterwards so whatever IT wrote is already accounted for. A
  timer would have been worse twice: it assumes a latency the file system does not
  promise, and it swallows a real edit that lands inside the window.
- **Measured rather than assumed:** `~/.claude` on this machine is a junction into
  the agent repo, and a watch that did not report through it would have looked
  wired and done nothing — it reports (one write, four events). Those four are
  also why the sweep is debounced.

## 3.477.0 - a Codex account was an identity with nothing behind it (X-279) (2026-09-13)

- **A captured Codex account started its sessions on the engine's defaults — your
  model, your MCP servers and your plugins reached none of them — and the birth
  contract called that slot COMPLETE.** Measured on this machine: `codex-murposta`
  held `auth.json` and one junction, because the adapter declared nothing else for
  the contract to ask about. Two clauses are not a short contract, they are an
  empty question, and a gate that cannot fail is the Principle 1 fault this whole
  family exists to end.
  - **`config.toml` now travels**, the way `settings.json` does on Claude: the
    model, the reasoning effort, every MCP server and every enabled plugin.
  - **So does `hooks.json`**, which is the live wire. Without it a session started
    under a captured Codex account posted no event and was invisible on the Live
    Timeline — the X-265 deafness again, on the other engine. **‼️ Carrying it is
    necessary and not yet sufficient, and nothing here pretends otherwise:** Codex
    will not run a hook without a persisted trust record, and that record sits in
    `config.toml` keyed by the hook file's absolute path, so it names the main
    directory and does not match a slot's own copy. The clause asks whether the
    file is the fleet's and claims nothing about the wire being live; granting the
    trust is a security decision and is the user's (X-295).
  - **`skills` and `plugins` are LINKED, not copied**, on X-273's grounds: what
    you installed once belongs to the fleet, and a copy would let one account fall
    behind an install it never heard about.
- **‼️ And carrying a file is not always rendering it.** Everything in the carry
  machinery parses JSON; Codex keeps its behaviour in TOML. Rendered the Claude
  way, `config.toml` would have arrived as `{}` — the whole configuration replaced
  by an empty object — and the drift check would then have compared `{}` with `{}`
  and called the slot current for ever: two silent failures from one assumption. A
  carried file is now copied BYTE FOR BYTE unless something actually has a claim
  inside it (the fleet's `requiredEnv`, or a key-level `ownership`), derived from
  the adapter rather than from a list of file names.
- **Codex isolation is now `measured` rather than `declared`** — and the line that
  said the CLI was not installed here was simply false. Measured 2026-09-13
  against codex-cli 0.149.0: pointed at an empty directory, `codex login status`
  answered "Not logged in" while the main directory was signed in, and wrote only
  its own scratch helpers there; pointed at the captured slot it answered "Logged
  in using ChatGPT". A stated reason is a claim about the world, and a wrong one
  closes the question.

### Fixed

- **The Console's default filter had hidden the way back into a long transcript.**
  The scrollback boundary — the row carrying `↑ load 200 older` — is written as a
  system line, so the day the standing filter became Dialog (agent and user) it
  stopped being drawn and every long session opened with its own history
  unreachable. It is structure, not conversation, and is now exempt from the
  filter. No test had caught it because none had ever opened that card with the
  filter a reader actually gets.

## 3.476.0 - a permission is an answer, not a setting: the return leg (X-291) (2026-09-13)

- **A tool you approved at a terminal prompt inside an account session was
  deleted at the next gate, and the fleet was never told — so switching account
  asked you the same question again, for ever.** X-274 made the identity file's
  keys owned key by key, and `allowedTools` came out as the fleet's: right for a
  folder trust, wrong for an approval, because an approval is an ANSWER YOU
  ALREADY GAVE and it is yours, not that account's. The policy `merge` says so,
  and the gate now runs in both directions.
  - **Which keys.** `projects[*].allowedTools` in `.claude.json`, and
    `permissions.allow` / `ask` / `deny` in `settings.json`. `deny` and `ask`
    are named here because they are answers to the same prompt; everything else
    under `permissions`, `defaultMode` first among them, stays the fleet's.
  - **Which do NOT.** No scalar, ever — there is no clock on a `model` or a
    `defaultMode`, so "last writer wins" cannot be measured and an account
    silently changing a fleet setting is the fault this whole family exists to
    end. No MCP server definition. And nothing inside a folder the main
    directory has not trusted itself, because creating that entry would carry a
    FOLDER TRUST into your own file off the back of a permission list. A folder
    first opened under an account therefore still asks once in the main
    directory — a stated limit, pinned by a test, not an oversight.
- **‼️ And a union without a base is not a merge, it is an accumulator that can
  never forget.** `fleet ∪ slot` alone would have resurrected every permission
  you had just revoked in the main directory, silently, at the very next gate:
  from two sides, the fleet deleting something and an account adding it look
  identical. So every merge key carries a BASE — the value both sides converged
  on at the previous gate, kept in `slot-keybase.json` beside the journal and
  never inside an account (an account carries the least possible, X-270).
  Present in the base and gone from the fleet is a REVOCATION and leaves the
  account; absent from the base and present in the account is YOUR NEW ANSWER
  and goes to the fleet. A revocation wins.
- **The order of the two legs is load-bearing, and it is measured rather than
  said.** The projection runs first, against the OLD base — it is the only step
  that can tell the two apart. The return leg runs after and records what both
  sides now agree on as the next base. Promoting first would overwrite that base
  and hand every revocation straight back. `fleet ∪ (slot \ base)` is the same
  set as `(fleet ∪ slot) \ (base \ fleet)`, so one gate converges and the second
  one writes nothing — pinned, because a gate runs at every start, capture,
  launch and press.
- **It does not ask, and it is not silent.** Promotion at the gate without a
  prompt is the decision: you had already answered the question once. But it
  writes your own `~/.claude.json`, so every promotion is a row in
  `slot-promotions.json`, an `↑N` badge on the account's card beside the `↻N`
  repair badge, and `accounts.promotions` on the bridge has every row with the
  key path it came from. `accounts.complete` now answers `promotions` too.
- `carry:settings.json` no longer claims `permissions` — one fact, one clause.
  It is derived from the adapter's own `ownership`, so naming a second key there
  needs no second edit and the two clauses cannot come to disagree about who
  owns what. The fleet's own file is written whole or not at all (rename over
  the target): `~/.claude.json` is rewritten by every Claude process you start
  outside an account, and a torn file there would cost you the sign-in and every
  folder trust in it.
- The repair journal and the promotion journal now share one body
  (`core/jsonJournal`) — the second copy of a load/rotate/write would have
  guaranteed a third, and that a fix to one never reaches the others.
- Console: the conversation line filter defaults to Dialog mode (agent and
  user).

## 3.475.0 - one question for a migrated machine: did it work (X-283), and the account dirs travel (X-276) (2026-09-13)

- **Every fault in the X-270 family proposed its own Doctor line, and the
  result was ten places to look on a new machine and no answer to the one
  question.** `migration.verify` on the bridge asks it: one pass/fail composed
  out of the checks the fixes already left in the code — and nothing of its
  own, because a gate with its own logic forks from the behaviour the moment
  either changes and then reads green while the system is broken.
  - Items: `root:claudeDir` / `root:globalStorage` (a real folder on the
    system drive is data that dies with the next format; the fix names
    `_setup\Link-Folders.ps1`), `slot:<id>` (the whole birth contract per
    account — `accounts.complete`, read-only), `twins` (one uuid in two slots,
    X-282), `portable-dirs` (X-276, below), `state:titles` / `state:marks`
    (the S-61 adoption: merged, once, never overwritten — legacy rows kept
    out on purpose are reported as such, not as a fault).
  - **Every failing item carries what a program can run**, in the shape the
    `_setup` Doctor already uses (X-209: id · label · op · args · danger):
    `accounts.complete dryRun=false id=…` for a repairable clause,
    `accounts.forget` (HIGH) for a twin, `accounts.portable` for a stored
    absolute path. An identity clause is a `fix` for a person — nothing can
    sign in for them. A check that throws is a failing item with the error on
    it; the rest of the gate still runs.
  - `_REF/machine-setup.md` step 6b names it as the acceptance step once
    VS Code is up. The cockpit (X-281) can call it through `af.js`.
- **The account directories were stored as this machine's absolute path
  (X-276).** `agentFarm.accounts` is the farm's own store that happens to live
  in `settings.json` — a capture writes it, never the user — so it now travels
  like every other store: `${globalStorage}\accounts\<slot>` on the way out
  (`portableSlots`, at the one writer), this machine's path on the way in
  (`normalizeSlots` through `expandPath`, at the one reader), and an absolute
  path another machine recorded heals onto this one's storage on load. Rows
  written before the tokenizer existed are rewritten once, off the activation
  path; `accounts.portable` reads them (`dryRun` default) and rewrites them.
  A dir under no known root is written as an honest absolute and the gate
  names it as the person's job.

## 3.474.0 - a whole file has no single owner: the fleet's keys inside the identity file (X-274) (2026-09-13)

- **The folder trusts and MCP servers the user approves in the main directory
  never reached a slot once it was captured.** `.claude.json` is an `ownFiles`
  entry — copied once, never asked again — because it carries the sign-in. It
  also carries `mcpServers` and, per project entry, `allowedTools`,
  `hasTrustDialogAccepted` and five more grants, which are the fleet's; and 21
  telemetry fields per entry, which are nobody's. Measured 2026-09-13: 74
  top-level keys, 29 fields per entry, every trust key identical across the
  three slots today — and nothing keeping it so. The next folder trusted would
  have forked silently.
  - **The unit is the key, not the file.** The adapter gains `ownership`: per
    file, a policy per key — `fleet` (projected at every gate, absence
    included: a revoked trust leaves the slot too) · `slot` (`oauthAccount`,
    `userID`; never touched) · `ignore` (everything unnamed; never compared,
    never written). One level down for `projects.<path>`, in every entry the
    fleet has; a folder only a slot session trusted is the slot's and stays.
  - **The default is `ignore`, and that is what makes it safe to run at every
    gate.** Counting telemetry as drift would rewrite every slot file on every
    gate for ever — the 3.469.1 fault. `core/keyOwnership` compares by value.
  - The contract derives a `keys:.claude.json` clause from it (`CONTENT_KEYS`
    now names `ownership`, so the classification test guards it), asked right
    after the identity and before the behaviour file. It reads the differing
    keys by name, its repair projects the fleet's keys and nothing else, an
    unreadable slot file is a gap the repair REFUSES to write into (a
    projection into `{}` would erase the sign-in), and a slot with no identity
    file is the `own:` clause's fact, not repeated here. The card, the
    `accounts.complete` op, the journal and the `↻N` badge see the new clause
    with no change of their own.
  - **Pinned, on purpose, as the X-291 hole:** a tool a slot session approves
    in a folder the fleet knows reads as drift and is removed at the next gate,
    and the fleet is never told. `merge` and `promote` are X-291's, and the
    test that changes when they land is named.

## 3.473.1 - the new journal's first finding was its own false alarm (X-292) (2026-09-13)

- **Read against this machine within the hour, and the instrument accused a
  working repair of failing.** One repair primitive puts back ALL of an
  engine's shared paths in one call, so the first failing link clause wrote
  both junctions and `link:shell-snapshots` then found nothing left to do:
  `fixed: false` on a clause whose junction was on disk and fine, twice, on
  two slots. A diagnostic that cries wolf is worse than no diagnostic.
  - `fixed` is now the clause's reading AFTER the pass, not whether that one
    call wrote bytes. A repair that really failed still reads `false` and
    still carries its `error`. Pinned by the live case: a row with
    `wrote: false, ok: true` must not be reported as a failure.
- **And a fifth event, on a slot that had been checked by hand ten minutes
  earlier.** `claude-aicozums` was measured whole at 09:52 with a
  `.last-cleanup` from the previous evening; by 10:02 the stamp had moved and
  both junctions were gone, and the `launch` gate put them back. Five for
  five, and `projects` has still never gone.

## 3.473.0 - a repair is an EVENT, and the thing that keeps breaking it has a name (X-292) (2026-09-13)

- **The contract healed the same two junctions over and over and no surface
  ever said so.** All three gates threw the answer away - `try {
  completeSlots(); } catch {}` - so a slot repaired at every gate read
  `complete` at every gate. Measured again this morning, 70 minutes after the
  previous session verified all five links on all three Claude slots:
  `claude-wmmuratvural` had lost `todos` and `shell-snapshots` again, and its
  `.last-cleanup` stamp was eight minutes younger than that verification.
  Four events now, four for four, and `projects` has never once gone.
  - **And the open question from X-273 is answered: the pool is NOT touched.**
    The pool's `todos` and `shell-snapshots` still carry the mtime they had
    before the cleanup ran, which is the signature of an unlink rather than a
    walk - a recursive remove sees a junction as a link and removes the link.
    Nothing has been lost; the slot loses the path, the contract puts it back.
  - `slot-repairs.json` beside the other stores holds what was put back:
    the clause, the slot, which gate ran (`start` · `capture` · `launch` ·
    `press` · `ask`), and **the reading it was repaired FROM** - after a
    repair every reading says the slot is well, which is the exact sentence
    that hid this.
  - **The cause is DERIVED, never declared.** The adapter names the file the
    ENGINE itself stamps when its own housekeeping runs (`housekeeping`;
    Claude: `.last-cleanup`), the stamp is read BEFORE the repair, and
    `accounts.repairs` reports per clause how many repeats followed a stamp
    that had moved - beside the denominator it was counted out of. A declared
    cause rots the first time the engine changes; a counted one reads zero.
    Pinned by its counter-case: the same four repairs with a stamp that never
    moved read `afterHousekeeping: 0`.
  - **And it is on the card, on the row that says `complete`.** A `↻7` badge
    appears only once a clause has been put back on that slot more than once -
    a first repair is a capture or a fresh clone - and its panel names the
    clauses, how often, when, and how many repeats the engine explains.

## 3.472.0 - what the user installed is the fleet's: plugins and skills reach every account (X-273) (2026-09-13)

- **Every isolated session had been running without the plugins and skills
  the user installed.** `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` moves the whole directory, and
  `plugins` and `skills` live in it - so a session on a slot could reach
  neither. Measured on this machine: the fleet holds a plugin marketplace
  (447 files) and two global skills, one of which the agent constitution
  names as a trigger; all three Claude slots had none of it.
  - Both are `sharedPaths` now, so the contract derives `link:plugins` and
    `link:skills` clauses by itself and the three gates make the junctions.
    Nothing there is an identity: installing a skill once and losing it on
    the next sign-in is the X-270 fault under another name.
  - The test fixture builds whatever the adapter names instead of a hand
    written list of three folders, so the next shared folder needs no test
    edited; and the `accounts.complete` describe stopped enumerating the
    folders it does not own.
  - Read against this machine: the new clauses found the real gap on all
    three Claude slots, which is what the item said would be there.
- **And a fault found on the way, filed as X-292.** The slot whose engine
  cleanup ran most recently is, in both measured events, the slot that lost
  its `todos` and `shell-snapshots` junctions - never `projects`. The
  contract repairs them at every start, so the recurring cause has been
  invisible; `cleanupPeriodDays: 36500` does not prevent it.

## 3.471.0 - a slot that was born complete now has to STAY complete (X-272) (2026-09-13)

- **The birth contract asked whether the file existed. Existence was never
  the question.** Measured against the real functions: a setting the user
  added to the main `settings.json` after a slot was born never reached it, a
  changed value stayed at the old one, and a permission they deleted lived on
  in the slot for ever - and the contract read `complete` through all three,
  on every one of its three gates. Reproduction has always rendered the
  fleet's whole file over the slot's, so the permissions, model and effort
  the item is named after could always travel; nothing ever told it to run.
  - The `carry:` clause now asks whether the slot's copy is still the
    fleet's projection, and names the keys that drifted on the row the
    Engines card and Doctor already print: `settings.json is a stale copy -
    model, permissions no longer match the fleet's .claude/settings.json`.
  - **Compared by value, not by bytes.** The fleet's file is whatever the
    user's editor left behind while the projection is re-serialised, so a
    text comparison would have called every healthy slot stale over
    indentation and rewritten three files on every sweep - the 3.469.1
    lesson, where a permanently wrong badge was the whole defect. Pinned by a
    test that changes the indentation and the key order and expects silence.
  - **And the carry clause does not fight the hooks clause.** Hooks are
    re-pointed at the live port AFTER the render, so counting them as drift
    would have the two clauses overwrite each other on every pass for ever.
    The exclusion is derived from the same condition that creates the hooks
    clause, and the mutation test shows it is load-bearing: remove it and the
    X-284 acceptance gate fails too.
  - Read against this machine before packaging: all four slots complete, no
    row changed its answer, nothing rewritten.

## 3.470.0 - the same notice posted twice is answered rather than obeyed (2026-09-13)

- **The user was seeing one question on the board twice, and the transcript
  says exactly how.** An agent piped its own `notices.post` answer through
  `head -8`, could not see the id it had just been handed, and ran the
  identical command again to read the fields it had cut off - a write op
  re-run as an inspection. 7.6 seconds apart, byte-identical, both on the
  board.
  - `notices.post` now REFUSES an identical agent+title+body+sections within
    ten minutes: nothing is added, the first notice is handed back
    (`posted:false`, `duplicateOf`), and the answer says in one line what to
    do instead. The second leg never runs either, so a re-run can no longer
    rewrite the report file under a notice the user is already reading.
    `allowDuplicate:true` is there for saying something twice on purpose.
  - **And the retraction that was not one.** The agent then "withdrew" the
    copy with `notices.resolve` and verified on its own pending list, which
    came back with one - while the user kept seeing two. `resolve` only marks
    a question handled and removes nothing; it now says so, and `dismiss`
    (undoable) says out loud that it is the op for taking something off the
    board, so a catalog search for "retract / remove / delete" finds it.
  - Pinned by a test that was mutation-checked: removing the guard drops four
    assertions, including the one that the report file is not rewritten.

## 3.469.1 - the link clause resolved one side of the comparison and called a healthy fleet broken (X-284) (2026-09-13)

- **Found by running the shipped contract against this machine before loading
  it.** `~/.claude` is itself a junction into the agent repo, so a slot's
  `projects` link resolved through TWO hops to a `D:` path while the path it was
  checked against had been resolved through none. All twelve link clauses read
  as gaps on a fleet with nothing wrong with it — and a badge that is
  permanently wrong is the Principle 1 failure the whole item exists to end.
  Both sides are resolved now; where the pool does not exist yet the unresolved
  path is what to compare against, which is also what the repair refuses to
  invent. A link pointing into some other folder is still a gap, with where it
  goes on it — pinned, so the fix did not buy its green by going blind.
- The honest reading of this machine: two slots are each missing `todos` and
  `shell-snapshots`, the other two are complete.

## 3.469.0 - a slot's contents are one contract, asked at every door instead of remembered at three (X-284) (2026-09-13)

- **Every fault in the X-270 family was the same fault.** Something a session
  needs was copied into an account slot once, at capture, and nothing ever asked
  again: the settings file (X-265/X-269), the live hooks, the pool links (X-271).
  Each got its own repair, its own gate and its own Doctor line - and the
  eleventh thing added tomorrow would have been forgotten the same way, because
  three call sites had to agree with each other by comment.
  - **The list is DERIVED, not written.** `core/slotCompleteness` walks the
    engine adapter's own fields - `ownFiles`, `carryFiles`, `requiredEnv`,
    `sharedPaths` - and turns each into a clause that can be read and, where it
    is the fleet's rather than the account's, repaired. A new slot-content field
    with no clause fails the build rather than somebody's memory.
  - **Activation, capture and launch now ask that one list.** The launch gate is
    the preventive one: once `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` points at an incomplete slot the
    transcript is already being written inside it and the system-prompt variable
    has already been read. Capture copies the identity and stops, then asks the
    contract the moment the row exists - so a RE-capture repairs a slot that had
    drifted, which the copy-if-absent line it replaced could never do.
  - **`accounts.complete`** on the bridge (a question first: `dryRun` defaults to
    true), and a **[Complete]** press on the Engines card wired to the same host
    function, so the button and the op cannot answer differently.
- **And the card now says whether a slot is whole.** `complete`, or `n missing`
  with every absent clause named in its panel in the product's own words - a
  count nobody can act on is a worse silence than none. The sign-in is not
  counted there: the verdict badge on the same row already owns it, so no row
  reads `complete` and `needs signing in` in one breath.
- **The contract has an exam, and it is the user's own claim.** Wipe a slot
  folder off the disk, forget its row, capture the account again: every setting
  and permission comes back byte for byte, the fleet's env guarantee is there
  although the user's own file never carried it, the live hooks are current, and
  the transcript written before the wipe is still in the pool and reachable
  through the rebuilt junction. A slot is an identity and nothing else - now
  measured rather than asserted.
- **Doctor gained `engines / claude slot contract`,** which found four missing
  junctions on this machine the moment it was written. It is offline (no
  extension host has run at migration time), so it reads file presence only and
  NAMES `accounts.complete` as the authority rather than keeping a second list.

## 3.468.0 - the index reconciles with the disk on a clock and on demand, because a Windows watcher drops a burst without a word (X-290, X-289) (2026-09-13)

- **654 transcripts were put back into the pool in one go and the tables saw two
  of them.** `fs.watch` on Windows hands events out of a fixed kernel buffer; a
  burst that overflows it is dropped silently, and until now the only rescan was
  the palette's Refresh — which had no bridge form, because the parity manifest
  called it "navigation: nothing produced that a read op does not already
  return". Measured 2026-09-13 restoring the transcripts Claude Code's 30-day
  prune had taken (X-289): every read op stayed 652 sessions behind the disk
  until a settings toggle provoked a full scan.
  - **The listing is the guarantee, the watcher is the accelerator.** `SessionIndex.sweep()`
    is the cheap half of `scanAll` — the directory walk, no stat, no parse —
    checked against what the index already knows (admitted, dropped, pending);
    only a file in none of those is read. It runs every 60 s while watching and
    costs a few hundred `readdir` entries.
  - **`sessions.rescan`** — the bridge op: default is that reconcile; `full:true`
    is the palette's Refresh (re-stat everything, re-parse only what the cache
    does not hold). Answers `{ mode, picked, claude: { before, after }, ms }` so a
    caller can see whether anything moved. The manifest now maps `agentfarm.refresh`
    to it instead of exempting it.
  - **`tools/restore_pruned_transcripts.js`** — the recovery used today: every file
    the agent repo's history records as deleted under the pool (or a slot's
    `projects/`) and missing on disk is written back from `git cat-file`, its mtime
    set to its last message, idempotent, `--dry` first. 481 transcripts + 173
    side files, 568 MB, 29–33 days old at deletion on every sample.
  - **The prune is off.** `cleanupPeriodDays: 36500` in the fleet's one source;
    X-269 reproduced it into every Claude slot with no hand on any slot file.
    The user's decision: transcripts are kept locally for good; growth is a
    problem to design for (see the growth report in the project's `10_Notes`),
    never one to solve by deletion.

## 3.467.0 - a slot's settings file is reproduced, not stored, so every session gets the FULL system prompt (X-269) (2026-09-12)

- **The behaviour file inside an account slot was a photograph, and every session
  Agent Farm ever started under an account paid for it.** Anthropic ships a
  SIMPLIFIED system prompt unless one `env` key says otherwise, and the standing
  decision is the full one. `carryFiles: ['settings.json']` copied the user's file
  into a slot once, at capture, and only when it was absent — so a key added
  afterwards reached no slot that already existed. Measured 2026-09-12: not one of
  five `claude-*` slots carried `CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0`, the variable
  is read when the process STARTS so no running session could ever have been
  repaired, and no surface in the product could say it was happening.
  - **Reproduced, not merged.** `core/slotSettings` renders the slot file out of the
    fleet's own source — the user's `settings.json` as the BASE, so their model,
    permission mode and live hooks travel, with the contract as the OVERLAY, which
    wins. The slot copy becomes a single-use output: there is nothing left to go
    stale, and forgetting the account takes no setting with it (X-270).
  - **Three gates, because a contract enforced once is a photograph:** every
    activation, at capture, and before a launch is handed a slot — the last is the
    one that PREVENTS the fault rather than repairing it. Idempotent by comparison,
    so a slot that already says it costs a read.
  - **The engine decides what it needs.** The contract lives on the adapter
    (`requiredEnv`, naming its own file), so nothing writes a Claude-shaped
    `settings.json` into a Codex slot that has never heard of one.
  - **And it is visible, or it is not a rule.** The Engines account card carries a
    `full` / `simple` badge with a `Fix prompt` press beside a slot that drifted —
    and draws NOTHING for an engine that guarantees nothing, because an empty gap
    list is two different answers. New op `accounts.repairSettings` (with `dryRun`)
    is the same function the button calls; `Doctor.ps1` grows a
    `claude slot prompt` item whose one-click action is `_setup\Repair-SlotSettings.ps1`.

## 3.466.0 - a recovered session name was kept and not shown: the old machine's 54 names are on the table (S-61) (2026-09-12)

- **A name that arrives from outside is SHOWN, not merely kept.** 3.465.0 stopped
  the file from being written over; what it did not do is tell the running
  window. Measured with the old machine's `state.vscdb`:
  `tools/adopt_state_vscdb.js` merged 54 titles and 11 marks (no conflicts) into
  `session-titles.json` / `session-marks.json`, the files held 151 and 19 — and
  every session table still drew the derived first-prompt title, because the
  session index is HANDED the map once at activation and nothing re-hands it.
  `PortableMap.reloadIfChanged()` answers "did the file move?" with one stat and
  no parse, and activation now runs a 20-second beat that pushes titles and
  marks into the index and repaints the trees and open pages only on a real
  move. So a recovery, or a `git pull` of the agent repo on the other machine,
  lands on screen without a restart.
