## 3.465.0 - a name added to the file by another hand was one rename away from being lost (S-61) (2026-09-12)

- **The session-name cache is checked against the file, never trusted.** Measured
  right after 3.464.0 loaded: the extension read 95 names at start,
  `tools/adopt_state_vscdb.js` added two from outside, and the next rename would
  have written the cached 95 back over them — the same thing a `git pull` on the
  other machine would suffer. `PortableMap.read()` now stats the file and
  re-reads when its mtime or size moved; one stat per read is the price of
  never losing a name.

## 3.464.0 - nothing of the user's is bound to a machine or a slot any more: session names travel (S-61), a forgotten account leaves no orphan (X-282), a backlog write says what took (X-287) (2026-09-12)

- **AN ACCOUNT FORGOTTEN IS AN ACCOUNT GONE — AND THE SAME SIGN-IN NEVER GETS A
  `-2` (X-282).** Measured: five `claude-*` folders on this machine, three
  accounts. "Forget" dropped the row and left the folder out of fear that a
  transcript might still live in it; the next capture of the same sign-in saw
  the name taken and minted `claude-x-2` — a second folder, a second
  `projects/` tree, and a fleet counting two five-hour windows where there was
  one. Three changes, one invariant:
  - **The uuid is the key.** `readClaudeIdentity` reads
    `oauthAccount.accountUuid`; a capture matches a stored row by it first, and
    the same address with a different uuid is another plan, not this row.
  - **A forgotten folder is taken back, not counted past.** Capture reads every
    slot folder under the root, stored or not (`slotsOnDisk`); one carrying
    the uuid being captured is re-sealed under its own name (`adopts`), one
    carrying another uuid is a name the mint may not hand out again.
  - **Forgetting deletes, and deleting is safe because it drains first.** The
    slot is emptied into the pool (X-271) before the folder goes; if anything
    cannot be moved, or a session or task is running as that account, NOTHING
    is forgotten and the refusal names it. Measured: `rmSync` unlinks the
    junctions inside the slot without following them. The page shows what
    goes and what stays, then asks — "keep folder" is offered by name.
  - A card carries the short uuid, and two cards carrying one are each
    marked **duplicate** — the only feedback that makes the fault visible. An
    account id that names no stored slot reads `⚠ not on this machine: <id>`
    wherever a task or session quotes it, instead of looking like one more
    account. `accounts.forget` answers `pooled` and `refs` and says, every
    time, that local deletion is not revocation: the tokens stay in the agent
    repo's git history.
- **A SESSION'S NAME, PIN, TAGS AND COLOUR NOW TRAVEL WITH THE FLEET (S-61).** They
  were kept in VS Code's `globalState`, which is a single row inside
  `%APPDATA%\Code\User\globalStorage\state.vscdb` — not in the extension's own
  folder, not in the repo, not carried by the migration. A new machine came up
  with every transcript present and every name gone. They are now plain JSON
  (`session-titles.json`, `session-marks.json`) inside the extension's
  `globalStorage`, which is junctioned onto the agent repo and therefore
  committed, pushed and cloned like every other fact.
- **It is the same fault as X-271, one layer up.** There the wrong owner was the
  account slot; here it was the editor's per-machine store. A session record
  outlives both the account it ran under and the machine it ran on.
- **‼️ A RECOVERY IS A MERGE, NEVER A COPY.** The old store is not deleted and
  not distrusted — it is merged in the first time the file is found missing,
  and an id the file already knows always keeps the value it has. That rule is
  what makes the same path safe for a `state.vscdb` carried over from another
  machine: the machine you are recovering onto is never empty (this one already
  held 95 names and 8 marks), so overwriting would repair one loss by causing
  another. Once, not at every start: the old row is never written again, so a
  repeated merge could only resurrect a name the user has since removed.
- A write goes to a sibling and is renamed over the target, so a crash mid-write
  leaves the previous file rather than half of the new one; a file that fails
  to parse reads as empty but is never cached as empty, and the next write
  keeps it beside the new one as `.corrupt` rather than renaming over it.
- **`node tools/adopt_state_vscdb.js <state.vscdb>` recovers what a machine left
  behind.** The extension adopts its own leftover row by itself; what it cannot
  reach is a `state.vscdb` carried over from another machine and the row
  written under the old publisher id (`miropharm.agent-farm` — measured: two
  names live only there). The tool reads both rows of any such file into the
  fleet's files: a dry run by default, `--apply` adds only what is missing, and
  an id both sides know with different values is listed side by side and left
  alone until the user says `--prefer incoming`. Measured on this machine: 95
  + 2 names and 8 marks, a second run writes nothing.
- **A backlog write that wrote nothing answered `ok` (X-287).** `backlog.add`
  and `backlog.set` read tags only under `kinds`; a caller passing `tags` — the
  word on the line — had them silently dropped, and `set` returned a full item
  as if it had taken. Both now read `kinds`/`kind`/`tags`/`tag`; `add` puts them
  BESIDE the `#byAI`/`#byREQ` stamp, never instead of it; and `set` answers
  with `asked` (the axes named) and `updated` (the axes whose value really
  differs on the re-read line, `backlogAxesChanged`) — an empty `updated`
  carries a note, a call naming no axis or an unknown priority/effort is
  refused rather than answered `ok`.
- **The parity gate had been green by accident on every capability wired
  through `deps.store`.** `valueOfKey` matched `…its own store: a mark` inside
  a doc comment and stapled 38 KB of host code onto both sides, so two sides
  with nothing in common "shared" everything; deleting that sentence for S-61
  failed `settingsPanel.ts#docOpenSet`, which nothing had touched. Comments
  are now blanked before the scan, and a dep value that is a bare host name
  (`store: docOpenStore`, `convertToQueue: convertNoticeToQueue`) is read
  through to what the host built — one hop — so the real link (`DocOpenStore`,
  `titleOf`/`dismiss`/`addSpawnedItem`) is what the gate sees.
  `node test/test_parity.js --why <capability>` now prints which symbols each
  side has, so a drift is named instead of hunted.

## 3.463.0 - a transcript is never left living under an account: the slot is emptied into the pool, before the launch and again after the session (X-271) (2026-09-12)

- **AN ACCOUNT IS A QUOTA, NOT A PLACE TO KEEP ANYTHING.** A sign-in can be
  closed, replaced or thrown away tomorrow; a transcript is the record of the
  work and outlives every account it was written under. The previous release
  found the sessions trapped inside a slot and made them visible; it still left
  them there, reported as `stranded`, because folding them back was "a move and
  a move is the user's call". That was the wrong line: leaving a record under a
  disposable owner is the fault, not a state to be tolerated. A real folder
  found where a junction belongs is now DRAINED into the one pool and the
  junction made over the emptied folder.
- **Nothing is overwritten and nothing is thrown away.** A name already taken in
  the pool by a file of the same size and mtime is the same transcript — the
  test the session index itself trusts — and only then is the slot's copy
  dropped. Any other collision lands under a second name carrying the slot id. A
  file the engine still holds open cannot be renamed on Windows: it stays, it is
  named in the answer, and the folder waits one more round.
- **Three moments, and the middle one is the only preventive one.** The repair
  runs at every activation (as before); **before a launch is handed a slot**, so
  the first byte of a new transcript lands in the pool instead of inside the
  account; and **once more after a session ends**, which is the moment the
  engine finally lets go of the file it was writing. Start-up alone is too late
  and pre-launch alone cannot reach a file the running session holds.
- `accounts.repairLinks` now answers `moved` beside `linked` / `stranded` /
  `failed`, and with `dryRun` it names what *would* move without touching it.

## 3.462.0 - a session started on a captured account could not be seen, because the link that pooled the transcripts had not survived the move (X-271) (2026-09-12)

- **A CAPTURED ACCOUNT IS A `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, SO THE TRANSCRIPT IS WRITTEN
  UNDER THE SLOT.** What kept that from mattering was a junction, made once at
  capture, folding the slot's `projects` into the one pool the index reads. A
  junction is not something git can carry, and it does not survive a folder move
  or a new machine either - so on this machine two slots had no `projects` at
  all and a third had a REAL folder with live sessions inside it. Those sessions
  were in no table, no cost figure and no watch. The index now reads every
  captured Claude account's directory directly, deduped by what `projects`
  really resolves to, so an intact junction is still read exactly once and a
  broken one costs nothing but a second folder to walk.
- **AND THE LINKS ARE CHECKED AT EVERY START, not only at capture.** An absent
  link is remade; an existing junction is left alone; a real folder **with the
  user's files in it is never touched** and is reported as `stranded` instead,
  because folding those transcripts back into the pool is a MOVE and a move is
  not something a window does behind somebody's back. `accounts.repairLinks`
  asks for the same pass on demand (`dryRun` to only look). The repair refuses
  to create the pool it would link into - an absent pool means this is not a
  machine whose links can be repaired.

## 3.461.0 - fifteen boxes on the Tasks page were narrower than the words in them, and every one of those words was written twice (audit B-07) (2026-09-11)

- **AN OPTION LABEL IS THE VALUE, NOT THE VALUE PLUS ITS EXPLANATION.** The
  select sweep, run over the Tasks surface for the first time, found 15 visible
  boxes holding text wider than themselves - and in every one the half that was
  cut was an explanation somebody had written into the LABEL: `headless - runs
  and exits` at 149px in a 127px box (nine of them), the route's `- none:
  nothing injected, nothing cleared -` at 259px in 124px, the account's `- the
  standing choice, else the main sign-in -` at 271px in 124px, the tier's `opus
  - kimi-k2-thinking` at 143px in 124px. The explanation was never missing:
  `C.option` already puts label + detail on the option's own native title
  (U-130), so each sentence was written twice and the copy that could not fit
  was the one on the screen. Labels are now the bare value - `headless`,
  `- none -`, `- standing choice -`, `opus` - and the sweep answers **0 cut**.
  The tier was the same defect with a worse ending: the model that name is
  served by rode in the label while the hover carried only the standing
  sentence, so it now opens the hover as `Served by: kimi-k2-thinking`.
- **THE SAVED-PROMPTS FOOTER PUT ITS LONGEST FACT FIRST AND LET THE ELLIPSIS EAT
  THE ONE THAT MATTERED.** 775px of text in a 678px line, and what the clip took
  was "clicking one PASTES it into the box - nothing is sent", because the whole
  vault path sat in front of it. Clipping a path is the worst of both worlds
  anyway - it keeps the drive and loses the file NAME. The line carries the name
  now, the title carries the whole path, and nothing is cut.
- **AND THE SWEEP IS NOW A GATE ON THIS SURFACE.** `test_settings_control_width`
  measures the Tasks page too - 162 boxes in one render, the biggest form in the
  product. Mutation: one label put back, and it fails naming the box and the
  pixels. Two assertions in `test_tasks_webview` that pinned the old WORDING
  rather than the claim were rewritten to hold the claim.

## 3.460.0 - the agent name was painted over its own engine badge, and the measurement that cleared it had asked the wrappers (2026-09-11)

- **THE FACTS ON THE COMPOSER ROW NOW KEEP THEIR SIZE AND THEIR PLACE; THE
  BOXES ARE WHAT GIVES WAY.** The user reported it live, mid-session: narrow the
  Console panel and the agent name under the conversation box climbs on top of
  the engine badge beside it. 3.459.0 had shortened the model value for exactly
  this row and declared it clean at 640px - the defect was never the value. The
  identity chip was `flex:0 1 auto`, so its WRAPPER shrank while the text inside
  it, which nothing clipped, stayed 48px wide and spilled straight over its
  neighbour. Measured on the live row of the `console` fixture before the
  repair: at **900px** the name ran **10px** over the Codex badge, at 760px
  **23px**, at 640px **35px** - 900px being an ordinary panel, not a corner.
  The chips that state a FACT (the agent the session opened in, the engine, the
  route) no longer shrink at all, and the name clips with an ellipsis at 190px
  instead of shoving Send. After: zero overlap at 1030 / 900 / 760 / 640px.
- **AND THE REASON IT PASSED FOR A DAY: THE EARLIER SWEEP MEASURED THE WRAPPERS.**
  Every control on that row is an AFTip wrapper, and those report a width of
  zero - ask them and the row answers "clean" at every width. The new guard in
  `test/test_console_identity_width.js` measures the painted LEAVES, pair by
  pair, at four widths, and names the pixels it finds. Mutation: the two rules
  removed, it fails with the three figures above.

## 3.459.0 - the running row said `claude-opus-5` beside a badge that already said Claude (2026-09-11)

- **THE LIVE MODEL BOX SHOWS THE ALIAS, NOT THE ID THE CLI REPORTED.** 3.457.0
  taught the running row to name its model instead of `Default` - and named it
  `claude-opus-5`, the resolved id, inside the narrowest control on the row,
  next to an engine badge that already says Claude. The engine written twice,
  and worse: a long option is a min-content floor a `<select>` will not shrink
  under, so on a narrow panel the row stopped giving ground and the agent name
  and its badge were drawn over each other. The user saw both in one look.
  One shared rule now (`AFLaunch.aliasIn`, loaded by page and host alike): the
  value a box SHOWS for a report is the one catalogue id that is a whole
  segment of it - `claude-opus-5` → `opus`, `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` →
  `haiku` - and the raw id only when the catalogue has no such row or several.
  The value SENT is untouched. Measured after: `opus` in the box, and the row
  narrowed to 640px with zero overlaps and zero spill.

## 3.458.0 - two engine names cut on the plan card with a thousand pixels to spare (audit B-06) (2026-09-11)

- **THE PLAN-USAGE STRIP READ `Antigra…` / `OpenCo…` WITH 1,028px OF PAGE
  UNUSED TO ITS RIGHT.** Measured: Antigravity needed 60px and had 59, OpenCode
  the same. The handles were `flex:1 1 0` - a basis of ZERO, so five of them
  split the card into five equal fifths whatever their names measured. Same
  family as the model id drawn in a box narrower than itself (audit B-04.4) and
  the voice pickers (B-05.5): a control narrower than its value, with room
  beside it. The basis is the name now: each handle starts at its own width and the
  SPARE is what they share equally, so an ellipsis appears only when the sum of
  the names really exceeds the card - the one case U-40's one-row rule was
  written for - and never before. Measured both ways on the laid-out DOM: at
  the card's own width no handle is cut and every strip is still one row; on a
  card forced to 200px the strip is STILL one row, nothing spills past its edge,
  and the names give ground proportionally (the longer name keeps more).
  `test/test_planusage_tabs_width.js` holds both, mutation-proved - put the
  zero back and it names the six cut handles with their pixels.

- The Dashboard surface is closed in the audit ledger: two fixtures, all six
  scenes photographed at their own size and looked at, two of them in the light
  theme too. One trap for whoever measures next, recorded there: a mutation run
  re-renders `dist/render/` with the MUTANT stylesheet, and `shoot_page.js`
  photographs whatever render is on disk - restore the source AND render again
  before you look, or the picture you approve is of the defect.

## 3.457.0 - every box on the Console was describing a session that was not running (S-58 · the launch layer that never reached a control) (2026-09-11)

One complaint, five defects, all of the same family: **a control that draws a
value it did not resolve.** The user set `developer` to `opus` at `xhigh` for
Claude in Farm Settings, opened a session, and read `Model: Default` beside
`Effort: xhigh` - two answers to one question, one row apart, both of them from
the same row of the same settings page.

- **THE AGENT'S OWN SETTING WAS A LAYER THAT NEVER REACHED A BOX.** The order
  is written in `core/launch.ts` and every door resolves it AT THE SPAWN: this
  launch -> what the agent last ran as -> what the agent is SET to for this
  engine -> the fleet. The third layer existed only at the spawn. Every door
  seeded its boxes from the memory and fell straight through to the fleet, so a
  model or an effort chosen in Farm Settings was applied to the session and
  invisible in the control that offers to change it. It is a LAYER inside
  `seedLastLaunch` now, so all ten doors inherit it by calling the function they
  already call, and it is resolved per FIELD - a memory holding an effort and no
  model must not silence the layer holding the model, which is exactly the shape
  that produced the report.
  Two readers, deliberately: the SPAWN's still returns an empty model on Claude
  (its CLI reads the agent's own `settings.local.json`, so a flag would be a
  second source of truth), and the BOX's folds that file back in - because
  `Default` is the one word that is false about an agent set to `opus`.

- **‼️ AND A `<select>` DRAWS AN UNKNOWN VALUE AS ITS FIRST OPTION, WHICH ON
  EVERY LAUNCH BOX IS `Default`.** The bridge reported `model: claude-opus-5`
  for the running session while the box beside it read `Default`: the Claude
  catalogue publishes four aliases and the CLI reports the resolved id, so the
  value matched no row and the browser fell back to the first. Not a missing
  value - a value silently redrawn as its own opposite, on the one control whose
  whole job is to say what the conversation is running on. The composer has had
  the rule since S-34 (`withCurrent`); the running row never called it.
  The permission box is the same defect with a reason in front of it: a live
  session's list drops `bypassPermissions` because you may not raise a running
  conversation into it - true about CHOOSING, and it was deciding what the box
  could SAY, so a session really running on bypass drew `default`.

- **‼️ AND THE ROW WAS NEVER DRAWN AGAIN ANYWAY.** The shell key was
  `selected | ended | pinned | account`, and those three boxes are markup: a
  `<select>` only moves when the markup does. A card is selected the instant its
  process starts, before the CLI has resolved anything, so the model it was
  built with was the model it showed for the rest of the session. Widening the
  option list could not have helped on its own.

- **‼️ AND ELEVEN FILTER MENUS STOOD PERMANENTLY OPEN OVER THE COMPOSER.**
  `hidden` is an attribute the browser enforces from its own stylesheet, which
  any class selector outranks - so `.crow .afms > *`, written so the hover
  wrapper would be the flex child, un-hid the picker's own menu. Laid out as a
  ROW, because flex with no direction is a row, which is why all that showed was
  the tools line and a horizontal scrollbar over the message box. The component
  shuts itself now rather than asking nine pages to remember, and the page rule
  names the trigger instead of every child.

- **S-58 - THE CARD'S ✕ WAS OUTSIDE THE CARD, AND ITS WRAPPER COST EVERY CARD A
  ROW.** `cardTip` wraps the button in an AFTip span and `cls` lands on THAT
  span; the positioning was left on the button. Measured: `right:4px` against a
  0px-wide wrapper put the ✕ at x=29 where the card starts at x=36 - seven
  pixels outside its own left edge, behind the border, unreachable however long
  you hovered. And the wrapper, still an in-flow `inline-block`, contributed a
  line box: every session card carried an empty row above its own name
  (identity row at 25px, now 8px, which is the card's own padding).

Every one of these had correct markup and passed every string test in the
suite. Four of the five are geometry or computed style, so the guards are
measurements on the laid-out DOM (`test_console_identity_width.js`,
`test_console_show_width.js`), and the fifth is a payload
(`test_console_agent_default.js` section 5 - sections 1 to 4 measure the spawn
and were green the entire time the box was wrong). The borrowed-back permission
row had none and now does, mutation-proved: with `withCurrentFrom` taken out,
the guard names it.

**And two guards went red on this work with no defect behind either** - both the
same shape, a test that pins the LINE it is about instead of the CLAIM it is
making. `test_console.js` held the entire shell-key expression as a literal, so
the shape that finally redraws the running row read as a broken pin; it names
the key line and asks for the pin now, which is what it was ever about.
`test_shot_height.js` TYPED the Console fixture's scene count, so adding two
scenes failed an assertion about CROPPING; it counts the fixture. And while that
file was open: its probe reused whatever `dist/render/` already held - measuring
the past and reporting it as the present, in the one file whose whole subject is
that failure in the shooting tool. It renders every time now.

## 3.456.0 - the axis was eating the value, the mirror was showing yesterday, and "Default" was naming what you already had (audit B-03.21 round 2 · S-57) (2026-09-11)

Round 1 of this item asked "which of these boxes is which?" and answered it out
of the value's own width. Round 2 is the user's answer, and it costs the value
nothing.

- **A ~100px picker with its axis written in front of its value shows the half
  that never changes.** Measured on `dist/render/console.s9.png`: the row that
  starts a session drew `model → Defa`, `effort → Def`, `perm → De`, and
  `xhigh` no longer showed even its first letter - which it had before the
  repair. A `<label>` beside the box is the same theft of width by another
  route, which is why round 1 refused it and why this does too.
  The third way costs nothing: an **`<optgroup>` heading**. The browser draws
  it at the top of the OPEN list and refuses to let anybody select it, so the
  axis is named exactly where somebody is choosing - once - and the collapsed
  box is left entirely to the value.

- **‼️ AND THE HOVER WAS A MIRROR OF A VALUE THAT HAD BEEN REPLACED.** MIRROR
  asks a narrow control to put its CURRENT value on the first line of its
  panel, and every panel in the product is written into the markup once, when
  the page draws itself. So the rule held exactly until somebody used the
  control: the box read `xhigh` and the panel under it still said
  `Effort → Default`. That is worse than no panel - a reader who has learned
  to trust the hover is being told the wrong thing with confidence. The live
  half is in the COMPONENT (`AFTip.syncAxis`), bound once, rebuilding from
  data the markup already carries (`data-axis-name` · `data-axis-std` ·
  `data-why` per option) - so it is right on the same event, with no round
  trip, and no page has to remember to call it.

- **‼️ AND ONE ROW WAS ANSWERING ONE QUESTION THREE WAYS.** Four boxes had an
  AFTip panel, five had a native `title`, and three of those had a `<span>`
  label beside them - on the same row, at the same height. Every box on both
  control rows is one shape now: no label, an optgroup heading, and a panel
  that says the axis, its value, the chosen row's own line and then the
  standing sentence once. The two `fixed` chips beside them were the last
  native tooltips on the row and went the same way. The standing sentences
  were cut back to that one scale while they were being moved: an account
  paragraph that re-explained a row the list already explains, and a route tip
  joined into one wall by ` · `, are four facts on four lines now.

- **The promise about the next turn moved from the label to the box.** With no
  label left to carry it, a pending account swap is an arrow beside the box and
  the value itself in warning yellow - still readable across the row without
  hovering, which is the whole of X-213's claim.

- Also: the console's clipped-value count fell from **49 boxes to 16**
  (audit B-04.6's console half), and the sixteen are 4-20px short rather than
  values destroyed. Three ceilings were raised into slack that was already
  there (`c-agent`, `c-account`, `c-account-live`).

New gate `test/test_axis_mirror.js` drives the component itself: change the box,
the heading has to change with it, the separator has to change with it
(`:` is a choice, `→` is what the engine resolves to), and a nested panel must
not be mistaken for the box's own. `test/test_console_axis_labels.js` was
rewritten to the shape it now measures - no box may spend its own width saying
what it is, none may wear a label, all of them must be axis boxes, and every
option must carry the line the panel will need. Both were mutation-checked.

Nine test assertions pinned the old shape (the option prefix, `.rtlbl`,
`.permlbl pend`, the native titles, the width rules on the selects). Reversed,
not deleted - the claims are unchanged, only the shape they are read in. One
`console.log` debug line left behind in `test_console_page.js` was removed.

### …and the same repair on Farm Settings, plus the chain the boxes describe

The console half above was round 2 of the axis item. The Farm Settings page was
still on round 1, so one question was answered two ways in one product — and
underneath it the per-agent defaults those boxes write turned out not to reach
the sessions the Console starts.

- **`model: sonnet` / `effort: high` in front of every option, gone.** The same
  `<optgroup>` heading the Console moved to, for the same measured reason: the
  prefix is the part that never changes, so it is the part that survives the
  clipping. The gate that used to REQUIRE the prefix now measures the two facts
  separately — every chip box carries an optgroup whose label is its axis, and
  no option repeats the axis in its own text.

- **‼️ AND THE `Default` ROW WAS NAMING THE VALUE YOU ALREADY HAD.** It read
  `Default → sonnet` on an agent whose model IS `sonnet` — the name of the one
  thing you cannot get by picking that row, because picking it clears the
  agent's own answer and falls through to the fleet. The resolution behind it
  walked every layer including the box's own. `resolvedZero` is the same
  resolver with this agent's layers left out, and the row now reads
  `Default → haiku`: what would really apply after the clearing. The sentence
  that used to sit inside the label — `(the CLI decides)` — is in the hover,
  where the rest of that explanation already was.

- **‼️ AND THE PER-AGENT DEFAULT NEVER REACHED A SESSION STARTED FROM THE
  CONSOLE.** Farm Settings draws a model box and an effort box on every agent
  chip and writes `agentFarm.agentEngineDefaults`. Every launch door resolves
  through that layer — the ▶ on an agent row, `sessions.start` on the bridge, a
  terminal start — except one: the Console composer read `launchDefaults()` and
  nothing else, so an empty box jumped straight over the per-agent answer to the
  fleet-wide one. An agent set to `xhigh` in Settings started at the fleet's
  effort and nothing said so: a control that stores what it is told and changes
  nothing, which is the exact shape this store was created to end. The order is
  now the box → this agent on this engine → the fleet, in the composer and in
  both of the panel's other start paths, through the SAME function the other
  doors call rather than a second reader. New gate
  `test/test_console_agent_default.js` measures the value that reaches
  `host.start`, not the source of the panel.

- **The `show` picker gives ground when the composer row is crowded.** It
  reserves the widest text it can ever print — right, so the row does not rock
  as the choice changes — and was therefore the widest control on a nine-box
  `nowrap` strip and the only one that could not help. Measured at 1030px it
  held 142px while the boxes that hold a VALUE were squeezed to single digits.
  Unchanged where there is room; down to half, never below, where there is not.
  The floor is computed from `--afms-w`, the width the component itself
  reserved, rather than a number typed into the page that would go stale.

- **‼️ S-57 — THE STRIP AFTER A RESTART SAID `$20.94 · 1step` AND NOTHING
  ELSE.** No duration, no tokens, no round trips, no model or effort. The
  information was not lost and not hidden: **it was never collected, because the
  turn was never opened.** Three functions open a turn and all three are the
  WINDOW speaking; a revived conversation has a fourth case none of them cover —
  the CLI answers on its own, because it was given the prompt before this window
  existed. That branch set `status` to `working` and nothing else, so the turn
  ran with no clock, no token baseline, no round-trip counter and no
  model/effort pair, and the `result` line closed it with `undefined` for every
  one of them. Reproduced through the reducer alone, on the exact shape
  reported, then repaired: a turn nobody in this window started is opened where
  it is first seen — before the line's own blocks are read, so the call that
  started the turn is charged to it.

- Also: `test/lib_afms_dom.js` insisted a picker's tag ENDED at
  `data-afms-wrap`, so the day the component gained a second attribute eleven
  page tests stopped finding any picker at all. One parser breaking, reported as
  eleven pages breaking.

`test/fixtures/engines.js` now DERIVES its resolutions from `resolveDefault`
instead of stating them by hand — the same rule B-05.6 applied to the
Superpowers and Sentry scenes. Typed out, they had already drifted into a
contradiction no string test could see: one agent claimed `launchDefaults` gave
it `haiku`, and the same agent on another engine claimed nothing was set
fleet-wide at all. One `launchDefaults` cannot be both, so the photograph was
showing a state the product cannot produce.

## 3.455.0 - the search grammar under "Mute the farm", and a bridge that said "answering" while it refused (audit B-05) (2026-09-10)

The Farm Settings surface was opened for the audit ledger: seven fixtures,
nineteen scenes, every one of them photographed at its own size and the three
machine sweeps run over each. Five defects, and two of them were in the
pictures themselves.

- **Twenty-one controls on Alert sounds explained boolean search syntax.**
  `AFQuery.tip(subject)` is the SEARCH BOX's tooltip - it returns the subject
  and then the whole query grammar - and it reads like a generic "make me a
  tooltip", so it was used as one. Hovering `🔇 Mute the farm` taught you that
  `OR must be uppercase`; so did `Quiet hours`, `rate`, `vol`, the reminder
  tone, the voice picker, the announcement template, the five per-event sound
  pickers, the three sound-library name fields and all four column headers of
  the table. Exactly one of the twenty-two was a search box. No string test
  could fail on it: every sentence was well-formed and every SUBJECT was
  right - the defect was the paragraph bolted on after it. Measured from two
  ends now (`test_tooltip_subject.js`): every `AFQuery.tip` call says what is
  SEARCHED, and on a laid-out page only an `<input>` you type a query into
  carries the grammar.

- **The alert table painted the rows that still ring, and left the silent one
  plain.** On the scene whose own title is "armed events whose sound cannot be
  played", `error` was armed with nothing on this machine able to play it -
  SILENT - and drew in the ordinary foreground, while the two rows that fell
  through to a working default drew in warning yellow. The badge above them
  said "1 armed event cannot be played" and pointed at the one row the table
  did not mark. A fallback is a warning; an armed event nothing can play is
  silence, and it is now the badge's own expression that decides the colour,
  so the two cannot drift apart.

- **The Telegram card said "Polling Telegram and answering the chats on the
  allowlist" over a red, over-budget bar.** `chatRunPrompt` refuses every
  prompt in that state ("Today's chat budget is used up"), so a green
  `connected` badge was telling somebody their phone could start a run when it
  could not - the exact failure the card's own header was written about.
  `over-budget` is a sixth bridge state now, ranked below an empty allowlist
  (nothing reaches the budget at all with one) and above `connected`, and it
  says which number to raise. `/status`, `/agent` and `/cancel` still answer,
  and the sentence says so.

- **`wikiEngine` drew a picker with nothing in it.** `agentFarm.wikiEngine`
  and `agentFarm.wikiEffort` name `''` in their own enum and default to it, so
  the schema-driven picker rendered an option whose text was the empty string:
  a blank box three rows under one reading `high`. Unset, broken and still
  loading all looked identical. It reads `— not set —` now, with the panel
  saying the setting is left out and whoever starts the work decides.

- **Two boxes narrower than the value they hold**, on the surface the width
  sweep had never been run against: the per-event sound picker (a user-named
  sound plus its state, 185px in 170px) and the announcement voice (every real
  voice on this machine, 333px in 306px, with 830px of unused row beside it).
  Both ceilings moved to where a real value fits, out of a column that had
  slack.

- **And the scenes themselves were wrong in two places.** The Superpowers
  fixture typed its rows out by hand and left `shape` off, so all three of its
  scenes had been photographing the raw JSON box U-110 replaced - a control the
  product does not have, in the file whose whole job is to say what that
  section looks like. The Sentry fixture built the refusal sentence itself
  under a comment claiming it was the resolver's, verbatim, and hardcoded
  `${vault}` into every one: the no-vault scene showed the `${projectNotes}`
  row warning about a variable that row does not contain. Both are derived from
  the product now, and `test_settings_fixture_truth.js` holds every settings
  fixture against `buildSettingsModel` and every refused path against the
  variables its own template carries.

## 3.454.0 - a box that says nothing but "Default", and a percentage under the wrong window (audit B-03/B-04) (2026-09-10)

Two defects of the same family, found by looking at scenes nobody had looked
at: a control that does not say what it controls, and a figure that does not
say what it is a figure OF. Plus the sweep that had been blind to both.

- **The row that starts a session drew three boxes reading nothing but
  "Default".** Which was model, which was effort and which was permissions was
  answerable only by hover, while the RUNNING row four inches below names all
  four of its boxes. The axis travels inside the value now - `effort: high`
  when somebody chose it, `perm -> Default` when the engine decides - and the
  hover is an AFTip panel rather than a native title: the axis spelled out in
  full, what it is set to, and what that choice means, without the standing
  sentence being repeated. A separate label was refused by measurement, not
  taste: `.crow` is `flex-wrap:nowrap` and had 69px of slack where four labels
  want ~166. The same thing was true of the agent chips on Farm Settings
  (`developer [gpt-5.6-terra] [high]`), and they got the same treatment.

- **Seven places named an account's quota window and only one was right.** The
  Codex card read `Current week 72%` while its own hover panel said `72% of the
  five-hour window used` - the same figure under two window names, one of them
  a lie with a real number in it. Each of the seven had typed the words out;
  the seventh had a capital F and survived the sweep that found the other six.
  The reading names its own window now and the host fills the silence exactly
  once (`windowNameOf`), so no page derives anything. Two silences, filled
  differently: an engine that named none is on the five-hour window, but a
  disk-backed reading nobody has taken yet is a `usage window`, because its
  length is IN the reading it has not had.

- **A model id was cut to 25 characters on a row with 1,106px to spare.**
  `opencode/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free` needs 173px; the box was pinned at
  150. The ceiling was raised, not removed. And the reason nine surfaces of
  audit walked past it: a native `<select>` is invisible to both standing
  sweeps - its `scrollWidth` never exceeds its box and its value is not a text
  node. A third sweep measures the option's text in the select's own font;
  over all 30 fixtures it answers with 77 clipped boxes on four surfaces.

- Also: the settings subtitle said "1 settings".

## 3.453.9 - a window that turned over hours ago said "in 0m" (audit B-04) (2026-09-10)

The Engines surface was opened for the audit ledger. Two cards in one picture,
two different clock times, both reading **(in 0m)** - and they cannot both be
right.

- **A five-hour window that has already turned over was drawn as one about to.**
  `resetsAt` comes off a READING of the account's usage file, so an account
  nobody has run on for hours carries a turnover that has been and gone. The
  wait was `Math.max(0, ...)`, which kept a negative from being printed and
  printed "about to happen" instead: `work@studio` said "turns over at 02:17
  (in 0m)" beside `personal@gmail` saying "turns over at 05:40 (in 0m)". It
  matters because of the percentage next to it - that is what an account
  rotation is decided on (X-169, X-226), and once the window has turned over the
  figure belongs to the OLD one. The row says so now, in the past tense, and
  names the staleness the line beside it was already admitting ("this figure was
  read 3h ago"). The wrong rule was nailed down in `test_af_account.js` ("a
  reset already past waits zero, never a negative") - reversed, not deleted.

## 3.453.8 - the tool that every visual verdict rests on was measuring the window (audit B-03) (2026-09-10)

The Console surface was swept scene by scene, and the first thing the sweep
found was the camera. Three defects, one of them in the measuring instrument
itself.

- **`shoot_page.js --scene N` answered 1400x2305 for all seventeen scenes of the
  Console** - the height of the measuring window, not of the scene. A fixture
  carries the PAGE's stylesheet, and `media/console.js` declares
  `html, body { height:100% }`, so `body.scrollHeight` reports the window back
  whatever is inside it. Measured: sixteen of seventeen scenes removed, the
  surviving `#app` 55..418, the body still 2308. Nothing said so - the picture
  was right at the top and empty below, and a reader scaling 2305px to fit shrank
  a 418px scene to a fifth for nothing. This is A-12.10's defect from the other
  end, where the tool CUT instead. The height is the lowest edge anything is
  DRAWN at now: a closed AFTip panel (a 5,169px block inside a fixed shell) is
  not painted and is left out, a scrolled-away row is clipped and is left out,
  and the body is not treated as a clipper. All thirty fixtures were compared
  against the old figure - twenty-eight identical to the pixel, and the one that
  moved was 85px of invisible panel the old number had been counting.
- **A letter fragment floating beside the open "/" picker.** The picker hangs off
  the composer's textarea wrapper (309..1339) and covers the "still working"
  strip on its way up - but the strip was on a ruler of its own, `padding: 4px`
  against the composer's 1px border plus 8px, so its right-aligned meta line
  ended at 1344. Five pixels, and with the picker open they were the only part of
  the covered line still on the screen. The strip is on the composer's ruler now;
  `test/test_console_column_ruler.js` measures the column rather than the number.
- **A card's whole spend beside "0 turns".** The two halves of the session line
  counted different things: `sessionSpend` adds the RUNNING turn to the cost and
  the tokens (that is what the `~` means) and the turn count is of FINISHED
  turns. Measured on a live card: 23,928,519 tokens, 149 api calls, `turns: 0`.
  Every figure was right; reading them side by side was not. The running turn is
  named now (`2 turns - 1 running`) instead of being left for the reader to add
  back.

## 3.453.7 - columns that were not columns, and a name squeezed to zero pixels (audit B-02 · B-03) (2026-09-10)

Four layout defects, none of which could fail a string test: the markup was
correct in every one of them. They were found by measuring the laid-out page
instead of reading it, and each repair now carries a test that measures too.

- **The Missions delegation table drew its column headers in the right third of
  the page.** `Agent · Task · Status · Tokens · Cost · Evidence` sat at
  x≈918–1356 while their own data sat at x≈60. The cause was a NAME, not a
  layout: `.srow` was also the mission composer's `display:flex` form row, 350
  lines away in the same file, so the `<tr>` became a flex container, its cells
  stopped being table cells, and the `<thead>` was left to lay itself out
  against nothing. The step row is `.steprow` now, and
  `test/test_table_row_display.js` reads every page script for the collision.
- **Three team rows of the same five axes, none of them in the same column.**
  The account picker is drawn only where this machine holds a sign-in for that
  member's engine (X-225, and right: a box with no referent is forbidden). But
  `.tmrow` is a flex row, so dropping the sixth control let the other five grow
  — one member's ENGINE box sat under the row above's MODEL and its PERMISSIONS
  under that row's ACCOUNT. The box still is not drawn; what holds its place
  says why the axis is missing, which is more than the hole was saying.
- **A session card's first fact — whose session it is — was not on the screen.**
  The list is a fixed 250px column on every window, so a card carrying engine +
  route + tokens + 🔖 beside the name is the ordinary case. Measured: the name
  was squeezed to **zero** pixels, and below one character there is not even an
  ellipsis to say something is missing; on the tightest row the eight-character
  id was clipped too and the card read `(#:`. The badges are one group now, so
  the line breaks between the identity and them rather than through them, and
  the identity has a floor.
- **A round table that clamps its duration, a scene that answers the host, and
  scenes that were photographing the scene above them.** `missions/history` is
  labelled "the recorded history strip, panel open" and had no way to open one;
  `missions/form-preview` exists to prove the refusal list a draft collects and
  had never drawn one, because it answered with a token the page discards. A
  scene now names the panel or menu it needs on itself, and
  `test/test_scenes_differ.js` refuses an undeclared duplicate — it found two
  more in other fixtures.

## 3.453.6 - the sentry scenes were drawn in words the product does not have (audit B-02) (2026-09-10)

The surface sweep of Missions, the most-touched page in the corpus. A-12.8 had
added four scenes because the sentry chip's own states had never been drawn —
and three of them were drawn from vocabulary nobody writes.

- **BLOCKED said `no-item`, and there is no such rule.** An empty backlog is not
  blocked at all: it is `idle` / `nothing-to-take`, because only the user ends a
  campaign. Its sentence ended in a bare `⛔` — a mark that belongs on a backlog
  line, not a word — so on screen the reason read as cut off mid-thought. The
  scene added to prove "the panel carries the reason" was carrying a reason
  nobody could ever meet. It now carries `pool-empty` verbatim, the longest one
  the product really writes, which is also the honest test of this line's 150
  character cap and its panel.
- **WAITING said `finish` / `round-ended`.** `finish` belongs to MISSIONS, a
  different machine; `SentryAction` is `start | sleep | idle | blocked |
  stopped`. The chip reaches WAITING as its fall-through, so an invented action
  landed on the right picture for the wrong reason while the panel's header read
  "finish — round-ended" over a `why` about starting X-178.
- **Five scenes were idle and mid-round at once.** Every state derived from
  `sentry-live` sets `running: false, live: null` and went on inheriting a round
  table whose last row said `running` with no `endedAt`.
- **And settling that row exposed a real one: `Took -24m`.** The round table's
  duration was `Math.round(endedAt - createdAt)` with no floor, so a row whose
  stamps are out of order printed a round that finished before it began. The run
  table one screen up in the same file already clamps the identical figure.
- **`test_sentry_fixture_truth.js`** reads the vocabulary out of `src/` — the
  declared union for actions, a scrape that understands ternaries for rules —
  and holds every fixture against it, so the next invented word is red before it
  is ever photographed. Bitten four ways.
- The why panel is named `sentry-why`, so `render_page.js --tip` can open it.
  Past 150 characters that panel is the only place the whole reason exists.

Looked at, not read, one scene at a time: `missions.s8.png` · `s9.png` ·
`s10.png` · `missions.light.s10.png`. 325 files, 20,323 passed, 0 failed.

## 3.453.4 - an op that answered ok to work it never did (audit A-25) (2026-09-09)

`projects.backlog.archive` sweeps a whole file. Handed `code` and `note` it
dropped both without a word and still answered ok — so a session cancelled an
item by calling it, read `ok: true`, and wrote the cancellation into its
closing summary and its handover note while the item stayed open, still
stamped as the user's own request. The next session found it and spent its
own budget on the repair.

- **The op refuses a single-item aim** instead of ignoring it: it names the
  arguments it would have swallowed and names `projects.backlog.check`, which
  is where closing or cancelling ONE item actually lives. Its contract says so
  too, so nobody has to run it to find out.
- **Pinned on both sides** — the dispatched behaviour and the real handler in
  `src/extension.ts` — because a harness that only tests its own copy of an op
  is how this got shipped in the first place.

Also, in the audit's own tooling: `tools/audit_extract.js` printed a session
window in UTC directly above a commit list `git log` renders in local time — a
7-hour skew on this machine, so a dossier showed commits stamped 17:35 and
19:13 under a window ending at 12:17 and called them "in the window". The
selection was always right; only the reader was misled. One clock now, and it
is named in the line.

## 3.453.3 - every MIRROR gap in the product was being swallowed (audit A-12.9) (2026-09-09)

MIRROR asks a control to put its CURRENT value on the first line of its panel,
**then a blank line**, then the description. Every panel in the product was
written that way and **not one of them drew the blank line**: `AFTip.lines`
drops an empty string, because that is how a caller passes a conditional line.
The rule read as applied everywhere and the screen ran the value straight into
its paragraph — the failure Principle 1 is about, in a shared component.

- **`AFTip.GAP`** — the second intention with its own name. It is a single
  space: a line that IS there and is blank, so it survives `lines`,
  `filter(Boolean)`, a bare `.join('\n')` and a native `title` alike, and no
  joiner has to learn about it. 57 separators across ten pages moved onto it.
  `media/missions.js` had already found the problem and kept a local `GAP = ' '`
  to itself, fixing exactly one panel; that copy is gone.
- **`test/test_aftip_gap.js`** holds the two intentions apart (an empty string is
  still dropped, a `GAP` is still drawn) and refuses a bare `''` written on its
  own line anywhere in `media/` — it is either a gap or an argument, and both
  read better named.
- **‼️ `render_page.js --tip` could not open an `AFTip.cell` panel at all.**
  `cell` writes the caller's classes and then `af-tipw` (`class="turncol
  af-tipw"`), and the matcher was anchored at `class="af-tipw` — so every cell
  panel in the product answered "nothing carries it", and the tool **rendered
  the page anyway**, so the screenshot that followed photographed a closed panel
  and was filed as evidence. Every class attribute is read now, and a `--tip`
  that opens nothing exits non-zero.

Looked at, not read: `dist/render/A129-barren-gap.png` (the brake's three
figures now stand off their paragraph) and `A129-turns-gap.png` (the same
through a page that joins its own lines with `filter(Boolean)`).

## 3.453.1 - the pin was written, tested and never plugged in (2026-09-09)

**X-267, the second half.** 3.453.0 shipped the pinned-context mechanism with
twenty-nine green assertions and it did nothing at all. `ConsoleHost` takes
`pinProjectContext` as its ninth constructor parameter, defaulted — like every
one of its siblings — to `() => {}`. `extension.ts` was never changed to pass
it. The build compiled, the suite stayed green (it constructs the host itself,
with all nine arguments), and the Console silently never pinned a single
conversation: measured on a live session started under 3.453.0, the `pinned/`
folder had not even been created. Every revive went on re-composing the brief
the pin existed to reuse.

- **The wire.** `extension.ts` — the `new ConsoleHost(…)` call site now passes
  `pinProjectContext` as its ninth argument. Headless rounds and the mission
  planner were already wired (they pass their callbacks by name, in an options
  object, where a missing one is a compile error).
- **The gate that would have caught it, `test/test_wiring.js`.** A missing
  *argument* is invisible to the type checker — that is what the default is for
  — and invisible to a suite that builds its own object — that is what a mock is
  for. It can only be caught by reading the call site, so that is what this
  does, derived rather than declared: the parameter list is parsed out of the
  class, the argument list out of the `new`, and neither is written down in the
  test to drift. **The rule:** a constructor parameter whose default is a
  no-op-shaped callback must be passed at every `new` site in `src/`. A `?`
  optional parameter is exempt (absent means something there); a real default
  (`= 'claude'`) is exempt too (leaving it off asks for that value). Run over
  the whole of `src/core`, this was the only such gap in the codebase.

## 3.453.0 - a resume was regenerating its own system prompt, and paying for the whole conversation again (2026-09-09)

**X-267.** Console session `4b0c8af8` was resumed after a 29-second extension-host
restart. Anthropic's answer on the first turn back, from the transcript:

```
"diagnostics": { "cache_miss_reason": {
    "type": "system_changed", "cache_missed_input_tokens": 219488 } },
"usage": { "cache_creation_input_tokens": 303987, "cache_read_input_tokens": 14811 }
```

**303,987 tokens re-billed as cache creation** on a conversation that had not
changed by one character — the 5-hour window went from 72% to 96% in a second.
`system_changed` names it exactly: Agent Farm re-**generated** the project
context on every spawn, and that text carries a `generated HH:MM` stamp and the
project's latest worklog lines — lines the resumed session had itself just
written. A prefix cache matches from byte zero, so one changed minute in the
system prompt throws away every token behind it.

The context genuinely does **not** survive `--resume` (measured long ago,
`smoke_project_context.mjs`), so dropping the flag would delete the feature to
save the cache. What a resume gets now is the **pinned copy**: the same bytes
that opened the conversation.

- **The pin.** `core/projectContext.ts` — `pinnedContextFileName` (the CLI
  session id plus the ordinary file's name, so project, audience and the
  Superpowers switch are all still in the key) and `resolveContextTarget`, which
  is the whole rule with no filesystem in it: serve the pin · write **into** the
  pinned slot when a resume has none yet · use the shared per-project file on a
  fresh spawn.
- **Three resume paths were regenerating it.** The **Console** (`consolehost.ts`
  now names the conversation it is continuing, and takes the pin itself once the
  `init` line reports the id), **headless rounds** (`tasks.ts` — the loudest
  case: a round is a `--resume`, so the whole thread was re-billed once per
  round), and the **OS terminal resume**.
- **And a fourth was DROPPING it, which is the same defect running the other
  way.** The mission planner passed no context file on a round at all, on the
  belief that the brief was already in the conversation. It was not — an
  appended system prompt is not a message and does not survive `--resume` — so
  every mission round after the first ran with **no project**; and removing a
  block from a system prompt changes it exactly as much as rewriting one, so it
  re-billed the thread regardless. It now gets the pinned copy like everything
  else, which restores the brief *and* the cache.
- **A resume is no longer re-briefed, on purpose.** A pinned hit composes
  nothing and does not refresh `_AF/BRIEF.md` either. The freshest brief is
  always one `_AF/BRIEF.md` read away; a fresher worklog line is not worth the
  conversation's whole prefix cache.
- **And it fixed the overwrite race for free.** A resume with no pin writes into
  its own slot, so another window spawning under the same project can no longer
  replace the bytes underneath it.
- **Known limit, stated rather than hidden:** a conversation that started before
  this build has no pin, so its *next* resume composes one and pays one last
  cache miss. Every resume after that is free.
- `test_context_pin.js` (29) pins the rule, both wirings and all four call
  sites.

## 3.452.0 - the page that came back came back twice, so it was taken back out (2026-09-09)

The half of 3.451.0 that reopened the Console PAGE after a revive is withdrawn.
Measured on the user's screen: the reader got **two Console tabs**. VS Code
leaves the old webview tab exactly where it was when the host went down — it
just never re-attaches it, because we register no panel serializer — so a page
opened by the revive is a *second* tab beside the dead one, not a recovery.

- **Withdrawn:** `consoleOpen` on the restart stamp, `ConsolePanel.isOpen()`,
  and the deferred `ConsolePanel.show()` at the end of the revive.
- **Kept:** everything the same release fixed about the numbers. The revived
  card still carries its conversation's own totals (turns, tokens, cost) rather
  than counting from zero — that half was verified live, twice, and is not
  touched here.
- **Pinned as an absence, not as a comment.** `test_console_revive.js` now
  asserts that none of the three exist: no `reopenConsoleSeat`, no
  `consoleOpen`, and still no `registerWebviewPanelSerializer`. All three have
  to move together, because a serializer arriving on its own — or a `show` from
  the revive on its own — is the two-tab bug walking straight back in.

The honest way in, when someone takes it up again: adopt the tab VS Code is
already holding with a `WebviewPanelSerializer`. The tab is VS Code's; the job
is to re-attach it, never to open another one beside it. That changes how the
Console panel is constructed — the product's most critical surface — so it is
asked before it is built.

## 3.451.0 - the revived card counted from zero, and the page that was showing it never came back (2026-09-09)

X-232 brings a Console conversation through a restart. Two things it did not
bring, both reported by the user in one breath, and both the same measured
fact as X-267: inside `activate()` the transcript index has answered NOTHING
yet, so everything read off it at that moment comes back empty.

- **What the conversation already spent comes back too.** `carried` is read off
  the index row, so on a revive it was always `undefined` and the card started
  at zero: an hour-old conversation under a line reading "$0.0000 · 0 tokens ·
  0 turns this session" — the composer describing this window’s turn at the
  session instead of the session, which is the exact reading `CarriedTotals`
  exists to prevent. The scrollback was already retried when the scan caught
  up; the totals now wait in the same subscription and go in the same way. The
  baseline is ADDED, never assigned, because a seat that was mid-turn is nudged
  to carry on the moment it comes back and may have spent something of its own
  by then. A context reading already on the card is left alone — live beats
  disk — and Codex’s per-turn baseline is set only if that thread has not
  already completed a turn in this seat.
- **And the Console page comes back with it.** VS Code restores no webview of
  ours (there is no panel serializer), so a revive put the seat back and left
  the reader looking at an editor that never reopened: the session was working
  and the screen said nothing about it. The restart stamp now records whether
  the page was open while the host is still up, and the revive reopens it on
  the seat that was mid-turn — or the first one, if none was. A page that was
  NOT open is not opened: a Console session can outlive the tab that started
  it, and opening an editor nobody asked for is not a recovery. It is deferred
  by a tick and wrapped, because activation is not the place to build a webview
  and the conversation must never go down with the page.

## 3.450.0 - one row ticking was clearing the handles of all eight, and the play took the selected row for the pressed one (2026-09-09)

3.449.0 stopped the play button on an agent row from asking which agent. The
user pressed it and got the other half of the same defect: no picker, but
sometimes *"▶ arrived without its row"* — and once, an agent they had not
pressed. Both are the same mechanism, read out of the running extension host
rather than guessed at.

**A change event with no argument clears every handle in the view.** `sb(t)`
deletes only the CHILDREN of the elements it is given and leaves each row’s own
handle standing; an empty event runs `tb()`, which empties the map for the
whole view. An inline ▶ whose handle is not in that map reaches its command
with no argument at all. Gating the redraw on whether the rows changed (3.449.0)
did not help where it mattered: on a live fleet a token count on ONE row
genuinely ticks every few seconds, and every one of those ticks was throwing
away the handles of all the others.

- **The row that changed is refreshed by name.** The Agents view now fires with
  the elements that actually changed, so the other rows keep their handles and
  a press between two draws still knows which agent it belongs to. The rows are
  the same objects from draw to draw, because the host finds a refreshed
  element by object identity — one built fresh on every draw is found nowhere
  and would go stale in silence. The view is still cleared outright when the
  rows themselves change (an agent added, removed, renamed, reordered), which
  is the one thing no per-row event can say.
- **And the row’s play no longer falls back to the SELECTED row.** Pressing an
  inline action does not select its row, so the selection is whatever was last
  clicked: press ▶ on one agent while another is still selected, lose the
  argument, and a session starts as somebody else with nothing on screen saying
  so. That belt was a reasonable recovery while the argument was lost several
  times a minute; now that the loss is the rare case, a rare dead press that
  explains itself is worth more than a rare silent impersonation. The Command
  Palette door keeps the belt — there the selection is the only thing the
  caller has, and the surface dialog names the agent before anything starts.

## 3.449.0 - the play button on a named row asked which agent, and the view was being rebuilt four times a second (2026-09-09)

S-48 was closed once. The user pressed the inline play on an agent row, was
shown "Select an agent" again, and said so a second time: *"every single thing
they do gets broken one more time."* It was the same defect and the cure had
been the wrong shape.

**What actually happens under the pointer.** Read out of the running extension
host: when `onDidChangeTreeData` fires with no argument, VS Code empties the
whole handle-to-element map for that view (`tb()` -> `this.j.clear()`) and
rebuilds the rows. A play pressed into an action bar that is being replaced
arrives at its command with **no argument at all**. S-48 answered that with a
250 ms throttle, which narrows the window and never closes it: `live` fires on
every hook event of every session, so a busy fleet rebuilt the view four times
a second, for ever, and almost every one of those rebuilds drew the same eight
rows.

- **The redraw is now gated on the drawing.** `AgentsTreeProvider.refreshIfChanged()`
  renders the top-level rows and reads back what a person would see - label,
  description, icon, context value - and fires only when that differs from the
  last drawing. Not a hand-written list of "the fields that matter", which would
  drift the first time a row learns to show something new: the signature is the
  drawing itself, so a token count that reaches the row only through its
  `description` still redraws at once. A quiet fleet now costs the view nothing,
  and the bar under the pointer stops being replaced for no reason.
- **The row’s play is its own command, because only the palette is entitled to
  ask.** `agentfarm.startSession` is reached from a row (which names the agent),
  from another command (which names it too) and from the Command Palette (which
  names nobody and MUST ask) - so an empty argument meant two opposite things on
  one id, and it kept resolving that clash the palette’s way. The row now has
  `agentfarm.startSessionRow`: kept out of the palette, it resolves the argument,
  then the view’s own selected row, and if neither can name an agent it **says
  so and stops**. A press that does nothing and explains itself is recoverable;
  a session quietly started as somebody else is not. The start itself is not
  reimplemented - it is the same door, called with the agent named.
- **And a run that was carried on stops telling you to start it.** Measured live
  on 3.448.0: the headless revive works, and the original row’s last event still
  read *"back on the queue, press start to run it again"* - written by the reload
  sweep minutes before the decision to carry it on was taken. A person doing what
  the row says pays for a second run of the original prompt beside the
  continuation that is already working. The carry-on now writes itself onto the
  row it came from, the way a refusal already did.

## 3.448.0 - the night shift stopped at the restart, and nobody was there to press start (2026-09-08)

X-232 got a Console card across a restart of the extension host, and it was
tested live and it works. The half beside it was never given a verdict: the one
headless test ever run died 25 seconds in, on a weekly plan limit, before the
restart could even be fired. Both halves turned out to be broken, and the ledger
had the second one recorded as working.

**What a headless run actually did.** The reload sweep puts it back on the queue
— and `launch()` clears `autoStart` before it spawns, while `pump()` only ever
picks up rows that have it. So a run cut by a restart sits `queued` with
`autoStart` false, which is a row nothing relaunches. Not "it starts again from
the beginning", which is what the audit ledger said: it does not start at all.
The manager's own comment says exactly this about the terminal case — *"nothing
on this earth relaunches it"* — and the plain headless case had the same hole
with a sentence addressed to a person in it: *"press start to run it again"*. At
three in the morning that is nobody.

- A restart that says `resume` now carries the headless runs too, in the same
  breath as the console sessions and for the same reason. The run is picked up
  in its OWN conversation — `runSessionId` was written down when the launch
  bound and it survives in the store — with the continuation words M-10 wrote
  for exactly this, never the original prompt, which would tell an engine with
  no memory to redo work it cannot see.
- It goes through the same copy path a retry goes through, so it runs the way
  the original ran (engine, model, effort, route, account, folder, sound). A
  resurrection is only as honest as its dimensions. What it is NOT is
  "(retry 4)": the work did not fail three times, the window went down under it,
  so the row says `continued` and the event says `resumed`.
- **Only on a restart that asked for continuity.** An ordinary window reload, a
  crash or an update leaves the runs exactly where they were. Spawning CLI
  processes that spend money on every reload is not a default anybody chose.
- Three refusals, each with its reason written on the ROW and not only in a
  toast that is gone in five seconds: no session id (nothing to resume BY), a
  run somebody already started, and a run picked up 3 times already — the
  boot-loop guard's sibling, because a host restarting in a loop would otherwise
  respawn the same work all night.
- Workflow steps are untouched: still cancelled, still offered to a person. That
  was a deliberate decision ("a resumed run can spend money/agent time, so the
  user decides") and changing it is a separate one.

**And the wall that killed the test is now recognised as a wall.** The run
printed `You've hit your weekly limit · resets 7pm (Asia/Bangkok)` and its own
record answered *"no retry — the failure was not a session limit, and this run
only retries those"*. `isLimitFailure` knew every phrasing of the SESSION limit
and none of the weekly one — and that one predicate gates three things at once:
whether to retry, whether to hand the run to another sign-in (X-226), and how
the session is diagnosed. A weekly-walled night run therefore did not wait, did
not move to a free account, and simply died.

- The weekly wall is a limit failure, and `limitWindow()` says which of the two
  it was. A monthly SPEND ceiling deliberately stays out: nothing reopens it but
  a person raising it, so a run that waits for it waits for ever.
- `resets 7pm` with no day is not an answer for a window that resets in days.
  `parseLimitReset` now reports which branch produced its number, and the weekly
  window refuses a bare clock reading rather than waking at a 7pm nobody said
  was today — and says so in the sentence on the record. An absolute stamp or a
  duration carries its own calendar and is trusted for either window.

Found by the retrospective audit track (B-03.8), whose own recorded measurement
of this row was wrong and has been corrected against the code.

## 3.447.0 - the badge got three states and the sentence under it kept two (2026-09-08)

X-220 split the account verdict into three because the two bad ones are not the
same fact: 🟠 knows whose account it is and cannot refresh it, 🔴 cannot tell you
even that. Its own tooltip says so out loud — *"this is NOT an expired sign-in"*.

Two lines below that, the window line said **"needs signing in again, so nothing
was read"**, and its panel said *"the stored credential no longer refreshes"* —
🟠's sentence, word for word, under a 🔴 badge. The reader was told the opposite
thing twice in two lines, and the one that was wrong was the one carrying the
detail. The engine chip's own list did the same: every non-ready account was
captioned "needs signing in again" there too.

**Why nobody saw it.** The third state had never been on a screen. It was
checked by mutating the payload inside a test — which proves a string and
photographs nothing — while every fixture the page is drawn from carried only
🟢 and 🟠. So the caption could go on testing `health !== 'ready'` for as long as
it liked and the whole suite stayed green.

- Three silences, three sentences: read it and it was dead · read it and nothing
  could be made of it · nobody has looked yet. The 🔴 panel names the difference
  rather than repeating 🟠's, and points at the 🔑 beside it, which is the thing
  that actually fixes this one.
- The state now has its own SCENE — `enginesbroken`, a variant of the engines
  panel fixture, with all three verdicts on it at once. It is a variant and not
  a sixth row in the existing picture, because that picture's counts are pinned
  on purpose (four quiet greens against one yellow is the design) and a state is
  not made visible by spoiling the picture that proves something else.
- Drawn and looked at, dark and light, at 760 px: `node test/render_page.js
  enginespanel --only enginesbroken` → `node test/shoot_page.js enginespanel`.

Found by the retrospective audit track (A-06.7), which also confirmed the two
halves that were sound: X-219's 🔑 really is on screen and really is drawn only
where there is something to renew, and X-220's duplicate protection really does
match on engine+address, refuse to guess at an unreadable address, and refuse a
hand-arranged directory by name instead of quietly dissolving it.

## 3.446.0 - a revived session takes the WORK up again, not only the conversation (2026-09-08)

The user's decision, in their own words: *kaldığı yerden devam etsin.*

X-230's header says the thing it exists to stop is a deadlock on an unattended
night shift — the loop stops until a human comes back. X-232 got the card back
into its seat with its whole transcript, and then it sat `idle`: `reviveInit`
carries no prompt and nothing spoke into it. So the night shift still stopped,
one step later than before, and the card said "ask again" to a room with nobody
in it.

A revived seat is now asked to carry on. **Only one that was mid-turn** — that
figure was already measured for the notice, and it is the honest scope: a
session sitting idle was waiting for a human, so nudging it would not be
resuming work, it would be inventing it.

Measured rather than assumed, and the assumption written first was wrong: a
resumed seat comes back `starting`, not idle — it has a transcript to load
before it says anything. So the nudge waits for the engine's own first quiet
moment. It also may not wait for ever: an engine that never announces itself
would leave the shift stopped in the one way nothing reports, and a prompt
written into a `starting` seat IS delivered (the message lands and the seat goes
to `working`). After 30s it is sent slightly early rather than not at all.

The prompt names what was lost and what was not, and it ends by telling a model
that cannot tell where it was to say so and stop rather than guess at work it
may already have done.

## 3.445.0 - the hidden-lines banner, looked at (2026-09-08)

U-133's third round, verified the way the item keeps asking for: rendered and
read, in both themes and in both arities.

The note moved into the transcript's frame in 3.444.0, at the top — as far from
the ask card as the panel goes. Its rule was on the wrong side: as the frame's
first child a `border-top` only doubled the wrapper's own border, and the
comment beside it called the element a footer while it sat at the head. The rule
is now on the bottom, where it separates the note from the lines it is about,
and the comment says what the element is.

Looked at: `console-asking-hidden` (one question and a show filter — the two
things the user reported colliding, in one frame at last) and
`console-asking-one` (no filter: the banner is absent and leaves no stray line),
dark and light.

## 3.444.0 - the version string is not the build, and a boot the farm did not plan (2026-09-08)

Both found by the audit walking into them, live, on this machine.

**`build.pending` compared two version strings, so it could not see the one
case the dev loop produces every time.** `npm run package` then
`code --install-extension --force` under the SAME version number is what
happens between commits: VS Code replaces the extension folder in place and the
running host keeps the code it loaded. Both strings still read `3.443.0`, so
`farm.health` answered `pending:false` while the build on disk was a different
one — measured here, package.json written at 09:38 against a host that booted
at 09:24. The agent believed its own code was live, and A-02.7's "the restart
loaded nothing" trap came straight back, silently, because nothing about the
name had changed.

A version number cannot express "a different build of the same version", so the
FOLDER's identity is carried instead: the host takes the mtime of the
`package.json` it was loaded from at boot and compares it live. Unreadable at
either end stays `undefined` — an unknown is not a mismatch, the same rule the
version comparison already followed. The sentence changes with it: two equal
numbers are never reported as differing, it names the folder.

**And `farm.health` was working "pending" out a second time, on its own.** The
planner learnt the new rule and the surface could not, which is exactly how an
op and a page come to disagree. It now reads the planner's answer.

**A boot the farm did not plan now says so.** VS Code restarts the extension
host by itself — a `--force` install, the Extensions card's own button, a crash
— and when it does there is no stamp, so there is no revive plan and no console
session comes back. It happened here twice in one morning: `bootId` changed and
the console seat was replaced while `selfRestart.json` was eight hours old.
Whether to RECOVER from that is a decision (reviving after an unplanned death
would also revive after the user deliberately closed VS Code), so this build
only stops it being invisible: `farm.health` carries `bootPlanned`.

## 3.443.0 - the resume exemption that was tested on a world the product never sends (2026-09-08)

Found by the retrospective audit, in the wiring rather than the rule.

**`resume:true` could never exempt a single session.** X-232's promise is that a
console session the engine has already named is not a loss to weigh against a
restart — it comes back on the other side, so it is not a reason to wait.
`liveBlockers()` implements exactly that, keyed on `sessionId`, and eight tests
pin it. But `restartWorld()` in `extension.ts` mapped the console list down to
`{id, agentName, status}` and dropped the fourth field, so the branch those
tests cover was unreachable from the running extension: every `resume:true`
restart counted its resumable sessions as blockers, armed, and waited for them.
Nothing failed — the tests built their own world and handed it the field the
product does not send. The map now carries `sessionId`, and the shape of the
world `restartWorld()` actually sends is pinned against the source next to the
rules that read it.

**And the swap that rebuilds a revived card's scrollback rests on an ordering
nobody had written down.** It is put in by an `index.onDidUpdate` handler that
`reviveAfterRestart()` registers, and the event fires once, at the end of
`index.scanAll()` — which `activate()` starts thousands of lines earlier. The
only thing that makes the subscription earlier than the event is that no
top-level `await` sits between them. One added anywhere in that stretch would
put every revived card back to a permanent "not in the index yet" placeholder,
with all 3.442.0's tests still green. That ordering is now a test.

## 3.442.0 - the revived session that came back empty, and the resume that forgot whose account it was (2026-09-08)

Both reported by the user, on the first restart that actually loaded a build.

**A revived card could never rebuild its scrollback. Not sometimes — never.**
`reviveAfterRestart()` runs inside `activate()`, and the transcript index is
filled by an **async** `scanAll()` started in that same activation. So
`index.all()` is empty for every id at that moment, and the read that rebuilds a
card's history always took its "Agent Farm does not have this session in its
index yet" branch. The session came back, said it had been taken up where it
left off, and showed nothing above that line; clicking changed nothing, because
"load older" goes through the same index. The only way back to the conversation
was to end the card and resume it off the shelf by hand — which is precisely the
manual step X-232 exists to remove.

The placeholder was honest and stays. What was missing is the second read: the
row is now **swapped for the real scrollback where it stands**, the moment the
index can answer. Nothing restarts for it, and nothing the card has said since —
the revive notice, anything already typed — is dropped or reordered. The
subscription lets go of itself once the last seat has its history, and a seat
closed in the meantime is simply dropped.

**And the shelf's resume door stated no account.** It is the eleventh door onto
a launch and it builds its `start` from a hand-written field list, so every
dimension added since had to be remembered there by somebody — `account` never
was. A conversation that had been running on a slot came back reading `Machine
Global`. It now states the account the run actually used, read through
`sessionAccountOf` — the one reader every other surface already asks. The
transcript cannot answer this (every slot's `projects` folder is a junction onto
one shared root, so the file names no owner); only the launch manifest recorded
it at the spawn. A session with no manifest states nothing and takes the
standing choice, which is the truth rather than a slot invented for it. A *fresh*
session started from that door deliberately does not inherit it — it is not that
conversation.

`test_launch_parity.js` now measures that eleventh door against its source, the
way it already measures the surfaces that live inside message handlers.

## 3.441.0 - the restart that restarted nothing: a host bounce never loads a build you just installed (2026-09-08)

The user reported it: after `farm.restartExtensionHost` the whole window looked
like it had come back, and yet the Extensions card still carried its **Restart
Extensions** button — as if everything had restarted except Agent Farm. Pressing
that button restarted it a second time and the button went away.

**The button was telling the truth.** Measured in VS Code 1.103.2's own
`workbench.desktop.main.js`:

- `workbench.action.restartExtensionHost` is `stopExtensionHosts()` then
  `startExtensionHosts()` — with **no argument**. `startExtensionHosts(e)`
  applies a delta only `if (e)`; otherwise it starts the hosts from
  `_registry.getSnapshot()`. The extensions folder is never re-read, so the host
  comes back running the **same folder** — the old version.
- The card's button is `updateRunningExtensions()`, the one and only call site in
  the whole bundle that passes `startExtensionHosts({toAdd, toRemove})`. That
  delta is what swaps the code.
- The button's own condition is `installedVersion !== runningVersion`. It is not
  a stale badge; it is the difference, read live.
