So X-230's central promise — "restart the extension host so a build you just
installed is the one running" — was false from the first day, and the poll loop
it told every agent to run (*wait until `version` is the new one*) could never
come true. Measured on this window: 3.440.0 was installed at 17:31, the host was
restarted at 17:37 (the restart stamp records `fromVersion: 3.438.0`), and the
running version only became 3.440.0 at 17:43 — when the user pressed the card
button by hand.

There is no command an extension can invoke for `updateRunningExtensions`, so the
only thing that loads a newly installed build without a human is a **window
reload**, which does re-scan. Therefore:

- `farm.restartExtensionHost` now reads the version sitting in the extensions
  folder and, when it differs from the running one, **plans a window reload
  instead** — reporting it in `build.escalatedFrom` and in one `note` sentence
  carried into the armed plan's own `reason`. `loadBuild:false` bounces the host
  as asked and is told what it is leaving behind.
- `farm.health` gained `build { installed, running, pending }`. That, not
  `version`, is the reading that answers "did my build load?".
- The escalation changes what blocks the restart — an open terminal blocks a
  window reload — so an unattended build-load belongs in a Console session with
  `resume:true`, and the wait says so instead of deadlocking in silence.

## 3.440.0 - the first two audit findings: a restart that could never fire, and a rule wired to one of its two doors (2026-09-08)

The retrospective audit's first pass over four closed sessions, and both repairs
are for defects that every one of those sessions certified as done.

**A turn in flight blocks a restart. A seat does not.** `farm.restartExtensionHost`
counted every console session that was not `ended` or `error` as a live loss —
including `idle`, which is a card whose turn is OVER and which is waiting for the
user to type. The session that ASKS for the restart is on the screen asking, so
what it armed could never fire: the note said "restart armed" and the user came
back to find nothing had happened and had to restart by hand. Measured twice in
the record, two days apart — one handover reports an arm that had been waiting
**five hours** for a card nobody was going to close, and treats it as the user's
job rather than a defect. A protection mechanism that removes the autonomy it
was written to protect.

`SESSION_IN_FLIGHT` is now `starting` and `working`, and nothing else. This
dissolves the caller's special case without a special case: the asking session
is `working` while it asks, so the plan is armed; its turn ends, it drops to
`idle`, and the watcher fires within 5s. The waiting sentence counts turns now,
not cards — "3 console turn(s) still running", because "3 console sessions"
reads as three things on the screen and things on the screen stopped being a
reason to wait. The old rule was pinned by tests; they were inverted rather than
deleted, so it cannot drift back.

**And X-260's `/context` account reached one of its two doors.** The reason that
parameter exists is written in the code itself: the capture resumes the user's
own session, and every slot's `projects` folder is a junction onto one shared
root, so the transcript is found either way — *the capture succeeds and the
wrong plan pays*, a failure with no symptom. The viewer's button was wired to
the resolver. `sessions.context`, the door the FLEET uses, was left spawning as
whatever account the VS Code window happened to hold. Now both are wired, and
the test COUNTS the call sites out of the sources rather than spot-checking one,
so a third door cannot reopen it silently. Measured: the test is red without the
fix.

Audit rows: `10_Notes/DENETİM - Sicil.md` → A-02.4/A-02.5, A-04.1/A-04.2.
Suite: 319 files, 20029 passed, 0 failed.

## 3.439.0 - a retrospective audit, because "done" was the defendant's own testimony (2026-09-07)

Twenty-eight sessions over five days closed item after item on the automatic
Pro-account switching work, and every one of them was certified by the agent
that did it. Nobody ever went back. The defects the user keeps finding by hand
— a stray control sitting on top of the Live Timeline's text, a restart
mechanism that blocks its own console session — are what that leaves behind.

This ships the machine for going back, not another rule asking agents to be
careful.

**The unit of audit is a CLAIM, not a session.** Three sources, and only one of
them is binding: the user's own turn (the specification), the agent's closing
note (the claim — the defendant's testimony), and today's code and screen
(reality, measured). A discrepancy between them is a finding. An audit that
reads the closing note has audited nothing, which is precisely how each of
these sessions certified the one before it.

- **`tools/audit_extract.js`** — a closed session's transcript is 5-8 MB, so
  nobody could re-read 28 of them and nobody did. This cuts one into a ~2 KB
  dossier: every user turn **verbatim** (never summarised — it is the law), the
  agent's closing prose, the handover note by name, the files it wrote, the
  commits in its window, the item codes it named. `--list` prints the corpus
  newest-first. Measured: `dbbbd9e7` → 6.5 KB out of 6.9 MB.
- **`tools/audit_lint.js`** — the gate. A verdict other than ⬜ without a
  `kanıt:` is refused; a citation of the form `path:line` that points at a file
  that is not there, or a line past its end, is refused. **And `fix@` may not
  equal `@`: nobody closes their own repair** — the agent that fixed it leaves
  🔁 and the next one verifies. That separation has never existed here, and it
  is the only structural difference between this and what already failed.
  `--next` hands the baton to the next agent (the first unexamined row, or,
  when there are none, the oldest repair still waiting for an independent
  check). `--seed` appends missing session blocks; `--stats` counts verdicts.
- **`test/test_audit_ledger.js`** — a gate that lives in a script nobody runs
  would repeat the failure it was built to end, so the gate is measured: 14
  checks proving it REFUSES each violation on its own fixture, that a legend's
  example rows inside a fence are documentation rather than verdicts, and that
  the real ledger is clean where the vault is mounted.

The ledger itself is the user's document and lives in Obsidian, beside the
project: `10_Notes/DENETİM - Sicil.md`. It holds the position across sessions —
a handover note points at it, it does not replace it. Two tracks: **A**, the 28
sessions newest-first; **B**, the surfaces, ordered by a measurement rather than
a guess (how many of the 28 sessions wrote to each one — missions 9, console 7,
engines 4, …). Track B exists because a stray checkbox appears in no claim
anybody made, so a claim-by-claim audit would never find it.

The agent-side procedure is `_REF/audit.md`, triggered from the constitution.

## 3.438.0 - the rule U-133 cost twice: draw the arity the user actually gets (2026-09-07)

Documentation only, and it is the part of U-133 that will outlive the CSS.

The fold control on the ask card was pushed to the right edge by a rule that
lived on the **answered count**, and the count is only drawn when there is more
than one question. The fixture scene asked **four** and so did the item's own
test — the single arity where that layout came out right. So every picture ever
taken of the card showed the control neatly in the corner, the suite stayed
green, and the card an agent actually puts up (one question) dropped the control
into the middle of the row. **The looking glass and the test suite certified the
bug for a day**, and the user found it in one look at their own screen.

So a fixture draws the arity the user really gets, not the one that shows the
feature off: **empty, one, many and too-many are different layouts** wherever a
count, a wrap, a scroller or an `auto` margin is involved — and the smallest is
the scene to add first, because the rich one is already there, built by somebody
demonstrating the feature. Written into `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` → "Looking at it".

## 3.437.0 - U-133 again: the fold control was in the middle of the row, invisible, and the card was see-through (2026-09-07)

**Reported by the user with a screenshot, after the first fix had shipped.** All
three faults are things **no render ever showed**, and that is the real lesson of
this item.

**1. The control sat mid-row, not in the corner — and the fixture is why nobody
saw it.** The rule that pushes the right-hand end of the header to the right
lived on the *answered count*, and the count is only drawn when there is **more
than one question**. So on a single-question card — the card an agent actually
puts up most of the time — nothing carried the free space and the fold control
landed directly after the words "is asking", mid-row, where nobody looks for a
control. The fixture scene and its test both asked **four** questions, which is
the one arity where the old layout came out right, so both drew it neatly in the
corner and both passed. A layout rule that only holds at one arity is not a
layout rule: the growth now lives on the element that is **always** there (the
name of whoever is asking), which also makes a long tool name truncate instead of
shouldering the controls aside. **A single-question scene has been added to the
fixture** — the picture that would have caught this.

**2. It did not look or behave like a control.** Its box was about thirteen
pixels tall with a `#4444` hairline around it, on a background the same colour as
the card. Being that small, the reader had to land the pointer on the **glyph
itself** — measured by the user, in their own words: *you have to hit exactly the
line*. It is now 24×24 with the glyph centred, drawn in the card's own focus
colour so it reads as part of this card, and it fills on hover. And it carries
its **tooltip in the markup**, so the control is never unexplained before the
first paint; the paint still writes the MIRROR text (the state it is in, then
what pressing does) over the top.

**3. The card was 90% transparent.** Its background was mixed against
`transparent`, so the transcript underneath printed straight through the header —
the user's screenshot shows the "load older" bar sitting inside the "waiting on
you" badge. Same tint, mixed against the editor's background instead of against
nothing. The thing holding a running turn still has to be the thing you can read.

## 3.436.0 - X-251 closes: the sessions table says the sign-in in WORDS (2026-09-07)

**Closes X-251.** The item's last clause asked for a per-row account chip beside
the engine badge. **It was put to the user and refused**, and the reason is the
one the measurement had already raised: in a fleet where every row carries the
same sign-in, a chip repeated down the column is noise, and the fact already
lives one hover away in the row's launch panel. A test now pins the absence, so
nobody re-adds it from the backlog text alone.

**But the hover was printing an internal id.** The session viewer and the Live
Timeline both resolve through `statedAccountLabel`, so they say
`aicozums@gmail.com` while the table said `claude-aicozums` — the same fact in
two spellings, one of them a directory name the reader never chose. The three
tables that carry launch manifests (Dashboard, agent page, Sessions page) are now
handed the same resolver the console already uses; the projects page passes no
manifests, so it has no account line to spell.

**The resolver is handed in, not imported**, for the reason every other optional
on `sessionRowPool` is: a table can be asked for rows before the account store
exists, and a missing resolver degrades to the raw id — an id nobody can read
still names the right account, a blank names none. A run that injected no
sign-in stays **empty** and the resolver is never asked: absent stays absent.

## 3.435.0 - X-265: the Live Timeline went deaf the day an account became a directory (2026-09-07)

**Closes X-265.** Live Claude sessions had been running for a day — hundreds of
tool calls — with **nothing on the Live Timeline**, under a cockpit card
reporting "every session on this machine is covered" in green. Three causes, all
of them the same shape: a feature that shipped correctly broke another one that
never knew it existed.

**1. The hooks never reached a captured account.** `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` moves
which `settings.json` the engine reads. A slot directory held `.credentials.json`,
`.claude.json` and a `projects` junction — and **no settings file at all**, so an
isolated session inherited no hooks, no model and no permission mode. Measured on
this machine: the last real Claude hook event was 2026-09-06 20:01.

**‼️ Measured live, on the running machine, and the proof is exact.** The
previous session (`dbbbd9e7`, hours of work under slot `claude-aicozums`, which
had no settings file): **0 hook events, ever**. This session (`e6116c62`, started
09:40Z under `claude-murvietnam-2`): nothing until **10:08:24Z** — the minute the
repair below wrote `settings.json` into its slot directory — and 81 events in the
eight minutes after. Claude picks the file up without a restart.

The adapter now says the file travels (`carryFiles`), and it is a list of its
**own** — an empty `copies` is how a failed capture is recognised, and a settings
file must never make a slot with no credentials in it look sealed. Slots captured
before any of this existed are repaired on every activation
(`syncHooksToAccounts`), under three rules: **the user file decides** (no hooks of
ours there, nothing written anywhere — somebody who removed them meant to), **a
slot is seeded from the user's whole file** rather than given a hooks-only stub
(an account that reports its work faithfully while doing it under different rules
is worse than one that is silent), and it is **idempotent**.

`hookTargets` — the one list of "every file the live hooks can live in" — now has
three kinds, so `hooks.status`, `hooks.install`, `hooks.remove` and the cockpit
page all learn about accounts in the same breath. **User scope carries through to
them**, because "every session on this machine" is only true if the directory the
engine actually reads gets one. What was written into a slot can be taken back out
by the button that removes hooks.

**‼️ And the verdict can now go amber for the failure that happened.** User scope
installed plus an unhooked account is `partial`, naming the account — a card that
cannot report the commonest failure is decoration.

**2. The hook gave up on a host that was merely busy.** `-m 3` was there to stop a
dead listener blocking the agent and never did that job: on 127.0.0.1 a missing
listener is REFUSED in about a millisecond. What three seconds cut off was a
listener that IS there — measured 0.28–0.54s idle, **6.7s under load** — and it
failed silently, because `|| cd .` swallows the timeout. Now
`--connect-timeout 2 -m 15`: the connect is bounded (the only hang a dead listener
can really cause), the exchange is not. A file still carrying the old line is
repaired in place on activation — "installed but stale" is the worst state,
because every surface says it is fine.

**3. The Console refused to mirror Claude.** "Claude is never mirrored — its CLI
fires the real hooks" was right for as long as a Claude session could be relied on
to fire them. Now Claude is mirrored **only while its own hooks are silent**, and
the dedup is exact rather than hopeful: a real CLI hook never carries `engine`,
so one arriving stands the mirror down for that session for good. This is the
safety net, not the fix.

**‼️ And a fourth thing, found while measuring the first three: the test suite
was editing the machine it runs on.** `test_activation.js` says in its own first
paragraph that it is "activation on a machine with an untouched configuration —
the coldest start there is". It was not. `cfgValueRaw` asks the vscode registry
first and, when it answers `undefined` — which a stand-in always does — falls
back to **reading the user's own settings.json off the disk**. So `activate()`
ran there with this machine's real `agentFarm.*` values and a real `os.homedir()`,
and a suite run rewrote `~/.claude/settings.json` and seeded all three captured
account directories. Nothing was damaged (those were the writes the feature is
meant to make), but the next `fs` write inside activation might not be so
harmless. The home and the three Windows profile variables now point at an empty
temp directory, and the isolation is **asserted** rather than assumed — a test
that quietly stops being isolated is how this happened in the first place.

## 3.434.0 - X-254 (d): an item whose sign-in is at its wall WAITS (2026-09-07)

**Closes X-254.** `queue.list` takes `ready: true`, which drops the items whose
**stated** sign-in is full right now and reports how many were held and until
when.

**‼️ And this is not a new rule — it is the sibling of one already shipped.**
`carryOnAccount` (X-211) moves a walled run onto another sign-in and refuses to
for a run pinned to `@machine`, in its own words: *"'nothing is injected' is an
instruction the user typed into the form, and a handover would inject one"*. That
is the whole distinction, and it must not be reasoned about a second way: a
**resolved** account may be handed over; a **stated** one is an instruction.
`WorkItem.account` is always the stated kind.

**Three answers that look like details and are not.** An item that names no
sign-in is never held — empty means "the resolved account decides", and holding
it would enforce a decision nobody made, leaving the queue quiet at 3 a.m. over
plans no item ever asked for. `@machine` is never held: nothing is injected, so
there is no window to be at the end of. And a sign-in nobody has **read** is not
at the wall — `-1` and `100` are opposite facts (X-256), and this is the
dangerous direction: treating unknown as full stops work on a plan that may be
empty.

**Off by default.** A list op that quietly started returning fewer rows would
change what every caller written before today sees, and the rows it removed are
the ones somebody is looking for. The caller about to take work asks, and gets
both halves.

"At the wall" is now one number (`ACCOUNT_WALL_CEILING`), named beside the
rotation that already used it rather than invented a second time at the queue.

## 3.433.0 - X-254 (2/n): the Work Queue draws its fourth axis, and a dead sign-in cannot hide in it (2026-09-07)

**The axis shipped in 3.430.0 and the page could not draw it**, because the page
was never handed the sign-ins at all. It has them now, from the one place the
Tasks form and the Console read them, so the row's route boxes are four: engine,
**account**, model, effort — in that order, because an account belongs to ONE
engine and cannot be offered before one is named.

**‼️ And the box would have LIED.** A `<select>` whose value matches no `<option>`
falls back to its first one — here "— account —", i.e. UNCLAIMED. So an item
pinned to a sign-in the user has since deleted would have read, on the one
surface where somebody decides what to hand out, as work anybody can take. The
stray id is offered by name and marked, and the row itself carries the mark too:
that is broken work, and seeing it should not cost a click. Found by rendering
the page and reading the markup; every string test passed over it.

**Moving the engine drops a sign-in of the old one** — a narrowing
`AFEngine.narrow` cannot do, because it knows nothing about accounts. A row
asking for a sign-in the new engine cannot read is a setup that looks answered
and cannot be served. 💻 Machine Global survives it: it is not any engine's
account, it is the absence of one stated outright.

**A fifth filter: Accounts.** "What is queued against this plan" is the question
the engine filter stopped answering the day one engine held five sign-ins, and
every engine's are listed together because the reader asking it is not asking
about engines. Unclaimed is an option rather than an absence, on the same rule
the engine and project filters follow. Drawn only where sign-ins have been
captured — a picker whose only row is "unclaimed" is a filter that cannot
filter.

Each row in the picker carries the five-hour figure, because that is the fact
the choice turns on; the queue still starts nothing and spends nothing.

**Still open on X-254:** (d) — an item whose sign-in is at its wall WAITS rather
than being slid onto another. It belongs to whatever TAKES the item, not to the
queue, which dispatches nothing.

## 3.432.0 - X-260 (2/n): a turn fired while VS Code is closed spends the sign-in written on it (2026-09-07)

**‼️ And the measurement this corrects is our own.** The item was paused as a
POLICY question — "whose plan pays for a turn nobody is at a window for" — off a
reading of `src/core/automation.ts`, which is the trigger's PRECONDITION module,
has never carried a route of any kind, and is not where the answer lives.
`FarmSchedule extends RunDimensions` and a trigger's `{ kind: 'task' }` action
does too, so the account is written on the item when the user makes it, already
persisted into `farm-tasks.json`, and already honoured by the extension's own
runner. There was nothing to decide. One hop was missing.

**The hop.** `farmService.ts` read the file, dropped the field on the floor and
spawned `claude -p` with no environment at all — so whichever sign-in the
machine happened to hold paid for every schedule and every watch trigger that
fired overnight: outside the rotation, unattributable, and invisible because the
run itself succeeds.

**One order, not two.** The service resolves exactly as the extension does —
stated account, then the standing choice for that engine, then nothing injected
— through the same functions (`resolveAccount`, `accountRefusal`,
`accountEnvFor`), now reachable from a process with no `vscode`. A second order
would disagree the first time one of them changed, and 3 a.m. is the worst place
for that to surface.

**‼️ A sign-in that cannot be resolved STOPS the run.** A slot the user deleted,
one belonging to another engine, or a service that has not been handed the table
yet: the run is skipped and the reason logged where the "while you were away"
digest reads. Falling through to the main sign-in is the silent wrong spend this
whole family exists to end, and with nobody watching it is worse, not more
forgivable.

**The table travels, and it is kept fresh.** An account is a config DIRECTORY
and the id→directory map lives in VS Code settings, which a plain node process
cannot open — so the extension writes it into `service-config.json` beside the
agent map. Unlike the agent map it is rewritten whenever the sign-ins move: a
stale copy is not a cosmetic lag once a run can be refused, because a schedule
pointed at this afternoon's new slot would be skipped tonight for a reason that
stopped being true hours ago.

Each headless run's own report now names the sign-in that paid — the transcript
cannot, because every slot's `projects` folder is a junction onto one shared
root. And an item asking for an engine this service cannot spawn is SAID in the
log rather than silently served by `claude`.

## 3.431.0 - X-253: a saved launch profile remembers the sign-in, softly (2026-09-07)

**Closes X-253, and the user chose the middle answer in their own words:** the
profile remembers a sign-in, the launcher opens on it, it is not a lock, and a
profile may be saved with the box deliberately empty.

**The exemption this replaces was honest, and its risk is now answered by name
rather than avoided.** `profileDoor` carried a written reason for dropping the
account — "a profile is a SETUP and an account is a STATE; stored, it would pin
a saved launch to a plan that may be exhausted by the time anybody presses it".
That risk is real. Leaving the dimension out is not the only way to answer it,
and it cost the reader the one fact a row offering to spend a plan should state
before it is pressed. So all three halves are built instead: a profile pointing
at a sign-in that is no longer on this machine opens EMPTY and says which one
went, by name; a stored one is a seed the reader may move before starting; and a
profile that stores none launches on the resolved account exactly as before.

**‼️ And it is deliberately NOT a lock in `matchProfile`.** That function is what
tells the launcher "you are looking at this profile", and every profile on this
machine was saved before the account was a dimension while a launcher always
carries a resolved one — so comparing it strictly would have made the row stop
recognising all of them at once, which reads as "it forgot my profiles". A
profile that says nothing about the sign-in matches whatever answered; one that
names a sign-in must agree, because the reader may move the box after loading
it and the row must not go on claiming a setup that is no longer on screen.

**Empty stays a real answer.** "Says nothing" is the first row of the picker
rather than an empty box — it is what every profile saved before this means, and
it is what the user asked to stay possible. The row is drawn only where the
engine can isolate a sign-in and at least one has been captured, the same rule
the launcher's own Account row follows.

`profile` is the last door on the launch matrix to carry the account; no door
claims an exemption from it any more.

## 3.430.0 - X-254 (1/n): the work queue's fourth route axis — whose plan pays (2026-09-07)

**The file counted three of four.** `WorkItem` carries `engine · model · effort`
and its own comment calls that the question a fleet of five engines asks:
"which engine, on which model, at what effort". On a machine holding five
sign-ins under ONE engine the remaining question is whose PLAN pays, and the
word `account` did not appear in `workqueue.ts` once.

**And the queue is where the autonomous fleet takes its work from.** Without the
axis a runner cannot be told "do this one on that plan", the queue cannot be
filtered by sign-in, and one account hitting its wall cannot change what is
picked up next.

**It behaves exactly like its three siblings, on purpose.** Optional and
independent; an empty one is a real answer — "this item does not care, the
resolved account decides" — so nothing is defaulted at capture, because a value
invented there is indistinguishable from one the user chose. `(none)` on the
axis asks for the items nobody claimed a sign-in for, and omitting the axis
still means every item, claimed or not. Each axis moves on its own: setting the
engine never clears an account somebody set from another surface.

**‼️ And it is NOT lower-cased, unlike the two beside it.** `engine` is an id
and `effort` is a word, so both fold. An account is a SLOT ID the user minted,
and folding its case names a directory that does not exist.

`queue.add`, `queue.list`, `queue.edit` and `queue.route` take it and say so in
their own `describe` — same commit, per the bridge rule.

**Still open on X-254:** the Queue page's own account picker and filter, and the
rule that an item whose account is at its wall WAITS rather than being slid onto
another sign-in.

## 3.429.0 - X-251 (2/n): a session's own page and its timeline card say whose plan ran it (2026-09-07)

**The half that was worse than a missing label.** The session viewer resumes the
user's OWN conversation to capture `/context` (`claude --resume <id> -p
"/context"`). `runContextCapture` has taken an `account` argument since X-260 —
and nobody passed one, so the capture ran as whatever sign-in the VS Code window
happened to hold. Because every slot's `projects` folder is a junction onto one
shared root, the transcript is FOUND either way: the failure was silent by
construction, the capture succeeded, and the wrong plan paid for it. It now
spawns on the sign-in the session was recorded on.

**And it is asked of the host, not taken from the page.** Which plan a spawn
spends is not a fact a webview should be able to state — the same rule the
origin verdict has followed since S-37.

**Two surfaces that said nothing now say it.** The session viewer names the
sign-in in the engine badge's own panel, and the Live Timeline card does the
same — that panel already answers "what ran this", and a second panel for the
sign-in would be the ONE SUBJECT rule broken. The sessions table keeps it in its
launch panel, where the rest of the recorded setup lives; the other two pages
have no launch panel, so the engine badge is the honest place.

**One reader for both.** `sessionAccountOf` in the extension answers off the
launch manifest and nothing else — `index.byId` → `manifestOf` → the slot, then
its label. Two resolvers would disagree the first time one of them met a slot
the other had not, which is the shape this family of items keeps closing. Both
parts travel: the LABEL is a thing to read, the ID is a slot, and only the
capture needs the id.

**‼️ Absent stays absent.** A session with no manifest, or one whose launch
injected no sign-in, says NOTHING — never "this machine", never a guess at the
standing choice. On a farm with five slots under one engine that guess is the
claim most likely to be wrong, and a gap is visible where a wrong attribution is
not.

Looked at: the timeline fixture now carries a recorded sign-in on two cards and
none on the rest, so the panel is drawn in both states.

## 3.428.0 - X-249: the leader turn chooses its engine, and an unwired one is refused by name (2026-09-07)

**CLOSES X-249.** The user's own reading opened it: "we are building a sentry
system, we are making the work multi-engine — but you cannot even pick an
engine other than Claude for the leader agent; they have not made the system
they just built multi anything."

**`LEADER_ENGINE` is gone, and it was not laziness while it lasted.** Its own
comment said what it was: the runner could spawn one engine and read one reply
envelope, so a settable field over it would have been a box that lies. Both of
those halves are the engine adapter's now (`core/oneShot.ts`, 3.427.0), so the
constant became `LeaderCaps.engine` — a real axis, resolved campaign → setting
→ default exactly as the model beside it is.

**What the runner spells now: nothing.** It takes three engine-specific facts
from the adapter and no more — ARGV, ENV and ENVELOPE. The command name and its
flags come from `oneShotArgv`, the environment from `oneShotEnv` (the same
assembly every other spawn in the farm goes through, so "the route wins over
the account wins over the window" is argued once), and the reply is read by the
adapter that built the line rather than by a Claude-shaped reader that would
return `null` for anything else.

**‼️ And the leader KEEPS its own process management, deliberately.** It was
measured before it was moved: `execOneShot` builds a shell string and puts the
prompt inside `-p "…"`. The leader's prompt is several kilobytes of the user's
own words, quotation marks and newlines — putting it through a shell is exactly
the class of damage a dozen inner rounds of `sanitizePrompt` exist to avoid. So
the adapter publishes a SPAWN form beside the shell form (`argv(want)` → command
and argument vector, prompt down stdin), and the leader keeps its own cut, its
own kill sentence, its own streams, and its habit of handing the prose over when
the envelope cannot be read. A plain move onto `execOneShot` would have been a
regression wearing the shape of a cleanup.

**An engine nobody has written an adapter for is refused BY NAME** — and the
refusal names the ones that can really be spawned AND read. Never a
fall-through to `claude`, which would spend a window on a model nobody chose
and report it as the one they did.

**On the form, a choice of one is not drawn.** The Leader row gets an Engine box
only when a second adapter has really been measured; today there is one, so no
box appears. When it does appear it cuts the two lists under it — the Model box
offers the named engine's catalogue and the Account box only the sign-ins that
engine can read, because a form offering one engine's models beside another
engine's accounts draws a setup that cannot launch. Both states are pinned by
page tests against the real page.

Also: `agentFarm.sentryLeaderEngine` (the farm-wide answer when a campaign names
none), `leaderEngine` on `sentry.start` and on the Missions form's own message.

309 files + 1 · 19 new tests in `test_leader_engine.js`, 10 in
`test_sentry_form.js`, 9 in `test_one_shot_adapter.js`.

## 3.427.0 - X-249 (2/n) · X-260 (2/n): a one-shot turn is a per-engine adapter, line and envelope together (2026-09-07)

**Partial — the shared path both items were blocked on. Neither item closes here.**

**Why an engine axis was never "one more select".** X-260 (1/n) gave the
fleet’s dozen short turns an account, and stopped at Claude: `oneShotLine`
refuses any other engine by name rather than quietly spawning `claude`.
X-249’s remaining half was measured to be blocked from the other side, and the
blocker is not the command line — it is the ENVELOPE. `parsePlannerEnvelope`
read Claude’s `--output-format json`: an object carrying `result`,
`session_id`, `total_cost_usd` and a `usage` block whose four token fields are
summed. The flag, the field names and the cost field are all Claude’s.

**So the two halves are now declared together, per engine** (`OneShotAdapter`
in `core/oneShot.ts`): build the line, read what came back. Splitting them
across two files is how an engine ends up spawnable but unreadable — which is
worse than being refused, because it spends a window and returns looking like a
model that said nothing. The test refuses a registration that has only one half.

**`parsePlannerEnvelope` kept its name and lost its copy.** Four call sites
import it; the envelope is a fact about the ENGINE, not about missions, so the
function now delegates to the adapter. Two readers of one envelope is exactly
the shape this family of items keeps closing.

**And no format is invented.** There is still only a Claude adapter. Codex’s
`exec` envelope has not been measured, so asking for it returns `undefined` and
reading with it returns `null` — the same refusal-by-name `oneShotLine` always
had. A guessed field name would not fail loudly: it would parse to `null` at
3 a.m. inside a mission round and read as an empty reply.

**Still open on both items** (unchanged, and deliberately not decided here):
the leader spawn at `extension.ts` still holds its own `cp.spawn` and has yet
to move onto `execOneShot`; `LEADER_ENGINE` is still a constant; the headless
`farmService` still has no account of its own (it has no extension to ask, so
the account must travel in its `ServiceConfig`); and `OneShotCaps.runtime` is
still uninstalled, because the route resolver answers per AGENT and a
fleet-wide sweep has no agent to answer for — inventing one would be a policy
nobody chose.

## 3.426.0 - X-262: a surface that inherits a sign-in says which one, before the click (2026-09-07)

**The launch doors were never wrong.** `doors/projects.ts` and
`doors/webviews.ts` both call `withAccount(ctx, pick(ctx.seed(agentId), …))`,
and `withAccount` really does resolve the account. What neither surface did was
DRAW it: the agent page’s three start controls and the project page’s "Start a
session here" opened a session and the reader learned whose plan was paying
afterwards. This is a visibility fix; it decides nothing and it does not touch
S-34 — the remembered setup is still a layer, and this states what that layer
resolves to.

**Why the account gets its own sentence.** Of everything inherited, it is the
only dimension that goes stale by itself. A model is today whatever it was
yesterday; a window fills on its own and a sign-in falls over on its own. So
the account is not merely named — it is drawn with its live figure through the
same component every picker uses (X-263), because "what you last ran on" can
already be false by the time somebody reads it.

**One reader, not a second opinion.** `nextLaunchReadout` seeds from the same
`seedLastLaunch` the doors seed from and resolves through the same
`launchAccountSlot` they resolve with. A readout that computed either itself
would be a page confidently describing a setup the door will not use.

**And where it stays silent, which is the part worth keeping.** The project
page’s start button may open a QuickPick: a project naming no agent, or naming
several, does not know WHO it will run as until after the click, and a setup
stated then would be a guess. The host sends the readout only where there is
exactly one answer — and `startSession` now resolves the agent through that
same `projectStartAgent`, so the button’s readout and the launch cannot become
two answers that agree most of the time. Where it cannot be known the tooltip
says the agent is chosen when you press it, rather than saying nothing.

Also: the agent-detail fixture now carries a `nextLaunch`, so the hover can be
looked at instead of only exercising the absent case.

## 3.425.0 - X-263: a sign-in picker says how much of that plan is left (2026-09-07)

**Five pickers drew the same account, and they had already stopped agreeing.**
The composer box, the live session box, a mission member’s delegation account,
a workflow step’s account and the task form’s account each carried a
hand-copied option body. The Console’s two had since grown the five-hour
figure; the other three had not — so one account read `murvietnam-2 •` on the
Tasks form and `murvietnam-2 • 42% used` in the Console, and the one figure the
choice actually turns on lived on a third page.

**An account is drawn in one place now** — `media/afAccount.js`, in the pattern
`afEngine.js` and `afProject.js` set. It owns the SHORTHAND row label (warning
sign, name, figure, standing-choice dot), the MIRROR hover under it, the two
sentinels that had been typed into three page files, and the "window turns over
at…" sentence the Engines page owned — six callers, one answer. Writing the
figure into three more copies is how a sixth is born.

**What is deliberately NOT in the component: the fixed rows.** Every one of
those pickers opens with "— the standing choice —" and 💻 Machine Global, and each
page says something different and correct in them: a mission round *spawns*, a
workflow step *fires*, a console session *starts*. That prose is about the site,
not about the account (ONE SUBJECT), so it stayed at the call site.

**And the figure really reaches the pages.** Measured: `accountsFor` sent
`percent`, but the three pickers that lacked it read `engineAccountMatrix`,
which sent no figure at all — a component formatting a percentage nobody hands
it would draw an em dash on every row for ever, with every test green. Both
host readers now take `percent` and `resetsAt` from one `accountFigure()`, out
of the same in-memory snapshot (X-170) the Engines page reads.

**-1 is not 0% (X-256), restated where it gets broken.** "Nobody has read this
account’s window" and "none of it is used" are opposite facts, and an empty
space in a picker reads as good news. An unread account draws `· —` and says so
in words; it never draws a zero.

Also: the Console fixture now carries three sign-ins, so the account box is
drawn in the looking glass at all — it never had been, and every change to it
shipped blind. And `test_tasks_webview.js` builds its sandbox from the one
shared list instead of the ninth hand-written copy of it, which is how this
change first showed up: as `Cannot read properties of undefined`.

## 3.424.0 - X-261: a sign-in that falls over is announced whether or not a campaign is running (2026-09-07)

**X-178's announcement was real, well written, and could only fire inside a
campaign.** Its one caller sat in the sentry turn, and
`applySentrySlotHealth` opens with `if (!this.sentry) { return undefined; }`.
So a token that died on a Tuesday afternoon — while the user was working across
three accounts by hand, which is most of the day — was noticed by nothing and
said by nobody. The account simply stopped being chosen, and the user found out
by wondering why one of them had gone quiet.

**The announcement now hangs off the thing that MEASURES.**
`AccountUsageService` gained one seam (`onRead`), called after every settled
figure with everything known at that moment — through a single funnel, so it
cannot end up attached to three of the four ways a figure lands and still look
connected. Judging what CHANGED is the listener's job, not a second memory
inside the service.

**The fleet keeps its own record of what it has already said**, in global state,
so it outlives every campaign — which is exactly the case the old gate lost.
The campaign keeps `sentry.downSlots`, because that answers a different
question: which accounts THIS campaign may still run on.

**And it is the only announcer.** Two of them would mean two notices per fall,
so the sentence moved out of the sentry turn rather than being copied; a
campaign is now a CIRCUMSTANCE the body mentions when there is one, not the
reason anybody is told. The notice carries the slot as data (X-257), so two
falls of one sign-in read as one story.

A listener that throws never costs the figure: the measurement is the product's,
the announcement is a courtesy on top of it.

## 3.423.0 - X-257: a notice says WHICH sign-in it is about, as data (2026-09-07)

**The board could not be asked a question about accounts.** X-178 closed with
the farm announcing a slot whose token had fallen over — and it announced it in
PROSE: the slot's name was written into the title and nowhere else. The word
`account` did not appear in `core/notices.ts` at all.

So three things were impossible on a farm whose scarce resource IS account
quota: the repeated failures of one slot could not be grouped, the board could
not be narrowed to one sign-in, and an agent could not ask `notices.list`
whether an account has an open warning against it **before** sending work there.

**A notice now carries `account`** — the same class of axis as `agentName` and
`projectId`: **stamped by whoever posts, never derived.** A notice about no
particular sign-in carries none, and that is an answer rather than a gap.

- `notices.post` takes it and reports it back; `notices.list` filters by it,
  with `"(none)"` for "the ones about no particular account" — because absent
  asks nothing about the axis, which is a different question.
- **The producer fills it:** the sentry slot-health notice stamps the slot it is
  about instead of leaving it inside the sentence.
- **The board draws it:** a 🔑 chip beside the project mark, carrying the slot's
  short form with the whole name in its panel (SHORTHAND — five slots of one
  engine differ in their last word, and a row is the wrong place to read them),
  plus an **Accounts** filter whose options are derived from the rows
  themselves. A slot nothing has ever been said about is not a filter anybody
  can want, and a stamp naming a slot that has since been removed must stay
  reachable — otherwise its rows become the ones nobody can filter to.

## 3.422.0 - X-260 (1/n): the fleet's own turns run on the account the rotation chose (2026-09-07)

**Agent Farm runs a dozen short turns nobody starts and nobody sits in** — the
judge behind A/B and evals, the pulse sweep, the quality scan, the suggestion
pass, the weekly summary, the memory distiller, the dispatcher, the command bar,
and the two verification judges inside the task runner. Every one of them was
written the same way:

```
cp.exec(`claude ${judgeArgs} -p "${prompt}"`, { cwd, timeout }, cb)
```

**No `env`. So each of them ran as whoever the MACHINE was signed in as** —
outside the pool the user allowed, invisible to `pickAccount`, and spending a
window no surface in the product could report. A sweep firing at 3 a.m. could
eat the plan the user was saving for the morning, and nothing anywhere would
say that it had. Every other launch in the extension — task, session, console,
terminal, leader turn — has gone through the account resolver since X-169.
These twelve were the one hole left in an otherwise closed system.

**And the same line nailed the engine into a template string**, so the axis
every other launch carries could not even be stated here.

**There is now ONE seam** (`core/oneShot.ts`). `core` says what it wants —
engine, account, flags, prompt — and the extension, which owns the slot list
and the engines' adapters, hands in how to answer it, exactly as it already
does for the Console and the task runner. The environment is assembled by the
same `spawnEnvironment` every other spawn uses, so "the route wins over the
account wins over the window" is stated once rather than argued twice, and a
layer that says `null` still REMOVES a name (X-211).

**Nothing installed is the documented absent case, not a failure:** the seam
hands back `undefined` and the turn inherits its environment byte for byte, so
the headless service and every unit test behave exactly as before.

**An engine with no one-shot form yet is REFUSED by name** rather than quietly
spawned as `claude` — the same mistake X-259 found one layer down. Making the
other engines real needs a per-engine envelope reader, which is X-249's second
half and is deliberately not smuggled in here.

**‼️ And the sharpest one: the /context capture resumes the USER'S OWN session.**
It, too, passed no environment. Because every slot's `projects` folder is a
junction onto one shared root (X-251), the transcript is FOUND either way — so
the failure is silent by construction: the capture succeeds and the wrong plan
pays for it. It now takes a stated account; naming the one that session actually
ran as is the session viewer's half of X-251, where the manifest reaches that
surface.

**Left open (X-260, 2/n):** the headless service (`service/farmService.ts`)
spawns while VS Code is closed and has no extension to ask — its account has to
travel in its own config, which is its own piece of work. The seam's route half
is wired for but deliberately not installed: `engineRuntimeFor` answers per
AGENT, and a fleet-wide sweep has no agent to answer for.

## 3.421.0 - X-264: a schedule that fires once IS its moment (2026-09-07)

**A `once` schedule installed over the bridge was stored with no time at all.**
`schedules.add` documents its moment as `"YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM"` — the same words
`schedules.edit` and the command bar use — but the seed parser behind it
(`parseSeedSchedules`) accepted a **number only**. The documented form arrived,
failed a `typeof` test, and was dropped on the floor. What was kept was a
schedule that is enabled, listed on the page, counted by the forecast, and
**can never be due**: `scheduleDue` asks `!!s.onceAt` first.

Nothing said so. The call returned `ok`, the row appeared, and the run simply
never happened — a rule that fails silently is not a rule. It was found the
only way it can be: by installing one and reading the store back.

**The parser now reads the moment the way it is written** — the spaced form,
the ISO form, and epoch milliseconds as a number or as its digits — and a
moment nobody can read stays `undefined` rather than becoming "no time".
**And `schedules.add` REFUSES a `once` schedule without one**, at the door,
in front of the caller who can still fix it. The contract says which forms it
takes, so the two halves cannot drift apart again.

## 3.420.0 - X-256 + X-234: the card names what actually limits the farm, and its buttons work (2026-09-07)

**Farm Status had no row for accounts** — live · tasks · triggers · workflows ·
media · engines, and the word "account" appeared nowhere in the module. On a farm
whose scarce resource IS account quota, the card a person opens to ask "is this
all right" could not say how many sign-ins there are, how many have fallen out,
or how much room the rotation will find.

**The row states the figure that decides tonight: the EMPTIEST account's room**,
because that is the one `pickAccount` reaches for. An average would read as
healthy on a farm with one free account and four walls. A slot that cannot sign
in is named on the row rather than left to the Engines page — the point of the
card is that nobody has to go looking. **And an unread account is not counted as
room:** "nobody has read it" and "0% used" are opposite facts, and treating the
first as the second is how a campaign gets sent at a wall. It is read from the
CACHED usage every other surface shows, never a refresh — drawing a status card
must not put five accounts into a request queue.

**‼️ X-234 — and the Engines button finally does something.** The panel's
`statusAction` handler tested the command against a **hand-written set of
three** and `agentfarm.openEngines` was not in it, so the press was dropped
without a word. X-203 had just fixed that button's *disappearance*, so the user
finally had a control to press and still got nothing — the worst of both.

The fix is not a fourth string. **The allowed set is now DERIVED from the card
that was just published**, so a door this module can draw is a door the panel
will open, by construction; a test pins the derivation rather than copying the
list into a second place. And a refused command now **says so** instead of
vanishing: replacing one silence with another would only move the defect.

The accounts row carries its own door label ("Accounts", the same command for
now) — two adjacent buttons both reading "Engines" are two controls a reader has
to tell apart by counting rows. When the accounts page of its own arrives
(X-235/X-236) only the command changes.

## 3.419.0 - X-251 (1/n): the run records whose plan paid for it (2026-09-07)

**Nothing knew which account a session had run on, and nothing could work it
out.** Measured on this machine: an account slot's `projects` folder is a
**junction onto one shared directory** — `…/accounts/claude-wmmuratvural/projects
-> C:\Users\rotam\.claude\projects` — so five sign-ins write their transcripts
into the same place and **the file cannot name its own owner.** The live console
card held the account in memory (`consolehost` `state.account`) and nothing
persisted it, so the answer died with the card. The spawn is the only moment it
exists.

**`LaunchManifest` now carries it**, beside `cwd` and `identity` rather
than inside `requested` — because it is a **resolved** fact. An empty account
box does not mean "no account": it means the standing choice answered, and the
standing choice is the one that **paid**. Recording the request instead would
answer a question nobody asks of a finished run. Absent stays absent: "nothing
was injected" and "we do not know" must not become the same reading years later.

**Resolved in one place.** Every door reaches the spawn through `recordLaunch`,
so the slot is resolved there and all ten are covered at once — asking ten call
sites to remember is the shape this family exists to refuse, and a source-shape
test now pins it.

**And it is readable.** The sessions tables already join the manifest by
`launchId` to show the requested half beside the reported one; the launch hover
gains an `Account` line, and `describeManifest` names the account in the one
line a notice quotes. **Both stay silent when nothing was injected** — "it ran as
this machine" is the ordinary case, and a line repeating it on every row is one
the reader stops seeing.

**Still open on X-251:** the session viewer header and the timeline, and the
console's own live card (which knows the account but writes it nowhere). The
record now exists, which is what everything downstream was waiting for —
including X-252, cost and quota attribution per account, which cannot be
measured without it.

## 3.418.0 - X-249 (1/n) + X-259: the turn that commands the rotation now runs inside it (2026-09-07)

**The leader turn spawned with no environment at all.** It is the short, cheap
turn that reads how the last session ended and decides what the next round says
and *which account it opens on* — and `cp.spawn` was called with `{ cwd,
windowsHide, shell }` and nothing else. So it ran as whatever sign-in the
machine happened to be holding: **outside the pool the user allowed, invisible
to `pickAccount`, and able to wall the very account it was about to choose.**
It is the only place in the extension that spawns an engine directly, which is
exactly why the account layer had never reached it.

**`LeaderCaps` takes an account, and the runner takes an environment.** The
slot id travels as part of the ask; what variable isolates it stays the engine
adapter's business (`accountEnv`), and `spawnEnvironment` is where a layer's
`null` means REMOVE rather than blank — both already solved once for every
other spawn in the farm. Every `ModelAssist` now records the account it spent,
**including the failed turns**: a turn that burnt somebody's five-hour window
and produced nothing is exactly the burn worth finding.

**‼️ An unnamed account is the POOL's answer, not the machine's sign-in.** That
distinction is the whole item. `campaignPick` is new in `core/sentryRun.ts`
— the one place that turns a campaign into `pickAccount`'s options — and both
`planSentry` and the leader call site go through it, so the round and the turn
that chooses for the round cannot answer differently. There is deliberately **no
machine-wide setting** behind it: the other four caps are policy, an account
belongs to the pool a campaign was given.

**The form grew an Account box on the Leader row** (`leaderAccount`, also on
`sentry.start`), narrowed to the engine the runner actually spawns. **The
machine's own sign-in is not on offer** — reaching it is the defect, and putting
it back under a nicer name would reopen the hole.

**‼️ X-259 — `runArgs('claude', …)` was handing back Codex's command line.**
Measured: `["exec","--skip-git-repo-check","-c","sandbox_mode=…","-m","haiku","-"]`,
because `case 'claude'` fell through to `codexRunArgs` — the one exception to
this function's own written doctrine that an engine "must never fall through to
another engine's". Nothing broke, and that was the danger: Claude is the
persistent engine, so its one-shot line is built as a string in `spawnHeadless`
and no live caller ever reached the branch (`engineFlagFor` even guards against
it by name). The next caller to take an engine as a *parameter* would have got a
plausible, working, wrong command line — and the leader runner is exactly such a
caller. It now refuses, in prose, naming where the line really is built.

**Still open on X-249:** the leader's ENGINE. `LEADER_ENGINE` remains a
constant because the runner spawns one engine; making it a choice means a
one-shot adapter per engine (each publishes its own envelope, and
`parsePlannerEnvelope` reads Claude's), which is the item's other half.

## 3.417.0 - X-250: the model box the user was pressing (2026-09-07)

**The popup drew itself at the far left of the row, and the reason was already
written down in the same file.** U-97 measured it on the mission delegate rows:
Chromium anchors a `<datalist>` on the flex PARENT rather than on the box, so
the second press puts the list somewhere the box is not, and a repaint while it
is open collapses it to a single line. That fix landed — and the two boxes in
the **sentry campaign form** were left behind, which is the form somebody
actually fills in to start a campaign: the round's own **Model** and the
**leader's Model**. Both are `<select>` now, fed by the same `AFEngine`
catalogue every other launch surface reads.

**‼️ And the list belongs to the engine the campaign named.** It used to be the
flat alias vocabulary whatever `Engine` held, so a **Codex** campaign was
offered **Claude's** words while `modelListOf(engine)` — four hundred lines
above, in the same file — had been doing it right since U-64. Changing the
engine now redraws the form, and a word the new engine does not publish is
**kept, marked ⚠, and explained** rather than deleted while the reader is
looking at another control (U-101: telling is not clearing).

**‼️ A green test was holding the defect in place.** `test_sentry_form.js`
asserted that the leader's box *carries* `list="s-models"` — the very thing
U-97 had removed everywhere else — while `test_missions_webview.js` asserted
the page ships no `<datalist>` at all. Two tests, one page, opposite claims,
both passing, because they render different fragments. The assertion now reads
the other way and the form is measured to ship no datalist.

**The leader's engine is named once.** A `<select>` has no placeholder, so the
figure in force moved into the empty option (`— setting: haiku —`) and MIRROR
still holds without opening the box. Which catalogue that box offers is the
host's answer, not a word typed into the page: `LEADER_ENGINE` in
`core/sentryLeader.ts` is the one place that knows what the leader runner can
actually spawn — a constant rather than a setting, because a settable field over
a runner that ignores it is a box that lies. **X-249 turns it into a real
axis**: today that runner is `cp.spawn('claude', …)` with no `env`, so the
turn that commands a multi-engine, multi-account campaign is itself locked to
one engine and burns an account outside the rotation.

## 3.416.0 - X-208 (1/n): the live hook, spelt for the shell that will actually run it (2026-09-06)

**Codex's Stop hook has been failing, and the reported reason was the smallest
of three.** Every engine's hook file carries one line — a `curl` POST to the
live listener with `|| cd .` on the end to force exit 0 — and it works in sh,
bash and cmd. Under **Windows PowerShell 5.1**, where Codex runs its hooks on
this machine, it fails three separate times:

1. **`||` is not a statement separator there.** It is a *parse* error, so the
   command never runs and the engine reports the hook as failed. This is the one
   that was reported.
2. **‼️ `curl` is not curl.** In Windows PowerShell 5.1 it is an alias for
   `Invoke-WebRequest`, handed curl's flags. Fixing (1) alone leaves the hook
   calling a different tool.
3. **‼️ An unquoted `@-` is the splatting operator.** PowerShell eats it before
   curl sees it: measured, the process exits 1 and **the body never arrives** —
   the worst of the three, because a shell reporting success while posting
   nothing looks exactly like a listener that has gone quiet.

`hookCommand(port, shell)` now has two spellings. The sh/bash/cmd one is
unchanged to the character — Claude's hooks run on it today and this item is
about the other shell. The PowerShell one names `curl.exe`, quotes the dash, and
forces the exit code with `; exit 0`; measured, it both parses and delivers, and
a dead listener still leaves exit 0.

**‼️ And there is no single string, which is why there are two.** `; exit 0`
looked like the one to standardise on — until it was measured under **cmd**,
where it exits 0 and posts **nothing**: cmd hands the semicolon to curl as an
argument. Every candidate for one line is silently wrong in some shell that
really runs these, so the shell is named rather than guessed.

`hooks.status` and the Infra panel now publish **both**, because deriving the
second one by hand is exactly what produced the broken Codex hook.

## 3.415.0 - U-133: the question can be folded down to its line without letting go of the turn (2026-09-06)

**The card was covering what the question was about.** The ask card sits between
the conversation and the composer and may take half the window, and it stays
there until it is answered. But the paragraphs a question is *about* — what the
agent found, what it is proposing, why it is asking at all — are written in the
flow moments before it. So the one thing you have to read in order to answer was
the one thing the card put out of reach.

It now carries a fold control in its fixed header. Folded, the card keeps its
line: the **❓ waiting on you** tag, whose it is, and how many questions are still
open — the session is still visibly held, which is the whole reason the card is
loud in the first place. Everything else gets out of the way, and the
conversation is yours to scroll.

**‼️ Folding is a VIEW act and nothing is re-drawn.** The card is holding your
picks, your half-typed sentence, your caret and your place in a list taller than
the window, and every one of those is carried across a rebuild *by hand*. A fold
that went through a rebuild would be a fifth thing to carry — and the one that
cannot be: a body under `display:none` reports a scroll position of zero, so
unfolding would have thrown you back to question one. The class is toggled in
place, so what comes back is not a reconstruction of the card. It is the card.

That is also why the button's **markup never varies with the state**: the card's
html is compared against its last write to decide whether to rebuild, so a glyph
or a title baked into it would have desynced that cache and made the next
repaint rebuild the very DOM the fold exists to leave alone. The glyph is CSS;
the tooltip is set on the element.

**A fold belongs to THIS question.** One that outlived its question would hide
the next one behind a button nobody knows to press — a held turn that looks like
a hung one, which is exactly the failure this card was built to prevent. A new
request always arrives open, in the same act that clears the picks.

Nothing else about the card moved: same shape, same ceiling, same scroller, same
answer strip, same words.

**And the card now has a picture.** Every other state of the Console had a
fixture scene and the only one that stops a running session dead did not, because
`pendingAsk` was null everywhere. Four questions with described options — the
shape that gave the card its ceiling in the first place — is now drawn.

**Also: the page shims can write attributes.** `setAttribute` was missing from
both test DOMs, so a page that set one at runtime threw. Swallowing them would
have been the worse fix — every assertion about the attribute would then pass on
a page that never set it, which is the one thing those shims exist to prevent.
They are written and read back now.

## 3.414.0 - X-220: an account is an engine and an address, and the card says which state it is in (2026-09-06)

**Two rows, one account.** Signing in again and pressing *Capture this sign-in*
— the ordinary way to fix a dead credential before there was a 🔑 on the card —
minted `claude-work-2` beside `claude-work`. Same person, same plan, same
address; one row stale, both offered in every picker in the product, and the
figure under each of them read from a different file. The id counts up past a
name it has already used, which is right when two plans really do share an
address and wrong every other time.

An account is an **engine and an address**. Capturing one that is already stored
now **refreshes that row** — same id, same directory, the moment and the tier
updated, the name the user gave it kept unless they type a new one — and the
list does not grow. `accounts.capture` says which of the two things it did:
`reseated` carries the row's id, or is null when a real account was added. A
caller told "captured" either way would be counting an account that was already
there.

**‼️ The quiet merge stops at the directory.** Merging without asking is right
only where the refresh writes exactly the files the capture would have written
anyway. A row filed somewhere other than where this machine keeps accounts is a
distinction somebody drew by hand, and dissolving one of those unasked is the
single move this system forbids outright — so it is refused **by name, with the
folder in the sentence**, and nothing is written. An address the engine never
reported is not a match either: that says *unknown*, not *new*, and guessing
there would merge two strangers.

**The verdict is now always drawn, and three states are three states.** The card
wore a badge only when something was wrong, so a healthy row said *nothing* —
and nothing is also what a row nobody has looked at says. The one question a
reader opens this page with was answered by an absence. Worse, **needs signing
in** and **unreadable** wore the same yellow and the same sentence, while one is
a credential that can no longer refresh and the other a file that cannot say
whose account it even is. Now: 🟢 *ready* drawn quietly (shouting the ordinary
case costs the other two their only advantage), 🟠 *needs signing in* in the
yellow this page already uses for "your move", 🔴 *unreadable* in the red it uses
for a fault — each with its own panel saying what that state requires of the
reader.

And the engine on each card is drawn in **the product's own badge**
(`AFEngine.badge`), the component the Console, the agent page and the slash
picker have always used. This card was writing the raw id in lowercase grey: the
same fact in a second spelling.

**Also fixed: a gate that was passing by accident.** `test_path_vars.js` counted
`configuredFolder(\n` in the source. `core.autocrlf` is true here, so a fresh
clone hands every file CRLF — and one `git stash` flips one on the spot. The
gate then reports that a resolver nobody touched has gone missing. It is
line-ending agnostic now; what it counts is the call on its own line.

## 3.413.0 - X-219: a dead sign-in can be renewed from the card that reports it (2026-09-06)

**The card stated the problem and offered nothing to do about it.** An account
whose stored credential stops refreshing wore a yellow *needs signing in* badge
whose own tooltip ended "Nothing here can renew it" — accurate, and the reason
one account's debt has stood open for seven sessions. A diagnosis with no
treatment is where the reader leaves the page.

Renewing a plan sign-in is a **browser** flow that only a person can finish, so
the extension's honest part is small and this release is exactly that part and
no more: it opens the **engine's own** sign-in command with the environment that
points it at **that account's own directory**. Nothing is copied over the live
sign-in (X-168), no browser is driven, and no other row moves — the flow writes
the new credential straight into the row that asked for it.

**‼️ The command is the engine's own, and it was measured rather than assumed.**
The request asked for `claude login`; there is no such command. Read off the
CLIs' own `--help` on this machine: Claude Code signs in with `claude auth
login` and reads back with `claude auth status`; Codex uses `codex login` and
`codex login status`. A button wired to the requested command would have failed
on its first press. Each adapter carries its own pair, so an engine that cannot
hold a second sign-in offers no command at all rather than a wrong one.

**‼️ It never declares the outcome.** The flow can be abandoned halfway, and a
card that assumed success would be lying about the one fact it exists to state.
So the plan hands back `statusArgs` — the way to MEASURE the result — and the
card, when the terminal closes, is READ AGAIN from disk with its cached identity
dropped first. The badge changes because the files changed.

**It refuses more often than it agrees, and every refusal comes with no command
at all:** never for the main sign-in (it is the ABSENCE of a slot, and the
session talking to you runs as it), never for an engine with no verified way to
keep two identities apart (the login would land in the one directory both of
them read), never for an id nothing is stored under.

`accounts.reauth` on the bridge and the 🔑 on the card are the same function —
`planReauth` — so a page and an agent cannot come to mean two different things
about which sign-ins may be renewed.

**‼️ And a refusal is now pinned as prose, not only as a match.** Two of the
three refusals shipped as a template literal that had swallowed its own
concatenation: the reader would have been handed `…may have been ' + 'forgotten`,
source and all, on the one surface whose entire job is to explain itself. Every
string test passed — they all matched a word near the front. The new gate asks
what the sentence *looks* like: no concatenation residue, no newline, ends in a
full stop.

## 3.412.0 - X-231: the fleet's waits, in one reading and one shape (2026-09-06)

*"An autonomous process must also know that it is waiting for other reasons.
Whoever uses this function, let them HAVE that knowledge — let them give the
command willing to wait, and if the command is making them wait, let them
understand that with its reason."* — the condition on X-230's approval.

**The root cause was not a missing figure, it was a missing vocabulary.** Every
wait in this extension was already reported correctly on its own surface: a
parked run says which ceiling holds it, a mission says it is waiting for an
approval, a sentry says when it wakes, an armed restart says which session it is
behind. What nobody could do was ask ONE question — "why am I not moving?" —
without calling five ops and reading five different shapes. And when a sixth
reason appeared, nothing told anybody.

`farm.waits` answers it once. Every row carries the same answers whatever
produced it: `kind`, `subject`, `reason`, `since`, `until` where a clock decides
it, `blockedBy` — and `clearedBy`, which is the only part a caller can act on:
**clock** (it ends by itself), **event** (when something else finishes),
**human** (nobody is coming). Where an op ends the wait, it is named, so a
caller can act instead of poll. Ordered by when relief comes, with the ones
nothing will end by itself last and the longest-standing of those first.

**Nothing here writes a second sentence.** The reason is the one the source
already wrote — the parked row's own line, the run's own "what it is doing",
the campaign's last plan, the armed plan's own words (which are now KEPT on the
record instead of being rebuilt). Two sentences about one wait is exactly how a
surface and an op come to disagree about the same fact.

**And the op that MAKES you wait speaks the same dialect as the op you ask
afterwards.** X-230's `decision:"armed"` was the first example of this shape, so
it now carries a `wait` built by the same function — an agent reads the wait it
is handed and the wait it asks about later as one object.

**‼️ The vocabulary is guarded by the sources, not beside them.** `test_waits.js`
reads `launchBlock` out of `tasks.ts` and the `MissionRunStatus` union out of
`missions.ts`: a sixth block code, or a new `waiting-…` status, that nothing
translates FAILS THE BUILD and is named in the failure. Both gates were proved
by breaking them on purpose. A hold this build has no name for is still
reported, as `task-unknown` — a wait that vanishes from the reading is worse
than a wait with a dull name.

**Two things the measurement corrected.** The account handover is NOT a separate
wait: `tasks.ts` writes it into the parked row's own sentence (`notBeforeWhy:
'account handover · ' + carry.why`), so it arrives as the `reason` of a
`task-clock`, and a second row would be the copy that goes stale. And the task
side is not one wait but a family of five — the codes `launchBlock` really
produces — so all five are translated rather than the one the item named.

**The person reads the same answer.** The Dashboard now carries a *Waiting* tile:
the count, the clock/event/human split under it, and every wait named on hover.
Zero is drawn on purpose — a tile that vanishes when nothing is held up cannot be
told apart from a page that never learned to ask. The page counts and draws; it
derives no wait of its own, and there is exactly ONE place the fleet's waits are
assembled, which the build checks.

**And the parity scanner learned the difference between naming an op and
registering one.** A wait says which op ENDS it, so a plain data table now holds
`tasks.unpark` and `missions.approve` — read as second registrations, they failed
the build for a duplicate nobody had written. The discriminator is the registry's
own contract: `{ op, describe, handler }`, so an object literal carrying neither
half is a reference. The hollow check keeps its teeth.

## 3.411.0 - X-218: one press for every account, and the two costs under it (2026-09-06)

*"And at the very top of the Accounts section, a general [🔄 Refresh all
accounts (All Engines)] button that makes no distinction between engines."*

Every engine already had its own group-wide read; what was missing was the
press above them — all of them, whichever engine. The item's warning is the
whole design: the two halves do not cost the same thing. A Claude figure is a
REQUEST against a budget the whole fleet shares (five seconds apart, and a 429
pulls every account back); a Codex figure is a file under that account's own
folder. One button that paced the file reads behind the requests would make the
free half wait for nothing, and one that paced nothing would spend the budget
the line exists to protect.

**No new rule was written to keep them apart, because the split is already**
**there.** `queueAccountRefresh` reads a slot whose figure is on disk here and
now and never puts it in the line (X-215). So the button hands every readable
slot of every engine to the function that already knows the difference —
`data-acrefreshall=""`, which means on this side exactly what
`refreshableSlots('')` already means on the other — and spends its sentence
saying which half of the press waits and which half does not.

**The line is drawn moving.** A card knows its own place (X-206); the section
knows how much of the line is left, so while it runs the button reads
`◍ 3 in the line` and its panel opens with `3 in the line — 1 being read, 2
still waiting`. A press that acts over half a minute with nothing changing is
one nobody presses once and everybody presses five times.

**And it is not drawn where it would be the button below it, twice.** With a
single engine on this machine, "all engines" and "all Claude Code accounts" are
the same press, and a control whose only distinction is its position is
furniture — the group button already reads every account there is.

## 3.410.0 - X-232: the console sessions that survive the restart (2026-09-06)

*"Even when I am at the desk working in the Console — I would rather not press
F1 and restart it myself; let the agent do it, and let our conversation carry
on where it left off."*

X-230 had measured the loss and drawn the only conclusion available then: a
Console card's handle lives in the extension host's memory, so a restart
loses every live one — therefore wait for the window to go quiet, or `force`
and lose the conversation. This is the third way.

`farm.restartExtensionHost { resume: true }` writes what is running into the
stamp the cooldown already lives in — the same synchronous write, for the same
reason: it has to survive the death it is about. On the other side every row
is started again by the id its engine gave it, in its own seat, with its
scrollback read back from the transcript and what it already spent restored.

**And a resume changes the decision, not just the aftermath.** A session that
will be taken up again was never a reason to wait, so it stops being a blocker
and the restart happens at once. A session the engine never NAMED still is one:
there is nothing to resume it by, so it is reported as lost rather than quietly
dropped — the reader saw a card there. A terminal is never saved by any of
this, so a window reload still waits for the terminals.

Two refusals to fake anything. The row that travels is DERIVED from
`RunDimensions` — add a dimension there and the build fails until a revived
session carries it too, because a session brought back on another account or
route is not that session, it is a new one wearing its transcript. And a
session killed MID-TURN says so in its own first line: the transcript has what
was said, nothing has what was being said, and a reader who is not told waits
for a reply nobody is writing.

The plan is consumed before it is acted on. A plan left in the stamp is a plan
the next activation obeys as well, and the same session spawned twice is worse
than not spawned at all.

## 3.409.0 - X-217: the account cards stop drawing a promise the code refuses to keep (2026-09-06)

*"The On/Off switch on the cards is MISLEADING — it looks as though more than
one could be on at a time; but only one account per engine can be active."*

It could not, and never could: `normalizeActive` has always enforced one
standing account per engine. So turning a second switch on turned the first
one off by itself — which is not what a switch means anywhere else in this
product, or anywhere else at all. The control was drawing an arithmetic the
code does not have.

A single selection is now drawn as one: the standing account wears a STATE
badge (`🟢 standing`) and every other card carries an ACTION chip
(`⚡ Use this one`). Both are the same class in two states, both announce
themselves as `role="radio"` with exactly one `aria-checked="true"` — so the
shape says "one of these is chosen" to a reader looking at pixels and to one
that never will.

Pressing the badge is still the way back to the main sign-in, which is the
one gesture with no card of its own: the main sign-in is the ABSENCE of a
slot, and a page that can enter a state it cannot leave is a trap.

ONE SUBJECT: the head pill that also said `standing` is gone. The fact is
drawn once, by the control that owns it — two drawings of one fact are two
things that can disagree.

## 3.408.0 - X-230: the farm can load its own new build (2026-09-06)

*"We are setting up the autonomous shift on Agent Farm, but normally after a
new package is made the agents tell me to restart it. How is that going to
work unattended? Can the agent not do the restart itself?"*

It could not, and the developer rule said so in writing: *"the user only
restarts VS Code."* At the desk that is friction. During an unattended night
it is a deadlock — the loop stops until a human comes back to press Reload
Window, and the one repository where that happens is this one.

Three ops — `farm.health`, `farm.restartExtensionHost`, `farm.reloadWindow` — over one
core the rule actually lives in (`core/selfRestart.ts`). Two things it refuses to
do, both measured rather than assumed:

**It never restarts inside the handler.** `processBridge` writes the response
AFTER the handler returns and unlinks the request after that — so a handler
that kills the host dies with its own request still on disk, and the next
activation reads it and restarts again, for ever, with no caller left alive to
clean the file up. The command is fired on a timer, inside the gap the response
is written in, and a cooldown stamp written synchronously to disk refuses a
second restart within 20 seconds. `force` does not open that guard: force is
about sessions, the loop is about the bridge.

**And it never destroys work silently.** A Console session is a spawned child
whose handle lives in the extension host's memory, so a host restart loses
every live one of them; an integrated terminal belongs to the window and
survives — which is exactly why an agent working in a terminal can restart the
host under itself and live to verify the result. So the default
(`when: "auto"`) ARMS the restart and fires it by itself once the last session
ends, and says in the same answer what it is waiting for.

The bridge is single-file (`bridgeBusy`): a handler that waited would freeze every
other agent's every op for as long as it waited. So waiting is REPORTED, never
held — `farm.health` carries the armed plan, what blocks it, and a `bootId` that
changes on every activation. That id is the proof an autonomous agent has been
missing: not that the VSIX installed, but that the build now running is the one
it installed.

## 3.407.0 - X-216: the standing account the indicator did not follow (2026-09-06)

*"When we make an account standing for Claude on the Engines page, the Dashboard
