and the status bar turn to it — a standing **Codex** account should do the
same."*

X-212 wired exactly one half of that. `usageCredentialsFile` and
`usageAccountLabel` follow `activeAccounts['claude']`; the Codex side of
`usageProbe` went on reading a FIXED root — the `agentFarm.codexHome` setting,
or this machine's own `~/.codex`. So making a Codex account standing renamed the
heading over the figure and changed nothing underneath it. That is the worst
shape a control can have: it looks like it worked.

The root is now the standing slot's own folder, derived by `slotSessionDir` —
the same function the account cards read a slot's figure with (X-215), so the
indicator and the card can never point at two different folders. Nothing
standing is the ordinary answer and is unchanged: the setting, then `~/.codex`.

The repaint half turned out to be right already, and is pinned by a test so it
stays that way: both surfaces are repainted before any engine-specific branch,
and the engine matrix behind them is read live — so for an engine whose figures
are files, a repaint IS the new reading. The Claude-only branch below it buys a
fresh ENDPOINT read, which is the one thing that is Claude's alone.

## 3.406.0 - X-215: the sentence that kept the Codex cards blank (2026-09-06)

The user found this by comparing two surfaces of one product: *"the status bar
says week 72% for Codex — why is that not on the account cards?"* The cards were
not missing a feature. They were being told, in a stamped sentence, that there
was nothing to read:

```
quotaSource: () => ({ kind: 'none',
    reason: 'Codex keeps no readable quota figure on disk' })
```

‼️ **That sentence was false, and a wrong reason is worse than a blank bar
because it closes the question.** `core/engineUsage.ts` has read
`rate_limits.primary` out of the tail of the newest rollout since U-27 — it is
where the status bar's "week 72%" comes from. `accountUsage.ts` read the stamp,
not the world, and dropped every Codex slot from the list of things it could
read.

`QuotaSource` has a third branch now — `session-tail`, the engine's own
transcripts under **the slot's own directory**, which is what makes the answer
per account rather than per machine. One parser serves both roots: the status
bar asks `readCodexUsage` for the machine's `~/.codex/sessions`, a card asks the
same function for its own folder, and a second copy is how the two would come to
disagree about one week.

‼️ **A FILE READ IS NOT A REQUEST, and nothing here may pretend otherwise.**
Every gate in `AccountUsageService` — the five-second floor, the one-request
round robin, the 429 backoff — exists so that asking how much quota is left
never becomes the thing that spends it. None of that is true of a file on this
disk, so a `session-tail` slot takes no turn in the robin, waits behind no
floor, and joins no refresh queue. Three sentences in the UI that promised a
request, a line and a five-second spacing now say what actually happens.

And the card names the window it drew. "five-hour window" is right for every
Claude row and wrong for the row this item exists for: Codex publishes a **week**,
and 72% under those words would have been a lie with a real number in it.

## 3.405.0 - X-226: the run that slept until 07:50 while three accounts sat at 4% (2026-09-06)

The X-211 family promised one thing: *when the quota runs out mid-work, change
account and carry on.* It was built into the Console window (X-213) — the
surface that needs it **least**, because a person is sitting in front of it and
can move the card by hand. The surface that needs it most had none of it: a
headless run at 03:00 meets a usage limit, `retryDecision` reads **one** plan's
reset (M-10) and parks the retry until that window reopens. Three signed-in
accounts can sit at 4% for four hours while the work sleeps.

‼️ And the commonest case is worse than the documented one. `resetAware` ships
**off**, so an unconfigured run does not wait for a window at all — it waits its
policy's forty minutes, on a plan that is walled for four hours, and fails
again. Six times. There was never a reset to be aware of; there was another
account.

`carryOnAccount` (`core/accountUsage.ts`) answers the one question the Console
answers with a person: **which sign-in should carry this work on.** It does not
decide *which* — `pickAccount` does, X-207's own answer to whose turn it is,
because a second rotation rule is how the campaign and the queue come to
disagree about the same night. What it adds is who may be asked at all, and it
refuses more often than it agrees:

* never the account that just refused the work, whatever its last read says —
  the refusal is fresher than the figure;
* never another engine. The sentry may cross engines because it opens a NEW
  round; a carried-on run resumes a transcript, and a transcript belongs to one
  CLI;
* never out of an empty pool — the absence of a slot is the main sign-in
  (X-172), and it cannot be asked how much room it has;
* never a run pinned to `@machine`. *"Nothing is injected"* is an instruction
  the user typed into the form, and a handover would inject one;
* never for a failure that was not a limit. A broken script breaks the same way
  on every sign-in, and moving it spends a second plan to prove it.

A handover starts as soon as the pump can take it: the wait it replaces existed
to outlast a wall this run has just stepped around. `resetAt` is deliberately
**not** written on a handed-over row — it would label a run "waiting for 07:50"
that is about to start on a plan whose window is already open.

‼️ **And two surfaces could not say whose plan a run spent.** The run's own
setup list — engine, model, effort, permissions, route, tier, folder, priority
— never carried the **account**, and neither did `bridgeDimsOut`, so neither a
person reading the board nor an agent calling `tasks.get` could answer "which
sign-in was billed for last night". Both say it now, and both say when it
**moved**.

## 3.404.0 - X-225: the mission that was not allowed to say whose plan it spends (2026-09-06)

`missionDoor` declared the account **exempt**, with the reason written on the
door: *"a mission runs for HOURS across rounds and its delegates spawn one at a
time. An account frozen into the mission would pin round nine to a plan that
round two exhausted."* The risk is real. Refusing the dimension is not an answer
to it — it is the decision taken away from the person who owns the plans, on the
one surface that runs longest, while the model, the effort and the permission
mode beside it were overridable both mission-wide and per member all along.

‼️ And the exemption bought nothing it promised. It ended *"each delegate run
resolves the account at its own spawn, from the one place that holds it."*
Measured: the delegate was queued as a task with **no account on it at all**, and
`missionPlannerCallOnce` — the call that carries a mission from round to round —
spawned with **no `env` whatsoever**, so the planner ran as whatever the VS Code
window happened to be holding. Neither half of that sentence described any code.

Two axes now, because they are two questions:

* **`account`** — whose plan every delegation is billed to, on exactly the axis
  `engine` is; a member overrides it with its own. The ladder is member →
  mission → **nothing**, and the floor is deliberate: there is no per-agent and
  no fleet rung, because `activeAccounts` is not a default to fall through to,
  it is what the spawn resolves when nothing was stated. Nothing stated leaves
  every mission behaving exactly as it did.
* **`plannerAccount`** — whose plan the orchestrator itself spends. One headless
  `claude` in the lead's folder, called once per round for the life of the run.
  A long mission whose planner and whose workers share one sign-in is precisely
  the run that stops in the middle.

Refused, not narrowed, at creation: an id this machine does not hold, or one
belonging to another engine, is answered before a planner turn is spent — and a
member's is judged against the engine that member will really land on, not
against `claude`. On the form, a row whose engine moves loses an account that
engine cannot take, said out loud in the row's own note, exactly as its model and
effort already were.

The form gained an **Account override** in the Orchestrator block and a sixth box
on every member row. ‼️ There is **no mission-wide box**, and that is U-101's
rule rather than an omission: a mission-level fallback the rows cannot see is a
form disagreeing with itself. `MissionSpec.account` stays for the bridge, for
specs already on disk and for child inheritance — as `MissionSpec.engine` does.

## 3.403.0 - X-228: the step card that could not say what runs it (2026-09-06)

A workflow step card asked six questions — what the step IS, its title, its
agent, its prompt, its mode and (since X-224) whose sign-in pays — and drew **no
launch box at all.** No engine, no model, no effort, no permissions, no route.

The measurement is what makes it a defect rather than a gap: the host was ready
in BOTH directions. `stepSeed` published `sengine`/`smodel`/`seffort`/
`spermissionMode`, `stepFromDraft` read them back, `WorkflowStep extends
RunDimensions`, and `runExtras(step)` carried every one of them to the run. The
data model, the persistence and the run path were all in place; there was
nowhere to SAY it. So every step of every chain built on this page fell to the
fleet default, and a value written through the bridge was invisible on the one
page that edits it — surviving the round trip only because `readStep` writes
back the keys it names and leaves the rest alone. An invisible setting is worse
than a missing one.

The route was not even seeded, so a step could be pointed at an endpoint from
the bridge and from nowhere else. It is seeded now (`sproviderId`/`stier`), and
a tier with no route under it is dropped — the same refusal `runExtras` makes
one layer down, because `opus` is a different model on every route.

‼️ And the rows are BUILT ONCE. The engine picker, the permission paragraph and
the route/tier pair used to be written out inside the task form, which is
exactly where a second surface would have copied them from — X-149's four copies
of one narrowing rule, one screen over. `ntEngineRow` / `ntPermTip` /
`ntRouteRows` are shared now, and the step narrows through `stepNarrow`, which
VIEWS the step as a run and asks `media/afLaunch.js` and the form's own
`ntNarrowRoute` / `ntNarrowAccount`. Moving a step onto another engine drops the
model, the effort, the route, the tier and the sign-in that engine cannot take.

Pinned by a sweep derived at both ends: `RunDimensions` read out of the source,
the card's own `s` prefix as its vocabulary, and `stepSeed` as membership — so
the next dimension seeded into a step is unreachable from this page until it is
drawn here and read back here too.

## 3.402.1 - X-229: round two answered the conversation as somebody else (2026-09-06)

Found while fixing X-227, one screen away from it: the **third** hand-copied
dimension list in `core/tasks.ts`. The one that queues the next round of a
multi-round task carried thirteen fields and dropped five — **account,
providerId, tier, finishSound, superpowers.**

This is worse than X-227, and the reason is two lines further down in the same
literal. A round is not a new run: it is a REPLY, and it goes back into the same
conversation by `resumeSessionId`. So round two `--resume`d a transcript on a
sign-in that had never seen it — the mid-run drift the whole X-211 family was
built to end, arriving through the front door of the feature that produces the
longest runs in the product. The route mattered too: with it dropped, the second
half of a chain spoke to a different model behind the same word.

Fixed the way X-227 was: `runExtras` is the ONE carrier of `RunDimensions`, and
this literal now goes through it, with the round's own fields written after so
they still win — `rounds` here is what is LEFT to say, not what the task started
with. Measured in `test_retry.js` against `RunDimensions` read out of the source,
in a second region beside X-227's; both named their missing fields out loud
before the fix.

Three lists, three readings, one carrier. If a fourth appears, the test that
found this one is the shape to copy.

## 3.402.0 - X-227/X-224: the retry nobody is watching, and the chain that ate one plan (2026-09-06)

**X-227 — the unattended retry was dropping seven dimensions, and this one was
found by reading rather than reported.** There are two retries in the product.
`retryTask`, the one a person presses, carries every dimension of the original
across by hand and says why beside each: *"a retry that quietly moved to the
agent's standing endpoint is a different run wearing the same name."*
`maybeScheduleRetry` — the one that fires BY ITSELF when a run fails, typically
at 03:00, with nobody at a window — had its own shorter hand-written list.

Measured against `RunDimensions`, it was dropping **account, providerId, tier,
finishSound, superpowers, interactiveTarget and interactiveClose.** Each has its
own cost, and the first is the worst: `retryDecision` reads the engine's
published reset time and WAITS for one plan's window to reopen (M-10) — and then
the run went to whichever account happened to be standing. The wait and the run
disagreeing about whose window was being waited for. The route was next: the same
word names a different model on two of them, so the run that finally succeeded
was not necessarily the run that had been asked for. And the finish sound, on
the one path whose whole justification is that nobody is watching it.

The fix is not a longer list — a longer list is the same bug with a later date.
`runExtras` already exists as the ONE carrier of `RunDimensions`, and a schedule,
a trigger, a template and a workflow step all travel through it. This retry now
does too, with the retry's own fields written after it so they still win. The
rule is measured in `test_retry.js`, derived from `RunDimensions` in the source:
when it was written it named all seven out loud.

**X-224 — a workflow step can be billed to its own sign-in.** A chain is the
shape that needs this most: every step is headless, so three steps on one plan
eat it and the chain hits the wall in the middle with nobody in front of it.
`WorkflowStep extends RunDimensions` and `runExtras(step)` has always carried the
account to the run — the step's two readings and its card were the only places
that could not say it. `stepSeed` now returns it, `stepFromDraft` reads it, and
the card asks for it with the same `[machine global]` row the task form got in
3.401.0. The fixture `tasks-step-account` draws the card that holds it, in both
themes, because a card nobody photographs is a layout nobody checked.

Still open on the same card, and now written down as X-228: the step card draws
NO launch dimension boxes at all — engine, model, effort, permission and route
are on the type, are seeded by the host, are read back by the host and are
carried to the run, but there has never been anywhere to type them. They can be
set over the bridge and nowhere else.

## 3.401.0 - X-221/X-222/X-223: the Tasks form had an account box that went nowhere (2026-09-06)

An audit of the X-167 and X-211 families — asked for because the user remembered
functions being discussed that they could no longer find — turned up a closed
item whose wire was never connected.

**X-169 put an account box on the Tasks form, seeded it, tested it against mock
launch doors, and closed.** The box drew. The page posted the value. And
`src/panels/tasksPanel.ts` never read the field: `task-new` carried nine
dimensions to `addTask` and not that one, the retry branch carried eleven and not
that one, and `dims()` — the automation path, the one that matters most because
a schedule fires at 03:00 with nobody at a window — collected fifteen and not
that one. Measured before the fix: the word `account` appeared **four times** in
a 2,400-line panel, and none of the four was a wire.

So every task written from that page for four months ran on whichever sign-in
happened to be standing, silently billed a plan nobody named, and offered the
box back the next time the form was opened. `scheduleSeed` and `triggerSeed` did
not read it back either, so editing a saved automation's *time* wrote the
emptiness over an account somebody had chosen on purpose.

**The measurement that could not see it, and the one that now can.** The existing
sweep (`test_task_seed.js`) pins one direction: every `RunDimensions` field comes
back OUT of a stored task and into the form. The mirror was never stated — a
dimension the form is SEEDED with is a dimension the form can be SAVED with — so
a box could be alive, carry a value, and be dropped one line before the store
with every test green. That return leg is now measured on all five readings
(three save paths, two automation seeds), derived from `RunDimensions` in the
source, so the next dimension somebody draws a box for fails until its wire is
connected. When it was written it went red on exactly one name: `account`.

**And the third answer reached the form (X-223).** X-211 gave the Console a
`[💻 Machine Global]` row — not a fancier way of saying nothing, but the answer
that *clears* the engine's config variable, which the VS Code window may itself
be carrying. That row never came to the Tasks form, so the bridge could write
`account: "@machine"` on a task and the form that edits the same task could not
say it back. Two doors into one field, disagreeing about what the field can hold.
The row is now on the form, and — the trap found while wiring it — it survives an
engine change: a slot belongs to one engine and is narrowed away when the engine
moves, but the machine's own sign-in belongs to none, and dropping it would have
turned "run this as the machine itself" into "run it as whatever is standing" the
moment somebody touched the engine box.

No host plumbing was missing: `addTask`, `retryTask` and `launchAccountEnv` have
all honoured the field since X-169/X-211. This release is the four lines between
the form and them, plus the test that will not let them go missing again.

## 3.400.2 - the Codex account card said something that was not true (2026-09-06)

The Codex adapter answered, whenever anybody asked why its account cards show no
quota: *"Codex keeps no readable quota figure on disk — its plan limits are only
visible inside the CLI itself."*

That is false, and it has been false since U-27. `core/engineUsage.ts` reads the
figure off the tail of the newest rollout under `sessions/`
(`rate_limits.primary.used_percent`, `window_minutes`) and the status bar and the
Dashboard have been drawing it — "week 72%" — the entire time. The user found it
by comparing two surfaces of the same product and asking why one of them knew
something the other said was unknowable.

**A stated reason is a claim about the world, and a wrong one is worse than a
blank bar: it closes the question.** The `kind` stays `none`, because the account
cards genuinely are not wired to that reader yet — that is X-215, opened for it —
but the sentence now says which of those two things is true, so the next person
to read it is pointed at the work instead of away from it.

No behaviour changed. This is the half of the fix that can be shipped honestly on
its own; the plumbing needs the read path in `AccountUsageService` to grow a
branch that does NOT go through the shared network budget (a figure read from
disk must not wait behind a 5-second floor meant for an endpoint), and that is
not a change to make halfway.

## 3.400.1 - X-203: the Engines button vanished exactly when the page became worth opening (2026-09-06)

The user's report: *"Dashboard/Engines satırı sonunda buton var demiştin ama
yok."* They were right, and the reason is a one-branch mistake with a general
lesson in it.

`farmstatus.ts` put the `Engines` action on the **dormant** branch only — the
branch that means "only Claude Code is ready here". The moment a second engine
was installed, or any foreign session existed on disk, the row became `ready` or
`active` and drew no button at all. So the door was offered to the machine with
nothing to look at and withdrawn from the machine with four engines and 35
sessions.

**A row's action is a way to the SUBJECT of the row, not a fix-it prompt for a
subsystem nobody switched on.** The action is now on the row in every state,
under one label, because it is one door.

And the reason it survived a page anybody could have screenshotted: the
dashboard fixture carried `farmStatus: []`, so the card was never drawn in any
render. It is now built through the REAL `buildFarmStatus` — the same rule the
missions fixture follows for its conditions — describing a machine in the ACTIVE
state, which is precisely the state the button used to disappear in. A fixture
that types its own rows photographs a card the code cannot produce.

**Second way in:** `agentfarm.openEngines` was in no `view/title` menu at all, so
with the Dashboard button gone there was no click-path to the page. It sits in
the Toolbox view's title bar now, beside Secrets — both are facts of the MACHINE
(which CLIs are installed, which sign-ins are captured) rather than of the fleet,
and the Agents title bar already carries eight doors. The alternative was the
Agents bar, which is more prominent and more crowded; the Dashboard row is the
prominent path and this is the standing one.

## 3.400.0 - X-207: the accounts a campaign is ALLOWED to spend, and the engine it falls back to (2026-09-06)

The user's own complaint, and it had two halves: *"nöbet sistemi limiti boş olan
herhangi bir hesaba motor gözetmeden mi atlıyor? … kullanıcının izin verdiği
hesaplar arasında rotasyon yapmalı, izinsiz hesaba dokunmamalı"* — and then
*"peki kullanıcı şu motordan 3 hesap bu motordan 2 hesap seçip toplam 5'i
arasında rotasyon isterse?"*

Neither was expressible. The pool was every account of the campaign's engine,
built in one line of `sentryTick`, and there was nowhere in the record, the form
or the bridge that even held the IDEA of permission. A sentry left running all
night on the account somebody was keeping for their own work was not a bug you
could point at.

- **‼️ THE POOL IS A WHITELIST, IN THE ORDER IT WAS PICKED.** `pool` on the
  campaign names the accounts it may spend; with one, nothing else on the
  machine is touched, whatever room it has. **Absent is the old answer and stays
  the old answer** — every record already on disk plans identically to the day it
  was written, which is why "no pool" is a distinct value rather than an empty
  list somebody has to interpret. The order is the priority, so no second field
  states it: two fields for one question disagree the first time one is
  reordered.
- **‼️ AND IT MAY CROSS ENGINES.** Three Claude sign-ins and two Codex ones are
  ONE pool of five. `rotation` picks how it is walked: **free** (the default, and
  what every campaign did before) takes the most room anywhere in the pool;
  **tiered** keeps to one engine — the campaign's own first, then the pool's own
  order — and crosses only when EVERY account of the current one is at or above
  the ceiling. That is the fallback the item exists for: the night used to end in
  a sleep while a signed-in Codex account sat idle. Every tier walled still
  sleeps, and it wakes at the earliest reset in the WHOLE pool, which is sooner
  than one engine's.
- **‼️ THE ROUND OPENS ON THE CHOSEN ACCOUNT'S ENGINE.** The round spec took
  `campaign.engine` unconditionally, which was right for exactly as long as a
  pool could hold one engine. Let it cross and that same line opens a Claude
  session pointed at a Codex sign-in — a round that dies looking like a broken
  account. **And the campaign's model is dropped when the engine changes**,
  because a model name belongs to an engine: `opus` means nothing to Codex, and
  carrying it would turn a working fallback into a round that fails on its first
  line.
- **‼️ AN ACCOUNT THAT IS NOT CAPTURED IS REFUSED AT 21:00, BY NAME** — rather
  than skipped every round and found as "no usable account" at 03:00. And one
  FORGOTTEN while the campaign runs is news, not a gap: the strip names it, and a
  pool that has lost all of them BLOCKS (`pool-empty`) rather than falling back to
  every account — falling back would spend exactly the sign-ins the user fenced
  off, which is the one thing this item exists to prevent.
- **The form got the control the idea needs.** Every captured account, grouped by
  engine, each carrying the room it has right now — because the figure is already
  measured and sending the reader to the Engines page to look it up, in order to
  come back and tick a box, is a click DENSITY says must not be charged. The tick
  ORDER is drawn (1. 2. 3.), since it is a real input to the tiered walk and an
  input nobody can see is not an input. MIRROR on both fields: empty says what
  will happen instead. The running campaign's strip trades "rotates claude
  accounts" for the count, the engines and the strategy, with the list and the
  rooms in its panel.
- **Bridge, same commit:** `sentry.start` takes `pool` (array or comma string)
  and `rotation`; `sentry.status` answers `pool`, `rotation` and `poolMissing` —
  the last being the only place "a pool of five running on three" can be
  explained.

Written design first, as the item itself demanded: `10_Notes/A-PLN - Nöbet Hesap
Rotasyon Havuzu ve Çok Motorlu Yedekleme - X-207 - 260906.md`.

## 3.399.4 - the extension could not be switched on, and no test could see it (2026-09-06)

**‼️ 3.399.0 through 3.399.3 DO NOT ACTIVATE.** Not a broken page — no pages.
`activate()` threw on its first surface and every command in the product
answered "command not found":

```
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'storedAccounts' before initialization
    at usageAccountLabel  (extension.js)
    at PlanUsageBar.heading → tooltip → paint → new PlanUsageBar
    at activate           (extension.js)
```

**The root cause is one of position, and one line long.** X-212 (3.399.0) gave
the status bar the words for WHOSE plan it is showing — `usageAccountLabel`,
declared beside the indicator it serves and reading `storedAccounts` out of the
accounts block 470 lines further down. Ordinarily that is fine: a closure is
allowed to name a `const` declared after it, because by the time anybody calls
it the declaration has run. `PlanUsageBar` is the case where nobody waits — it
paints inside its own constructor, so the very first thing that happens after
`new` is a call back into a binding still in its temporal dead zone. The two
readers are declared at the top of `activate()` now, with the rule written where
they sit: **anything constructed during activation may call its dependencies
before its constructor returns, so a reader handed to one is declared first.**

**‼️ AND THE PART THAT MATTERS MORE — 18 972 assertions could not see it.**
The suite was green, the vsix verified 16/16, the package installed, and the
product was dead. Every file in `test/` tested a piece; not one had ever called
`activate()`. Being able to switch the extension on is the precondition of
everything the other assertions describe, and it was the one claim nothing
checked — a rule that fails silently is not a rule.

`test/test_activation.js` loads the COMPILED extension against a stand-in
`vscode` whose `getConfiguration` returns every reader its own default — the
coldest start there is, and the one a first install actually gets — then calls
`activate()` and insists it comes back. Four claims, in the order they fail:
it loads · it does not throw · it registers its doors · **every command id
`package.json` declares is live afterwards**, which is the symptom the user saw
stated as an assertion. Verified by putting the defect back: the test reproduces
the host log stack line for line, then goes green on the fix.

It sorts first in the run, so from now on the suite answers "does it turn on?"
before it answers anything else.

## 3.399.3 - X-196 (part 2): the hover that repeated the row (2026-09-06)

The Settings page's sentry section came through the audit clean — every path row
already shows what its variables resolve to, every box holds its own value, and
no description is cut. One thing on the same page did not: a declared object's
field description is drawn on an ellipsised line, so a hover is right — but it
was a native `title` carrying the IDENTICAL string. That is the exact complaint
the panel component was built for: the platform tooltip repeats what is already
on the row and then stops wherever it feels like stopping. The cut line is the
SHORTHAND now and the panel is the sentence, whole and scrollable. The wrapper
takes the row's sizing, because wrapping a line makes the wrapper the flex child
and a column sized by the line's own rule silently stops being sized.

## 3.399.2 - X-196 (part 1): the sweep reaches the sentry block and the account cards (2026-09-06)

The user's own instruction behind the item: read the finished backlog, see what
we have complained about, and take the interface out of it. Three of those
complaints were still true of this family's own surfaces.

- **‼️ A SHORTHAND WORD WITH NOTHING BEHIND IT.** Six state words came out of the
  sentry chip — OFF · PAUSED · STOPPED · RUNNING · SLEEPING · WAITING — and not
  one had a panel. WAITING and SLEEPING are the same picture to a reader who
  does not already know that one is between rounds and the other is sitting out
  a quota wall; BLOCKED said nothing about what was blocking it. Each now opens
  with its long form and then the campaign's own figures — what it works
  through, as whom, how many rounds, the last decision and when, and for
  SLEEPING the clock that is the whole difference.
- **‼️ PROSE IN A NATIVE `title`.** Five labels on the campaign form carried two
  and three sentences inside a platform tooltip: cut at a length nobody
  controls, unscrollable, and gone the moment the pointer reaches for it. They
  are AFTips now. **And MIRROR:** Ceiling %, Safety min and Failure brake are
  empty BY DESIGN and empty means "the setting decides" — so each panel opens
  with the figure in force and where it comes from, because an unset ceiling and
  a ceiling typed at the same number are not the same answer.
- **A thin cell is a bug, and an undefined column is one too.** Status, Opened
  and Took had no `<th>` definition at all; Took drew `20m` and nothing else. The
  columns are defined once, on their headers, and the cell carries the figures
  the row already implies — opened, ended, took, status. A round still on the
  board says so rather than drawing a figure that is stale as it is painted.
- **‼️ THE BLOCK THE ACCOUNT CARD IS FOR HAD NO PANEL.** A bar, a percentage and
  one line about the reset — and how much is LEFT, which is the figure somebody
  is actually after, was nowhere: 38% used and 62% left are the same fact and
  only one of them answers the question being asked. The window block now
  carries used, left, the reset, how old the reading is and whose plan it is; an
  account with no figure says WHICH of the two silences it is in.
- `AFTip.label` joins `AFTip.cell`: a form label whose whole area is the trigger
  and which stays the element its row is laid out with. Wrapping a `<label>`
  puts a span between it and its flex row, and the row then lays out the span.

## 3.399.1 - X-195 closed: and WHICH handover note the words were built on (2026-09-06)

The last line of the item, and the one a reader cannot check for themselves. A
continuation prompt is largely somebody else's note: "the previous session left
this behind" is a claim, and until now nothing said which file it was or which
source offered it. The round's record carries `handover` now — the note's path,
the source that found it and the score it was chosen by — and both panels draw
it. **A search that found nothing is its own answer** (`found: false`) and says
so: it is what explains a thin prompt, and reading it as "never looked" hides a
search that failed.

## 3.399.0 - X-211 family closed, and X-195: every round says why it opened on those words (2026-09-06)

Three surfaces named an account and a fourth ran the process. Every item below
closes one of those gaps; together they are the X-211 umbrella.

- **‼️ X-212 — the status bar and the Dashboard read the account that is
  STANDING.** `PlanUsageService` was pointed at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`
  and nothing else, which was right for exactly as long as there was one
  sign-in: make an account standing on the Engines page and every session ran on
  it while the indicator went on reporting the main account's window. The reader
  is dynamic now, the cached snapshot remembers WHICH file it came out of (a
  cache that outlived an account switch would put the new name over the old
  figures), the heading says `Claude Code (murat@…) — plan usage` /
  `(Machine Global)`, the Dashboard card carries the same owner, and making an
  account standing repaints and re-reads in the same gesture instead of waiting
  up to five minutes for the next beat. `usage.plan` answers with `account` too.
- **‼️ X-211 — "the machine's own sign-in" is a VALUE, not a blank
  (`@machine`).** The empty account was two answers wearing one face: *nobody
  chose*, which falls through to the standing account and must, and *I chose the
  machine's own*, which must not. They are different values now, and the second
  one CLEARS the engine's config variable rather than merely not setting it —
  a window that itself carries one used to hand it to the card while every
  surface named something else.
- **‼️ X-213 — the ghost selection, and the lock.** The composer's box had no row
  for the machine's own sign-in, so the browser drew the FIRST account as
  selected while the composer stated nothing. It has a root row now, it OPENS on
  the standing account with its dot, it is drawn on any engine that can hold a
  second sign-in (a machine with nothing captured is the case that most needed
  it), and what it shows is what `start` states. One layer down: three of the
  four session-start paths never recorded the account on the card's state, so
  Claude — the engine this family is for — re-spawned as `undefined`.
- **‼️ X-213 — and the box no longer locks when the session starts.** A window
  that hits its five-hour ceiling mid-task used to mean a second terminal, a
  `/login`, and `claude --resume` by hand. Now the account box stays open on a
  live card: pick another sign-in and the next message ends the process and
  brings the SAME conversation back up on it with `--resume`, carrying the
  running totals so the conversation does not get cheaper for changing account.
  The old process is watched out of the CLI's own registry rather than assumed
  away, and a hold-out is reported. On a per-turn engine there is no process
  between turns, so the change is simply true and says so. New op
  **`console.setAccount`**.
- **X-214 — a terminal resume names its account too.** That door passed no
  account layer at all. It asks now — the standing account first, so Enter does
  what the machine would have done — and cancelling opens nothing.

Two gaps found REVIEWING that family, and fixed here rather than written down as
caveats:

- **‼️ A HELD MESSAGE KEPT NO PROMISE.** `send` re-sealed the session for a
  message said into an idle card, but a message PARKED while a turn was running
  is released somewhere else entirely — straight down the pipe of the process
  the conversation is leaving, with the card still saying the swap was pending.
  The reader was told the next message would run on the other sign-in and then
  watched it spend the old one, with nothing on screen saying so. It re-seals
  there too now, taking the held text out of the queue WITHOUT opening a turn so
  the resumed session says it exactly once.
- **‼️ THE TERMINAL RESUME CLEARED THE VARIABLE ON A MACHINE WITH NO SLOTS.**
  Nobody was asked, so nobody answered — and `@machine` is an ANSWER, one that
  removes the engine's config variable. On a machine with no captured account
  the window's own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is the only sign-in there is, and the
  Console's own spawn inherits it: two surfaces, two identities. Nothing stated
  is what it answers now.

### X-195 — the account of why a round opened on the words it did

`roundWhy` existed, was tested, and was called from NOWHERE: a record nothing
ever built. The rounds table showed status, account and duration and nothing
anywhere said WHY a round was given the prompt it was given, so a night of eight
rounds left eight prompts nobody could account for and the one that cost money
was indistinguishable from the seven that did not.

- **The writer.** `sentryTick` builds the record at the one moment both halves
  are in hand — the verdict that judged the round that ended, and what the
  leader actually DID about it — and carries it on the round spec, so it is
  written to the row and outlives the closure that made it. `path` is the
  leader's REAL outcome and never the verdict's wish: a verdict of `leader`
  whose turn timed out, refused or answered prose produced a TEMPLATE round.
- **The mark, on the row.** `L` a leader chose the words · `M` a template did
  and nothing was asked · **`M!`** the leader WAS asked and gave nothing usable,
  which is the only case that spends money without buying words and is the only
  one drawn as an alarm. The panel opens with the long form and carries the
  conditions that fired, the ones nobody could judge, the diagnosis and the
  bill. A round opened before this record existed says so rather than being
  drawn as free.
- **What the thinking cost, on the campaign's own line** — the night's total
  with the turn-by-turn ledger as its hover, red only when the leader has
  actually stopped waking rather than for one turn that gave nothing usable.
- **And on the Console strip**, where the morning reader's eye already is: the
  last round's account, in the strip's panel.
- `sentry.status` answers with `why` and `whyMark` per round, so an unattended
  agent reads the same account the page draws.

## 3.398.0 - X-194 closed: what every condition reads today, AND parts, and the leader's own purse (2026-09-05)

The editor could WRITE a rule and could not show what the rule was about. Three
things finish it.

- **‼️ Every condition row says what its field reads TODAY** — `repo.dirty | is
  more than | 0 | now 3`. The reading comes from the round that ended last,
  through the evaluator's OWN reader (`factsSnapshot` runs `read()` over the
  field dictionary), so the figure on the row is by construction the figure the
  condition will be compared against. A field added to the dictionary turns up
  with a reading without either side being touched. With nothing measured yet
  the row says "not measured yet" rather than showing a zero — "nothing fired"
  and "nothing was read" are opposite answers.
- **And whether it would fire tonight, ASKED rather than guessed.** The page
  posts a debounced probe on every repaint of the draft and paints what the real
  evaluator answered: the rows that hold are marked, and the set says in one
  sentence whether "a round ending like the last one would wake the leader",
  naming which conditions did it. New op **`sentry.probe`** is the same function
  behind the bridge, so an agent can ask before a night is spent finding out.
- **‼️ AND groups.** `Condition.all` has been in the core since X-190 and the
  editor drew a flat OR list, so the only policy anybody could build was "any one
  of these". A line can now be given AND parts: the lines are ORed, the parts of
  one line are ANDed. "The repo is dirty AND the item did not close" is a real
  night; either half alone is an ordinary one. Take the last part away and the
  line goes back to being a plain condition.
- **The leader's own leash, per campaign.** `leaderCaps` has been on the record
  since X-191 with no writer anywhere, so every campaign spent the machine-wide
  settings. Three boxes — the model its short deciding turn runs on, the dollars
  per calendar day, and what one turn may cost before the next is refused (not
  the round's model or budget). All three empty by default, and empty means the
  setting decides: **MIRROR** puts the figure in force on the first line of each
  panel, because an empty purse and a purse of zero look identical and one of
  them switches the leader off. An untouched box sends nothing, so changing the
  setting later still changes this campaign. Also on `sentry.start` as
  `leaderModel` / `leaderDailyUsd` / `leaderMaxUsd`.
- **Three defects found on the way.** The mode strip said `custom · from hybrid`
  over a set nobody had edited (a value was compared by TYPE, so `0` and `"0"`
  were two questions); reading the form back walked inside each row and so
  measured nothing in the page harness, leaving every row holding the first
  row's boxes; and `+ condition` named a new row by the count, handing out a
  name already on the board after a delete — and the verdict names conditions by
  their handle.

## 3.397.0 - X-194 (part 2): the sentry form gets a mode and its conditions (2026-09-05)

The host has taken `preset` and `conditions` since 3.390.0 and the round has
read the policy since X-191 — but no surface could SET one, so every campaign
anybody actually started fell to the mechanical default and the leader never
woke. This is the half that was missing. **‼️ X-194 is not closed:** each row
still has to show that field's CURRENT value (so you can see whether the
condition would fire today), and the lead settings — model, daily budget, round
ceiling — are still to come.

- **A mode strip above the conditions:** Not set · Mechanical · Intelligent ·
  Hybrid. They are not code paths — pressing one FILLS the condition set from
  `core/sentryPolicy.ts`. "Not set" is a fourth position and not the absence of
  one: no policy is written at all and the round's own default decides, which is
  what every campaign started before this control existed did.
- **‼️ The mode is READ OFF THE CONDITIONS on every paint, never remembered.**
  Edit a row and the strip says `custom · from hybrid`; undo the edit and it
  says Hybrid again by itself. A preset name printed over five edited conditions
  is a label that lies about what will run tonight.
- **A condition editor fed by the dictionary.** Fields, operators and presets
  all come from `sentryPolicy.ts` over the page's data, so a fact the round
  learns to measure turns up in the editor the day it is added and the page does
  not change. A row offers only the operators its field's TYPE admits, a closed
  set gets a picker, an operator that takes no value gets no value box, and a
  field the dictionary no longer names is kept, marked and explained rather than
  silently swapped for whatever sits first in the list.
- Rows can be added, dropped and reordered, and the order is not cosmetic: the
  conditions are ORed and the verdict names the ones that fired in the order
  they were written. The block says that in one sentence, where the decision is
  made.

## 3.396.0 - U-131: right-click is the second position of the switch (2026-09-05)

The Console's `show` box is opened, scrolled and re-ticked all day to do one
thing: drop to the conversation and come back. That is not a choice between
eight options, it is a switch — and a switch that costs a click, a read and two
ticks is not a switch.

- **Right-click the trigger and it flips**, without opening the menu:
  everything → the picker's first preset; the preset → unfiltered; **any other
  combination → the preset first**, because somebody reaching for a shortcut in
  the middle of a hand-built filter means "take me there", not "throw my filter
  away".
- **It lives in the component** (`media/afFilters.js`), so every `AFFilter.multi`
  that declares a preset has it — the same box is drawn on nine pages, and one
  written per page would have been nine gestures that disagree.
- **‼️ A picker with no preset does not take the gesture at all** — no listener
  and no `preventDefault`, so the platform's own menu is untouched. A gesture
  that silently does nothing on the other pages is worse than no gesture: the
  reader learns it, tries it, and stops trusting it.
- The hover says the gesture exists and names what it flips to, built from the
  same list the listener reads. A feature nobody is told about is a feature
  nobody uses.

## 3.395.0 - U-130: 2 205 options that said nothing, paid off in full (2026-09-05)

A `<select>` cuts its own text and the popup it opens is drawn by the operating
system, so no hover panel of ours can reach into it — the option's native
`title` is the only surface there is. U-128 measured the damage and fixed the
Console; the other twenty-two pages were left on a budget. That budget is now
**zero**, on every page.

- **One emitter, not twenty-three copies.** `C.option(value, label, { selected,
  disabled, detail })` and `C.optionTip(label, detail)` live in `media/charts.js`
  — already on every page as `window.AFCharts`. The option's own text comes
  first, then a blank line, then the detail: the same order MIRROR puts a
  control's current value before its explanation.
- **And the detail is a FACT, not a restatement.** A settings enum says which of
  its values is the default; an alert tone says where the file lives and why a
  greyed row is greyed; a voice says which language it reads and what picking it
  writes into the setting; a queue position says how many items it jumps; a
  project says the same `Label: value` readout its own row hover carries. The
  three shared components (`afProject`, `afForm`, `afTelegram`) were fixed once
  and paid for six pages at a time.
- **The gate is now a ban rather than a budget.** `test/optiontips.manifest.json`
  is empty and `bare` is `0`, so a page missing from it must be at zero — a new
  picker cannot arrive silent. A `<datalist>` option is no longer counted: it is
  a suggestion behind a text box, it opens no popup, and no browser shows a
  `title` on it, so counting it invited markup nobody can ever see.
- **‼️ And a test that hand-wrote its own `window.AFCharts` now borrows the real
  one** (`test/lib_charts_stub.js`). Thirteen sandboxes each carried a partial
  copy, so the day a shared helper was added every one of them died with `C.<new
  thing> is not a function` while the extension itself was fine — a false alarm
  on one side and no alarm at all on the other.

## 3.394.0 - X-197: one atomic writer, and a failure you can retry (2026-09-05)

A `projects.backlog.add` call fell over with `EPERM: rename Backlog.md.af.tmp ->
Backlog.md` because Obsidian had the file open. The real damage was not the
failure — it was that the caller could not tell a refusal from a half-applied
batch, retried, and wrote six items TWICE, spending their codes for ever.

- Both writers (`reportBridge.atomicWrite`, `projectDocs.safeWriteDoc`) now go
  through the one `core/atomicFile.ts` introduced with X-204, instead of each
  keeping its own copy of temp+rename.
- **The rename is retried** through a short backoff (150/300/600/900 ms) while
  the target looks locked — EPERM, EACCES, EBUSY. On Windows those locks are
  measured in milliseconds, so waiting is the honest answer. A fault that will
  never clear (a missing directory, a read-only volume) is reported at ONCE
  rather than after two seconds of hoping.
- **‼️ And the failure carries the guarantee that makes a retry safe:** the error
  states that NOTHING WAS WRITTEN, names the file, and names the kind of process
  that is probably holding it. The temp file is swept up, so nothing is left
  behind that could be mistaken for the document.

## 3.393.0 - X-206: read them all, in a line (2026-09-05)

Before switching accounts you have to see which one has room — and there was no
way to ask. The page-wide beat reads ONE slot per turn, whichever is stalest, so
the card you were looking at could be minutes old and nothing on the page would
tell you: it printed  beside a percentage, which is the age of
the ACCOUNT, not of the figure.

- **‼️ "Refresh all" is a LINE, not a burst.** `accountUsage` still refuses to
  have a `refreshAll()` — the new `core/accountQueue.ts` holds an ORDER and
  starts one read every five seconds through the same single-slot door. N
  accounts are still N requests; the spacing is the only thing that keeps asking
  how much quota is left from becoming what spends it, and it is the SAME
  constant the manual floor is built from rather than a second number.
- **The queue is drawn, because a queue nobody can see is a hang.** A waiting
  card wears its PLACE in the line (a number you can act on, not a spinner that
  says soon); the one in flight spins; **pressing a waiting card takes it back
  out** — a queue you cannot leave is one you learn not to join. A slot already
  being read cannot be cancelled and says so: the figure will land either way.
- **One engine, one group.** A Claude account and a Codex account are never
  alternatives to each other, so the flat list made you filter by eye before you
  could compare anything (ONE SUBJECT). Each group carries its own `⟳ all`,
  which is the press somebody actually makes before switching.
- **Every card says when its own figure was read** (`read 40s ago` / ), beside when the account was filed. The two answer different questions
  and only one of them decides a switch.
- New bridge op **`accounts.refresh`** (id = toggle · engine = that group · all).

## 3.392.0 - X-205: the standing account is a switch, not a sentence (2026-09-05)

`Use next` read as *hand the next one to whoever is next* — the opposite of what
it did. It makes THIS account the one every new session of that engine opens as,
and the state is binary and exclusive per engine, which is what a switch is for.

- The two text buttons (`Use next` / `Main account`) are now **one control in its
  two positions**: a switch, ON in the same blue the standing badge and the card's
  left rule already wear — one colour for one fact, read down a column of cards
  without stopping to parse a label.
- **MIRROR** — a control with no words opens its tooltip with the position it is
  IN (`ON — the standing Claude Code account` / `OFF — switch to this account`),
  then the whole consequence: that turning one on turns the other off, and that
  nothing already running moves either way.
- `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`, so the state is not only a colour.
- The Console account box and the launcher dimension no longer point at a button
  by a name that no longer exists.

## 3.391.0 - X-204: an expired access token is not a signed-out account (2026-09-05)

MEASURED, and it cost an account to learn. Two things were true at once and only
one of them was in the code that decided whether a session could start:

- `engineAccounts.readClaudeIdentity` has always said an expired access token is
  routine and only a dead REFRESH token needs a person.
- `accountUsage` read HTTP 401 from the usage endpoint as `expired`,
  `slotIsUsable` refuses an expired slot, and the sentry's own fleet filter
  (`extension.ts`, `sentryWatch`) drops it. So an account whose token had simply
  aged out of its few hours **left the fleet**, and the user was sent to a browser
  to fix nothing. Not a cosmetic alarm: the account could not be switched to.

- **The grant's short half is now refreshed** the way the CLI refreshes it in the
  same directory — `platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token`, endpoint, client id and
  body shape READ OUT OF THE INSTALLED CLI rather than invented (`oauthRefresh.ts`).
  A 401 is refreshed and retried once; a token already expired on the clock is
  refreshed **before** the request, so the machine's shared budget is not spent on
  a call that is known to fail.
- **‼️ A REFRESH IS NOT A READ.** Measured against the live endpoint: Anthropic
  ROTATES the refresh token on every exchange and REVOKES the access token that
  was in force. Two rules follow, and both are in the code rather than in a note:
  - a slot with a **session running on it is never exchanged** — that would take
    the credential out from under somebody's turn. It is re-READ instead, because
    the engine using it refreshes the grant itself and has usually already
    written the answer to disk;
  - the rotated grant is parked in a **sidecar** (`.credentials.json.rotated.json`)
    BEFORE the real file is replaced, and a sidecar found on the next read is
    adopted. The window between "the server rotated" and "the file says so" is
    where an account is lost, and it is now survivable.
- **Weather is never reported as a sign-out.** An unreachable endpoint, an HTTP
  500, a locked file: the slot stays USABLE with an honest sentence. `expired`
  now means only what it says — the refresh grant itself is gone, or a token
  minted seconds ago was refused.
- **One atomic writer, and its failure carries a guarantee** (`atomicFile.ts`).
  The rename is retried through a short backoff while the target looks locked
  (EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY — Windows, an editor or a scanner, milliseconds), and when
  the attempts are spent the error states that NOTHING WAS WRITTEN, which is what
  makes the caller's retry safe. A fault that will never clear is reported at
  once rather than after two seconds of waiting.

## 3.390.0 - X-194 (part): a campaign can be STARTED with a mode (2026-09-05)

MEASURED: the campaign record has carried `policy` since X-190 and the round has
read it since X-191 — and **nothing could set it**. `sentry.start` took no preset
and no conditions, so every campaign anybody could actually start fell to the
mechanical default and the leader X-191 built never woke once.

- `sentry.start` now takes **`preset`** (`mechanical` · `intelligent` · `hybrid`)
  and **`conditions`**. They are not three code paths: one condition set with
  three fillings, so a preset FILLS the conditions from the dictionary and your
  own `conditions` win over it, with the preset kept beside them so a surface can
  say what they were edited FROM.
- **‼️ A preset nobody knows is REFUSED BY NAME**, never quietly mechanical —
  that silence would turn a night of thinking into a night of templates and tell
  no one. Same rule X-190 applies to an unknown FIELD, at the other end of the
  same dictionary.
- **Asking for no mode still starts a campaign** and writes no policy at all: the
  round already has its own default, and inventing one here would be this
  function deciding something nobody asked for.
- The Missions page's own door takes the same two arguments, so the form X-194
  still owes has nothing left to invent on the host side.

‼️ **X-194 IS NOT CLOSED BY THIS.** The mode selector and the condition editor —
its visible half — are still to build; this is the host-side gap that made them
impossible to wire.

## 3.389.0 - X-193: the sentry gets a section, and every path says where it points (2026-09-05)

Thirteen settings for one unattended campaign were scattered down a page about
task concurrency and dispatch rules. Each of them was filed there for a reason
that was right about that one setting and wrong about the set: somebody tuning
an overnight run had to hunt for the words it starts on, the folders it reads,
the leader's leash and three thresholds, one at a time, in alphabetical order.

- **Its own section, and four questions instead of thirteen boxes.** *Where it
  looks for the handover note · The words it starts the next session with · The
  leader, and its leash · When a round is going nowhere.* Each group says what
  the question IS, not just which keys are in it.
- **‼️ A key the grouping has never heard of is still drawn**, under **More**.
  The grouping is hand-written editorial and will go stale; a settings page that
  HIDES a setting is worse than one that groups it badly.
- **‼️ EVERY PATH ROW SAYS WHERE IT POINTS.** `${vault}\00_AGENT_AREA\…` in a
  box tells you nothing about the folder it opens, and that gap is where an
  unattended campaign reads the wrong place and reports "no handover note" about
  a folder nobody ever opened. Each row now carries the real resolved path
  underneath it — no click, no dialog (DENSITY). A path that cannot be built
  carries the REASON instead and no path at all, because a half-built path looks
  usable and points somewhere nobody meant.
- **The variable legend is DRAWN from the dictionary**, not repeated on the
  page: a variable added to `core/pathVars.ts` turns up here untouched. MIRROR —
  each chip's panel opens on what the variable IS on this machine, then a blank
  line, then what it means. One with nothing behind it is marked, because that
  is the case that silently cancels a path.
- **The order is the value, so a row can be moved.** `handoverSources` is tried
  most-truthful-first and the instruction pool decides whose block wins;
  reordering used to mean deleting a row and retyping it at the bottom. Rows now
  drag, and carry ↑/↓ for the hand that would rather not drag and the keyboard
  that cannot. Nothing is saved by moving — **Save the list** still is.
- **Which settings get all this is DERIVED from their own schema** (`x-af-browse`),
  never from a list of keys — the disease that key was introduced to cure.
- **Bridge:** new `settings.paths` — where a path setting actually points on this
  machine, through the same resolver the page and the campaign use, so all three
  agree. With no arguments it answers for every path setting plus each variable
  and what it is here; `templates` resolves a value you have not written yet.
- **U-128 paid down while passing through:** the list editor's dropdown rows and
  the setting-set picker now title their options, so six other pages' budgets
  came down with them and `spsettings` reached zero.
- What deliberately did NOT move: `answerDir` (where an answer is WRITTEN — that
  belongs to the work queue) and `automation.*` (the master gate over every
  unattended thing on this machine, not over this one).

## 3.388.0 - X-192: one pool of your own words, read twice (2026-09-05)

Your saved instructions were never a second file to invent. `sentryTemplatesFile`
already held blocks you had written; the campaign just refused every heading that
did not name a verdict and then **threw the block away**. So "always give it the
session id", "after 3am keep it short" — the things you actually type by hand out
of the right-click menu — had nowhere in the machine to live.

- **One pool, two uses.** A block whose heading names a verdict (`item-done`,
  `clean-handover`, `nothing-to-continue`, `hit-the-wall`, `*`) is a TEMPLATE and
  the mechanical round fills it, exactly as before. **Every** block — including
  the ones under a heading of your own — is MATERIAL the leader blends into the
  next session's opening words. Same file, same format, read twice.
- **‼️ A refusal is no longer a loss, and it says so.** A heading naming no
  verdict is still refused BY NAME (dropping it silently is how somebody spends
  an evening wondering why their template never fires), but the sentence now
  ends "it is kept as material for the leader" — because a refusal that reads as
  a loss teaches people to stop writing the blocks this exists to collect.
- **The pool is a LIST, not a file.** New `agentFarm.sentryInstructionFiles`,
  taking the X-188 path variables (`${vault}`, `${projectNotes}`, `${today}` …).
  `sentryTemplatesFile` is read first and the list follows it — they are
  **assembled**, not chosen between, so nobody's precedence changes and a file
  named in both is **read once**: a doubled instruction would be a doubled prompt
  on a model metered by the word.
- **The leader is not handed the whole pool.** `materialFor` gives it your
  standing instructions plus the ONE block that answers the round that actually
  happened, and the catch-all. The other verdicts' wording is noise it pays for
  and, worse, something to copy.
- **Still self-contained (X-179).** With nothing configured the pool is empty,
  every verdict still has a built-in answer, and no folder of yours is needed
  anywhere. A path whose variables will not resolve is SKIPPED **with its
  reason** rather than pointed at the wrong folder (X-182); a path that is gone
  is reported and the rest of the pool still reads.
- **Bridge:** new `sentry.instructions` (what the leader receives, and with
  `outcome` what a leader woken on that verdict would receive); `sentry.templates`
  now reports `files`, `missingPaths` and `skipped` alongside what it already said.

## 3.387.0 - X-191: the leader wakes, takes the situation in hand, and goes back to sleep (2026-09-05)

This is the defect the whole X-167 family was reopened for. `ModelAssist` and
`modelNeeded()` were WRITTEN and never wired: `sentryStep({…})` had never once
been handed an `assist`, so the sleeping leader you designed did not exist. What
shipped filled a template and could not think.

And the reason it was not built is the thing to get right. The `automation.ts`
precedent burned $70.90 over five nights asking a model something that could
have been counted, and the agent that wrote this family over-corrected into
"never call a model". ‼️ The answer was never "do not call" — it is **govern
when, and how much**. New pure module `src/core/sentryLeader.ts`.

- **Six leashes, each of them tested as a leash.** The leader wakes only when a
  condition fires, so a routine night costs nothing at all · the model is cheap
  by default (`haiku`) and the default is named in one place · a turn has a time
  ceiling and a cost ceiling · a campaign has a DAILY budget · every turn is
  recorded as a `ModelAssist` (model, ms, $, ok) · N failures in a row drop the
  mode to mechanical and say so.
- **‼️ Not one of them is a brake on the WORK.** Budget spent, brake tripped,
  turn cut, answer unreadable, runner missing — every path opens the round
  anyway, on the template. A leader that could halt the night is a worse failure
  mode than a leader that is occasionally wrong, so nothing thrown inside a
  leader turn leaves it.
- **What the leader may do is deliberately narrow:** replace the WORDS, pick the
  ACCOUNT, or say WAIT. It cannot overrule your hand, the failure brake, the
  automation gate or the quota wall — all of which are decided around it, never
  by it. Waiting is `idle`, not stopped, and the words it wrote are carried to
  the round that does open.
- **The brief tells the truth about what is not known.** X-174's law travels
  into the prompt: a fact nobody measured is presented as unmeasured, because an
  absent fact is an invitation to invent one.
- **The reply is read with a string-aware brace scanner**, not a regular
  expression — the thing the leader writes is a PROMPT, and prompts here are
  full of `{placeholders}` and stray braces.
- New: `sentry.leader` on the bridge (read-only and free — an op that spent
  money to answer a question about spending money would be the same bill with an
  extra step) · five settings under Tasks & Automation with the campaign's other
  brakes · `SentryRecord.leader` / `.policy` / `.leaderCaps`.
- `sentryTick` is now async, and its port settles the promise rather than
  letting a rejection walk past the `try`/`catch` into the extension host.

## 3.386.0 - X-189: the handover note is looked for where it was actually written (2026-09-05)

The sentry looked for the last session's handover note in ONE hard-coded folder
under ONE millimetric name pattern. An agent that wrote its note anywhere else,
or called it anything else, was invisible — and the campaign then diagnosed
`hit-the-wall` about a session that had handed over perfectly well. That is not
a missing measurement, it is a false one: it sends the next round after the
wrong thing, and you find out in the morning. New pure module
`src/core/handoverDiscovery.ts`.

- **‼️ Four sources, in order, and the order is the argument.** `transcript`
  first — the files the finished session ITSELF wrote, read back out of its own
  transcript, because where the agent actually wrote beats where a setting says
  it should have. Then `configured` (`agentFarm.handoverFolders`, with X-188
  path variables), then the project's own `10_Notes`, and only then the folder
  this extension shipped with. A folder reached twice is listed once.
- **‼️ Scoring replaced the all-or-nothing pattern — not the identity check.**
  The session id in the name or the session having written the file (+3), the
  word devir/handover (+2), a date near today (+1), the full canonical name
  (+2). The canonical name is still preferred; it is just no longer required.
  But one of the two identity proofs is REQUIRED at any score: adopting another
  session's handover note is a worse failure than finding none, and "devir +
  today + canonical" describes every note in the folder.
- **‼️ A folder nobody could read is unknown, never empty.** X-174's law makes
  the trip intact: `measured:false` means say nothing about whether a note
  exists. A skipped source reports the reason in the caller's own words.
- **The near misses are kept**, ranked, with the components that scored — so the
  answer to "why was my note not picked up" is on the record rather than in
  somebody's head.
- **The legacy vault folder is now a named constant** reached last by both its
  readers, never a `||` default. X-188's test tightened accordingly.
- New: `sentry.handover` on the bridge (read-only, calls no model, writes
  nothing) · settings `agentFarm.handoverSources` and
  `agentFarm.handoverFolders`, both filed under Tasks & Automation with the
  campaign's other brakes.

## 3.385.0 - X-190: the sentry gets a policy, and the three modes stop being three code paths (2026-09-05)

The sentry that shipped was purely mechanical: measure, fill a template, open
the next round, never think. You asked for the switch instead — mechanical /
intelligent / hybrid — with condition inputs wide and flexible, because "çok dar
kalıplara sıkışmış bir hibrit sistem çok etkili olmaz". New pure module
`src/core/sentryPolicy.ts` decides, and it costs nothing to decide.

- **‼️ The three modes are three PRESETS over one condition set, not three
  branches.** Mechanical is the empty set, intelligent is a set that always
  fires, hybrid is whatever you build. Written as branches, two of them would
  rot unwatched — and three fixed modes would be exactly the narrow mould. As
  presets, the mechanical path is exercised by every hybrid round that fires
  nothing.
- **Seventeen fields, ten operators, AND groups.** Fields cover the diagnosis,
  the handover note and where it came from, the repository, the round, the
  quota, the accounts and the raw output. Conditions are ORed; a group's parts
  are ANDed; an empty group is not "always".
- **‼️ An unknown field fails with its eyes open.** It does not fire — firing on
  a name nobody implemented spends money at 3 a.m. — and it is not swallowed
  either, because a condition that quietly never fires is a rule that failed
  silently. It comes back by name, and a broken row never disarms the working
  ones. Same for a regular expression that will not compile.
- **The verdict names what woke the leader**, so a round can say why it was
  opened the way it was.
- The dictionary lives in one exported list, so the missions editor (X-194)
  draws it rather than repeating it: adding a field touches no UI.

Nothing is wired to it yet — the leader turn itself is X-191. This is the
decision, tested on its own, with no way for it to spend anything.

## 3.384.0 - X-188: a folder setting you can write, and a resolver that refuses to guess (2026-09-05)

Three folders in this extension ended in one person's Obsidian vault, spelled
out in the source: the wiki root, the report folder and the answers folder. Your
words about it were exact — a program is written open-ended and elastic, not
against today's folder — and about what may survive: today's folders may stay,
**as a fallback and nothing more**.

- **`${vault}` `${workspace}` `${home}` `${today}` `${date:YYMMDD}` and nine
  others now work in every one of those settings.** The syntax is `${…}` because
  that is what the settings file next to it already speaks (`${workspaceFolder}`,
  `${userHome}`), and both of VS Code's names work as aliases. Prompt templates
  keep their own `{name}`: two subjects, neither borrowing the other's
  punctuation.
- **‼️ An unresolved variable CANCELS the path — it never becomes an empty
  string.** `${vault}/01_CEVAPLAR` on a machine with no vault skips that folder
  rather than looking in `\01_CEVAPLAR`, finding nothing and reporting it as an
  answer. An unknown name and a known one with nothing behind it are told apart
  in the reason: one is a typo you can fix, the other is a machine that has no
  such thing.
- **New setting `agentFarm.vaultDir`** — say where your vault is once, and the
  three folders derive from it. The built-in defaults are now
  `${vault}/00_WIKI`, `${vault}/…/10_REPORT`, `${vault}/…/01_CEVAPLAR`, so the
  legacy absolute path is only reached when neither your setting nor the
  built-in template can be BUILT. Nothing changes for you until you set it.
- A resolved value is not re-expanded, so a folder literally called `${home}`
  cannot loop or reach anywhere it was not pointed.
- The dictionary of variables lives in one exported list, so the settings
  surface X-193 adds can draw it instead of repeating it.

## 3.383.0 - X-187: the Engines page asks for the quota it draws (2026-09-05)

You captured three accounts, opened Engines and saw no limit anywhere — no bar,
no reset countdown. The page was telling the truth: nobody had ever looked.
`AccountUsageService` was built with three doors (`beat()` for a timer,
`readOnEdge()` for a turn that just ended, `refresh()` for a person) and on the
day it shipped exactly one of them was wired — the bridge's own `accounts.list`.
The page read `current()`, which never touches the network, so on a cold host
every card drew percent -1 and resetsAt 0.

- **Opening the page asks for a reading, and revealing an open one asks again.**
  The answer lands as a fresh payload, so the figures arrive somewhere the page
  actually redraws from.
- **Capturing, standing up or forgetting an account asks too** — each changes
  which accounts there are to have figures for.
- **One timer for the page, never one per account.** The service already walks
  the slots in turn behind a single machine-wide floor and backoff, so three
  accounts still do not mean three times the requests. The timer is skipped
  while the tab is hidden and cleared when the page closes.
- The old guard "this panel schedules nothing" was a proxy for what actually
  matters — nothing may spend a TURN on its own — and is now stated that way,
  with an allow-list of exactly one thing a timer here may call. A usage reading
  is a free GET; an engine test costs your plan, and still runs only from the
  button.

## 3.382.0 - U-130 (1/n): the sessions table pays its own hover debt (2026-09-05)

The first page off the budget U-128 opened. The shared Sessions table's sort box
drew six options that said nothing; each now opens with its own name and then
says what picking it DOES — which is a different fact from what the figure means
(that is the column's `<th>`), so neither repeats the other.

- Because the table is shared, one fix lowered four pages at once: **sessions
  30→0, agentdetail 6→0, dashboard 39→33, planusage 156→132.** Fleet total
  2 291 → 2 225 and the budget is relocked at the new floor, which is the whole
  point of a number that may only shrink.
- The Duration option says out loud what S-52 changed: it sorts on the longest
  RUN, never the longest span.

## 3.381.0 - U-128: an option in a narrow box says its own name (2026-09-05)

You asked why the Console's project picker did not show a project's full name on
hover when the boxes beside it did — and answered it in the asking: our own
design principles already said it had to. The measurement was worse than the
report. **2 291 of the 2 639 options this extension draws carried no usable
`title` at all**, including 126 on the Console itself, because options were built
as `title="${detail}"` and most lists carry no detail.

- **Every option the Console draws now opens its hover with its own text**, and a
  detail follows after a blank line — the same order `boxTip` puts the current
  value before the standing explanation. One helper (`optionTip`) that all six of
  the page's option builders go through, so the next list cannot forget it.
- **The project picker** carries the whole project name; **the agent picker**
  carries the name and the folder the session will open in — the thing that
  box's own tooltip has always promised.
- **‼️ And it is measured, so it cannot come back.** `test/test_option_tips.js`
  renders every page fixture and counts the options that say nothing;
  `test/optiontips.manifest.json` holds a per-page budget that may only SHRINK,
  exactly like the parity gate's `gapBudget`. A page missing from the manifest
  must be at zero, so a NEW page cannot arrive with the defect in it. The
  Console is at **0 of 249**; the other 23 pages are recorded at today's numbers
  and can be paid down one at a time.

## 3.380.0 - S-52: a session you resume tomorrow did not run for a day (2026-09-05)

The Sessions table measured Duration from the first message to the last. That figure is
true, but it was the only one on the row — so a conversation picked up again the next
morning read as a day and a half, and every rate derived from it was divided by a night's
sleep. Measured on this machine: **36 sessions** carry a gap of over an hour, the worst of
them reporting 1 247 minutes for 144 minutes of work.

- **Duration is now what the session RAN**, with the span it ran ACROSS beside it —
  `50m ⋯25.8 h` — in the same shape the token column already uses for its second figure.
  A session that was never put down is drawn exactly as before, mark and all absent.
- **‼️ Absence is measured BETWEEN turns, never inside one.** A three-hour headless round
  is the work itself; a rule that called a long turn absence would subtract exactly what
  the figure exists to show.
- **‼️ Nothing is subtracted on no evidence.** A session whose turns were not recorded is
  unmeasured, not idle: active falls back to the wall clock rather than to a guess.
- **The rates follow the work.** Cost per hour, minutes per turn and seconds per API call
  are divided by what ran; below an hour of real work no rate is stated at all, where the
  wall clock used to manufacture one out of the sleep (23 cents an hour said nothing).
- The cell's hover carries the absence, how many times it happened, and the wall clock it
  was carved out of — and says none of it on a session that has none.
- `agentFarm.sessionBreakMin`, default 30 minutes, decides when a pause stops being
  someone thinking and becomes someone away. **0 switches the split off** and Duration
  goes back to being first-to-last.

## 3.379.0 - X-178: the watchdog, and a sign-in that falls at two in the morning (2026-09-04)

The campaign's loop is driven by rounds ENDING. That left one state nothing could
recover from — a round that never ends — and the quota does not break it either,
because a session parked on a permission prompt spends nothing.

- **A watchdog on the beat the farm already keeps** (no second scheduler): the same pump
  tick that asks "is the campaign due?" now also asks "is the round on the board still
  alive?". Silence is measured from the run's own output, so it is engine-agnostic and a
  thinking turn is never touched. `agentFarm.sentryStallMin`, default 45 minutes, 0 to
  switch it off.
- **‼️ The stalled round is ended as FAILED, never as cancelled.** Cancelling the round
  the sentry is running is your hand on the campaign and stops it — the opposite of what
  a watchdog is for. Failed is a barren round, so three stalls in a row still hit the
  failure brake and a genuinely broken setup still ends. It is **not retried**: the row a
  retry would re-run is the row that went quiet.
- **The reason is written down in three places** — the row's own event, a level-2 notice,
  and the campaign's next decision. Silent stopping is forbidden by the item's own words.
- **A fallen sign-in is now reported.** It never stopped the campaign (an expired slot is
  already refused and the rest carry the work) — but nobody was told, which is the same
  loss in slow motion. Told **once per fall**, re-armed when the slot answers again, and
  raised to level 3 with different words when it was the last usable account.
- `sentry.status` now carries `stallMin` and `downSlots`.

## 3.378.0 - X-177: the sentry, in one line, where your eye already is (2026-09-04)

The other half of the item. Missions carries the campaign's setup and its history; the
**Console** — the page you are already looking at — now carries what is true this second,
and no fact is drawn on both.

- **A one-line sentry strip under the Console header.** Running, it says which round is
  open on which item, as whom, on which sign-in, and **how much of that account's
  five-hour window is left** — the one figure no task row can carry. Sleeping, it says
  when it wakes and why it is waiting, in the campaign's own words. Paused, it says so.
  Stopped, it is still drawn, faded, saying what stopped it — because a campaign that
  ended at three in the morning is exactly what somebody needs to read at nine.
- It has **no controls of its own**: pressing it goes to Missions, where they are. The
  whole sentence, the project, the round count and the words the next round is already
  holding are one hover away.
- **‼️ The live clock left Missions.** That block already said in its own comment that
  what is true this second is the Console's subject, and then drew the campaign's wake
  moment anyway. It is now in one place.
- **‼️ Fixed: a wait destroyed the sentence the next round was holding.** `backlog.next`
  gives nothing while every remaining item is XL or waiting on an unfinished ⛔ — a WAIT,
  which says nothing about whether the words still fit. They were dropped there anyway,
  so the item back at the top ten minutes later opened on the campaign's FIRST-round
  sentence: the same failure 3.377.0 fixed, through another door. Only a DIFFERENT item
  drops them now. And words built while the backlog had nothing to give — they name an
  empty item — are no longer kept over words that name a real one.

## 3.377.0 - X-177: the sentry has a face, and a pause of its own (2026-09-04)

The campaign shipped in 3.376.0 could only be reached from the bridge. It now has the
surface it belongs on: **Missions**, which is already the page for work that runs while
nobody is watching. No third panel was opened — the item forbids one by name.

- **A Sentry block at the top of Missions.** Off, it says what a campaign would do before
  you press anything. Set up, it is four rows of controls: the project whose backlog it
  works through, the agent it runs as, the engine (naming one is what turns account
  rotation on), the model, the permissions, the ceiling, the safety buffer, the failure
  brake, and the words the FIRST round opens on — which are yours because every
  continuation sentence is built on "the previous session" and the first round has none.
- **Running, it is the campaign's own account of itself:** the state in one word, the
  last plan IN ITS OWN WORDS (why nothing is happening right now is the question a
  surface has to answer), what it is working through and as whom, the barren streak
  against its brake, the moment it wakes if it is sleeping off a quota wall, and every
