  round it has opened with the account each one spent.
- **‼️ Pause is now the campaign's own, not the farm's.** The automation master switch
  stops every schedule there is; wanting the sentry to stand still for an hour is not
  wanting that. A paused campaign opens nothing, still holds the one campaign slot, and
  keeps everything it had worked out — above all the sentence it had already built for
  its next round. Resume looks at the backlog AT ONCE rather than serving out the poll it
  was paused in the middle of. `sentry.pause` and `sentry.resume` on the bridge.
- **‼️ A round that ends while the campaign is paused is still read.** The verdict and
  the next session's words are free to compute, so a hold does not throw away what the
  round earned.

## 3.376.0 - X-176: the sentry campaign actually runs (2026-09-04)

X-174 could say what a finished session left behind and X-175 could say what to tell the
next one, but nothing CALLED either of them. This release is the runner: switch a campaign
on for a project, and it takes the next item off that project's backlog, opens a clean
unattended session on it, watches that session end, diagnoses it, writes the next
session's opening words from the verdict, and opens the next round — until you stop it.

- **A round is an ORDINARY TASK ROW.** The same runner opens it, the same terminal is
  watched, the same cancel button ends it, the same pump launches it. That is how "no
  second scheduler" — the item's own condition — holds all the way down to the launch.
  The price is that the task board fills with campaign rounds, which is the accepted cost.
- **‼️ Only you end a campaign.** There is no round budget and no time budget, so an
  EMPTY BACKLOG IS A WAIT rather than a finish: an item written tomorrow morning finds
  the sentry still standing there. The brakes that do exist are the ones that already
  existed — the automation gate (master switch, pause, quiet hours), the five-hour
  ceiling per account, and a sleep until the earliest MEASURED reset plus a safety buffer.
- **‼️ Cancelling the round cancels the campaign.** The sentry runs one session at a
  time, so reaching for cancel on the round it is running is you saying stop. The machine
  is reading your switch, not inventing one of its own.
- **‼️ A failure brake, which is not a round budget.** A campaign whose sessions produce
  NOTHING, over and over, is a broken setup opening empty sessions all night — and no
  quota stops it, because a session that fails instantly spends nothing. Three barren
  rounds in a row switch it off with a notice; the streak is wiped by the first round that
  achieves something. `agentFarm.sentryFailureLimit` changes it, `0` switches it off, and
  a campaign may carry its own.
- **‼️ What nobody measured is not a measurement**, all the way through the runner. An
  answers folder that would not list is not "no handover note"; a `git status` that would
  not answer is not "clean"; and one unreadable repository makes the whole repo fact
  unmeasured, because "clean" is a claim about all of them. Those land in the verdict's
  `unknown`, where they ask instead of assuming.
- **‼️ Engine-agnostic, by name.** A campaign that names no engine runs every round on
  the main sign-in and rotates no account — choosing one would mean assuming an engine.
  `sentry.start` and `sentry.status` both say so (`rotatesAccounts`) rather than leaving
  you to wonder why nothing rotates.
- **On the bridge:** `sentry.start` (project, agent, the words the first round opens on,
  and the dimensions every round is launched with — including `permissionMode`, without
  which an unattended round can stop to ask and never end), `sentry.stop` (the record is
  kept; a round already on the board is left alone), and `sentry.status` (the last plan in
  its own words, the moment it wakes, the rounds it opened, the streak against its brake).
- **New settings** in Farm Settings → Tasks & Automation: `agentFarm.sentryFailureLimit`
  and `agentFarm.sentryIdlePollMin` (how often an idling campaign looks at the backlog
  again — it never shortens a measured sleep, so a three-hour quota wall is waited out
  rather than poked every ten minutes).

## 3.375.0 - X-174 · X-175: what a finished session left behind, and the sentence the next one opens on (2026-09-04)

The sentry (X-167) has to answer two questions every time a session ends, and both
of them used to be answered by asking a model: *what did that session actually
leave behind*, and *what do I say to the next one*. Neither needs a model, and the
precedent for what happens when you ask one anyway is on this repo's own bill —
a question that could have been counted cost $70.90 over five nights.

- **The verdict is counted, not asked.** `sessionDiagnosis` takes facts somebody
  MEASURED and reaches one of four verdicts: the item was closed, a clean handover
  note was left, there was nothing to carry on from, or the session hit the wall
  with work outstanding. It reads nothing itself — no disk, no git, no model —
  which is what makes "this is free" auditable rather than a claim.
- **‼️ What nobody measured is not a measurement.** A folder that was never listed
  lands in `unknown`; a folder that was listed and was empty is evidence. Collapse
  those two and the machine invents a verdict out of its own defaults, then starts
  the next session on it.
- **The decision ladder is a POLICY, not a rule carved in.** Four named keys, with
  the defaults spelled out, so a campaign can hand its own down; every verdict
  carries which policy produced it and which rule fired.
- **The prompt the next session opens on** is rendered from that verdict, the item
  `projects.backlog.next` picked and the path of the handover note. A model is
  called only while facts are missing, and the module says so as a decision —
  `assist.needed`, plus the questions worth asking — instead of making the call
  itself. What a call cost (which model, how long, how much) travels in the words
  the next session reads.
- **‼️ Every template ships INSIDE Agent Farm** and answers every verdict with
  nothing configured — no file, no vault, no folder of yours anywhere. Name a
  markdown file in `agentFarm.sentryTemplatesFile` (Settings → Tasks & Automation)
  and it REPLACES only the verdicts it answers, so adding a case is a block rather
  than a release. A heading naming no verdict is refused by name and reported: a
  template that silently never fires is an evening nobody gets back. A path that
  is not on disk is reported, never cleared.
- **On the bridge:** `sentry.templates` says which words are in force and where
  they came from, `sentry.prompt` turns measured facts into the sentence. Neither
  calls anything and neither writes anything, so asking twice costs nothing and
  answers the same.

## 3.374.0 - X-172: the sign-ins the Engines page can capture, stand up and drop (2026-09-04)

The chip slice made the Engines page SAY which account each engine is plugged
into and left every gesture on the bridge. A page that shows a state it cannot
change is the dead end this page exists to remove, in a new costume.

- **One card per captured sign-in** — the label, the address, the plan being paid
  for, and how much of the five-hour window is gone.
- **A bar only where a figure was really read.** `-1` is not 0%: an account nobody
  has read a percentage for and an account with nothing left would draw the same
  empty bar, and one of them is ready to work. The other two states say which one
  they are in, in words.
- **The way back exists.** The main sign-in is the ABSENCE of a slot, so there is
  no row to press: the standing card offers "Main account", which clears the
  engine rather than naming one. Without it the page could put an engine on an
  account and never take it off again.
- **Capture is offered only where two identities can really be kept apart** —
  three of the five engines have no verified way, and they say WHY in the
  adapter's own words rather than being left out of the list.
- **Both defaults are the op's, deliberately:** capturing does not become the
  standing choice, and forgetting does not delete the directory. The page says
  both out loud.
- `captureAccount` / `activateAccount` / `forgetAccount` are one function each,
  called by BOTH the page's buttons and the `accounts.*` ops — a page and its op
  cannot drift into meaning different things.

## 3.373.0 - X-169: which sign-in pays for the session, at every door (2026-09-04)

Three Claude Pro plans on one machine, switched by hand all day: `/login` in a
terminal, the right Chrome profile, sometimes a fresh Google sign-in. X-168
measured the way out — `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` isolates an account completely, so
switching is not copying files over the live one, it is pointing the SPAWN at a
different directory. This is that measurement turned into a launch dimension.

`account` is the seventeenth field of `LaunchOptions`, which means the matrix
that counts "every dimension, every door" grew from 208 obligations to 221 and
went red until every one of the thirteen had a verdict. Eleven doors carry it;
two say out loud why they do not.

- **The composer has a box for it**, beside the route, and it opens on whatever
  the standing choice is — so the account a session will spend is readable before
  Send rather than discoverable afterwards. Its hover says which one is set, then
  what "empty" means: the main sign-in, the identity this machine is logged in as.
- **The launcher has a row**, the Tasks form has a box, and `sessions.start`,
  `console.start` and `tasks.add` all take an `account` argument and answer with
  the one they really started as. A task is unattended, so "the nightly batch on
  the second plan" can only be said when the task is WRITTEN or it is never said.
- **An id naming no stored slot is REFUSED, not downgraded.** Falling back to the
  main account for a slot that was forgotten would start the run on whoever
  happens to be signed in — the exact accident this whole family exists to end.
  An account belongs to one engine and is refused on another.
- **The variable's NAME is the engine adapter's** (`engineAccounts.accountEnv`).
  No door and no runner spells `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`; an engine that cannot isolate
  a sign-in shows no control at all rather than one that pretends to work.
- **It is NOT remembered per agent, and that is the decision.** A model is a
  preference; an account is a STATE — how much of a plan is left, which changes
  hourly. Remembered, it would pin an agent to an exhausted plan and, through the
  S-34 layer order, would silently outrank the "use this next" gesture: a button
  that does nothing visible. `agentFarm.activeAccounts` holds it, per engine, and
  a launch that names one still wins.
- **One injection path, not a second one.** The environment goes in through the
  `layers` argument `providerRuntime.spawnEnvironment` and `terminalEnvOverlay`
  already take — the place that knows a name left OUT of a terminal overlay is
  not removed by leaving it out (only `null` removes it).
- **A card keeps the account it started on.** It is on the session state, like
  the route, so a re-spawn or a window reload cannot walk a live conversation
  onto whichever plan the button was last pressed for.

Nothing changes on a machine that has captured no accounts: no variable is
injected, no box is drawn, and every launch is byte for byte what it was.

## 3.372.0 - U-129: the install button types a command that can actually run (2026-09-03)

Every Install button on the Engines page typed `npm install -g …` into a terminal,
and on the machine that needs it most — a bare one, with no engine on it — that
machine has no Node either. So the answer was `npm is not recognized`, for all of
them, which reads as a page whose buttons do not work.

Three of the five engines ship an official installer that needs nothing at all, and
the user's own migration system (`_setup\Install-Engines.ps1`) already puts those
FIRST: the `Script` method is method #1 for Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity, with
npm as the fallback. This page now copies that table rather than giving a second
answer to the same question. Measured on this machine: `claude` resolves to
`~/.local/bin`, `codex` to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\OpenAI\Codex\bin` — both native
installs, neither from npm.

- **Claude Code · Codex · Antigravity** — the vendor's own script, picked by
  platform: `irm … | iex` on Windows, `curl … | bash` elsewhere. Antigravity had no
  install command at all before, only a sentence, so it was the one row the page
  could not put in front of a terminal.
- **Gemini · OpenCode** — still npm, because that really is where they come from,
  and the row now says the route needs Node.js v20+ instead of leaving the shell to
  say something unreadable.
- **The sign-in was wrong too, in the way that is hardest to see:** `claude /login`
  is not an error. It starts an ordinary session with `/login` as the prompt — the
  CLI opens, nothing signs in. It is `claude auth login`, read off the CLI's own
  help. Codex and OpenCode were already right.
- **And the line is typed into a shell that can run it.** On Windows the terminal is
  opened as PowerShell: `irm … | iex` typed into cmd is the same unreadable failure,
  one layer further out.

Nothing runs by itself. The command is still typed, not executed, and the user
reads it and presses Enter.

## 3.371.0 - U-126: the thing that opens is a dot, not a session (2026-09-03)

One press on a colour dot opened two palettes. Not always — only when the same
session was drawn twice in the left column, which is exactly when the reader is
most likely to press one.

The open state was the SESSION ID. `colorDot()` is called from three places for
the three card kinds — the live card, the "where you left off" shelf, the resume
list — and each of them drew a palette for any dot whose id matched. A session
standing on two surfaces therefore answered a single press with two pickers, the
second one hanging over a card the reader never touched.

The slot is not the answer either: the live cards and the shelf are both inside
`c-list`, and the same session really can be on both — a hosted session that has
ENDED keeps its card and comes back onto the shelf the moment it is no longer
running. So the key is now `<surface>|<sessionId>`, carried by the dot itself
(`data-cdot`), and the handler reads it off the button rather than off the slot
it was wired for.

The colour is still a mark filed against the session id alone. Only "which dot is
open" became per-surface — which is what it always meant.

## 3.370.0 - X-166: ticking a box and typing a sentence no longer costs you the boxes (2026-09-03)

The user answered four questions, ticked all four, added a sentence — and the agent
was handed the sentence alone. It read as an agent ignoring them. It was not.

**MEASURED, over every AskUserQuestion in the transcript history (26 calls, eight
months): when `response` is present the CLI renders `"The user responded: <text>"`
and DROPS `answers` outright.** Eight of those calls lost picks that way. The picks
were never lost from the RECORD — `toolUseResult.answers` has all four of them,
sitting in the transcript that same evening — only from the model's view. That is the
worst shape a bug can have: no error, no gap, an answer that looks complete.

`answerAsk` was sending both, because the composer always sends both: the picks it
has and whatever is in the free-text box. So `askInput` now folds the picks INTO the
response text, which is the only channel that survives, and still sends `answers`
alongside — it costs nothing, it is what the transcript records, and a CLI that one
day honours both would merely repeat itself. The failure worth avoiding is the silent
one.

Untouched: picking with nothing typed, and typing with nothing picked. Only the
combination changes, and only because the combination was the one that lost data.

Selecting and then typing is not exotic. It is what somebody does when the list is
nearly right — which is when their answer is worth the most.

## 3.369.0 - X-151: the doors are modules, and the matrix calls them (2026-08-31)

`test/test_launch_parity.js` wrote this file's reason down before it existed:

> "These live inside quickpick loops and message handlers in extension.ts, which
> nothing can call. **THE SOURCE IS THE HANDLE**, and a missing door here is the
> structural failure `_REF/agentfarm-dev.md` names."

So door parity was measured by throwing regular expressions at 30.476 lines of
source, and that measurement was wrong in both directions at once. A door that
passed a whole `LaunchOptions` through named none of its fields and read as
thirteen gaps; a door that merely MENTIONED a dimension in a comment read as
carrying it. And neither could say anything about a dimension nobody had thought
to write a regex for — which is exactly how `providerId` and `tier` reached the
type, reached the launcher, and never reached the composer.

**The 13 doors are modules now (`src/launch/doors/`)**, each with one job:
`collect(ctx)` returns the intent it has assembled. ‼️ **A door does not start a
session.** The spawning, the recording and the UI plumbing stay exactly where
they were — this is a live product, and extracting the ANSWER is all the matrix
ever needed, while extracting the ACT would have moved seven spawn paths at once
for no extra measurement.

**So the matrix stopped grepping and started calling.** Each door is handed EVERY
dimension there is and asked what it hands on. A dimension that does not survive
the call is not carried, whatever the source says. The gap count fell from **141
to 31** — and the 31 are not noise, they are findings, each one named:

| door | reaches it and stops |
|---|---|
| palette (continue) | model · effort · permissionMode · providerId · tier · variant · superpowers · cli |
| mission | providerId · tier · variant · superpowers · cli |
| projects · webviews | providerId · tier · variant · cli |
| treeMenu | providerId · tier · variant |
| composer | variant · name |
| profile | superpowers |
| bridge | superpowers |
| task · automation | variant |
| treeRow | cli |

**‼️ Not one of them was fixed here.** Whether a "continue" should re-apply the
remembered setup, whether a saved profile should store the discipline, whether a
mission should carry a route — each is a real decision with a real behaviour
change behind it, and this release is a hardening one. They are counted, named
and left for somebody to take.

**‼️ And a door that only DESCRIBES a call site is counted as such.** That is the
same trap one level up: a module modelling what `extension.ts` does is a second
statement of the rule, free to drift. So `wired` is a fact on each door, four of
them really are what the extension calls now (treeRow · treeMenu · launcher ·
projects), the count may only rise, and a test proves each wired door is
genuinely imported rather than merely marked.

Nine source-regex assertions were deleted rather than repointed at the new files
(eight in `test_launch_parity.js`, one in `test_run_surface.js`): their subject
had moved, and a regex aimed at a new file is the same measurement with the same
blind spot. What they claimed is now stated as facts about the doors, proved by
calling them.

## 3.368.0 - X-150 (2/2): 208 obligations, counted (2026-08-31)

"Every launch dimension is carried by every door that starts a session" is true,
important, and until now it lived only in prose — a 1.690-line SOP, a `_REF`
rule, and 74 hand-written regexes, all three of which need a person to read
them. A regex can only see the absence of something it was told to look for; it
cannot look for a rule nobody has written yet. That is exactly how `providerId`
and `tier` reached the type and the launcher and never got a box in the Console
composer with nothing going red.

**A matrix can.** 16 dimensions crossed with 13 doors is 208 cells, and every
one of them must now hold a verdict in `launch.matrix.json`: `carried`,
`exempt: <reason>`, or `gap: <reason>`. A seventeenth dimension therefore
arrives with THIRTEEN cells that have no verdict and the suite is red until
somebody says, per door, which of the three it is. The obligation is created by
the dimension, not by somebody remembering to create it — which is the whole
item.

**‼️ The first count is 67 carried, 141 gaps, and 7 of the 13 doors cannot be
pointed at at all.** That is not a regression; it is the first time anybody has
had the number. Most doors live inside quickpick loops and message handlers in a
30.476-line file, so their cells are declared rather than measured — and
declared as gaps, because `door not addressable yet` is a count and not an
excuse. Driving it to zero is X-151's acceptance criterion, stated in a figure
rather than a paragraph.

**And the half that already bites, bites today.** A cell declared `carried` on a
door that CAN be addressed is re-measured on every run, so taking a dimension
out of `runLauncher` goes red now, without waiting for X-151. `gapBudget` may
only be lowered: raising it means a door stopped carrying something, which is
the failure being counted. Reseed the observable half with
`node test/test_launch_matrix.js --fix` — it never invents an exemption, because
only a person can say a dimension does not apply to a door, and saying it
requires writing why.

The 74 source regexes in `test_launch_parity.js` stay where they are for now:
they are today's per-cell evidence, and deleting them before the doors are
callable would replace measured guarantees with weaker ones. They fall away in
X-151, when a door can be called with a fixture and asked what it collected.

## 3.367.0 - X-150 (1/2): the 16 launch dimensions are data now (2026-08-31)

A session here is described by 16 answers and can be started from 13 places.
That is 208 obligations, and the sentence stating them lived in a 1.690-line
document, in a `_REF` rule, and in 74 hand-written regexes — all three of which
depend on a person remembering to read them. What that costs was measured:
`providerId` and `tier` were added to the type, wired into the launcher, and
simply never given a box in the Console composer. Nothing went red, because
nothing was counting.

**The list is now a record, in `media/afDimensions.js`.** Each row says who the
answer belongs to, whether a launch writes it back, whether it is remembered per
ENGINE (X-145), whether changing it rebuilds the composer shell, where the
dimension does not exist at all — and one line of why it is the way it is. It
lives in `media/` for the reason the clock and the narrowing rule do: both sides
need it, and the shell key has to be computed BY THE PAGE or every repaint waits
a round trip. `src/core/launchDimensions.ts` is its typed door.

**‼️ The array is pinned to `LaunchOptions` in BOTH directions.** A field added
to the interface with no row goes red; a row for a field that no longer exists
goes red too. That is the difference between this and the constant it replaced.

**Three places that counted these fields by hand now fold over the list.**
`ENGINE_MEMORY_FIELDS` is derived rather than typed; the row `launchToRemember`
files under an engine is built from it; and the six engine-owned dimensions
`withLastLaunch` used to name one by one are inherited by the shape. A seventh
of them is a flag on a row now, not six edits somebody has to remember.

**‼️ Two remembered dimensions are exempt from that fold, and the exemption is
counted rather than assumed.** `engine` decides which row the other six are read
FROM, so it cannot be one of them; `superpowers` has three states and
`undefined` is the one that means "the agent's own default decides" (K-34),
which a fold over strings would spell as `''` and quietly turn into a fourth. A
test requires each flat dimension to still be inherited by name — a third one
arriving with nobody to inherit it fails the build.

**S-51 closes as a class.** The composer's shell key was a string built by hand
— the dimension list written a third time, incompletely, in a line that looks
complete either way. It is folded from `redraws: true` now, and the test proves
that every such dimension moves the key and that no other one does (a key that
moved on a keystroke would detach the caret M-33 protects).

Behaviour is unchanged throughout: the four dimensions in the derived key are
exactly the four the hand-written line already counted. Second half of X-150 —
turning the 74 source regexes in `test_launch_parity.js` into the generic
16x13 matrix — is still open.

## 3.366.0 - X-149: one narrowing rule, loaded by both sides (2026-08-31)

"The engine moved — what happens to the boxes under it" was answered in four
places: `narrowLaunch` on the host, `reconcileComposer` in the Console,
`ntNarrowEffort` in the Tasks form, and a fourth in the shared engine component
whose own comment admitted the other three "have not been moved here yet". They
were written from the same intention and they still disagreed — the host counted
`claude-opus-4-5-20251101` and the alias `opus` as ONE model while the pages
pushed the unrecognised value onto the list as a stranger. Nothing measured the
four against each other, which is the mechanical form of the complaint that
opened this work: one thing gets fixed and another breaks.

**There is now one rule and it lives in `media/afLaunch.js`**, the arrangement
the clock and the query language already proved: the pages load it in the
webview and the extension host loads the SAME FILE through
`src/core/aflaunch.ts`. The four bodies are gone, not shadowed — a page that
kept its own would have passed every test and stayed free to drift, so the
absence is measured: `defaultEffort`, the one piece of arithmetic the rule owns,
no longer appears in any of the three page scripts at all.

**‼️ It did NOT make the four agree — that would have changed behaviour on
surfaces that took months to get right.** The differences are real answers to
real cases, so they are PARAMETERS now instead of divergences hidden in a copy:
`keep` is S-34 (a setup a real launch on this engine used beats the catalogue),
`preferModelDefault` is the Console's "a model was just picked by hand",
`resolveAlias` is S-47/K-28 (`big-pickle` resolving to `opencode/big-pickle`),
and `takesEffort` is X-35 (an engine with no effort flag offers none, answered
at each call site because the two page surfaces resolve it differently before a
catalogue has landed). Every one of them is now a word somebody can read, and
converging them is a decision there is finally one place to take.

**`test/test_launch_narrow.js` is one fixture table and every entry point
answers all of it** — Node, a webview sandbox, and the host's own compiled
`narrowLaunch`. A case added there is a case every surface has to pass, and the
page's answer is asserted equal to the host's on all 23 of them, which is the
assertion the four copies could never make. Two source-text regexes in
`test_launch_parity.js` and one in `test_tasks_webview.js` were replaced by
running the rule rather than reading it: their subject had moved, and
re-pointing a regex at the new file would have been the same measurement with
the same blind spot.

First of the four moves in the launch-axis hardening (X-148).

## 3.365.0 - X-106: an unattended run can say which route serves it (2026-08-31)

Every launch dimension on a stored automation is there because of one sentence:
an automation fires with nobody at a window, so anything about the run has to be
stated when the automation is WRITTEN or it is not stated at all. The endpoint
the process really talks to was the one dimension that could not be stated
anywhere — a nightly job took whichever standing route the agent happened to have
at 3 a.m., which is a decision nobody made about a run nobody watched.

**It travels by the shape, not by ten call sites.** `providerId` and `tier` are
now part of `RunDimensions`, so a schedule, a trigger, a template and a workflow
step carry them without any of those knowing they exist — and a retry, a clone
and an edit inherit them the same way. Both spawn shapes in the runner (the
headless one and the interactive one, which live 400 lines apart) pass the task's
own route to the same resolver the Console and the terminals already use.

**Refused, not narrowed — and that is the difference between a composer and an
automation.** A composer redraws, so dropping an impossible value and saying so
is right there. An automation is written once and read months later, so a route
quietly discarded at write time is a run that silently takes the agent's standing
endpoint for ever after. A route this engine cannot be pointed at, a tier the
route does not map, a tier with no route at all, and a route beside a `cli`
profile are each refused by name at the moment they are written down.

Whether a route EXISTS is not a question `core/bridge.ts` can answer — it needs
the engine's adapter and the user's own profiles — so it arrives as a callback,
and the callback is attached in exactly ONE place. Ten doors passing their own
would be ten places to leave it off, and the one left off is the schedule that
stores a typo tonight and refuses it at 3 a.m.

**And the form offers what the bridge offers.** The New-task form has a Route box
(drawn only where the engine has a provider axis with something set up) and a
Tier box under it (drawn only once a route publishes tiers) — because `opus` is
`kimi-k2-thinking` on one route and `MiniMax-M2` on another, so the tiers ride ON
each route rather than in a list of their own. Moving the engine or the route
drops what the new one cannot carry, exactly as the model box already does.

## 3.364.0 - X-105 (6/n): the card says who served the last turn, not only who was asked for (2026-08-31)

X-102 keeps a run's DECLARED half and its REPORTED half apart because they are
allowed to differ, and the Console card had only ever shown the first. On the
engine that may change provider at a turn boundary that gap is a whole state: the
change lands, the next turn has not started, and the engine's own events still
name the provider that served turn four while the card is configured on another.
A card that could state only one of those was answering the wrong question for
the entire window between the two.

The route mark now carries three facts and each line is drawn only when it says
something the line above it does not: the pill is **who serves the next turn**,
`Started on:` is the launch record (untouched — the manifest is immutable),
and `Last turn ran on:` is **what the engine itself reported**, in its own words
rather than as the request. Both derived through the anti-guess reader, so a
prefix is a provider only where the engine published it — which is why this is
absent on Claude and always will be: the transcript names a model and never a
route, measured, and reading one out of the other is the one thing this family
forbids.

`console.sessions` and `console.switch` hand back the same three facts from the
same single reader, so an agent and the panel cannot come away with different
answers about one card.

## 3.363.0 - X-105 (5/n): a provider change is answered, not guessed (2026-08-31)

The item's second sentence is a POLICY, and it had no home in the code: Claude
forbids a provider change inside one conversation and wants a new session or a
fork, while OpenCode genuinely allows one at a turn boundary and records it as a
new turn identity. Until now nothing asked the question at all — `console.setModel`
on OpenCode moved the provider silently (the wire name **is** `provider/model`),
and the card went on naming the route it launched on.

**The verdict is the adapter's, and no engine is named to reach it.**
`src/core/providerSwitch.ts` answers one question — may this live session change
who serves it, and when — out of `providerScope` and
`canSwitchProviderAtTurnBoundary`. Four answers, and `unchanged` is one of them:
`unchanged` · `now` · `turn-boundary` · `refuse`. A refusal carries the remedy
(`fork` when there is a conversation to carry over, `new` when there is not),
because a no with nothing after it leaves the caller nowhere. The module names
no engine at all, and a test measures that: a sixth engine gets the right answer
by declaring its scope, not by somebody remembering to edit a list.

**`console.switch` is the one door.** It asks the policy, THROWS a refusal
rather than returning a success with a sentence beside it, and — on the engine
where the model names the provider — refuses to invent a model, listing what
that provider actually serves instead. `console.setModel` still changes what
answers; this changes who serves it, and on two engines those are different
questions.

**And the card says who is serving it NOW.** On OpenCode a mid-session model
change moves the provider, so a pill naming the launch value was pointing at an
endpoint the session had stopped talking to. Both facts are kept and neither is
stored twice: the current provider is DERIVED from the model the card is on
(through the anti-guess reader — a prefix is only a provider when the engine
published it), the launch record is untouched because X-102 made it immutable,
and the panel's first line is the current one with `Started on:` under it. Same
mark, no second pill, and the line is drawn only on a card that really moved.

## 3.362.0 - X-105 (4/n): the composer PICKS the route, and the bridge can too (2026-08-31)

X-103 made the route pickable in the launcher; X-105 (2/n) made the started card
say what serves it. Between those two the composer carried the pick **blind**: a
route handed over by a launcher was applied and had no box, so the person about
to press Send could not see it, change it, or clear it — and a composer opened
without one had no way to choose at all.

It has two controls now, and **the words are the engine's**: `Route` on Claude,
`Provider` on OpenCode, `Tier` under it — all read off the engine's own adapter
through the SAME `providerFormFor` the launcher's route row is built from and the
card's pill resolves through. A fourth reader is exactly what X-105's acceptance
line cannot survive.

**‼️ AND THE SUB-AXIS IS ONLY A BOX WHERE IT IS A TIER.** Where the engine's
sub-axis is the MODEL — OpenCode names one `provider/model` — that axis is
already on this strip, so a picked provider **narrows the model box that is
there** instead of adding a second one beside it. Two controls for one subject
can disagree within a click, and ONE SUBJECT is the rule that would break.

**‼️ Nothing is drawn where there is nothing to choose.** Four of five engines
have no provider axis, and the fifth gets no box until a route has actually been
set up — so the row measured at `nowrap` is unchanged for everybody who has never
made one. There is no variant control either, and that is the transport's answer
rather than an omission: a hosted card is spoken to over ACP, which declares only
model and mode. The form says why, in the route box's own hover.

**The narrowing stays where it belongs.** Picking a route, and moving the engine
underneath one, both go through the adapter's own `prunePick` — which says out
loud what it dropped, so a tier that stops existing is not something you discover
at Send.

**And the bridge got it in the same commit**, because `_REF/agentfarm-dev.md` is
explicit that a session dimension reaches every door or it is a structural
failure. `console.start` takes `providerId` and `tier`, **refuses** a route the
engine cannot be pointed at rather than dropping it, and answers with what it was
really pointed at — through the same resolver the card uses.

**‼️ S-51's lesson applied twice more.** Both pickers repaint on the spot instead
of waiting for the host's echo to arrive under the reader's hand. And because the
tiers under a route can only come FROM the host, the page now marks the one push
it is waiting for: an answer you asked for is not "a rebuild nobody asked for",
so M-33 lets that single push through and still defers every other one.

## 3.361.0 - S-51: the engine moves, and the boxes move with it (2026-08-31)

In the user's words: *"change the engine and the models and the efforts used to
follow it; now they do not. You go to open the model box yourself, and only once
you press it does it become what it should have been."*

That last sentence was the whole diagnosis. The model list, the effort list and
the hint that says what an engine changes about the composer are **all** drawn
off the composer's current engine, so none of them moves without a shell rebuild
— and the engine picker had no rebuild of its own. Its only one was the host's
echo of the choice, which arrives at the one moment the reader's hand is still on
the picker they just used, because a native `<select>` keeps focus after a
choice. M-33 read that as hands-on and put the rebuild on the slate; the debt was
then paid by the `focusout` of the user reaching for the model box — which is
precisely why the list corrected itself the instant they went to argue with it.

**M-33 was not the thing to loosen.** Its rule already says *only a rebuild
nobody asked for waits*, and this one was asked for by the very hand it was
waiting on. So the fix is the answer the model picker beside it has always used:
the engine picker repaints on the spot, and hands focus back to itself afterwards
so an arrow-key walk through the engine list still reaches its second step.

Measured on the page, with the hand held on the picker the way the browser holds
it — and the deferral it does **not** touch is measured in the same file: a
rebuild nobody asked for still waits while a box is held, and is still paid the
moment the hands come free.

## 3.360.0 - X-105 (3/n): one reader for the route, and the bridge says it too (2026-08-31)

`console.sessions` described every dimension of a hosted card except the one this
whole line of work exists to establish: **what is answering on the other side of
the engine.** An agent could read the engine, the shape, the model, the effort,
the permissions and the tokens — and still not know which company served the
conversation.

It says `route` now: the route's id and name, the engine's own noun for it, the
tier, the endpoint, the auth kind, and the engine's own words for how long the
pick lasts. `null` where there is none — and the op's description says what that
means, because otherwise a missing route reads as a missing feature.

**And it is the same reader the card draws from.** The resolution lives in one
place that both the page and the op delegate to, and it asks the engine's own
adapter — the same one the launcher's route row is built from — for the words it
uses. If those were two readings, "what the card says is what the process runs
on" could not be true by construction: it can only hold while there is one
statement.

## 3.359.0 - X-105 (2/n): the card says what it is served by (2026-08-31)

The engine badge has always said which **program** is running. It has never said
what that program is *talking to* — and two cards on the same engine can be
served by two different companies' models at the same moment. The Console has
carried the pick since 3.35x and said it out loud nowhere, which made the one
fact this whole line of work exists to establish the one fact you could not
check.

**The route is now its own mark, beside the engine badge.** Not a line inside
it: the engine is the program, the route is the endpoint, and a badge that
answers two questions is a badge that will eventually answer one of them wrong.

It appears only when there **is** a route. Four of the five engines have no
provider axis at all and most Claude launches pick none — a pill reading "none"
on every row would cost every reader something to learn nothing.

The pill carries the route's own short name; hovering it opens with the long
form, then the **endpoint** — the line that makes the mark checkable instead of
decorative — the tier, and the engine's own words for how long the pick lasts
(fixed for the session on Claude; changeable at a turn boundary on OpenCode).
Those words come from the same reader the launcher's route row is built from, so
what the card says and what the picker said cannot drift apart.

Nothing secret is anywhere near it: the endpoint is an ordinary setting, and the
credential is not read and has no field to travel in — measured on the rendered
page, not on the type.

Deliberately not in an engine colour: those five hues mean "which engine" on
every surface here, so a sixth pill wearing one would read as a sixth engine.

## 3.358.0 - X-105 (1/n): the Console card runs on the route the card says it is on (2026-08-31)

**The same defect, a fourth time — this time on the surface the Console exists
for.**

Three surfaces already hand the CLI a complete environment: the per-turn engines
since X-101, the OS terminal window since X-104. The Console's own Claude path
never did. It started the process with a working directory and nothing else, so
the session inherited whatever the VS Code window happened to be carrying.

What that produces is this family's quiet failure, and it is the reason it went
unnoticed: a card started on Kimi keeps Kimi on its state, writes Kimi into the
launch manifest and reports Kimi on every surface — while the process talks to
whichever endpoint the window held. Every surface agrees with every other one,
and all of them are wrong about the only thing that matters.

**And the card with no route chosen is the half that is easy to miss.** "No
route" is not "no statement": the official endpoint is reached by *clearing* what
was inherited. A leftover `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` in the window answered the exact
question the official route was picked to answer, and nothing here could say
otherwise because nothing here was said at all.

The card's **own** route is used — the one it was started on, not the agent's
standing one. A card started on Kimi stays on Kimi even after the setting changes
under it, because a route change is a different program.

Measured by driving a real session host and reading back what the process was
actually given: the route reaches it, the inherited one is gone rather than
outvoted, everything else the window carried survives (an overlay, not a
replacement), and a card with no route is no longer hijacked by a leftover.

*Deliberately unchanged:* the shared OpenCode runtime is one process for the
whole window and can carry no per-card environment — and does not need to, since
OpenCode's provider is its own native configuration.

## 3.357.0 - S-50 and U-127: the Console the door opened, and one Sessions column (2026-08-31)

Two long-standing wrongs, each fixed at the one place it was made.

### S-50 — the play button works even when the Console was closed

Every door that starts a session hands the Console the agent, the engine and the
whole setup: the ▶ on an agent row, the launcher's **Start Session**, "Talk to
agent", the project page. It worked — as long as the Console was **already
open**. Opened cold, none of it arrived: not the agent, not the engine, not the
model, effort or permission mode. The composer came up on the fleet defaults as
though nobody had chosen anything, on both doors at once, which is exactly why
it read as "the feature does not work" rather than as a timing bug.

The cause was one line of ordering. The page's shell was built inside the
panel's constructor, which runs **before** `show()` applies the caller's
options — so the first payload the page ever read described a panel nobody had
told anything yet. The refresh that followed pushed the real answers into a
webview whose script had not run, and **a push into an unloaded page is not
late, it is lost**. The preselected agent is deliberately one-shot (it seeds the
picker once and is let go), so that dropped payload did not merely arrive late:
it took the agent with it, and nothing could ever say it again. With no session
running, no host event fires either — so "later" never came at all.

Loading the page is now a step of its own, taken **after** the door has said what
it came to say. What was chosen is in the page's first payload. A refresh aimed
at a page that has not loaded yet returns instead of spending the one-shot on
nobody.

An already-open Console is untouched: it is revealed and pushed to, which is the
channel a loaded page reads — and that path is measured in the same test file, so
a fix to one can never be paid for out of the other. A plain **Open Console**
still opens a plain composer with nobody preselected.

### U-127 — one Sessions column, one vocabulary

In the Runs table, a Claude row said `bc384059`. The Antigravity row under it
said the word **transcript**.

Not the engine's fault — a question of where each CLI puts the id. Claude names
the *file* after the session (`<id>.jsonl`), so reading the file's name has
always been right for it. Antigravity names the *folder* and gives every
conversation a file of the same name
(`…/brain/<id>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl`), so the column printed
a constant. A column of identifiers with a constant in it is a column you cannot
match against a Console card, a swim lane or a log line — which is the whole
reason it is there.

The file is asked first (Claude, unchanged to the character), then the folders
above it, nearest first. The folder test is a full id on purpose: a looser one
would read Claude's own project folder as a session. Anything unrecognised comes
back exactly as it did before.

Measured against this machine's own run history, both engines:

| engine | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| Antigravity | `transcript` | `18b148ce` |
| Claude | `bc384059` | `bc384059` |

## 3.356.0 - X-104 (1/n): the OS terminal window runs on the route you picked (2026-08-31)

Of every surface that starts a CLI, the external terminal was the only one that
carried **no environment at all**.

The integrated terminal has taken an overlay since 3.34x — the agent's own
variables, plus the route's endpoint and key, plus the names to CLEAR so an
inherited Anthropic route cannot answer the same question a second time. The
external branch, three lines away, dropped every bit of it. So with
`Agent Farm: External Terminal` switched on, a session you picked as Kimi (or
MiniMax, or any custom route) opened on the **default** route — and the launcher
row, the engine badge and the launch manifest all said Kimi, because every one of
them reads what you SELECTED rather than what the process was given. Nothing
anywhere contradicted it. The same hole swallowed a custom CLI's own variables,
and it was there for both doors that open an OS window: a session terminal and an
interactive task set to "OS terminal window".

Both doors now hand the window exactly the map their integrated twin gets. Where
you want to watch a run has never been a statement about what it should run on.

**On Windows the values travel in a file the script eats, and they are not in
the script.** There is no in-memory channel to an OS window here: when Windows
Terminal is already running, `wt.exe` is a thin client and the window is opened
by a process that started long before this one, so an environment set on the
spawn reaches nothing. A route's value is an API key, so the design is about how
briefly it exists: the launcher script's first act is to read the file and
**delete** it, before it runs anything. A window closed later — with the CLI
still running, or killed — leaves nothing behind. Writing the values into the
script instead would have left them for as long as the session lasted, because
the script only removes itself on its last line and a session is exactly the case
that never reaches it.

This is measured rather than reasoned about: the generated script is really run,
and the test reads back what the process was actually given — a key with `+`, `/`
and `=` in it, a value carrying `%`, `!`, `&` and `<`, and a name that had to end
up genuinely unset.

On macOS and Linux nothing reaches disk at all: the shell is our own child, so
the `export` and `unset` statements travel in the command line, single-quoted so
a `$` or a backtick inside a key is not read as anything.

Partial on purpose — the other half of the item (an engine that takes its
provider as a command-line argument rather than as environment) is still to come.

## 3.355.0 - M-33 closed: the Plan tab can delete, and no page repaints under your hands (2026-08-31)

Two halves of one report. The first was fixed last release on the page it was
reported from; both are finished here.

### Plan rows can be deleted — in bulk, and one at a time

"I can tick the rows on the Plan tab, but all I can do with them is switch them
on and off. Why can I not delete them? Deleting several should ask; the ✕ at
the end of a row should not — just delete it."

Both, and the difference between them is the point. **The row ✕ asks nothing**:
one row, you are pointing straight at it, and a box in the way of every tidy-up
is the thing that made the page feel like it was arguing. What replaces the
question is an **Undo** — the object goes back with its own id and in its own
place, so a workflow that comes back is still the workflow its triggers point
at. Re-creating it from the title would have made a new one and left them aimed
at nothing. **The bulk delete asks first** and says what it counted, broken down
by kind: "delete 6 items" hides that four of them were workflows.

**Every row can be ticked now, not only the switchable ones.** A workflow and a
template have no switch, so they could not be picked at all — and the one act
that applies to all four kinds was exactly the one that could not reach them.
The two switch buttons say how much of your selection they can touch and grey
out when the answer is none; the ticks are pruned to what is actually on screen,
so "4 selected" always means four boxes in front of you and a filter change
cannot leave a hidden row inside a delete.

Underneath, the four kinds now delete through one call instead of four —
previously two asked their own question in the panel and two handed the press to
a command that asked again, which is why no bulk act could be built out of them.
Agents get `plan.delete`, which deletes across kinds in one call and refuses a
bare kind: "delete every schedule" is never a call worth honouring on a typo.

### The repaint guard, swept across the whole extension

Last release fixed the caret bug on the Tasks page, where it was reported, and
said the other pages were the next sweep. They are done: **twenty-four pages**
now hold a host push until your hands are free, instead of redrawing the box you
are typing in.

The Console is the one deliberate exception and it is not an omission. It
repaints incrementally on purpose — you watch a session's output while you type
your next message to it — so holding the whole paint back would be the opposite
bug. Exactly one part of it replaces the composer, and only that part waits: a
session ENDING elsewhere no longer takes your half-written message's caret with
it, while pressing a different session still answers immediately, because that
one you asked for.

And the rule is measured rather than remembered. A page that answers a host push
must route it through the guard or be named with the reason it does not; the
next page written cannot quietly copy the one line every page used to have.

## 3.354.0 - M-33: the caret stops getting thrown out of the box (2026-08-31)

"I start typing, I press space, and it is as if I pressed Page Down — the caret
leaves the box and the page scrolls. Not every time. Mostly right at the start.
And it is not only there: when another agent is running I cannot even pick from
a dropdown, it shuts as I press."

Space did nothing. Focus had already gone. When something changes elsewhere in
the farm the extension pushes fresh data at every open page, and a page answers
by redrawing itself completely — which detaches the box you were typing in, and
a detached box cannot hold the caret. The browser hands focus back to the page
body, and on the body space IS Page Down.

Every detail of the report follows from that one line. It is intermittent
because it depends on a push landing while you type; it bites when another agent
is running because that is what produces the pushes; it bites hardest right
after opening a page because that is when the first ones arrive; and it never
happened on the Backlog page because nothing pushes at it.

The rule against it had already been written — for the Tasks page's own
30-second refresh, with the comment "never re-render under the user's fingers".
The push simply did not go through it.

Now there is one guard, and it ships to every page rather than being something a
page has to remember. It knows three things the old check did not:

- **It defers rather than skips.** The timer's answer was to not repaint at all,
  which trades a stolen caret for a screen that never catches up on its own. A
  held-back repaint is owed, and it is paid the moment your hands are free.
- **Tabbing between two fields is not "hands free".** The browser announces the
  caret leaving the first box before it has landed in the second; answered on
  the spot, the page would repaint mid-journey.
- **A repaint YOU asked for still happens at once** — a tab pressed, a filter
  typed — because the field you are in is the thing that asked. Only the pushes
  that arrive from elsewhere wait.

A dropdown counts as hands-on for the same reason a text box does, which is the
other half of the report.

Wired on the Tasks page, where it was reported. The other pages have the
component and are the next sweep.

## 3.353.0 - X-102: what a run was asked to be, beside what actually answered (2026-08-31)

Agent Farm has always recorded which MODEL a session ran. It recorded nothing
about which ROUTE served it, which stored profile at which revision, or what was
REQUESTED as opposed to what came back — and no transcript carries any of those.
Measured on a real Claude JSONL (2.1.251, 1373 records): the file names the
session id, the folder, the version, the entrypoint and the permission mode, and
nothing else that matters here. So for those questions the launch manifest is
not the convenient witness, it is the only one.

The manifest itself has been written on every spawn since 3.352.0 — terminal,
Console and every automated run. This release is the half that makes it worth
having: the answer that comes BACK, and the two held side by side.

**What the engine actually said, read out of its own events.** One rule, and it
is the one the catalogs already followed: *the field, not the printed prefix*. A
provider is reported when the engine NAMED it in a field of its own; a model
spelled with a slash in it proves nothing. OpenCode publishes the same fact
three ways — its export, its JSON run stream, its ACP config options — and has
changed its wire shape twice already, so one scan collects the named fields
wherever they sit rather than three readers that each need remembering. The one
qualified name the engine states as its own current value is cut only where the
head is a provider that same engine published.

**Claude reports no route, and never will.** Measured in August against a local
fake endpoint: two Claude processes ran concurrently on separate routes under
one model name, and the transcript preserved neither. So `claude-opus-5` is not
evidence of Anthropic, the reported-provider list on this engine is permanently
empty, and that is an answer rather than a gap. The MODEL is a different field
and the transcript does name it — which is what the manifest now has to compare
itself against.

**Asked vs answered, one turn at a time.** Both halves genuinely move inside one
session: OpenCode may change provider at a turn boundary because the engine
documents that, and on Claude a compaction or a sub-agent is served by a smaller
model than the turn that spawned it. So the comparison is per turn, and it is
deliberately not a verdict. A launch asks for `opus`; the transcript says
`claude-opus-5`. Those are the same run — an alias and an id — and a check that
called it a mismatch would paint almost every honest session red, which is the
fastest way to make a correctness signal ignored. The states are `matched`, `not
proven`, `no model requested` and `no model recorded`, and `not proven` means go
and look, never "this ran on the wrong thing".

**And you can see it.** The Engine cell's hover now carries the route, the
profile revision, what was requested and how the two halves compare, directly
under the models that answered. A session with no recorded launch shows none of
those lines rather than a guess — most sessions are in that state for a while,
and the row says so by staying silent. The column's own header explains what the
four states mean, once.

Under it, the chain that was missing its last link: a binding knew which spawn
produced a transcript and never handed that id to the session, so no session
could reach its own manifest. It does now.

`launch.runtime { sessionId }` on the bridge returns the manifest, the per-turn
rows and the run's drift with a one-line note that is empty on an ordinary run.

## 3.352.0 - S-49 + S-48: the composer stops arguing with the hand on it, and the row you pressed is the agent you get (2026-08-31)

Two halves of the same complaint — the agent · engine · model · effort ·
permission matrix, where fixing one dimension has kept breaking another.

**S-49 — a DOOR seeds the composer; the composer never reseeds itself.** Set a
model, set an effort, set a permission mode in the Console composer, then change
your mind about WHO runs it — and all three answers were replaced by the newly
chosen agent's last-launch record. That rule (S-34) is right for a door that
OPENS the panel and wrong for a box the person is standing in: the last decision
of a launch was silently undoing the first three. The agent picker now REPAINTS
and does nothing else. Where the boxes open from is still decided once,
host-side, by the door that opened the panel (`ConsolePanel.show` →
`composerLaunch`); once they are drawn, the only thing that writes them is a
hand on them. The Superpowers chip follows the new agent exactly as before,
because an untouched choice is resolved against the agent the picker is showing
rather than written anywhere — and a chip the user HAS pressed now keeps their
answer for the same reason the boxes do.

**S-48 — the row you pressed is the agent you get.** Pressing the play triangle
on an agent row sometimes asked "Select an agent" anyway, and picking a
different name there really did start a different agent, so aiming at the row
meant nothing. It was a RACE, and it began when the engine work multiplied the
live events: `live` fires once per hook, every one of them rebuilt every row in
the Agents view including the inline action bar under the pointer, and a press
landing inside that rebuild reaches an action with no row behind it — so the
command arrives with no argument at all.

- **The cure:** the Agents tree is redrawn at most once per 250 ms instead of
  once per event. Below the eye's threshold for a status column, far above the
  width of a click — and cheaper on an old machine besides.
- **The belt:** the Agents view is now a real `TreeView`, so play can ask which
  row it is standing on before it asks the person. One row, an agent row, a
  visible view — anything less still falls through to the picker. It is not a
  silent substitution: the surface dialog that follows is titled with the
  agent's name.
- **And the argument NAMES an agent; the fleet ANSWERS** (`core/agentArg.ts`).
  A tree row's own `AgentInfo` is a snapshot of the fleet as of the last redraw,
  and it used to be believed on sight — an agent renamed or moved since then
  started a session in a folder that is not there any more. A caller naming
  somebody the fleet no longer has is now refused BY NAME instead of being
  turned into a menu, and a name two agents answer to is refused rather than
  resolved to whichever came first.

The other doors on that menu — Start Session…, Continue Latest, Start Session
With…, Talk to Agent — were measured and deliberately left alone: they take what
their caller published and ask when there is nothing, which is what the view's
own title-bar button is supposed to do.

## 3.351.0 - U-84: the Telegram bridge card, on the page that is made of its settings (2026-08-30)

U-84's first half put a live management card on the Toolbox. Its item asked for
that card in TWO places, and the second one was the harder half to get right:
Farm Settings already draws `telegram.enabled`, `allowedChats`, `maxDailyUSD`
and `defaultAgent` as four ordinary rows, and a card that repeated them would be
a page that can disagree with itself.

**So the card carries only what a settings row cannot.** The token is in the
secret vault, the day's spend is in the extension's own storage, and "is the
poller alive" is a fact about a running process — none of the three is in any
box, and all three are the reason somebody opens this page when their phone gets
no answer. The card says: token in the vault or not, which bot answered, poller
alive or stopped, how many chats the list admits, and what today has cost
against today's ceiling. Plus the two acts that are not settings at all —
connect a token, ask Telegram who this bot is.

**‼️ ONE CARD, and that is now structural rather than a promise.** The badge,
the tones, the budget bar and the wiring live in `media/afTelegram.js`, shipped
to every page by the shell; the data is composed once by `telegramCard()` in
`core/telegramCockpit.ts`; and every `svc-*` message both pages can post is
handled by one function in `panels/base.ts` — including the allowlist of the
three settings a webview may write, which is the thing a second copy forgets.
The tests fail if either page grows a tone vocabulary of its own.

**‼️ A SETTING WHOSE ANSWER IS A NAME THAT HAS TO EXIST NOW GETS A PICKER.**
`telegram.defaultAgent` was a text box, so the one way to get it wrong — type a
name no agent has — was the easiest thing to do and produced no error anywhere.
The correct values are not a fact of the manifest (they are whatever agents this
machine has today), so the schema names a SOURCE instead: `"x-af-values":
"agent"`, and the host fills it in on every draw. Derived, never a list of keys
on the page — the same rule `x-af-browse` follows, and `wikiAgent` gets the
picker for free. A stored name the host has never heard of stays selected and is
marked "not on this machine", because a page that silently swapped it would be
changing a setting nobody touched.

**Fixed while looking at the render.** The card's two buttons carried a class
(`mini`) that is defined nowhere in the extension, so they drew as full-size
primary buttons — two blocks of button-blue over the one thing the card exists
to say. An action on a status card is secondary by definition.

## 3.350.0 - X-103: the route is something you can PICK (2026-08-30)

X-101 built one entrance for resolving which route a launch runs on, and then
left the choice unreachable: it was read from
`agentFarm.agentEngineDefaults[<agent>]["claude"].providerId` and nothing wrote
it, so the only way to run a session on Kimi or MiniMax was to hand-edit
`settings.json`. The Start Session launcher now draws the whole axis —
**engine → route/provider → tier/model → variant** — from the adapter's own
catalog, and a saved profile stores it.

**The rows come from the adapter, never from the engine's name.** A form with
`if (engine === 'claude')` in it is a second statement of what each engine
offers, and the day an adapter changes its mind the form goes on drawing the old
answer confidently. The filter for what may be offered is the engine's own word
— `normalizeSelection`.

**‼️ Only what can actually run is offered.** The Claude catalog carries the
shipped route *templates* (Anthropic, Kimi, MiniMax) beside your own profiles.
A template is a SHAPE: no id to hold a credential under, nothing behind it.
Picked, it resolves to `unknown` identity and injects **nothing** — the session
would run on whatever the shell was already carrying while the row said "Kimi".
That is exactly the lie X-101 exists to prevent, so the launcher offers profiles
and the template list stays where you create one.

**Changing a row drops what is below it, and says so.** Pick MiniMax after
choosing a Kimi tier and the tier goes, named, with the tiers that route really
maps. Pick a different OpenCode provider and a model it does not serve goes.
Silence there is how a person stops trusting a form.

**"Default" is a word with a referent.** The route row says which of three
things is true: a route picked for this session, this agent's standing route
(and the setting it lives in), or nothing at all — which is **not "Anthropic"**.
It is inheritance, and this window may already name somebody else's endpoint.

**Two defects found by writing it**, both the same shape — a writer naming its
fields one by one instead of merging over the shape's own list:

- `withAgentDefault` rebuilt the record from `model` and `effort`, so **writing
  a model DELETED the route in the same record**. Every route hand-written into
  `settings.json` — the only way to set one before this release — was lost the
  moment somebody touched the model box in Farm Settings, silently.
- `rememberedOn` named the same three, so a Claude profile id **leaked across an
  engine switch** onto OpenCode, which has never heard of it.

**Measured against the installed CLI, not assumed.** `opencode models
--verbose` prints a bare `provider/model` line per model and then its JSON, so
one spawn now serves both readers — the id list the model box has always used
and the providers/variants/limits the new rows are drawn from. And
`opencode run --variant` exists while the bare TUI's `--help` has no such flag
and ACP declares only `model` and `mode`: the variant row is therefore a
question about the **transport**, not the engine. The same model publishes
`low/medium/high` and the honest answer is yes on a headless run, no in a
terminal, no on a hosted card — and the form says *which*, rather than looking
like the model has no variants.

Also: a saved launch profile now stores the route and the variant (two setups
differing only in endpoint used to be indistinguishable); `sessions.start` and
`launch.profile.set` take `provider`, `tier` and `variant`; a Console card keeps
the route it was started on in its own state, so a window reload cannot move a
live conversation to a different endpoint; and the registry's dependencies are
built in one place — the two hand-written copies had already begun to differ,
neither passing the OpenCode catalog, so `providers.runtime` reported "no
providers" on a machine whose engine publishes six.

## 3.349.0 - X-101 (3/3): the Console, and the acceptance line closed (2026-08-30)

The ACP host spawned with **no `env` at all**, which means it inherited whatever
the VS Code window happened to be carrying. On four engines that is correct; on
Claude it is a second answer to the question a route profile was chosen to
answer — the runner's defect, on the surface people actually sit and watch.

It now builds a complete environment through the same `spawnEnvironment` the
runner uses, from the same resolved runtime, handed in as a dependency: the host
reads no profiles and touches no keychain, and the suite fails the build if it
starts to.

**‼️ The item's acceptance line, closed and measured.** All four launch surfaces
— headless runs, interactive task terminals, session terminals and Console cards
— resolve through one symbol, `engineRuntimeFor(agentId, engine)`. The suite
reads the real source and fails if a second resolution appears beside it, or if
any spawn site returns to spreading `process.env` with the route still in it.

Three routes side by side (Anthropic, Kimi, MiniMax) and an OpenCode native
selection are measured not to contaminate one another: their keys never cross,
their endpoints never cross, and the first-party route — the one most easily got
wrong, since it has no base url and no key of its own — still clears an inherited
one rather than quietly running on it while the manifest says Anthropic.

Test: 251 files, 16709 assertions, 0 failures.

## 3.348.0 - X-101 (2/2): the terminal surfaces, where absence is not an instruction (2026-08-30)

3.347.0 isolated the route for spawned runs. A terminal is a different shape of
problem and not a duplicate of that one.

`cp.spawn` is handed a COMPLETE environment, so removing a name means simply not
putting it in. `vscode.window.createTerminal({ env })` is handed an OVERLAY that
VS Code merges onto the window's own environment — so a route name left out
changes nothing at all and the inherited one survives untouched. On that surface
the absence of an instruction is not an instruction.

Measured in the API's own declaration rather than assumed:

    env?: { [key: string]: string | null | undefined }

where `null` is the documented way to REMOVE a variable. Had it not been, an
isolated route would have been impossible here, and the honest thing would have
been to refuse the launch rather than run it on a route nobody chose. ‼️ `null`
and not `''`: an empty string is a variable the CLI still finds and still tries
to sign in with; only the removal makes it fall through to the credentials file.

Both terminal call sites now go through it — the interactive task terminal
(`core/tasks.ts`) and the session terminal (`launchClaudeTerminal`). The session
one resolves its agent from the working directory through `resolveAgentByCwd`,
the same reader every other surface uses to answer "whose folder is this", so a
terminal and a task opened on the same agent get the same route rather than two
readings of it.

**‼️ And all of them through ONE symbol.** `engineRuntimeFor(agentId, engine)`
in `extension.ts` is what the runner, the interactive terminal and the session
terminal all call, and the suite fails the build if a second resolution appears
beside it. That is the item's acceptance line stated as a symbol rather than as
an intention: three surfaces resolving a launch three ways are three answers to
"which route is this run on", and the transcript records none of them.

Still open on this item: the Console/ACP host (`core/consolehost.ts`) spawns
without an `env` of its own and therefore still inherits whatever the window
carries. That is the third surface named in the acceptance line and it is the
remaining work.

Test: 251 files, 16706 assertions, 0 failures.

## 3.347.0 - X-101: one entrance, and a route a run cannot be lied to about (2026-08-30)

X-98 wrote the adapter contract, X-99 the catalogs, X-100 the ownership and the
vault boundary. **None of them ran.** `readClaudeRouteCatalog` and
`readOpenCodeCatalog` were called from nowhere — measured with grep — and the
adapter interface had no implementations at all. This release is where the four
become one call: `resolveRuntime(engine, selection)` in
`core/providerRegistry.ts`, with the two real adapters behind it.

**‼️ The environment names were MEASURED, not remembered.** Read out of the real
`claude` binary on this machine, a 217 MB bundle:

    grep -ao 'ANTHROPIC_[A-Z0-9_]*' claude | sort -u    ->  75 names
    grep -ao 'CLAUDE_[A-Z0-9_]*'    claude | sort -u    -> ~200 names

The documentation lists a fraction of them. A list written from the docs would
have missed `ANTHROPIC_PROFILE`, `ANTHROPIC_CONFIG_DIR`,
`ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS`, `ANTHROPIC_UNIX_SOCKET`, the Bedrock / Vertex /
Foundry / Mantle families, `CLAUDE_CODE_HTTP_PROXY` and
`CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT` — every one of which moves the route somewhere else.

**‼️ And the two families get different treatment, which is the measurement
worth writing down.** All 75 `ANTHROPIC_*` names are route, credential,
model-mapping, alternate-backbone or organisation identity: there is not one a
run legitimately keeps while being told to use a different route. So that family
is a PREFIX rule, and a name shipped next year is covered before anybody hears
about it. The `CLAUDE_*` family is not like that at all — it holds the alternate
backbones and the plan credential AND the working context Agent Farm itself
depends on (`CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT`,
`CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`). Clearing that family wholesale would break the user's
own hooks in the name of isolating a route they never changed, so there it is
what a name MEANS that decides.

**‼️ Nothing chosen means nothing touched.** A user who has never opened this
feature is running on their own shell's setup deliberately, and sanitising it
because Agent Farm now *could* would break a working machine to enforce a choice
nobody made. The moment a route IS chosen the inherited ones all go — including
when the choice is Anthropic's own endpoint, because an inherited
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` would otherwise send that run to a third party while the
manifest recorded first-party. That is the exact lie measured in August.

**The two engines are opposite in the place that matters.** On Claude the route
is Agent Farm's: injected as environment, fixed for the session, and a resume
across a route change FORKS rather than pretending — measured in August, that
resume mixed two routes' models into a single transcript. On OpenCode the
provider is the ENGINE's: the choice travels as `-m provider/model`, it may
change at a turn boundary because the engine documents that, and Agent Farm
contributes no environment and clears none. A second copy of that credential
here would be a second vault, a second revision, and two truths that eventually
disagree.

Also:

- The provider is asked of the CATALOG, never taken off the front of a model
  name. `opencode/big-pickle` looks like it carries its own provider, and
  splitting on the slash would be right most of the time — which is exactly what
  makes it the wrong rule: a guess that happens to agree goes on agreeing
  confidently after the day it stops being true. With nothing read yet the
  answer is `unknown`, which this system is required to be able to give.
- The profiles ARE the catalog's user routes. Left apart they would be two lists
  of one thing with two revisions — the "two vaults" mistake one level up — so
  there is no second `agentFarm.claudeRoutes` setting.
- A Claude row in `agentFarm.agentEngineDefaults` may now carry `providerId` and
  `tier`, read by its own function rather than through `storedDefault`: a model
  and an effort are command-line flags, a route is an environment isolation with
  a credential behind it.
- New bridge op `providers.runtime` — what a launch of this agent on this engine
  would actually run on. ‼️ NAMES, NEVER VALUES: it reports which variables
  would be cleared and which would be injected, and no credential is returned or
  taken.
- A third-party route with no stored key is refused BEFORE the spawn, where
  somebody is looking, rather than reaching a stranger's endpoint
  unauthenticated and then reporting an auth error about the wrong thing.

Test: 251 files, 16695 assertions, 0 failures. Eight sabotages were planted and
all eight were caught by name — including the two that matter most: a spawn site
quietly returning to `{ ...process.env }`, and a credential reaching the public
identity. X-100 shipped a correct core that nothing called, so this suite reads
the real source and fails the build if the registry goes back to being a library
nobody invokes.

## 3.346.0 - U-84: the Telegram bridge, on a card that cannot lie about it (2026-08-30)

The bridge that lets a chat talk to your agents has been in the extension for a
while, and it announced itself through two `showWarningMessage` calls at startup
and then went silent. A token that expired on Tuesday looked exactly like a
bridge nobody had switched on, and the only way to change anything about it was
to find four settings by name.

The Toolbox page grows a **Services** tab — the first tab on that page that is
about something RUNNING rather than files on disk — holding a Telegram Bridge
card with its state, its sign-in, its allowlist, its ceiling and its default
agent.

**‼️ The card derives nothing for itself.** Every badge and figure comes from
`core/telegramCockpit.ts`, which is measured against what `applyChatBridge()`
really does. A page working out "is it running" from `enabled && hasToken` would
be a second copy of the launch rules living in a file nobody thinks of as launch
logic, going out of date the first time that function changes — in green.

**‼️ RUNNING and USABLE are two different questions**, and this was measured
rather than assumed: an empty allowlist does NOT stop the poller. It warns and
starts anyway, and every message that arrives is refused. A single badge
collapsing the two would call a live-but-deaf bridge "off" and send somebody to
restart a service that is running fine.

**‼️ A poll that returns nothing still reports that it completed.** The last
error used to be cleared when a MESSAGE arrived — but a bridge nobody is texting
polls all day and receives nothing, so this morning's timeout would still be on
the badge at teatime. `TelegramPoller` gained an `onPoll` signal for exactly
that, and an injectable transport, which is what finally made the loop testable:
until now it was the one part of the bridge no test had ever run.

**‼️ Two defects were found by LOOKING at the rendered page, not by a test.**
The ceiling row stacked a box, its unit and today's figure into three lines for
one fact; and the switch read "on — polling Telegram" underneath a red "no
token" badge, contradicting itself in two adjacent lines. Both are visible in
`dist/render/toolbox.png`; neither would have failed a string assertion.

Also here:

- `hasToken` is a boolean and never the token — the boundary X-100 draws with
  `hasSecret`, for the same reason. Nothing about the credential reaches a
  webview, and the new `telegram.status` bridge op neither takes nor returns one.
- The page may only write three named settings. A webview that could post
  `{key, value}` at the host would be a general-purpose settings writer nobody
  meant to build; `allowedChats` has its own two doors because adding an id has
  to be able to refuse — and it refuses BY NAME, since a button that silently
  does nothing is indistinguishable from a broken one.
- A group chat id is negative and is accepted as such; an id too long to hold
  exactly is refused rather than rounded into a number that belongs to nobody.
- Five new doors, five new parity entries, in this commit. The gap budget is
  unchanged at 34.

## 3.345.0 - X-100 (surface): the routes Agent Farm holds, and the boundary drawn where it can be measured (2026-08-30)

The other half of X-100. 3.343.0 shipped the core — who owns which fact, how a
secret is keyed, what the public half of a profile is — and shipped it with
nothing calling it. This is the surface, the bridge ops and the parity entry,
in one commit because the item's acceptance requires all three together.

**The failure this prevents is still two vaults**, and the surface is where that
becomes a thing a person can act on. So the Engines page now draws the ownership
table itself: engine × kind of data, each cell saying which side owns it and
carrying the reason in words on its hover. ‼️ The `selection` column reads
**Agent Farm on every engine** — which provider a run was actually started with
is history, not configuration, and no engine keeps it.

‼️ **That column was missing from the first drawing and it was found by looking
at the page, not by a test.** `ownershipTable` listed the rows in `OWNERSHIP`,
and `selection` is answered by rule rather than by row — so a kind that exists in
