the type and is enforced by `ownerOf` appeared nowhere a person could look. The
table is now derived from `ownerOf`, one call per cell: one rule, one reader.

**The routes themselves** get CRUD, copy, revision and credential status:

- ‼️ **The stored record IS the public record.** There is no private half of a
  profile — `StoredProviderProfile` is the public shape minus the one derived
  field, built by NAMING its fields. A `key`, an `apiKey`, an `authorization`
  header or a field invented next year cannot be stored at all. The acceptance
  line says settings, bridge, CLI, notice and export contain no secret; a filter
  applied at five surfaces is five chances to forget one, and a record that never
  held a key cannot leak one at any of them.
- ‼️ **And that promise is now MEASURED**, which the core release said it was not.
  `test_provider_profiles.js` puts a hostile record through both builders and
  then checks each surface really goes through them: the page is handed
  `publicProfiles` output and the panel cannot reach the store or the keychain at
  all; every bridge op answers with the public shape; the row renderer is checked
  field by field against the nine the public shape has, so `p.apiKey` on that page
  fails by name tomorrow.
- **The credential is human-only** — typed into the host's password box, stored
  in the OS keychain under the profile id, never in settings and never on the
  bridge. Same deliberate exception the Secrets vault has, for the same reason:
  the bridge is a plaintext request/response file channel.
- ‼️ **Replacing a key bumps the revision.** The same endpoint under a different
  credential is not what served a past session, and the credential is not a
  field, so the writer does what `setProfile` cannot see. A rename bumps nothing:
  the revision is a statement about the route, not a count of edits.
- ‼️ **Removing a route collects its key.** A row dropped with the keychain entry
  left behind is a working credential nobody can see and nobody can revoke.
- ‼️ **A profile for an engine that owns its own credentials is REFUSED**, not
  warned about, and the refusal names that engine's own way of signing in
  (`opencode auth login`). The two-vault failure arriving through a form is still
  the two-vault failure.
- **A base URL must be https, or http on loopback.** A key sent over plain http
  to another host travels in clear. Loopback is allowed by name because a local
  gateway is an ordinary setup and refusing it would push people to disable the
  check rather than obey it.

**Also in this release, found while wiring it:** `agentFarm.providerProfiles` had
no category in the settings model, which the settings gate caught by name.

**Bridge:** `providers.ownership` · `providers.list` · `providers.add` ·
`providers.set` · `providers.copy` · `providers.remove`. There is no op that
takes or returns a credential and there is not going to be one.

## 3.344.0 - X-145: a remembered setup belongs to ONE engine, and ▶ answers from Settings (2026-08-30)

**The reported fault, in the user's own sequence.** Start OpenCode from the
launcher without permissions (`manual`). Then press ▶ on the same agent's row and
choose Claude — whose default in `~/.claude/settings.json` is
`bypassPermissions`. The Claude session came up in `manual`. Nobody had ever said
`manual` about Claude.

Three separate defects were behind it, and this release closes all three.

**1. The memory had ONE box for an agent used on three engines.** The record kept
one model, one effort and one permission mode per agent, so every engine
overwrote the last. S-34 had already dropped the model and the effort on an
engine switch — half a fix, because dropping is not remembering: an agent used on
two engines has two setups, and emptying the boxes made the user retype the one
they had chosen on that engine an hour earlier. The record now holds `byEngine`,
one row per engine, and a switch **recalls** that engine's setup. The other
engines' rows survive every launch.

‼️ **And the permission mode falls with them.** S-34 kept it across the switch on
the grounds that `plan` is Agent Farm's word rather than any CLI's — true about
the spelling, false about the effect. It becomes a **flag**, and a flag beats the
engine's own settings file. Silence is what lets that file decide, so silence is
what an engine with no row of its own gets.

**2. ▶ answered four questions it never asked.** The ▶ on an agent's row asks
engine · project · where, and inherited the model, the effort, the permission
mode and the discipline from a record written by a **different door** on a
**different engine**, with nothing on screen mentioning any of them. But at that
door the agent is known and the dialog makes you choose the engine — both halves
of the Farm Settings key are settled before anything starts. So that channel now
resolves the way the Settings page draws it: this agent's per-engine default →
`agentFarm.launchDefaults` → the engine's own settings file. The same agent on
the same engine gives the same session every time.

It still reads the record for the two answers its dialog **draws as rows** and
labels "• last used": which engine to open on, and which surface. A value you can
see and overrule in the same breath is not the defect.

**3. Claude's per-agent EFFORT was a control that stored what it was told and
changed nothing.** `withAgentEngineDefaults` returned early for Claude, on the
correct ground that its CLI reads `<agent>/.claude/settings.json` itself and
passing the same **model** again would be a second source of truth. The early
return took the **effort** with it — and nothing anywhere reads an effort out of
that file; Claude Code has no such key. So Farm Settings drew an effort box on
the Claude row, wrote `agentEngineDefaults[<agent>].claude.effort`, and no session
ever carried it. Now only the model is left to Claude's own file; the effort goes
through the layer like every other engine's, as `--effort` on the command line.

**Not touched:** resumed sessions still reopen exactly as they were left — that is
a different question with its own answer, and this release does not go near it.
Launch Profiles are a separate store and are unchanged.

## 3.343.0 - X-100 (core): who owns which fact, and where the vault boundary runs (2026-08-30)

‼️ **The core half of X-100. The Engines/Providers surface, its bridge ops and
the parity entry are NOT in this release** — the item stays open.

**The failure this prevents is two vaults.** The obvious design gives every
engine the same provider-profile manager. For Claude Code that is exactly right:
a provider there is a route Agent Farm assembles, and if Agent Farm does not hold
it, nobody does. For OpenCode it is exactly wrong — that engine already owns
`/connect`, `opencode auth login`, `auth.json` and `opencode.json`, and a second
copy makes two vaults and two revisions where the stale one wins silently.

So ownership is a fact **per engine per kind of data**, in one table a surface
can draw, each row saying WHY in words a person can check. `core/providerOwnership.ts`
also settles three things once:

- **The secret is keyed by the profile ID, never the label.** A key built from a
  name moves the moment somebody edits the name, and the old entry stays in the
  OS keychain forever with nothing to collect it — the profile silently has no
  credential.
- **The public half is built by NAMING what is public, never by deleting what is
  not.** Settings, the bridge, the CLI, a notice and an export are the same
  question asked five times; a deny-list grows a hole the first time somebody
  adds a field. ‼️ Whether a credential EXISTS is public; the credential is not.
- **Agent Farm refuses to manage what it does not own** — and the refusal names
  the engine's own way of doing it (`opencode auth login`), because a refusal
  that does not say what to do instead is just a wall.

One kind is Agent Farm's on every engine, present or future: **which provider a
run was actually started with.** That is history, not configuration, and no
engine keeps it — Claude's transcript demonstrably cannot.

## 3.342.0 - X-99: what is on offer, from the two places that actually know (2026-08-30)

**Two engines, two owners, and the ownership is the design.** OpenCode owns its
provider list, its credentials and its config; Agent Farm reads the public half
and records what was chosen rather than keeping a second copy — two vaults, two
revisions and two contradicting truths being the alternative. So that catalog is
**measured**. Claude Code has no provider list at all: a provider there is a
ROUTE Agent Farm assembles (base URL, auth kind, tier→model mapping), so that
catalog is **declared** — and because living provider names must not require a
code change, the templates are DATA and a route the user describes in settings is
read by the same function into the same shape, replacing a shipped row of the
same name rather than appearing twice beside it.

`core/providerCatalog.ts` reads `opencode models --verbose` by brace depth (the
objects are multi-line and hold braces of their own, so a line-based split joins
two models the first time one gains a field), and takes the provider from the
`providerID` **field** — never from splitting the printed `provider/model` line.
That is X-98's rule one layer up, and it is one line of code.

**Measured on OpenCode 1.18.19 here, 30 Aug 2026 — three things the shape had to
be honest about:**

- **Reasoning is not the same question as variants.** All six models this machine
  reaches report `capabilities.reasoning: true`; exactly two publish a `variants`
  map. A level box drawn off the capability would offer the engine words it will
  not take, so only published variants are offered.
- **Zero is a figure; nothing is not.** The free provider really does cost zero,
  and calling that "unknown" makes an honest catalog unreadable. The other half:
  one model states no input limit at all, and reporting 0 there would be
  inventing a ceiling.
- **`ref === providerID + "/" + id` on every row** — so the printed line is a
  cross-check and the field is the source, which is exactly the right way round.

**A selection that cannot run is refused before the spawn** — a tier the route
does not map, a model the engine stopped offering, a variant it never published —
each named with what IS available. ‼️ **But silence refuses nothing**: a catalog
nobody has read yet is `not-fetched`, a different value from an empty one,
because absence of a list is not proof of absence of a model and refusing on it
would block every launch made in the first seconds of a window.

**And the X-98 gate earned its keep on its first day.** Run against this new
file it raised two findings, both false: it read across a comma into a separate
object property, and across `&&` into a separate condition — and it counted a
`===` comparison as a derivation. Sharpened to cross neither, it is still caught
both planted violations. A detector that cries wolf gets relaxed rather than
fixed, and then it is not a detector.

## 3.341.0 - X-98: who actually served this session, as one shape for every engine (2026-08-30)

The first item of the X-97 family. Nothing on screen changes — this is the
sentence the next twenty items are written against.

Agent Farm starts sessions on five engines and records, for each, which MODEL
ran. It records **no provider at all** — and the two engines that have a provider
axis do not mean the same thing by the word. On **Claude Code** a provider is a
ROUTE (base URL, auth, tier) that Agent Farm owns and injects, fixed for the
whole session: changing it is a different program, not a resume. On **OpenCode**
the provider is the engine's own identity and the first half of the wire name
(`opencode/big-pickle`), and the engine legitimately allows it to change at a
turn boundary. Written down as one shape that difference is a single field —
`scope`. Written down per surface it becomes an `if (engine === 'claude')` in
twenty places, and the first one somebody forgets is a session claiming a route
it did not run on.

`core/providerIdentity.ts` carries `ProviderIdentity`, `TurnRuntimeIdentity` and
the axes they turn on: `origin` (agent-farm-profile · engine-native · external ·
legacy-inherit · unknown · not-applicable), `scope`, and `proof` (launch-declared
· engine-reported · matched · unknown). `core/providerAdapter.ts` carries the
contract the engines answer — catalog, runtime, preflight, identity, resume,
billing — plus the complete answer for an engine that has no provider axis at
all, which three of the five do not.

**‼️ NOTHING GUESSES THE PROVIDER FROM THE MODEL NAME, and that is now measured
rather than asked for.** `claude-opus-5` does not prove Anthropic served it:
measured in August against a local fake endpoint, two routes answered under the
same model name and the transcript preserved neither. So a provider is DECLARED,
or REPORTED, or unknown — and `unknown` is an answer this system has to be able
to give rather than an absence it fills in. A record from before any of this
stays `legacy-inherit`, which says "nobody was asked" and can be backfilled from
real evidence later, rather than `unknown`, which would say "asked, no answer".

The rule is a rule about code nobody has written yet, so it is measured from
today while the count is still zero: the suite refuses a `provider…` field taking
its value from an expression that mentions a model, and a model string split on a
slash. Both shapes were planted and watched to fail. One exemption, named with
its reason — `tasks.ts` asks which IMAGE-generation service serves a model, a
different domain entirely — and the exemption itself is checked, so a line kept
for a site that has since been fixed is caught too.

## 3.340.0 - S-34 reopened: a remembered model belongs to the engine it ran on (2026-08-30)

**‼️ Switch the launcher from Antigravity to Claude, press Start, and the Console
came up saying Claude with the Antigravity model in the box beside it.** A setup
that cannot run, drawn as if it would. 3.339.0 taught the composer to keep a
seeded model the engine's published catalog does not list — right, because a
catalog is what an engine OFFERS and not everything it can run — but it decided
whether to keep by comparing the seeded value against itself, a comparison that
cannot fail. So the reconcile was not narrowed, it was silenced, and the one case
it exists for went with it.

Being per-engine is a thing that has to be **checked**, and three readers now
check it against the same rule (`rememberedOn`):

- **The memory layer.** `withLastLaunch` inherited the model and the effort from
  the record whatever engine the launch stated. `gemini-3-pro` is not something
  Claude can be asked to be, and the record is one row per agent — so any door
  that changed the engine carried the previous engine's model across. The model
  and the effort are the engine's own vocabulary and are dropped with it; the
  permission mode and the ⚡ discipline are this extension's own words, spelled
  the same on every engine, and stay.
- **The Console panel.** It reads the record directly rather than through that
  layer, so the rule did not reach it: told to open on Claude for an agent whose
  record says Antigravity, it handed the composer the Antigravity model.
- **The page.** A handed-over setup now names the engine it was built for, and
  the composer keeps it only while that engine is the one on screen.

‼️ **A record with no engine on it is still inherited.** It predates the engine
being recorded, so it cannot contradict anything, and treating silence as a
mismatch would empty the boxes for every agent that has not been started since.

**And two tests were reporting green on prose.** `test_run_surface.js` slices the
`startSession` command out of the source at a fixed length, and its last check had
drifted to offset 4190 of a 4200-character window — the command had not changed,
the comment above it had. `test_finish_sound.js` matched a bare `\n` and passed
only while that file happened to be sitting in the working tree with LF endings.
Both now measure the behaviour rather than the layout.

## 3.339.0 - S-34: it remembered, but not all of it — and the row never said what it would start (2026-08-30)

Three defects with one shape: a launch setup that is known and not shown, or
shown and not kept.

**‼️ "Sometimes it forgets the model, sometimes the effort" — and it was one line
in the page.** Every door seeds the composer's boxes from the agent's record; the
composer then reconciled them against the engine's published catalog and
**cleared anything the catalog does not list**. A catalog is what an engine is
OFFERING, not what it can run — an alias typed into the launcher's "Other…" box,
a model added to `agentFarm.modelAliases` and later removed, a level a catalog
stopped advertising. So the model vanished; and because the effort list is looked
up BY model, an emptied model then landed on a different list and took the effort
with it. A value a real launch on **this** engine used now survives the check,
and the select draws it. An engine CHANGE still clears both — those values belong
to a different program, which is the case the reconcile exists for.

**‼️ Starting an agent from a Projects page silently reset that agent's
remembered engine.** That door stated the fleet default engine as its own answer
— which beats the memory, because what a caller says wins — and then recorded it.
Two doors writing one record, one of them with an answer nobody gave: which is
the whole of "sometimes it insists on Antigravity and then suddenly it is Claude
again". It now inherits like every other door.

**‼️ The Start row said what was CHANGED, not what will run.** `describeLaunch`
drops the engine when it is Claude and the model when nothing was typed — right
for a toast, backwards on the row you press: the two facts that decide what a
session IS were the two it left out, and the line read `effort high · auto ·
superpowers on`. There is now a SETUP line, always in the same order —
**engine · model · effort · permissions · ⚡ · project** — and it prints the
resolved answer rather than the word "default", because a row saying "agent
default" makes you open a second screen to find out what will happen. Short on
purpose: the effort is the bare word, the discipline is `⚡on`/`⚡off`, and a field
nobody stated is left out rather than spending a column on "default". The model
is named either way, because "which model" is never a detail.

**‼️ And the ▶ picker now says what it will start, not only where.** It asks
three questions (engine · project · where) and inherits four more without showing
any of them, so "▶ then Enter" ran on a model and an effort that were nowhere on
screen. It carries the same setup line — and the engine row says where its answer
came from (`• last used for dev` / `• your default`), because the rule was always
fixed and always unreadable: two agents, two engines, nothing saying why.

## 3.338.0 - K-36 · M-32: the list the install actually has, and the form that gives it back (2026-08-30)

Two losses of information, both silent, both now measured.

**‼️ K-36 — the `/` picker offered 18 commands where the same machine's terminal
offers 49.** The catalog's one authoritative source is a running session's
`system:init`, and the composer's `/` is pressed exactly when there is not one
yet — so the picker fell back to the shipped table, and no shipped table can ever
close that gap: two thirds of the real list is skills and plugins, i.e. facts
about THIS install. So the report is now **remembered** (per engine, and per
agent where an agent has folders of its own), written by every door that sees one
and read by the ones that cannot. Nothing is spawned to learn it — a session
started for its own reasons pays for it once and every later composer is right.
`toolbox.slashCommands` reads the same record, so an agent asking "what could I
type here" is told what the picker offers.

**‼️ And a report is a COMPLETE answer, not an addition.** Measured against a
real Claude: 49 names, and `/cost` — which is in the shipped table — is not among
them. Offering it anyway teaches a command that answers "unknown", so once a
process has named its commands, a shipped row it did not name is dropped. The
disk is untouched by this: a file that exists is a command whether or not a
running session listed it.

**‼️ Two more answers out of the same event, replacing two guesses.**
`system:init.skills` names which of the reported commands are SKILLS — filing
them as the engine's own printed a claim about a machine as a claim about a
program — and `system:init.terminal_slash_commands` is the `tui` flag measured
rather than marked by hand (the CLI names `doctor` and `color`; the table guessed
five). Where the CLI says nothing, the shipped guess stands.

**‼️ M-32 — a saved task reopened in the form was not the same task.** Every door
that reopens a run ("like this one, but…", the retry form, a clone) draws the
form off ONE reading of the stored object, and that reading carried neither the
**round chain** nor the **conversation the run was set to continue** — so the
boxes drew their defaults over a run that had four prompts, and saving wrote the
emptiness back. Both are seeded now, and the rule is swept: every field of
`RunDimensions` is a box on that form, so every one of them has to come back out
of the stored task. The next dimension somebody adds fails the test until it is.

**‼️ …and a retry by hand now runs the way the original ran, like an automatic
one always has.** `maybeScheduleRetry` has carried the retry policy, the rounds
and the resumed conversation for releases; `retryTask` — the rerun button and the
retry form — carried none of them, so the same failed run retried by the machine
and retried by a person were two different runs. The form can still change any of
them: for these three a key that is PRESENT decides, so clearing the chain or
putting the policy back to the default really takes.

## 3.337.0 - K-32: the parity that matters is not "both exist" (2026-08-30)

The acceptance half of K-14. The bridge op, the merge and the picker were built
across K-29 · K-30 · K-31; this is what now **fails the build** if they come
apart.

**‼️ The Console's door and the bridge op are the same capability, and it is
pinned by DERIVATION.** `parity.manifest.json` already said so; what makes it
true is that the page's `slashCommands` handler calls the same
`scanSlashSources` + `getSlashCommands` rather than assembling a catalog of its
own. A second assembler would drift on the first engine anybody added, and the
symptom would be an agent being told about commands the picker never offers. The
sweep also checks the door hands over the **whole** catalog — the narrowing is
the page's, per keystroke, and a `q` on that message would be the round trip
K-29 was built to avoid.

**‼️ X-97's `provider` is carried and does not narrow — now measured as such.**
A provider decides which *models* a session may run on; nothing anybody has
measured says it decides which *commands* the CLI offers. The op accepts it and
returns the identical list, and the test says why: a filter invented here would
take commands away on the strength of a guess, and the loss would look exactly
like a catalog that failed to scan.

Also pinned: an engine this build has never measured is not an error — it gets
what is on disk plus whatever it reports, which is the honest answer for a CLI
nobody has sat down with.

## 3.336.0 - K-31: whose command it is, and the one it cannot run here (2026-08-30)

The picker's rows now say the two things a name and a sentence cannot.

**Whose command it is, in the badge every other surface draws.** A command the
CLI itself owns wears the ENGINE badge (X-110, the same colour as on a card, a
turn and a session row): `/model` on Claude and `/model` on Codex are different
programs' commands, and a list that called both of them "engine" would be hiding
the one thing that decides whether it can be typed here at all. A command that
came from a file is nobody's engine, so it says which kind of file instead —
**local · skill · workflow**.

**‼️ And the one it cannot run here.** `/model` with no argument opens an
interactive menu *in a terminal*. This session is hosted over stream-json and
has no terminal to open it in, so it can only answer with text — offering it
silently is offering a way to spend a turn on nothing. The row carries a ▤, and
the sentence is a **line in the panel that follows the highlight**: `▤ /model
opens a menu in a terminal. This session is hosted, so it can only answer with
text — give it its argument (/model [name]) and it acts.` It is not a hover,
because a panel over a list you are arrowing through covers the very rows you
are comparing.

The shipped table is now **swept rather than spot-checked**: every command in it
must carry a name, a sentence that ends, and an argument hint that is either
`<required>` or `[optional]` — the picker prints that hint beside the name, so
the brackets are the explanation. The failure this catches is a sixth engine
added in a hurry.

## 3.335.0 - K-30: the "/" picker, where the composer already is (2026-08-30)

K-29 built the catalog — **which commands this session could actually run**, as
a merge of what is on disk, what the running session reported at `system:init`
and a short shipped table per engine. This is the half you can see: type `/` in
the Console composer and the list opens over it.

**‼️ A TYPEAHEAD, NOT A WINDOW, and that is the whole design.** The saved-prompt
picker takes the screen because choosing a prompt is what you stopped to do;
this opens *while* you are mid-sentence. A window that took the focus would mean
typing the query twice — once to open it, once inside it. So the box keeps the
caret, the box keeps the query, and the list draws above it. There is no filter
input in the picker: **`/mod` in the composer IS the filter.**

- **The `/` icon in the box's bottom-left corner types the slash** rather than
  opening a second door. One rule decides when the list is open (`slashQueryAt`,
  read off the caret), so there is no second state machine to fall out of step
  with what is written in the box. Mid-word it puts the space in first, because
  `abc/` is a path and correctly opens nothing.
- **↑ ↓ move · ↵ inserts · Esc closes · a click on a row does what ↵ does.**
  Escape belongs to whichever is open: with the list up it closes the list, and
  the very next Escape stops the running turn the way it always did. Ctrl+Enter
  is never the picker's — with a list open or shut, that chord sends.
- **↵ REPLACES the query rather than adding to it.** The `/mod` under the caret
  is the query; an insert that only added text would send the engine
  `/mod/model`. What lands is the command and a space — and the space is what
  ends the query, so the list closes itself and the argument is your own text.
- **The catalog is asked for once per engine · agent · session**, when the
  picker opens — never on the payload, because this page rebuilds its data
  several times a second while a turn runs and the scan walks three folders.
  Typing narrows in the page. A late answer about an engine the composer has
  moved on from is dropped rather than drawn.
- Each row carries what you need to choose: the name, the argument hint the file
  declared, the description, and where it came from (engine · local · skill ·
  workflow). Nothing is sent — a pick lands in the box, still yours to edit.

The rule and the filter are mirrored into the page (`media/afSlashPicker.js`)
because they run per keystroke inside a webview, and the mirror is **pinned
against the compiled core** — the picker and the bridge's `toolbox.slashCommands`
cannot come to disagree about what a slash even is.

## 3.334.0 - Three answers the user gave: the red box, the hover nobody needed, the popup that would not shut (2026-08-30)

Small, and all three are the same kind of fault — a control that was almost
right and cost the reader something every time they met it.

**U-121, settled — the box stays, and it goes red.** The mark filed under
nothing keeps the ordinary checkbox, so it can still be ticked with four others
and dropped in one press; what it gets is a **red frame**. No icon beside it and
no second word: the colour is the whole message, and the sentence explaining it
already lives in the State cell (ONE SUBJECT). The pick button that briefly
stood there took the row out of every bulk act to say something the row could
say by looking different.

**The colour dot no longer opens a hover.** It said the same three sentences on
every card in the list — a colour is a mark, it is kept against the session id,
it survives the window closing — and it spilled under the conversation pane, so
it was unreadable exactly where it appeared. A hover identical on twenty cards
is not information; it is a paragraph dismissed twenty times. The dot is its own
answer: the colour it is drawn in is the colour it carries. The **dead** dot
keeps a short native title, because a control that refuses a press still owes a
reason — and a native tooltip is drawn by the host above every pane, so it
cannot be clipped by the one it sits in.

**The colour palette closes the way everything else closes.** It was openable
and un-closable: every control inside it stops the click, so the only way out
was the same dot that opened it, and it stood over the next card while the
reader worked on. A click anywhere else now shuts it, and so does Escape. The
listener is on the document and bound once — a repaint rewires the dots, and a
close handler rebound with them would stack up one per repaint — and it repaints
only when something was actually open.

## 3.333.0 - K-29: the slash command catalog, and whose answer it is (2026-08-30)

The groundwork for the `/` picker (K-14): a catalog that can say **which
commands this session could actually run**. No UI yet — that is K-30 — but the
answer exists and is readable from the bridge.

**‼️ The finding that shaped it, measured rather than assumed.** A real Claude
`system:init` on this machine named **47** slash commands, and the list mixed
the CLI's own (`/model`, `/compact`, `/context`) with the SKILLS this machine
happens to have installed (`/dataviz`, `/account-signup`) and two internal names
nobody types (`__remote-workflow`). No table shipped inside Agent Farm can be
right about that. So the catalog is a **merge**, not a table.

Three sources, and they do not carry the same authority:

1. **The disk** — `.claude/commands/**/*.md` namespaced by their own folders, so
   `commands/git/cleanup.md` is `/git:cleanup`; the skill folders; and an
   engine's own `.agents/workflows`. Read by the scanners the Toolbox page
   already uses, never by a second reader.
2. **The running session** — what it reported at `system:init`, the only source
   that knows THIS install.
3. **A short shipped table per engine** — for the one moment before any session
   exists to be asked. Antigravity's `/goal` and `/plan` are not Claude's
   `/compact` and `/context`, and offering one engine's commands on another is
   offering a way to break the session.

**Precedence is one-way: disk beats the session's report beats the shipped
table** — a file is the only source with a description somebody wrote on
purpose. A second `system:init` (a resume, a `/reload-skills`) **adds** rather
than replaces, so a picker never loses commands it had a moment ago. Internal
names beginning `_` are dropped rather than offered.

Each row already carries what the picker will need: `scope`
(engine · local · skill · workflow), the argument hint the file declared, the
source file, whether the session confirmed it, and `tui: true` for a command
whose whole job is to open an interactive menu — those can only answer with
text in a hosted session, which is what K-31 will warn about.

**New bridge op: `toolbox.slashCommands`** — ask it for an engine, an agent, or
a live session, and it answers with the merged list plus a count of what each
layer contributed, so a surprising list can be explained without reading the
merge.

## 3.332.0 - S-34: the setup an agent last ran with belongs to every door (2026-08-30)

Agent Farm has always remembered what an agent was last started with — the
engine, the model, the effort, the permission mode, the discipline switch and
the window it ran in. It remembered it in **one** place and offered it back in
**one** place: the multi-dimension launcher. Press ▶ on the same agent's row
instead, or open its composer from "Talk to agent", or start it from a project
page, and it ran on the fleet defaults, whatever it had been running as ten
minutes earlier. A memory nine doors out of ten cannot see is not a memory; it
is a feature of one picker.

**Now it is a layer, and every door stands on it.** The resolution order is the
same everywhere: what this launch states → what this AGENT was last started
with → the agent's engine defaults → `agentFarm.launchDefaults`. Reading is one
function (`seedLastLaunch`), writing is one function (`rememberLaunch`), and
what is kept is decided once, in the core — so the next dimension added to a
launch is remembered by the shape rather than by ten call sites, which is the
failure this item is named for.

Where you will see it:

- **▶ and the tree menus** open the surface picker on the agent's own last
  engine and last window, and the row says *last used for `<agent>`* rather
  than crediting the window for a choice that agent never made.
- **The Console composer** opens on the remembered model, effort, permission
  mode and Superpowers state instead of five boxes reading "Default".
- **Changing the agent in the composer's own picker** reseeds those boxes from
  the new agent's record — an agent chosen there used to keep the previous
  agent's setup, with nothing on screen saying so.
- **"Talk to agent" and the Projects page** start it as it last ran; only the
  project is new.

**‼️ What the composer shows is what runs.** The boxes are seeded from the
record and then left alone: an empty box is a person asking for the default,
and re-applying the memory at Send would be the panel arguing with a control
they had just cleared.

**‼️ And the bridge records without inheriting.** `sessions.start` writes the
record — the record means "what this agent was last RUN with", so a headless
start that skipped it would leave ▶ offering a setup that had been overtaken —
but it is never seeded from it: an unattended call that says nothing means the
documented defaults, not whatever a person last clicked. The new
`sessions.lastLaunch` op reads the record, so an agent can answer "how does
this one normally run" without guessing.

Neither a name nor a first prompt is ever remembered: re-applying them would
give the next session the same name and send the same opening message on your
behalf.

## 3.331.0 - M-31: the list follows the count (2026-08-30)

The figures at the top of the backlog answer two honest questions one press
apart — `⊞ every` line, or `⊟ wholes` with the parts folded into the jobs they
belong to. But the ROWS underneath never moved. Pressing for "how much work is
left" put the reduced number in the headline and left the full list below it,
so the strip contradicted the thing it was a strip for.

**Now the press moves the family filter with it.** `⊟` ticks *wholes only*, `⊞`
puts the axis back to *any* — and because "wholes only" is the SAME predicate
the roll-up counts by (nobody's part), the rows on screen are exactly the lines
behind the number, never a near-miss.

**‼️ The arrow points one way.** The strip writes the axis; the axis never
writes the strip. Narrowing to *part of something* is a question about the
family tree, not an instruction to change what the headline counts. And what
you pick AFTER a press stands — change the axis, or clear the filters
altogether, and nothing re-applies it until you press the figure again.

The press is unconditional on purpose: a press whose effect depended on what
the axis happened to hold is a press whose result you cannot predict. Both
hovers say so before it happens — the strip's, and the family axis's own.

## 3.330.0 - K-35: a colour label on a Console card (2026-08-29)

The left panel is a column of cards that all look alike — same shape, same two
lines of grey figures, and the agent name repeated down it because three of them
belong to one agent. Finding "the one about the wiki" means READING, every time,
and reading is what a panel you glance at cannot ask for.

**So a session can carry a colour**, picked from a dot at the bottom-right of
its card: ten fixed swatches, a colour of your own, and "none" to take it off.
It is a MARK — the same kind of thing as the pin and the labels
(`core/sessionmarks.ts`), keyed by session id and remembered for ever.

**‼️ Which is why the dot is on every card kind in that panel** — live, "where
you left off", and resumable. A colour that is right on two surfaces out of
three is a colour nobody trusts on any of them.

**And a card with no session id cannot carry one.** The mark is filed against
the id, and a process that has not written its first turn has not got one: that
dot is drawn dead and says why, rather than being pressable and saving nothing.

The value is validated in the store and nowhere else — it ends up in a `style`
attribute, so nothing but `#rrggbb` survives, whether it comes from the page,
from `sessions.color` on the bridge, or from a hand-edited globalState.

## 3.329.0 - U-122: every object on the vault strip is a path (2026-08-29)

The Wiki cockpit's vault strip named six things and let you press three. A path
you can see and cannot copy, a drop box you can read the name of and cannot
open, and the agent procedure rendered as a dead `<span>` are one omission with
three faces: the object is DRAWN but is not an object.

**‼️ `_REF/wiki.md` opens.** It is the file a compile is told to read first,
named on the one page that starts compiles, and it could not be opened from
there. It is resolved against the configured agent roots — the FIRST root that
really holds it wins — and on a machine where none of them do it stays plain
text rather than becoming a link that opens nothing.

**📥 `_RAW_` is on the strip, with the count that is the reason to look at it.**
The whole promised gesture is "drop a browser export in `_RAW_` and do nothing
else"; a folder you have to hunt for in Explorer is that gesture with a hunt in
front of it. Pressing it opens the folder.

**Everything on the strip has a right-click menu** — open it in the editor, show
it in the folder, copy the absolute path, and for the root, open Wiki settings.
Nothing there is new behaviour invented for a menu: each item sends the message
the strip's own press already sends, so the menu and the button cannot drift.

**And every named file states its four figures on hover**: how many lines, how
big, when it last changed — and, for the drop box, how many transcripts are
waiting and how many are already archived in `_DONE_`. A line count is refused
rather than guessed on a file past 2 MB.

A door that opens nothing is not drawn as a door: a drop box that is not there
yet and a root that does not exist are text, not links.

## 3.328.0 - U-120: a chip says which scope it belongs to (2026-08-29)

A mark on the WHOLE conversation covers turn 2, so pressing turn 2's badge
ticked it alongside a mark that covered turns 1–3 and nothing else. Two scopes,
one colour, one list — the aggregation illusion — and the next topic went under
whichever chip the eye landed on.

**A session-wide chip is now warm** (the editor's own warning pair, so it holds
its contrast in both themes) and a partial one keeps the ordinary accent. The
rule is the same from a turn's badge and from a session's, because both popovers
are the same panel.

**‼️ And what a chip reports is what pressing "Keep it" LEAVES BEHIND** — every
turn the topic is already kept on, plus the scope now chosen. That second half
is why it is worth repainting: choosing *Whole session* turns the partial chips
warm **before** the press rather than after it. The hover states the count the
way the cockpit says it (`Whole session (10 turns)` · `3 turns (3/10)`), then
the span (`Turns: 1–3, 7`), then where the topic stands today and what this
press would add.

X-58's exclusions are part of that arithmetic: a whole-session mark that leaves
two turns out reads `Whole session (8 of 10 turns) · except 9–10` rather than
claiming ten. They now travel with the mark on the wire, because a count the
compile will not honour is worse than no count.

The footer says what the window is not: it only ADDS topics — dropping, editing
and compiling candidates is the Wiki cockpit's job.

## 3.327.0 - U-121: the tick box stops being the compile's box (2026-08-29)

Three separate frustrations in the Wiki cockpit, all of them the same mistake:
the tick box was the COMPILE's box rather than a selection box.

**‼️ So the master box could only be pressed once.** It was drawn unchecked on
every repaint, which means a browser click always read as *turn on*: ticking
everything worked and untticking it was impossible — the one gesture that box
exists for. It now takes its `checked` from the rows themselves and its
`indeterminate` from a partial selection (a property, so it cannot be written in
markup and has to be set after the paint), and its hover says which of the two
presses you are about to make.

**And the `dropped` and `compiled` tabs had no boxes at all**, so five dropped
marks could only be brought back one row at a time — which is what made 🚫 Drop
feel irreversible even though every row has had its own ↺ all along. Every row
is tickable now except the one a run is out for, where anything you do fights
the run, and the bulk group gained **↺ Reopen**.

**‼️ And when the ticked set and the compilable set differ, every button says its
own number.** A selection of six that compiles two says `Compile Selected (2)`,
`Drop 1`, `Reopen 1`, `Remove 6` — each act taking exactly the slice it counted,
and the compile button's hover saying out loud how many of your ticks it is
leaving out and why. A button that says 3 and sends 6 is the silent narrowing
these counts exist to prevent.

- **The table's buttons moved to the table.** `Compile Selected`, `Compile All`,
  the bulk group and `Lint` were in the page header, among the global
  navigation — two strips away from the filters that decide what is in the table
  and from the ticks that change their numbers. They sit under the filter bar
  now, in the order the three things argue: what is shown, what is ticked, what
  happens. The header keeps what a header is for.
- A mark with no topic (U-117) is tickable like any other — it can be dropped or
  removed with four others. What it is never in is a compile: no compile button
  counts it, and the State and Topics cells both say why in words.

## 3.326.0 - X-140: the compile is told what a dropped file is, and where to put it afterwards (2026-08-29)

The brief and the compile prompt are written in the grammar of a CLI
transcript — a turn scope, turn numbers, what each turn opened with. A markdown
export somebody saved out of a browser has none of it, and it was being handed
to the run under a heading identical to every other heading, with `turn scope:
whole file` under it. A run reads that and goes looking for turns.

So a dropped file is now **declared** in the first line of its own block:
*EXTERNAL FILE — NOT A CLI SESSION*, read the whole of it, it has no turns. Its
note travels as **⚠️ KULLANICI DİREKTİFİ** rather than "why it was kept" — on a
file that is not context, it is the only way a person can say which part matters,
because there are no turn numbers to narrow it by, and the prompt says outright
that it outranks the run's own judgement.

**‼️ And a compiled drop is moved into `_RAW_/_DONE_` — by the agent, in the same
breath as the report.** The extension never learns that a page was written; only
`wiki.candidates.edit {state:"compiled"}` says so, so a file moved on the
strength of a run that then wrote nothing would be filed as done while the pool
still said pending. One actor, one moment. The prompt names the pair together
and says what each half costs alone: a file left in the drop box is offered to
the next compile as though nothing had happened, and a file moved without the
report leaves the pool waiting for a file that is no longer where the mark
points.

The paths are **computed, never described**. A model asked to work out an archive
path works out a plausible one; a provenance link pointing at where the file
currently is breaks the moment the move next to it succeeds. So the brief carries
`rawArchive` (the exact destination) and `rawLink` (`_RAW_/_DONE_/<file>`, which
is what goes on the page as `- [YYYY-MM-DD] Harici Kaynak: [[…]]`), and the
prompt prints the move as `from -> to`.

- **Self-healing, at both ends.** `buildBrief` rebuilds `_RAW_/_DONE_` if it has
  been deleted — the root is already known good at that point, so it is the one
  moment this can be healed without guessing. The run is *still* told to create
  it, because the folder can go away between the brief and the move.
- **A drop whose file has been tidied away is skipped by name**, like any mark
  whose material is gone. It is the likeliest of them: this file lives in a
  folder the user opens and cleans.
- **‼️ And a compile with no dropped file in it is told none of this.** No
  archive folder, no move instruction, no `_DONE_` anywhere in the prompt — a run
  handed an instruction about a folder none of its marks came from is a run that
  may act on it.

## 3.325.0 - U-117: a dropped file stops pretending to be a session (2026-08-29)

X-139 put files in the cockpit that never happened in a CLI, and the table drew
them exactly like the ones that did. A conversation saved out of Claude Web
appeared as `raw:clau` — eight characters of a key that identify nothing —
alongside `whole session`, over a markdown export with no turns at all. It is
now what it is: **📄 the file's own name**, a `RAW` badge, and `DONE` once a
compile has archived it into `_RAW_/_DONE_`. Sessions carry 💬 in the same
column, because a distinction only one side of a pair signals is one the eye has
to work for.

**‼️ And the stage a drop arrives in is its own state, not `waiting`.** A raw
file lands with no topic on purpose — a topic is the key a page is filed under
and a scan will not guess one. So the row reads `🌱 needs a topic`, its empty
topics cell says `pick a category…` instead of a dash, and where the tick box
would be there is a 🌱 that opens the picker. Three stages, visible at a glance:
dropped → filed → compiled.

That is not a hint the page draws over a host that would have accepted the
press. `startCompileRun` now **refuses a topicless mark by name** — and names
the *file*, because an id tells you nothing about which drop you forgot to file.
`all:true` simply leaves such marks out, so one un-triaged file can never block
Compile All; and when leaving them out leaves nothing, the refusal says which
files are waiting rather than "nothing matched". The cockpit's counts follow the
same rule, so `Compile All Pending` never offers a mark the run would reject.

The rest of it, each fixing something that was quietly wrong:

- **The row editor's turn strip is REPLACED, not omitted.** A file has no turns,
  so the strip had nothing to draw — and an editor that simply left the line out
  said nothing about scope at all. It says the opposite in so many words: all of
  it is read, and the note below is where you narrow it. The note is relabelled
  **directive** there, which is what it actually is for a drop (X-140).
- **📄 Files** is a filter of its own next to the state segment — a source, not a
  state, since a drop crosses all of them. It carries the count, and its hover
  says how many still need a topic.
- **Clicking a dropped file opens the FILE.** It was being handed to the session
  viewer, which was being asked to parse a browser export as a CLI log; it goes
  through the same door a compiled page does.
- `candidateView` answers `raw` / `rawFile` / `rawDone` / `compilable` once, so
  no surface re-derives any of it from the engine string — and its `turns` reads
  `whole file` rather than claiming a session's range.

## 3.324.0 - X-139: the drop box becomes a pool, with nobody pressing anything (2026-08-29)

X-138 made `_RAW_`. On its own that is a box files go into and nothing comes out
of: the folder existed, and a conversation saved into it stayed a file. The
whole gesture is meant to be *save it in there* — so the pool notices, and it
notices on the calls that are already being made rather than on a button
somebody has to remember. `wiki.status` and `wiki.candidates.list` both sync
now, which means a file dropped a second ago is in the answer the cockpit is
drawing itself from.

A dropped file becomes an **untagged** candidate: whole-scope, `engine:
raw-file`, `addedBy: auto-raw`, and **no topics**, because what a file is about
is the one thing only a person can supply and a scan inventing it would file the
conversation under a guess. Its label is the file's first real line, with a YAML
front matter block skipped — an exported chat whose first line is `---` would
otherwise be listed as `---`. Only `.md` and `.txt`; a screenshot is not a
transcript.

Three rules, each the answer to a way this could quietly go wrong:

- **‼️ The file is the identity, not a turn range.** Every other row in this pool
  is "this conversation, these turns" and merges by exactly that. A dropped file
  has no turns, so it is keyed by its own name and a row is created only when no
  row holds that key **in any state** — which is what stops a candidate somebody
  dropped on purpose from being resurrected on the next scan, for ever.
- **It never creates a folder.** Healing the drop box is `ensureRawDirs`'s job
  and its callers do it first. A listing that silently made directories would
  also make them from a root that was mistyped.
- **‼️ A file that vanishes never takes somebody's work with it.** Moved into
  `_DONE_` means consumed, not gone: the path on the row is corrected (that path
  is what a compile reads) and the state is kept. Deleted outright may only drop
  the row when nobody has touched it — no topics, no note, still pending, added
  by the scan itself. A row a person tagged keeps its state and is told on its
  own line why it is stuck, because a mark that disappears from the cockpit is
  indistinguishable from one that was never made.

`wiki.status` reports what the call itself changed, by id, so a scan that
rewrites the pool is one somebody can debug.

## 3.323.0 - S-47: a resumed session comes back as itself on EVERY engine (2026-08-29)

S-45 was built and tested against the Claude parser alone, so four of the five
engines still came back from a resume wearing the fleet's current defaults. What
each of them actually records was measured, one at a time, and only what is
really written down is read:

- **Codex** — the figure was already here and the field was missing. The parser
  has tracked the last model since it was written (it is what prices the
  session) and never put it on the row, so the resume ladder fell back to
  `models[models.length - 1]` — a set in first-seen order, whose last element
  names the model the session **stopped** using. Measured: two rollouts of 110
  on this machine would have resumed on the wrong one. Its `turn_context` also
  states the **effort** per turn (60 of 110 rollouts) and the **sandbox** it ran
  under, which gives the permission mode back for 35 of them.
- **‼️ …and only half of that mode is readable.** A rollout records the sandbox,
  not the mode that was picked, and `default` and `plan` BOTH map to
  `read-only`. Reading it would put a word in the box the user may never have
  chosen, so `read-only` names nothing; `workspace-write` and
  `danger-full-access` invert cleanly and are the two that let a run write.
- **The Console's own mirror** — the record that never had to be inferred and
  was read least. It is Agent Farm's snapshot of a session Agent Farm launched:
  model, effort and permission mode have been written into it since it was
  invented, and only the model was ever read back, into the display list.
  Measured: 63 conversations, 55 with a model, 54 with an effort, 63 with a mode.
- **Gemini** — the same one-line omission, with one subtlety: `models` is only
  added to when a reply reported usage, which is right for a spend column and
  wrong for "what is it on now". A reply that answered without being billed
  still answered.
- **OpenCode** — its export records `big-pickle` while its catalogue publishes
  `opencode/big-pickle` (K-28), so the recorded name reached the resume gate and
  was dropped. A bare id that is the tail of **exactly one** published id is now
  resolved to it; a tail two providers both claim resolves to nothing. ‼️ The
  rule is inert by construction where ids carry no provider prefix — there every
  id is its own tail — so Claude, Codex and Antigravity cannot be affected.

Absence stays absence throughout: an engine, or a file, that never said which
model it was on says nothing rather than the fleet default wearing the session's
name.

## 3.322.0 - S-46: Antigravity keeps its model, and its effort (2026-08-29)

Choosing **Gemini 3.7 Flash** and pressing send got you a session that never
started:

```
invalid model selection (--model "gemini-3.7-flash" --effort ""):
--model gemini-3.7-flash requires --effort (available: low, medium, high)
```

while the effort box on screen read **Default → medium** the whole time. Both
halves of that were true, which is why it was invisible: X-26 made the row NAME
the effort it would send, but the field every reader actually asks —
`defaultEffort[model]` — was left empty for this engine alone. So an effort of
`''` had nothing to be completed to, survived every narrowing untouched, and the
`<select>` showed its first option because its value matched none of them. The
label was right and the value behind it was empty.

- **The catalog now states the default effort per model**, derived by the same
  call that writes the label, so the two cannot drift apart again. A model that
  takes no `--effort` at all still gets none.
- **And where nothing narrows** — a mission member, a task row, a bridge call —
  a model that cannot run bare is now **refused before the run** instead of
  dying at the CLI hours later. It is the catalogue's own shape that refuses,
  not a named engine, and only a model's OWN vocabulary may do it: an engine
  that says nothing about a model still refuses nothing.

**‼️ And the second half of S-45, on the engine it never reached.** Resume
inheritance was built and tested against the Claude parser alone, so an
Antigravity conversation came back on the fleet default — the exact failure S-45
exists to end, one engine over. This engine writes no model field anywhere; it
staples a sentence to the user's step, and that sentence is the record:

```
The user changed setting `Model Selection` from None to Gemini 3.7 Flash (High).
```

Measured across every conversation on this machine: **105 of 111 transcripts now
name their model and effort**, 15 of them having changed model mid-conversation,
which is why the LAST setting is the one a resume takes. The sixth is
`Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Thinking)` and it is deliberately left unread — that label is
`claude-sonnet-4-6` while `Claude Opus 4.6 (Thinking)` is
`claude-opus-4-6-thinking`, so the id is not derivable from the label and a
resume that quietly runs the wrong model is worse than one that asks.

`SESSION_PARSER_VERSION` is 3: without the bump every session already indexed
would keep answering with no model, which is exactly the set that gets resumed.

## 3.321.0 - B-20: the notices board's own actions, on the bridge (2026-08-29)

An agent could **post** a notice and then do nothing else with it. Four things
the board could do had no op at all, and the gap showed: a title that turned out
wrong stayed wrong, nothing could be kept at the top of a busy board, a run had
no way to mark which of forty results were the two worth reading — and a
dismiss was **final**.

- **`notices.edit`** — the board's own edit, on the same store. Pass only what
  changes. ‼️ The first edit snapshots the original, so the board can show the
  difference: a correction on the record, never a quiet substitution. An edit
  that changes nothing is refused rather than stamping the notice `edited` for
  no reason.
- **`notices.pin`** — hold it at the top, or let it go. A pin also protects a
  notice from the sweeps.
- **`notices.stars`** — rate it. ‼️ The scale is **0-3**, and anything outside it
  becomes **0** rather than clamping — so a "5" from a caller who assumed five
  stars *clears* the rating. The op says so, because that is the kind of thing
  an agent gets wrong forever otherwise.
- **`notices.undo`** — put the last removal back.

**‼️ And undo is why the store changed, not just the ops.** The board's Undo kept
the removed notices on the **panel**, which made it a property of a window: an
agent that dismissed the wrong batch over the bridge had nothing to take back,
and the person's own Undo vanished the moment the board was closed. The memory
lives on the store now, so the button and the op undo the same removal — one
deep, deliberately, because Undo here means "that was a mistake" and not "walk
back through the day".

Four named gaps in the parity manifest are closed with this: the gap budget goes
38 → **34**, and 326 capabilities now reach the bridge.

## 3.320.0 - X-138: the wiki's drop box, relative and self-healing (2026-08-29)

Groundwork for the wiki's Phase 3: a folder you can simply **drop a file into**.
A Claude Web answer, a ChatGPT export, something somebody typed by hand — into
`<wikiRoot>/_RAW_`, with no command, no conversion and no naming rule to get
right first. A compiled one moves to `_RAW_/_DONE_`, so the drop box stays a
to-do list rather than a growing pile.

**Relative to the root, never absolute.** `agentFarm.wikiRoot` is a setting the
user retypes on every machine, `%USERPROFILE%` and all. A path baked into the
code would be right on exactly one computer.

**‼️ Self-healing, because the folder lives in the user's own vault** — where
Obsidian, a sync client and their own hand all reach it. It *will* be deleted,
renamed, or simply absent on a fresh machine, and every one of those is a normal
Tuesday rather than an error worth a dialog. `ensureRawDirs` makes whatever is
missing, recursively and silently, and says what it had to make. It runs on
`scaffoldWiki`, `wikiHealth` and `wikiStatus`: asking "is something wrong here"
is the moment a user asks, so answering "`_RAW_` is missing" and leaving it
missing would be a diagnosis where the fix costs one syscall.

**‼️ And it still refuses to create the ROOT.** `mkdir -p <root>/_RAW_/_DONE_`
brings the root into existence too — and the root is a hand-typed path. A typo
would quietly become a real empty folder on the disk while the real wiki sat
untouched beside it, and the health check meant to *report* the problem would
have manufactured the evidence that there wasn't one. An unset root is refused
outright: `path.join('', '_RAW_')` is the **relative** `_RAW_`, which would
appear in whatever directory the process happens to be in.

`wiki.health` and `wiki.status` report the two paths and say in their own
descriptions that they repair them. The drop box starts with `_`, so it is not a
category and adds no pages — pinned by a test, because the day that stops being
true every wiki grows a phantom category.

## 3.319.0 - U-111: the agent page can be asked about a period (2026-08-29)

The dashboard has had a range row for a long time. The agent page — the one
place you go to ask about **one** agent — was frozen at *last 30 days* for its
chart and *all time* for every figure above it, so "what did this agent cost me
last week" was not a question it could be asked.

**The same row, on the agent page**: the first week day by day, then 14 / 30 / 90
/ 180 / 365, then two dates. It opens on **30d**, which is exactly what the page
already drew — the row arriving changes nothing about the first thing you see.

It governs the **cost card** (summed from the same daily buckets the chart draws,
so the number and the bars can never disagree), the **sessions card**, and the
**daily cost chart** — which now buckets weekly past 120 days, or a year of bars
would be a pixel each. Both cards keep their all-time figure in the sub-line
rather than trading one question for another.

**‼️ And the two cards it cannot govern say so.** Tool calls are kept per session,
not per day, so there is no honest way to cut them by a span; the memory count is
a picture of the present. A page where some cards are scoped and others silently
are not is worse than one where none are.

**‼️ Sessions are counted from their spans, not from the table.** The obvious
implementation — filter the sessions array — is wrong: that array is a *pool*,
the union of the true top-N per sortable criterion, built for a table you sort.
On a busy agent the count would quietly stop growing at the cap, and it would
look perfectly right on every quiet agent. The panel now ships two numbers per
session for **all** of them, every engine, and the page counts the ones
**overlapping** the span — a conversation opened on Monday and still being
written on Friday belongs to every day in between.

## 3.318.0 - K-33: a command is given to a shell that is ready for it (2026-08-29)

Right-click a live Console card, *Resume in Terminal*, and the terminal opened on
Claude's **login screen** instead of the conversation. Two races, both real.

**The shell was still starting.** Every terminal here was driven the same way:
`createTerminal` … `show()` … `sendText(command, true)` **on the very next
statement** — before the shell inside the pty had finished running the user's own
startup (a PowerShell profile, oh-my-posh, conda init). On a slow profile the
written line is swallowed by or interleaved with that startup's output, and a
`claude --resume <id>` that loses its tail runs as a bare `claude`: a fresh
process, no conversation, the onboarding screen. The session looks like it
evaporated. (The **external** terminal path was always immune — it writes the
command to a `.cmd` file first — which is why switching to it "fixed" it.)

**The line now waits for the shell to report in.** VS Code can only install its
own integration once the shell has started, so `Terminal.shellIntegration`
becoming defined is exactly the signal that was missing. ‼️ **The delivery is
unchanged** — still `sendText`. `shellIntegration.executeCommand` looks made for
this and is deliberately not used: it sends ^C first to interrupt whatever is
running, and what these terminals run is a full-screen TUI.

Three ways out, so a launch can never hang on it: integration switched off in
settings sends **immediately** (no ceiling paid for a promise nobody made), the
3-second ceiling sends anyway (today's behaviour, so the worst case of this
change is the behaviour it replaces), and a terminal closed first sends nothing.
And it happens **once** whichever of the three fires — a resume sent twice would
put two processes on one transcript.

**All three doors**: every terminal session the extension opens, the task
terminal (whose `exit` line is still second, and still after the command it is
meant to outlive) and the session viewer's own fallback.

**The second race: the handoff.** Moving a session out of the Console waits for
that process to release the transcript — and then **fell through and launched
anyway** when the wait ran out, which is precisely the second-process bug the
wait exists to prevent. The ceiling is an answer now: it says the process is
still finishing and opens nothing. Safe to refuse there and nowhere else in that
handler, because the Console card is already closed — the same right-click a
moment later just works.

## 3.317.0 - S-45: a resumed session comes back as itself (2026-08-29)

Picking a conversation back up handed it whatever the **settings page currently
said**. So a session you had deliberately put on a bigger model, at a higher
effort, under bypass, restarted on the fleet default every time — and the three
had to be re-chosen by hand on every sitting. Worse than tedious: nothing on the
row says the model changed, so the wrong one just runs.

**The transcript is the answer, and it is the right one.** A `/model` typed
INSIDE a session changes the run without Agent Farm ever hearing about it, so
anything written down at launch would be stale exactly when it mattered. The
file records what actually happened, so a resume now reads it:

- **the model that answered last** — `SessionInfo.lastModel`. ‼️ Not
  `models[models.length - 1]`, which every reader had been using: `models` is a
  set in first-seen order, so a session that went opus -> sonnet -> opus named
  **sonnet**, the model it had stopped using.
- **the effort it ran at** — new. The CLI writes it on the assistant line
  itself, beside `type` and `timestamp`; nothing had ever read it.
- **the permission mode** — X-124's field, now used rather than only shown.

**All four doors, not the two the report named.** The Console's own resume, the
terminal resume, *Resume in Console* (which already reached for the model — and
reached wrong) and the `sessions.start` bridge op. `sessions.context` was
resuming on the wrong model for the same reason and is fixed with them.

**‼️ Order, and one deliberate exception.** In the panels the transcript comes
**first**: the composer's boxes are *seeded from* the fleet defaults, so the
value travelling with a resume click is a default rather than a choice, and
anything placed after it could never win. On the bridge it is the other way
round — an argument a caller actually wrote is the most deliberate answer in the
room, so it beats the transcript, and the defaults are consulted only for what
neither answers.

The inherited pair still passes `narrowLaunch`: it is a fact about the catalogue
as it stood **then**, and an effort a model no longer offers is the X-30 error
with an older date on it. An inherited **bypass** is not trusted either —
`resolveEffectivePermission` still resolves it against the folder's own layers
(K-22), so a mode carried back from a transcript can never grant more than
starting a fresh session there would.

`SESSION_PARSER_VERSION` is bumped: without it every session already indexed on
your machine would come back with neither field — which is exactly the set of
sessions you resume.

## 3.316.0 - K-34: every door that starts a session carries the same setup (2026-08-29)

X-133 gave the Console composer a ⚡ chip. That is **one of ten** ways a session
gets started here, and the other nine went on deciding the engineering
discipline from a per-agent setting the person starting the session could not
see — so the same agent worked one way in the panel and another way in a
terminal, and a saved profile reproduced everything about a launch **except**
that.

**`⚡ Superpowers` is a launch dimension now**, like the model and the
permissions: on `LaunchOptions`, so the multi-dimension launcher, the sidebar
tree rows, the surface picker, a **saved profile** and the terminal itself all
carry it. The launcher shows what will actually happen —
*`agent default (on for developer)`* — rather than leaving the reader to guess
which setting answered.

**‼️ Three answers, and the empty one is not "off".** *Agent default* hands the
decision back to `agentFarm.superpowersDefaults`, which is what every session
started before this row existed did. A profile that says nothing about the
discipline **clears** it on load rather than leaving the last launcher's answer
standing — the same rule the model already followed.

**And the launcher no longer spawns behind you.** Picking *Where: the Console
panel* used to start the session the instant you pressed Start: the setup was
baked in, and every dimension became unchangeable at the exact moment you
finally had a window to change one in — a wrong model picked in a quickpick
could only be fixed by ending the session and starting again. **The composer now
opens *on* the setup**: the same answers, still editable, a first prompt sitting
in the box rather than sent, and nothing running until you press Send. The
terminal branch is untouched, because a terminal has no composer to preserve.

`test/test_launch_parity.js` measures it — a dimension that exists on
`LaunchOptions` and is missing from a door is the structural failure this suite
is here to catch.

## 3.315.0 - M-30: the discipline is a property of the JOB, not only of the agent (2026-08-29)

X-133 put the Superpowers engineering discipline — brainstorm before building,
a plan before code, systematic debugging before a fix — behind **one switch per
agent**. That answers *"how does `developer` work"* and cannot answer *"…except
for this job"*. A nightly lint sweep and a feature build are the same agent
doing work of two different kinds, and the Console composer's ⚡ chip could say
so only for a session somebody was sitting in front of.

**`⚡ Superpowers`**, in the new-task form beside Model, Effort and Permissions
— so a **task, a schedule, a trigger, a template and a workflow step** can each
say it, and an automation that fires at 03:00 says it when it is *written*,
which is the only moment anybody is there to say it.

**‼️ THREE ANSWERS, AND THE EMPTY ONE IS NOT "OFF".** *Agent default* hands the
decision back to the agent's own setting — which is exactly what every task ever
written before this row existed said, and what they all keep saying. *On* and
*Off* are a person overriding that default for this job alone. A checkbox would
have had two states and would have had to invent an answer for every existing
automation on the day it shipped.

**An explicit pick beats the default, and a retry inherits it.** A rerun that
quietly fell back to the agent's setting would be a different job from the one
being retried — the same defect the engine, the model and the finish sound each
had here once.

Over the bridge it is `superpowers` on `tasks.add`, `schedules.add`,
`triggers.add`, `templates.add` and `templates.run`; on `schedules.set` and
`triggers.set`, **`null` is its clear** — the string dimensions beside it clear
on `""`, and a tri-state boolean has no empty string. Omitting it is the third
answer, not `false`, in both directions: a schedule read back and written away
again cannot freeze today's default onto a run that never chose one.

## 3.314.0 - A-26: the farm reads the answer, not just the news (2026-08-29)

A tone says *something happened*. The announcement (A-20) says *which agent*.
Neither says **what it answered** — so the walk back to the screen happened
anyway, and for most turns the answer was one sentence long.

**`🔊 Read this session aloud`**, in the same right-click the mute and the voice
already live in (`Sound for this session…`). Turn it on for the ONE conversation
you walked away from, and every turn it finishes is read out loud in that
session's own voice.

**Per session, and only per session.** There is no fleet-wide "read
everything": eight agents reading over each other is a crowd, not a cockpit.
For the same reason there is **one reader for the window** — a newer answer cuts
short an older one still being read, on purpose.

**It is not part of the alert plan.** A session with every ♪ box unticked still
reads when you ask it to, and a muted fleet does not silence it: mute exists to
stop noise nobody chose, and this switch was thrown by hand. It does not go
through the alert queue either — that queue serialises short tones, and a
minute-long reading would hold every chime in the farm behind it.

**Only a FINISHED turn is read.** A turn parked on a question has not said its
answer yet, and a session ending would repeat the turn that was already read.
Markdown, code fences and links are stripped first; the text is cut at the same
1200 characters the timeline quotes, and *"There is more."* is spoken when it
did not fit.

`alerts.read { sessionId, on?, stop? }` is the same act from the bridge — with
`stop` as the panic button, which cuts the current reading short and changes no
setting.

**Fixed on the way:** a session's chosen announcing voice (A-20) was **lost on
every window reload**. It was written by its setter and asked for by the
announcement, but the store never read it back when loading — and a session
whose only preference was that voice was dropped entirely. Found while adding
the field beside it.

## 3.313.0 - U-123: the nudge has a control instead of a JSON box (2026-08-29)

The last raw box on the Alert sounds card, and the odd one out: the rest of the
gate — mute · quiet hours · the sessions muted on their own — has lived on one
line since A-22, while the **one control that makes a sound you did not arm** sat
three fields deep in `agentFarm.alerts.nudge` as JSON.

**`⏰ Nudge after [3] min, [2] × [tone]`**, on the gate strip, beside the two
switches that decide whether the FIRST alert is heard at all. That is where it
belongs: it answers the gate's question — *will a sound happen* — not the table's,
*which sound*.

**And what is waiting right now is on the strip.** `2 waiting` is the number of
questions actually armed for a reminder at this moment; a session that is
answered or leaves the list disarms itself, so it is what is outstanding rather
than a running total. **The card head says the nudge is on** too, beside the
armed count — a policy that produces an unrequested chime some minutes later is
worth a badge.

**The tone picker offers exactly what the op accepts.** One grouped list, shared
with the event rows, and a sound this machine cannot play is **drawn and
disabled** rather than dropped — a setting naming a missing file must go on
naming it. Off is `minutes: 0`, the setting's own word for it, so there is no
fourth field that could disagree with the other three.

Everything on the strip goes through the same host function `alerts.nudge` uses,
which is now one door rather than logic living inside an op handler.

## 3.312.0 - A-24: a run can say what it sounds like when it ends (2026-08-29)

The last piece of A-23, and it was held back for three releases by one honest
objection: **"Silent" could not be built.** The two authorities over a sound ADD
and neither may subtract from the other, so nothing a session said about itself
could make it quiet — and a three-option field with one option that does nothing
is worse than no field. A-22 answered it with the session mute, so the field is
now three real answers.

**Sound on finish**, on the New-task form and on the schedule and trigger
editors beside it: *Default* · a tone · *Silent — no sound at all*. Drawn for
every run, headless included — a headless run has no window to open, but it does
END, and it is the one nobody is watching.

**It adds no step to the alert chain.** The moment the run's session has an id,
the pick is written onto **that session's own step** — the one A-23 built, that
the resolution chain already reads and the Live Timeline already draws. So the
row goes on saying "this session's own choice" and is telling the truth.
Declared ids (a Console run, a resumed conversation) are stamped at the spawn;
an ordinary headless run is stamped the moment its transcript names it.

**Picking a tone also arms that session's ♪** — otherwise the choice would be
accepted, stored, drawn, and silent whenever the fleet switch happened to be
off, which is the defect the field exists to fix.

**And "Silent" mutes the whole run, not only its ending**, because that is what
it really does: silence is not a tone, it is the mute, and the label says so
rather than promising less than it delivers. Everything underneath it is left
alone, so unmuting restores the setup.

`finishSound` is a run dimension like the model and the permission mode: it
rides on `tasks.add`, `schedules.add|set`, `triggers.add|set`, `templates.add|run`
and every workflow step, it is refused **by name** where it is written down
rather than at 03:00, a **retry inherits it**, and reading an automation back
tells you what it will sound like. The word `silent` can never be a tone: every
built-in id is spelled out and every one of your own is `u-…`.

## 3.311.0 - A-25: the announcement has a face (2026-08-29)

A-20 built the whole engine and left it behind a raw JSON box. Seven fields,
one of them a voice NAME that has to exist on this machine — and a settings box
cannot know whether it does. **That was the worst of the four boxes this card
has now absorbed**, because the engine's answer to a name nothing answers to is
a FAILED announcement (`exit 5`), on purpose, rather than a quiet fall back to
English. The one thing the box could never show was the one thing that decided
whether the feature worked at all.

**The strip.** Under the gate, on the same card, in the order the two are read:
*is anything heard at all* → *and what does it say*. Switch · voice · rate ·
volume · the sentence · ▶ test. `agentFarm.alerts.speak` no longer appears as a
box beside it.

**Every voice on the machine, with its LANGUAGE on the row.** Both of Windows'
registries, asked of the machine and not guessed, sorted by language — because
an `en-US` voice reading Turkish is not accented, it is unintelligible. The
answer costs a PowerShell process, so it is asked once when the card opens and
kept; ↻ is for the language pack installed a minute ago.

**And which voice the setting ACTUALLY REACHES.** `Tolga` is a legal setting and
no voice is called that, so the picker selects the voice it *resolves to* —
`Microsoft Tolga - Turkish (Turkey)` — and a name **nothing** answers to is
shown as a warning here rather than discovered at the moment the alert does not
arrive. ‼️ Only where the list is authoritative: listing voices is Windows-only,
so on macOS the strip says the platform cannot answer instead of calling a
working setting broken.

**Which events are spoken is a 🗣 column in the table that already says what
they play** — not five more ticks three lines above it, which the reader would
have had to match up by name.

**And the ♪ right-click gained the third thing somebody says about one
conversation:** *announce this one in its own voice*. The engine and the store
shipped in A-20; only the surface was missing. It is in the same picker as the
tone and the mute because those three are said in the same breath.

Every gesture goes through the same host functions `alerts.speak` does — the
card and the bridge cannot part company on what a partial change means. The op
now answers `resolved` as well, so a caller learns the same thing.

## 3.310.0 - A-20: every voice on the machine, and one per conversation (2026-08-29)

3.309.0 shipped the announcement and told the user their machine had only two
en-US voices. That was wrong, and the user said so.

**Windows keeps its voices in TWO registries and `System.Speech` sees one.**
SAPI 5 reads `Speech\Voices\Tokens` — David and Zira, en-US. Every voice a user
has ever installed from Settings goes to `Speech_OneCore\Voices\Tokens`, and
`SelectVoice` can neither list nor choose one. Measured on this machine: SAPI 5
had two voices, OneCore had four — one of them **`Microsoft Tolga — Turkish`,
already installed and completely unreachable.** So the advice the last release
printed ("install a language pack") was for a problem the user did not have.

**The COM server underneath reaches both.** `SpVoice.GetVoices()` enumerates
