the SAPI 5 set only, but `SpObjectToken.SetId(<registry path>)` loads ANY token
by id, OneCore included — verified out loud, in Turkish, before it was written.
The Windows backend is now that, walking both registries to find a voice by
name: **`Tolga` finds `Microsoft Tolga - Turkish (Turkey)`.** Every voice on the
machine is selectable, in every language it has.

**The voice list says what it really is.** Six rows here, each with its culture
and which registry it came from, sorted by language — because the question a
reader brings to the list is "is there one that speaks mine?".

**A name nothing answers now FAILS, by name.** The old code caught the error and
fell back to the system default, so somebody who asked for a Turkish voice got
an English one and was told it worked. A wrong voice is not a smaller failure
than no voice; it is a harder one to diagnose.

**And a conversation can have its own voice.** One voice for eight lanes is the
wrong shape the moment two of them are worth telling apart by ear: the agent
whose questions are in Turkish is announced in Turkish while the rest are not,
and the difference carries from the next room without a word being understood.
Same chain as the tones — the session answers first, and having no opinion falls
through to the fleet rather than to silence. `alerts.speak { sessionId, voice }`
sets it, reads it, and clears it.

Underneath, the three sticky per-session fields (the chosen tone, the mute, and
now the voice) are carried by **one helper** instead of three spread expressions
repeated in three setters — a rule that held only until somebody added a fourth
field and updated two of them.

## 3.309.0 - A-20: the fleet can say which agent (2026-08-29)

The third part of A-20. Twenty voices answer "what KIND of news is this?" and
nothing else. With eight lanes running, the question you actually have from the
next room is **which one** — and no palette of tones can carry a name.

**A spoken line can, and it costs nothing.** `System.Speech` has been in every
Windows install for twenty years; macOS `say` and Linux `spd-say` are equally
already there. No network, no account, no model, no per-token anything.

**It is an addition to the tone, not a replacement.** A tone reaches the ear in
half a second and is recognised before it finishes; a sentence takes two and
cannot be told from a podcast in the next room until it is over. So the tone
still says what kind, immediately, and the sentence arrives behind it saying
which one. **Both ride in one queue ticket** — submitted separately, another
lane's chime would land in the middle of this one's sentence, which is the exact
overlap the queue exists to stop. It follows the same mute, the same quiet
hours and the same per-session mute.

**It ships off, and out of the box announces only `question`.** That is the
argument for the feature rather than a limitation of it: `question` is the one
event where an agent is STOPPED and the cost of not knowing is the whole run
standing still. A fleet that announces every finished turn out loud is one you
silence in an afternoon — and then you hear nothing at all, including the
question.

**The text never enters a command string,** which matters more here than for
the tones, not less: the sentence is written by you, in a settings box, and an
agent's NAME is substituted into it. On Windows it travels as an environment
variable, elsewhere as an argument of its own. An agent called `; rm -rf ~` is
a strange name and nothing else.

**The substitution is deliberately dumb.** `{agent}`, `{event}` and `{session}`
are replaced and everything else is spoken exactly as typed, so a mistyped
`{agnet}` is HEARD — a placeholder that silently vanishes is a bug with no
symptom at all.

**And it lists the voices — while saying plainly that the list is about the
PLAYER, not about the machine.** A Turkish sentence read by `Microsoft David`
is unintelligible rather than accented, so which voice is used matters. But
Windows keeps **two separate sets**: `System.Speech` is SAPI 5 and sees
`Speech\Voices\Tokens`, which usually holds only David and Zira; every language
pack a user has ever installed goes to `Speech_OneCore\Voices\Tokens`, which
this engine cannot reach at all. Measured on this machine: SAPI 5 has two en-US
voices, OneCore has four — **one of them `Microsoft Tolga — Turkish`, already
installed and invisible to the player.** So the list says so, instead of
telling somebody to install what they already have.

New op **`alerts.speak`**: read the configuration and the installed voices, set
any of it, and `say:` speaks a line RIGHT NOW as a test — even when the feature
is off, and it says so. "Does this machine talk at all?" and "is the
announcement switched on?" are two questions, and a test that answers the second
when asked the first teaches nobody anything.

Under it, the tone and the sentence now go through **one runner**: the timeout,
the shell-free contract, "a missing player is not a diagnosis" and the named
exit codes are written once and cannot drift apart.

‼️ **Still to come.** Two named pieces, both in the backlog:
**3b** — `agentFarm.alerts.speak` has no control in the Alert sounds card yet
and is drawn as a raw JSON box; the op and the setting are complete and
working. **3c** — reaching the OneCore voices, so an installed Turkish (or
German, or Japanese) voice can actually be used, which needs the WinRT
synthesiser rather than `System.Speech`.

## 3.308.0 - A-20: ten sounds that are ten different objects (2026-08-29)

The second part of A-20 — the palette. The nine tones A-18 generated are one
mechanism heard nine ways: a sine, an octave above it, and a decay. From the
next room they are recognisably relatives, and telling "your turn" from "it is
asking you" while doing something else was the condition this whole feature was
opened for.

**So the ten new ones are ten different OBJECTS.** The partials of a real thing
are not a harmonic series, and that — not the envelope — is what makes wood
sound like wood: a marimba bar rings at 1 : 3.9 : 9.2, a tubular bell at
1 : 2.76 : 5.40. Three new instruments in the generator (a struck body with
arbitrary partial ratios, a pitch glide whose phase is integrated so it does not
click, and a seeded noise transient) make: **Crystal** · **Intercom knock** ·
**Zen bowl** · **Deep sonar** · **Lullaby** · **Marimba** · **Pop** ·
**Thin ticks** · **Bell, urgent** · **Pulse**.

**And they are measured, because nobody can listen to them in a review.**
`node tools/make_alert_sounds.js --stats` prints each voice's length,
brightness and body, and checks the pairs that carry the feature. The two
defaults — Crystal for a finished turn, Intercom knock for a question — sit a
factor of **4.7 apart in brightness** and differ as much again in body: one is
struck glass, the other a knuckle on a panel with almost no pitch at all. That
is a difference you hear through a closed door, which a difference of melody is
not.

**All five defaults changed, and that is said out loud rather than shipped
quietly.** A default nobody hears is not a delivery. What is safe about it:
alerts ship OFF, so anybody hearing anything has been to the settings page
already; and a voice you CHOSE lives a step above the default in the chain and
is untouched. Only "sound on, never picked a voice" moves.

**The earlier ten stay, under their own heading in the picker.** A set that
disappears in an upgrade takes a setting with it. `chime-soft` still points at
`turn-ready.wav` — the exact bytes every install already makes.

**A label names the SOUND, never an event.** The first cut of these read
"Crystal — your turn", which is a lie the moment somebody picks it for `error`,
and which the picker cut off anyway.

**`verify_vsix` now looks inside `media/sounds/`.** It never did: it read
`media/` and stopped. A voice the archive does not carry is not a blank panel
somebody notices in a second — it is an alert that never plays, on a feature
whose whole purpose is to be heard from another room, while the settings page
still offers it by name. The list is derived from the compiled core, so a voice
added there and forgotten in `.vscodeignore` is caught here rather than by a
user. The test suite also checks every committed `.wav` is byte-identical to
what the generator produces: the character of each voice is supposed to be a
line of code somebody can read and argue with, and that is only worth anything
while the two agree.

**The settings fixture reads the core instead of restating it.** This release
is the proof of why: ten voices arrived, five defaults moved, and the fixture
went on drawing the old ones — every string test passed while the screenshot
lied about a page that no longer existed.

## 3.307.0 - A-20: the Windows alert was arriving eight seconds late (2026-08-29)

The first of three parts of A-20 — the player itself, before the sounds it
plays. It began as "add mp3 and flac" and turned up something worse on the way.

**Measured: every Windows alert was eight seconds late.** `MediaPlayer` is a
WPF `DispatcherObject`, and its `MediaEnded` event is raised on a Dispatcher
that `powershell -Command` never runs. So the event never came, the process sat
in its wait loop for 17.7 seconds, this module's own timeout killed it at eight,
the backend was reported as broken — and the sound you finally heard was the
SoundPlayer fallback, announcing a turn that had ended eight seconds earlier.
Nothing in the extension was in a position to notice: the fallback returned
success, so the alert was working, just late enough to be useless.

**The player asks the file how long it is instead.** `NaturalDuration` is
filled in by the media engine and needs no dispatcher — which makes it two
answers at once: how long to wait, and, when it never arrives, the codec saying
it cannot open this file. Measured end to end: **1.8 s for a `.wav`, 2.3 s for
an `.mp3`**, and a file no codec can open now reports that, in those words.
Before, a refused file left through the same silent loop with exit 0 and was
reported as PLAYED.

**And it was reported as played.** That is the second half of the same bug and
the more dangerous one: `.mp3`, `.flac` and anything else the codec refused
came back green. A user who pointed an alert at their own file was told it
worked and heard nothing, for ever.

**The format now picks the player, before anything is spawned.** An `.mp3` went
to the wav-only fallback as a matter of course, failed there, and — because the
LAST attempt was the reported one — ended carrying `SoundPlayer: wav only`,
while what the real player had said was already thrown away. A format nothing
on the machine can open spawns no process at all and names what does play.

**`.flac` is offered on Windows and macOS; `.ogg` deliberately is not.** Read
out of the registry rather than assumed: Windows carries Media Foundation
handlers for flac, mp3, m4a and wma, and **none for ogg** — the Web Media
Extensions that carry Vorbis are a Store package that is on some machines and
not others, and CoreAudio has never read it either. Promising it would be the
exact trap this table exists to prevent: the row says playable, the alert is
silence, nothing reports an error. Vorbis is offered through `ffplay`, which is
named in the row, so a user who wants it is told what to install.

**On a `.wav` the cheap player now leads.** `SoundPlayer` lives in `System.dll`
and is already loaded; `MediaPlayer` pulls in PresentationCore first — 0.6 s of
overhead against 1.2 s, measured. Every built-in voice is a `.wav`, so this is
the path almost every alert takes.

**When every player fails, the one that explains it is reported.** The chain now
ends on `ffplay`, which most machines do not have, so "the last attempt is the
answer" would reply to every silent alert with `spawn ffplay ENOENT` and bury
the sentence produced two backends earlier. A player that is absent is not why
the alert was silent.

Also: `pw-play` on Linux, for a desktop that has replaced PulseAudio outright.

## 3.306.0 - A-22: eight agents finishing together make eight sounds, not one noise (2026-08-29)

The other half of A-22. 3.305.0 answered "should anything sound"; this answers
"in what order, and what if nobody comes".

**One queue for the whole window.** Eight lanes is the normal case, and eight
players started in the same 40 ms do not make eight sounds — they make ONE
noise, out of which nothing can be told apart, which is the exact ability ten
named tones exist to give. The sounds now go one at a time, ordered by how much
the news matters: `question` first (the only event where the agent is STOPPED
and waiting on you), then `error`, `stalled`, `ended`, and `turn-ready` last —
the one that happens most and costs least to miss, because the Timeline shows it
anyway.

**The 500 ms gap is measured from the END of the last sound**, not its start.
The tones are up to 1.2 s long, so a gap counted from the start would let them
overlap, which is the whole thing the queue exists to stop.

**The queue has a small ceiling, and something IS dropped.** A backlog of twenty
chimes is twenty seconds of noise describing a fleet that has since moved on —
not merely useless but actively misleading. Over six waiting, the LEAST urgent
goes and says so. The same alert twice is one alert.

**A dropped sound is `skipped`, never `failed`,** and a sound that waited says
how long and behind how many: "the chime came four seconds late" is otherwise
indistinguishable from a slow player, and the two have opposite fixes.

**The second tap on the shoulder.** The sound exists so you can leave the room,
and a sound heard in another room with both hands busy is one that gets
acknowledged in a minute and then forgotten, while the agent sits at its
question for forty. If a question is still unanswered after 3 minutes, a light
reminder tone plays — up to twice, then it stops, because a chime that never
ends is one you mute for good. Its tone is deliberately its own and lighter than
the one you already missed; a second identical chime reads as a second question.

**Only `question` is nudged.** Reminding somebody about a finished turn is
pestering them about news that needs nothing from them. And **the sweep is also
the disarm**: a session that answered, ended or moved on is dropped by the beat
rather than by an edge somebody has to remember to wire — every edge that could
be missed is one reminder at 3 am about a question answered hours ago.

The reminder goes through the same mute, the same quiet hours and the same queue
as the alert it reminds you about. New op: `alerts.nudge`; `alerts.gate` now
also reports the queue depth and what is waiting in it.

**Deliberately not done:** `agentFarm.alerts.nudge` has no control on the Alert
sounds card yet — it renders as its own settings box, which works but is not
where the rest of the gate lives. The op and the setting are complete.

## 3.305.0 - A-22: the farm can be told to be quiet (2026-08-29)

Alert sounds could be configured and armed, and there was no way to make them
stop. Somebody walks into the room at 23:40 with eight agents finishing turns,
and the only remedy was to walk to the machine and untick five boxes they would
then have to remember to tick again. **A-22 adds the gate: a 🔇 in the status
bar, a nightly window, and a mute for one conversation.**

**Which sound and whether it sounds are two questions, and they stay two.**
`resolveVoice` answers the first and is guaranteed to always have an answer;
teaching it to resolve to nothing would make every fall-through in it
indistinguishable from a deliberate silence. The gate (`core/alertGate.ts`) sits
in FRONT of the chain, names who closed it, and edits no choice.

**🔇, one click, from wherever the eye already is.** A status bar item that
APPEARS the first time anything is armed — the whole family ships off, and an
icon sitting there for months on a fleet that has never made a noise is clutter
— and stays up while muted, because a control that hides itself once pressed is
one nobody can undo. It is the same act as `Agent Farm: Mute / Unmute Alert
Sounds`, the Settings card and the `alerts.mute` op: one function, three doors.

**Quiet hours WRAP MIDNIGHT.** 23:00→08:00 read as `from <= now < to` is quiet
for exactly no minutes of the day, and that is the only shape anybody sets. A
time that is not `HH:MM` is refused BY NAME rather than stored: a schedule that
reads as configured and silences nothing is the worst of the three outcomes.
Start equal to end is an EMPTY window, never all day, so a typo cannot mute a
farm around the clock.

**One conversation can be quiet while the others ring.** The fleet-wide switch
ADDS to a session's own ♪ selection and a union cannot subtract, so unticking ♪
never silenced a session while `alerts.on.question` was on. The session mute is
that missing authority — and it clears nothing: every armed box and chosen tone
stays exactly as it is, so unmuting restores the setup rather than the defaults.

**A gated sound is `skipped`, never `failed`.** Reported as a failure it raises
the broken-player warning and teaches the user to ignore the one message that
matters. The branch carries the reason instead, which is the answer to the only
question anybody opens the alert page with.

**Every authority is named, not just the first.** Unmuting at 03:00 and still
hearing nothing is a half-truth nobody can debug, so the card's badge, the ♪
panel, the status bar tooltip and `alerts.gate` all list every one of them.

Sounds only: the notification, the modal and the focus jump are separate
branches with their own switches. New ops: `alerts.mute`, `alerts.quiet`,
`alerts.gate`.

## 3.304.0 - X-142: reopening something archived takes it out of the archive (2026-08-28)

Ticking an archived item back open changed one character and left the line
hanging under `## 🗄 Archive`. That is the worst of both states: the item counted
as open, and every default view hides the archive — the page folds it away and
`backlog.next` reads the file from the top — so the work was neither shown nor
finished, and nothing anywhere said why it had vanished.

X-145 already diagnosed exactly this shape and built the carry-home. It only
ever ran on a deliberate `projects.backlog.tidy`, so the file stayed wrong until
somebody happened to run one. **The reopen is the moment the line becomes live
work, so it is the moment it goes home** — same machinery, called at the moment
that creates the problem instead of at some later moment that happens to notice
it.

**The line's text is not touched.** It is lifted and re-inserted verbatim; what
changes is where it sits. `setBacklogState`'s promise has always been that it
never REBUILDS somebody's line out of parsed pieces, and that still holds.

**Only that one item moves.** The full sweep is still a deliberate act: quietly
relocating four other mis-filed lines because somebody unticked a box would be
an edit they did not ask for, in a file they read by eye.

**One way.** A closed line under 🗄 belongs there and is never dragged out, and
nothing is ever auto-archived. If the item's area has no heading to go home to,
it stays where it is and the note says so — inventing a heading would be
restructuring somebody's document rather than repairing it.

Reported as a fact and not only in prose: `projects.backlog.check` answers with
`reseated: true`, because the line number a caller was holding is now the wrong
one. And the ⛔ that comes off when an item is started now comes off the line
that MOVED — it was named by a line number the reseat had just invalidated,
which would have left the hold silently on, on the one path where the item had
just been rescued.

## 3.303.0 - A-23: a conversation can have a tone of its own, and the row says which (2026-08-28)

Fifth step of A-18, and it closes a hole that had been open since the first one.
`resolveVoice` has always answered "which sound?" in four steps — **session,
agent, settings, default** — and the top step was **never wired to anything**.
Nothing in the extension could write it, so "give THIS conversation its own
sound" — the thing the item was opened for — quietly resolved to the fleet-wide
setting every time. The chain was right; it was reading a store that did not
exist.

### The `session` step, written at last

It lives in the SESSION preference store (`turnAlerts.ts`) rather than in a map
of its own, because everything a per-session preference needs is already there:
the **rekey** when a terminal lane learns the engine's real conversation id, the
TTL, the ceiling, the forget. A second copy of that machinery would have drifted
on the first change to either.

The two questions stay separate. Clearing a row's four boxes does **not** unpick
its tone, and clearing its tone is **not** muting it — an empty choice hands the
answer back to your setting for everybody and then to the built-in default.
There is no "this session is silent" in the chain; muting is the ♪ box, which is
a different question and a different control.

### Sound for This Session…

New right-click item, drawn only where the row IS something still running — a
Timeline lane, a Timeline card, the Console's live card. Offered on a search hit
it would be an item that refuses on nearly every click.

Two picks, both over lists that already exist. First the **event**, each one
carrying what it plays today and which step chose it, because the question is
comparative and five bare names cannot be compared. Then the **tone**, with ▶ on
every row: ten sounds called `chime-bright` and `ask-rise` are unchooseable from
the words, and the button plays one where you are standing instead of sending
you to Settings and back. It does not close on ▶ — the point is comparing two.

### The ♪ box says what it will play

It was a checkbox with a native tooltip, and a checkbox can only ever say
"armed" — which was never the question somebody hovers it with, now that five
tones exist precisely so two rows finishing in the next room can be told apart.
It is an **AFTip** now (MIRROR): the tone and the step of the chain that chose
it on the first line, both session events, then every step that was passed over
**with the reason**, then what the control does. The other three controls keep
their native tooltip — a boolean is the size a native tooltip is for.

Drawn in SVG and answered in HTML like the rest of this gutter (U-67), and the
box IS the control, so the two cannot disagree about which session was clicked.
The group under it keeps its role and its state: announcing one checkbox twice
is worse than announcing the drawing.

### The ⏱ test picks its edge

`live.alerts.test` has taken an `event` since A-20 and the page had no way to
name one, so the only rehearsable edge was `turn-ready` — the one thing the
feature exists to distinguish from `question` could not be heard on purpose. The
picker sits in the line that explains the ⏱, defaults to `turn-ready`, and
offers the three fleet-switch-only edges too, so their tone can be judged before
turning them on. The result strip names the edge and the tone that came out of
it; a row of ticks alone answers nothing now.

### Bridge

`alerts.voice.set` gains `scope: "session"` (with `sessionId`). It was refusing
every non-`settings` scope by name; that door is open, and it still says which
step of the chain it wrote to. The `agent` step has no surface yet and is still
refused by name rather than silently written to the wrong place.

## 3.302.0 - A-21: the alert sounds get a card that says which one will play (2026-08-28)

Fourth step of A-18. `agentFarm.alerts.on` and `agentFarm.alerts.voices` were
two JSON boxes on the settings page, and **both are empty objects out of the
box** — so the page showed `{}` twice for a feature that already plays five
different tones, and the one question a person opens that page with ("which
sound will I hear, and why that one?") had no answer anywhere on it. Only the
resolution chain can answer it, so the host now hands the **resolved** rows over
and the boxes are gone rather than decorated. Same lesson the wiki root (X-57)
and the Superpowers folder (X-136) each cost a week.

### The card

One row per event: the tick that arms it for every session, the sound picked for
everybody, **what would actually play and which step of the chain chose it**, and
a ▶ that plays it. The picker offers the default as a named option rather than a
blank, because "use whatever the default is" and "pin it to chime-soft" are
different answers and only one of them survives a version that changes the
default.

A chosen sound and a playing sound are drawn as different things, and they differ
exactly when something is wrong — a file deleted in Explorer, a format no player
here opens. The chain **falls through to the step below rather than going
silent**, so the alert still rings; the row says what it landed on and the hover
lists every step it passed over with the reason. An armed event that has run out
of steps entirely — a partial update that took `error-buzz` with it — is called
out on the card’s badge, because that is the one state where the sound really
would be silence, and silence is indistinguishable from the switch being off.

It sits **beside the notification switches on purpose**: those open a VS Code
notification, these make a noise, and "I turned the sound off and a notification
still arrives" is the confusion that keeping them apart-but-adjacent prevents.

### Your own sounds

Up to ten, any format a player on this machine can open. **The file is not
copied** — "wherever I like" was the ask, and a copy would mean the sound edited
tomorrow is not the sound that plays. The name is an editable box on the row
rather than a ✎ that opens a prompt (a webview has no `window.prompt`, so a
button wired to one does nothing at all), and renaming **never moves the id**: it
is written into the settings and into any session that picked it, so
regenerating it would silently unpick the sound everywhere it was chosen.

Removing a sound **clears whatever pointed at it** in the same breath, so no row
is left naming a sound nothing answers.

### On the bridge, in the same commit

`alerts.voice.add` · `alerts.voice.remove` · `alerts.voice.rename` ·
`alerts.play`. Every gesture on the card runs the same host function its
matching op runs — the page holds no rule of its own about reserved ids, the
limit of ten, or which formats play, so the two cannot drift. `alerts.voices`
now also says where a new sound is suggested to go and how much room is left.

## 3.301.0 - K-22 · U-118 · U-119: a blocked session stops being a dead end (2026-08-28)

Three items around one failure, reported the same morning: a session asked for
permission on a terminal nobody was watching and sat there for an hour and a
half. Every layer had a way of not helping.

### K-22 — bypass on the card has to mean bypass in the process (the CLI half)

The Console half was fixed in 3.135.1. **The terminal and headless paths were
still spelling bypass their own way**, and the spelling they used does not
enforce it: `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` is read through a branch the
CLI guards and `gad()` can downgrade, while `--dangerously-skip-permissions`
short-circuits at the top. Three places spelling one instruction is what this
item has been about from the start, so all three now go through
`permissionFlags`.

**And `Default` was never resolved at all.** A user whose own settings say
`permissions.defaultMode: bypassPermissions` got an asking terminal session —
the picker even promised it would ask. The layers are read before the command
line is built, exactly as the Console reads them, and the launcher's preview
shows the flags the launch will really carry. **A bypass that a policy forbids
refuses to start** rather than opening under a label it cannot keep: in a
terminal that failure is invisible, because nothing draws a card.

`launch.permission` on the bridge answers "what would a launch in this folder
really run in", with the three facts kept apart — requested, from settings,
enforced.

### U-118 — the queue can finally show what the agent said

Needs You drew `lastPrompt`, which the live monitor cuts to **ninety
characters** for a card, and then cut it again with an ellipsis. So the one page
a person opens to find out what the farm is stuck on could not show the question
it was stuck on: the answer was four thousand characters deep in
`lastPromptFull` and was thrown away one field before it was drawn.

**A row is a line and an opened row is the text.** Every row kind goes through
one reading standard now — a caret and a selectable block that keeps its line
breaks, plus an AFTip carrying the whole thing so the common case needs no click
at all. **The caret is drawn only when there is more behind it**: a triangle
that opens onto the sentence already on the row teaches a reader in two clicks
that opening rows tells them nothing. Opening one posts nothing and marks
nothing — a blocker is not a message. Queue, Tasks and the Timeline already
carried their full text; Needs You was the outlier.

### U-119 — answer it from the page

The row's offer was "⌨ Terminal": a signpost. Agent Farm knew an agent was
blocked ON THE USER and its best answer was to send them looking for a window.
Esc has been typed into these terminals since the interrupt was built, so the
channel was always there — only the other half was missing.

**Allow and Reject on the row**, and on the bridge as
`sessions.answerPermission`. A hosted conversation is answered properly through
the option id the CLI published; a terminal session has its answer typed in, on
the same resolution the interrupt uses (two answers to "which terminal is this
session's?" is how they drift, and typing an allow into the wrong window is
worse than typing an Esc into it). An external OS window is refused by name.

**‼️ And the claim is exactly what is known.** Nothing here can see the prompt
or read an answer back, so every path reports WHICH KEYS were sent and never
that the tool was allowed — the terminal is brought forward first, so the user
is looking at the prompt when it moves, and at the prompt that did not move when
it does not. **The keystroke is a setting** (`agentFarm.permissionAnswerKeys`),
because what a prompt accepts belongs to the CLI and has worn more than one
shape: a hard-coded key a later build stops honouring would make this button do
nothing, silently.

### A-20 (step 3) — the alert sounds get their settings

`agentFarm.alerts.on` (which events play a sound, for every session) and
`agentFarm.alerts.voices` (which sound each one plays). Both draw themselves as
forms on Farm Settings, from the schema, with nobody editing the page.

**‼️ The global switch ADDS to a session's own ♪ selection; it does not gate
it.** The design asked for all five entries off out of the box, and a gate
defaulting to off would have silenced the turn-ready sound every install has had
for months — on upgrade, with nothing on any page saying why. So there are two
authorities and they add: a session's selection is "alert me about THIS
conversation, in these ways" (the item's two events), and `alerts.on` is "play
the sound for this KIND of event, everywhere". The worst an empty setting can do
is nothing. It arms the SOUND only — nobody turning on a setting called "alert
sounds" is asking for modal dialogs across the whole fleet.

Bridge: `alerts.on`, `alerts.voice.set` (which names the step of the resolution
chain it wrote to), and `alerts.resolve` now returns the plan as well as the
voice — "would this actually ring?" is a different question from "which sound",
and a resolution that answered only the second reads as "it is armed".

Also: a form field that declares a default now uses it as its placeholder
instead of repeating the label six pixels to its left.

**Tests:** `test_permission_answer.js` (27), `test_needs_reading.js` (23),
`test_bypass_contract.js` +13, `test_alert_voices.js` +15. 231 files ·
15 147 assertions.

## 3.300.0 - A-20 (step 2): the farm says WHICH kind of attention it wants (2026-08-28)

**Step two of the auditory cockpit (A-18).** Step one built the ten voices and
the chain that picks one, and nothing was wired to it. This wires it: the live
monitor now reports every edge that wants the user, carrying the event that
names what happened, and the alert dispatch takes that event all the way to the
sound, the modal and the toast.

**`waiting-input` was two different endings wearing one status.** A turn that
finished hands control back; a turn parked on an `AskUserQuestion` is still open
and wants an ANSWER. They were the same beep and the same "your turn" modal, so
the only way to tell them apart was to walk back and look — which is the whole
thing the sound was for. `LiveConfig.pendingAskOf` is injected, because only the
host knows: a hosted conversation's pending ask lives in the Console, and the
monitor keeps its promise never to reach outside itself.

**Four edges, one emit site.** `waiting-permission` → `question`,
`waiting-input` → `question` or `turn-ready` depending on the parked ask,
`SessionEnd` → `ended`, the stall sweep → `stalled`. **Once per crossing**,
exactly as before: the "waiting" Notification and the `Stop` behind it are one
edge, and a session parked in a state does not keep ringing. `onTurnReady`
survives unchanged as the narrow view of the same emit — wire one or the other,
never both.

**A second permission ask in the same turn is no longer silent.** The dedupe key
was the prompt ordinal alone, so a question asked mid-turn would have swallowed
the turn's own ending, and a second tool approval would have made no noise at
all — precisely the case somebody is away from the screen for. The key now
carries the event and the tool ordinal too, and neither counter moves between
the two events that announce one turn ending, so that collapse still holds.

**A hosted lane's parked question reaches the timeline at last.** The turn stays
open while a Console ask is pending, so no status change ever carried it: the
card showed the question, the timeline showed a turn still working, and a user
in another room was told nothing at all. A permission ask now parks the lane on
`waiting-permission`, an `AskUserQuestion` on `waiting-input` where the injected
`pendingAskOf` names it a question rather than a finished turn. **And the agent
speaking unparks the lane** — without that the turn's real ending was no
crossing at all and rang nothing. Only Agent Farm's own mirrored event can do
this, so no CLI lane is touched by it.

**Only the item's two events dispatch.** `stalled`, `ended` and `error` are
emitted and ride the same mechanism for free, but arming them for every session
that ever ticked `♪` would make an ended session start beeping on a setting
whose whole text says "your turn". They ship silent and get their own switch
with the settings surface.

**Bridge:** `alerts.voices` (the ten plus the user's, each with whether THIS
machine can play it — answered from the player's own format table, never a list
kept beside it) and `alerts.resolve` (why that sound: the winning step, and
every step passed over with its reason). `live.alerts.test` takes an `event` and
reports the voice it resolved and where that choice came from.

**Tests:** `test_live_edges.js` (21 assertions) — every edge, once per crossing,
both endings of `waiting-input`, a second ask in one turn, a host that throws,
and nothing wired at all. `test_turnready.js` is untouched and green.

## 3.299.0 - A-20 (step 1): ten alert voices, and which one plays (2026-08-28)

**The first step of the auditory cockpit (A-18), and nothing is wired to it
yet** — this is the core plus its assets, in the build order the design note
lays out. The farm could make exactly one noise, on the one edge where a turn
finished. Away from the screen, "your turn" and "it is asking you something"
were the same beep, so the only way to tell them apart was to walk back and
look — which is the whole thing the sound was for.

**Ten voices, generated rather than sourced** (`tools/make_alert_sounds.js`).
The obvious way to get ten alert sounds is to download them, and then the
extension ships ten files whose licence nobody can state; these are written from
arithmetic, cost 340 kB together, and each one's character is a line of code
somebody can read and argue with. All are ≤1.2 s, 44.1 kHz mono, normalised to
−3 dBFS. **`chime-soft` is `turn-ready.wav` and is not regenerated** — it is the
sound every current install already makes, and a "nicer" replacement would have
changed it silently.

**`src/core/alertVoices.ts` — one place answers "which sound, and why".**
Session beats agent beats settings beats the built-in default, and the answer
says which step gave it, because "why did it play that?" has to be answerable on
the page. **A voice whose file is gone falls through rather than silencing the
alert**, and the step it passed over is reported with the reason: silence is
indistinguishable from an alert that never fired. Out of the box "your turn" and
"asking you" are different sounds — one settled chime, one rising double knock.

**Windows now plays through `MediaPlayer`, with `SoundPlayer` behind it.**
`SoundPlayer.PlaySync()` opens `.wav` only and blocks for the length of the
sound; the moment a user points an alert at a file of their own, an `.mp3`
handed to it throws and the alert becomes silence with no error anywhere.
MediaPlayer is the same Windows install, opens mp3/m4a/wma/wav and is
asynchronous. SoundPlayer stays as the fallback, because MediaPlayer lives in
PresentationCore and a Windows without WPF would otherwise lose the alert it has
today. Linux gains `ffplay` between `paplay` and `aplay`.

**Every backend now declares what it can open**, and `playableOn` reads that
table — so a page cannot promise an `.mp3` that the player cannot play, which
would be a row saying "playable" over an alert that makes no sound.

## 3.298.0 - U-110: a set of name → value pairs is a row editor (2026-08-28)

**Three settings are a free-form object** — `budgets`, `superpowersDefaults`,
`agentEngineDefaults`. Nothing can list their keys, which is why all three were
left as a JSON textarea, and it is the wrong conclusion: **the key is free, the
pair is not.** Setting a budget meant hand-writing `{"developer": 20}` including
the brace, the quote and the colon, and getting the agent's name right from
memory — with a misfiled name failing silently for ever.

One row per pair now: **a name box, an arrow, a value box, a ✕**, `+ add`, and
**Save the pairs**. The name box **suggests and does not constrain** — the fleet
the page is already holding is offered, and a name nobody has yet is still
typeable, because `*` is a real key and so is an agent created tomorrow.

**The three maps are not the same shape, and each now says so.** `budgets` is
name → **number** and gets number boxes; `superpowersDefaults` is name →
**boolean** and gets a yes/no picker that can still say "not set";
`agentEngineDefaults` declares nothing about its values and keeps their JSON,
honestly, in one cell. All read off `additionalProperties`. **Where the names
come from is a manifest fact too** (`x-af-keys`), because the three differ:
`budgets` takes agent names and `*` for the whole fleet, `superpowersDefaults`
takes names with **no wildcard at all** (it is an exact match), and
`agentEngineDefaults` is keyed by an agent's folder. One guessed list for all
three would have offered `*` where it does nothing.

**Four refusals a pair editor owes, all in words:** a value with no name, a name
with no value (writing `""` would file a budget of nothing under a real agent —
set-looking and inert), the same name twice, and a figure typed in words. The
draft is a **list** of pairs rather than an object, so a pair being renamed does
not jump around under the hand.

With this and U-109, **U-89 is closed: no setting on that page is a bare JSON
box any more.**

## 3.297.0 - U-109: the settings whose fields the manifest already declared (2026-08-28)

**Fifteen settings name every field of their value, type it, say which ones are
required and write a sentence about each — and the page drew a JSON textarea
over the top of all of it.** `taskRetry` declares SIXTEEN fields; the user was
asked to hand-write its braces and to remember that `backoff` takes one of four
words, while typing it into a box that accepts anything.

**One object with declared fields is now a FORM** (`taskRetry`,
`launchDefaults`) — one box per field, its own sentence beside it. **A list of
them is a TABLE** (`cliProfiles`, `launchProfiles`, `pricing`, `mediaPricing`,
`quotaWeights`, `modelPolicy`, `dispatchRules`, `relayFeeds`, `ingestFolders`,
`extraClaudeDirs`, `projectSkeleton`, `projectTemplates`, `livingChecks`) — one
row per entry, `+ add`, a ✕ to drop one, **Save the table** to commit. A closed
set is a picker rather than a box that accepts anything, a required column is
marked where it is asked for, and a number typed into with words is refused in
words rather than written as `NaN`. Both are chosen from `shape.kind`, so a
setting whose fields are declared tomorrow gets its editor with nobody touching
the page.

**A boolean field is a three-way picker, not a checkbox.** An unticked box
cannot say "not set", and here that is the opposite answer to `false`: a field
left empty is LEFT OUT of the object, so its own default stays in charge. A
checkbox would have turned one edit into an override of every field the user
never looked at.

**`livingChecks` got the items schema it never had** — label and precondition
required, level a closed set, every field described. It was the last box the
schema refused to describe; there are now none.

**A key the schema does not name survives the round trip.** A stored entry may
hold a field an older build wrote; rebuilding the object out of the declared
fields alone would have deleted it without a word. The remainder travels with
its entry — through a redraw, through a row moving up — and is written back on
save.

**Fixed, from U-108: "Edit as JSON" threw away what you had typed.** It read the
rows carefully into the draft and then drew the textarea from the *stored*
value, so every unsaved edit was silently replaced the moment you asked to see
it as JSON — the opposite of what the link promises. The box now carries what
was on screen in both directions, and a document that refuses to parse stays in
the box where you can fix it.

## 3.296.0 - U-108: a plain list is a list of boxes, not a JSON document (2026-08-28)

**Nine settings are an array of strings or numbers** — root folders, excluded
folders, model names, Telegram chat ids, queue targets, webhook events, allowed
hosts, pack gallery sources, insight categories. The schema says
`items.type: "string"` and nothing more: there is no structure to get right in
any of them. The page asked for JSON anyway — a textarea, a pair of brackets,
and a comma the user had to remember — which is the report U-89 was opened
about.

One box per entry now, a ✕ to drop one, one button to add one, and **Save the
list** to commit them. Adding and removing act on a DRAFT, so a list
half-edited and abandoned leaves the setting exactly as it was, and every
structural gesture reads the boxes first — type a path, press + on the row
above, and without that the path is gone. The value is sent as a **real array**,
which is the whole point of not making the user write the brackets: it cannot
fail to parse.

**Where the schema says the entries are PATHS, every row gets a Browse.**
Declared as `x-af-browse` on `items`, exactly as a scalar path setting declares
it on itself — so `agentRoots` and `excludeAgentDirs` get the picker as a fact
of the manifest, and the next list of paths gets it by one line there rather
than by editing the page. The row picker **saves nothing**: it posts the path
back and the draft takes it, because the list around that row is still being
edited and saving would commit every other row at the same moment.

**Which settings get any of this is nowhere written down.** `shape.kind`
chooses the editor, `shape.itemBrowse` the picker and `shape.itemAllowed` turns
a row into a dropdown — all three read off the manifest
(`core/settingShape.ts`), so a list added tomorrow gets the editor with nobody
touching the page. **And the JSON box does not go away:** a value the schema
cannot describe is always possible, so "Edit as JSON" is one click and comes
back, carrying what was typed either way.

One dead control removed on the way: **Example** writes into the JSON textarea,
and in the list view there is no textarea — it looked live and did nothing.

## 3.295.0 - M-27 (V2): the rounds a schedule could not keep, and the round that never opened (2026-08-28)

**M-27 shipped and did not work.** Three separate faults, each of which alone
was enough to make a multi-round task impossible; the audit that found them was
asked for because the feature visibly did nothing.

**1 — the chain died on its ordinary path.** A round is a reply, so it resumes
the conversation the round before it was answered in. That id was read at the
moment the run ended — and `opencode run --format json` is the ONLY engine that
knows it then. Every other engine, Claude included, is bound to a session
AFTERWARDS, by matching a transcript the index finds on disk (S-31), which lands
after the process has exited. So the check said "no conversation is bound to
this run", **dropped the whole chain**, and wrote a note nobody was going to
read. Round 2 of a Claude task had never once happened.

A round is now a ROW from that moment either way — created, visible,
cancellable — and HELD (`round:binding`) until the binding arrives.
`releaseRounds` fills the id in, and it is RE-DERIVED from the store rather
than driven by the event, so it is right on the first pump after a restart and
in a window that never saw the binding land. This is M-3's `progress:unknown`
park, for the same reason and in the same shape. A round whose run has been
deleted ends and says so instead of waiting for ever.

**2 — an automation could not carry a chain at all, which is the case the item
was written about.** "Run this every morning, and when it answers ask it the
next thing" is what an unattended session is FOR. The rounds were read on the
`task-new` branch only: the form drew the editor on a schedule, the page sent
what was typed into it, and `savePlan` dropped it on the floor — so a schedule
set up with three prompts fired a one-prompt run and looked exactly like one
that had never been given any. `rounds` is now a **RunDimension**, beside the
model and the retry policy, which is what carries it through `runExtras` to
schedules, triggers and templates in one move. The plan form saves it and gives
it back on edit, the row's anatomy says how deep the run goes, and the bridge
takes it on every op that takes run dimensions (`ROUNDS_NOTE`).

**3 — an interactive run was offered a chain it could never run.** Resuming is
a headless argument (`launch()` refuses it by name), so the rounds someone
typed became a row that failed at the spawn with a message they would not
connect to them. The core refuses it in words, the bridge refuses it rather
than storing it, and the form disables the block in place with the reason —
the same treatment the Conversation and retry pickers already had.

**And the test harness was hiding it.** `lib_page_dom` built an element's
`value` from its `value="…"` attribute, which a `<textarea>` does not have: so
every textarea came back EMPTY after a repaint, a page reading its own form back
wrote that emptiness into its draft, and the next repaint really did lose the
words. Every `<input>` on the same form survived, so the picture looked like a
page that loses only its big boxes. Fixed in the shim, where it was.

## 3.294.0 - U-89: the two settings whose panel was half a panel (2026-08-28)

`pricing` and `mediaPricing` declared their fields and described none of them,
so the new shape panel could only say `match · string` — which answers what to
type and not what it means. The schema was filled in rather than the page taught
to apologise: every field now carries its sentence, `match` says the rule a
reader cannot guess (**the first rule that matches wins, so order matters**),
and the fields a rule cannot do without are marked required. Every array-of-
entries and every object setting in the manifest now describes every field it
declares, and the test asserts that of all of them rather than of these two.

## 3.293.0 - U-89 (first layer): a JSON settings box says what goes in it (2026-08-28)

**Measured on this manifest: 129 settings, 27 of them drawn as a bare JSON
textarea — and for twelve of those the manifest ALREADY declared every field of
an entry, with a sentence about each one.** The page threw all of it away. So
the user was asked to hand-write JSON whose shape was documented six feet away
in the same file, and their report on that page was exact: a field they could
not use.

Every JSON box now carries a chip saying what the value **is** — `a list of
entries · 3 field(s)`, `a plain list of string`, `one object · 16 field(s)`,
`name → value pairs` — and a panel behind it listing each field, its type,
whether it is required, the values it accepts, and the sentence the manifest
already wrote about it. Beside it, **Example** writes a complete entry that
validates into the box. It saves nothing: the reader edits it and presses Apply
themselves, because a button that silently overwrote a live setting with a
sample would be the worst possible reading of "show me what goes here".

All of it is **derived from the schema** (`core/settingShape.ts`), never a list
of keys — a setting added tomorrow explains itself with nobody editing the page,
the same rule the Browse button already follows. The example takes the schema's
own default wherever there is one and a real allowed value from any enum, so it
is something to start from rather than something to correct first. Where the
schema genuinely says nothing (`livingChecks`, and that is the only one) the
panel says so instead of pretending.

Ten of the twenty-seven are a plain list of strings or numbers, where there is
no JSON to get right at all; three are name → value maps. Giving those their own
editors instead of a JSON box is the next layer of this item and is queued as
its own work.

## 3.292.0 - M-27: a task can go as many rounds as the work needs (2026-08-28)

**A task carried exactly one prompt, and that is not the shape of the work.**
"Read the file, then write the patch, then run the tests" is three turns of ONE
conversation; the only way to say it was to queue three tasks — three runs,
three separate conversations, and the second of them woke up knowing nothing
about the first. So the thing an unattended session usually needs could not be
asked for at all.

A ROUND is one prompt sent into the same conversation once the round before it
has been ANSWERED. The prompt box is round 1 — that is every task ever written
and none of them change. Under it, **+ another prompt** adds as many more as the
work needs, each with its own **wait** in minutes measured from the moment the
previous answer lands (0 = at once, up to seven days). Each round becomes its
own visible task row when its turn comes, carrying the moment it may start, so a
two-hour wait survives a restart, says when it will go, and can be cancelled —
the same lesson retries taught: a chain held in a closure is a chain the window
closing throws away.

**‼️ A RETRY IS NOT A ROUND.** A retry is the same round attempted again because
the run did not survive; a round is the next thing to say because the previous
one was answered. The retry carries the whole chain forward and does not move
the count — otherwise "round 3 of 5" would be a lie on any task that ever met a
usage limit, and a flaky network would silently eat the rounds the user paid
for. The retry that finally succeeds is the run that opens the next round.

A round is a REPLY, so a run with no conversation bound to it opens none and
says why on its own record, rather than starting a fresh conversation with a
prompt written for a context it does not have. A failed or cancelled run ends
the chain; a workflow step opens no round of its own, because the workflow
already owns what happens next.

On the board a chained run says `R2/4` beside its agent, with the whole sentence
in the hover — and nothing at all on a one-prompt task. On the bridge,
`tasks.add` takes `rounds: [{prompt, delayMin?}, …]` and reads back `round`,
`rounds` and `roundsLeft`. A round waiting on a ceiling now announces itself the
way a retry does: by round 4 the person who typed it left hours ago.

## 3.291.0 - X-130: the backlog is read once per change, not three times (2026-08-28)

**A backlog mutation cost two full parses of a document that never shrinks.**
Every op that changed a line read the whole file to find its target, wrote the
change, and then read the whole file AGAIN to hand back the one line it had just
written. Measured on this project's real backlog (495 KB, 396 items): **67 ms
per mutation, of which 34 ms was the second read.** The second read was not
dropped — "what does that line say NOW" is the honest answer to give a caller —
it was made cheap. `parseBacklog`'s loop body became `parseItemLine`, because
everything an item says about itself is on its own line and the only thing
needing the whole file is which HEADING it sits under; the changed line is now
sliced out by offset and read alone, with its heading context carried from the
item that stood there a moment ago. `setBacklogHold`, `setBacklogFields` and
`addBacklogItem`: **67 ms → 34 ms.**

The thing a single line cannot decide is what a `parent` field names, and that
is checked against the list the caller is already holding, with the same
function the full pass uses — a link that quietly stopped being verified would
have been the worst possible thing to trade a millisecond for.

**And the file watcher was re-doing the work the mutation had just done.** Every
write to `Backlog.md` wakes the directory watcher a second and a half later, and
it ran the entire reconcile pass again — over a document nobody had touched
since, because the writer was Agent Farm and it had already run that pass
inline. Measured cost of that echo: a 44 ms parse, a ledger read, a log render
and a 454 KB cache rewrite, on **every single mutation.** The watcher now reads
the file and compares the bytes first: identical text means there is no outside
edit to reconcile, so it stops there — **54 ms → 6 ms.** A real edit still pays
the full pass (plus 6 ms for the read that proved it was real), because
anything weaker than the bytes would be a guess, and a guess here loses a round
the user actually typed. The suppressor is deliberately not persisted: a window
that opens must compare against what the file said when the last one closed.

The 454 KB snapshot cache is also no longer rewritten by a pass in which no
item's wording changed.

## 3.290.0 - X-145 / X-135: new items stop landing in the archive, and stop being born undated (2026-08-27)

**A new item was being written into the history section, and nobody could see
it.** An item is seated "after this area's last item". Once an area's items have
been archived, its last one is at the BOTTOM OF THE FILE under 🗄 — so every new
item in that area went into the archive: coded, open, queued by nobody, and
hidden from every default view. Measured on this project: `B-16`..`B-21` and
`X-132`..`X-133` all landed there and it was only noticed when the list came up
short. The seat now skips archived lines, and the test is the HEADING the line
sits under, not "below the archive line" — a `## X — …` heading written after
the archive opens a section that is not the archive.

**And the repair was blocked by the rule that protects the archive.** `tidy` left
anything under 🗄 alone — right for a CLOSED line, which is a record, and exactly
wrong for an OPEN one, which is live work nothing will ever show you. An open or
doing line under the archive is now diagnosed on its own line by the parser and
carried back to its own area by `tidy`, named in `reseated`; closed lines are
left where they are, and the sweep still only ever moves `[x]` and `[-]`.

**Second: an item was born with no date, so the newest thing in the file drew as
the oldest.** Every event the track ledger had was something that happens to an
item that already exists; nothing recorded one coming into existence. So a
freshly written item was a code the ledger had never heard of — `openedAt` and
`touchedAt` both null — and both time orderings sank it below work last touched
months ago. Measured: 43 open items, 5 with any history, so **"last touched"
answered the same code every single time it was asked, for months.**

`opened` is now an event, written by whichever door creates the coded line (the
bridge add, the panel add, and classifying an inbox capture — that last one is
where an uncoded thought first gets a handle the ledger can hold). Written once,
and never fatally: an item that reached your file is an item, stamped or not.

**And a stamp was quietly throwing exact dates away.** `uncertain: 'none'` says
"no session could be named", which is a fact about AUTHORSHIP — it was read as a
fact about TIME and every record wearing it was dropped from the item's dates.
That is right for a box ticked in Obsidian and found out about later; it is
wrong for a first-hand write from a session Agent Farm did not spawn, which is
routine. Narrowed to what its own reason describes.

**Finally, all three time orderings widen the state filter, not just "closed".**
"What did I write down last" and "what did I work on last" are questions about
the whole record, and the last few sessions' work is the part most likely to
have been finished — so answering them over *Active* hid exactly the rows that
prompted the question. Queue order still puts the filter back to *Active*, and
every change says so on the page.

## 3.289.0 - X-136: the discipline gets a cockpit, and the empty setting stops naming one computer (2026-08-27)

**Two boxes, and neither could answer the question a person actually has.**
X-132 built the skills page and X-133 the switch; what was left was a text field
for the folder and a raw `Record<string, boolean>` for who starts with it on.
The folder box could not say the one thing that decides everything — without
`using-superpowers/SKILL.md` a switched-on session is handed **nothing at all**,
which from outside looks exactly like the switch being off. The defaults box was
keyed by an agent's NAME with no way of knowing which names exist, so a
misspelling was a default that never fired and never complained.

Settings now opens **Superpowers & Engineering Discipline** as its own section:
the resolved folder with what was typed above it when the two differ, the hook
drawn as a found/missing checklist row, every skill behind an AFTip with the
line saying when it applies, and **a box per discovered agent** — real names,
read off the agent roots, with the answer each one would actually get. A row
nobody wrote down is drawn as a *default* rather than as a choice, because it is
ticked by the built-in list and that list can change under it.

**And the empty setting no longer falls through to a folder on one computer.**
It resolved to a literal `D:\…` path — the same portability rule `agentRoots`
and the wiki root already obey, broken in the one place nobody would look. Empty
now means `_SKILLS/superpowers` **next to your agents**: under each agent root,
or beside it when a root names a single agent, first one holding the hook.

## 3.288.0 - U-106 / U-107: closed is not archived — the backlog says which, and hides the archive in one press (2026-08-26)

**Two rows, drawn identically, meaning completely different things.** An item
that was finished last week and an item moved under 🗄 Archive last year were
both just grey and struck through: "is this recent work, or is this history?"
could not be answered by looking, on the page or through the bridge.

The parser had known all along — and threw it away. `inArchive` was computed on
every line and spent on `...(inArchive ? {} : {})`, a no-op somebody left behind.
It is now `archived` on the item, on the row (a small boxed 🗄 beside the code,
saying what archived MEANS — the line is history and its code can never be
reissued), and on `projects.backlog`, where an agent quoting a code back at
somebody can tell the two apart. It follows the HEADING, not the state, so a
file whose owner typed `## Arşiv` by hand reads the same.

**And the archive can be got out of the way.** `🗄 archive N` on the filter
strip cycles through the three answers a reader actually wants — in the list ·
hidden · **only** the archive, which is how you go looking for what a code used
to be — one press each, saying which one it is on. It draws nothing at all when
the file has no archive, and it counts on the ⚙ filters chip like every other
axis, because a filter you have forgotten you set is indistinguishable from a
backlog that has lost your items.

## 3.287.0 - X-133: the switch that wakes them — one appended file, a chip beside the project chip, and a default per agent (2026-08-26)

X-132 built the page; nothing was reading it. **Text that is generated and goes
nowhere is not a feature**, so this is the half that puts it in front of a model
and lets it be turned off again.

‼️ **`--append-system-prompt-file` takes ONE file** (measured), so the project
brief and the Superpowers hook cannot be two flags: they are composed into a
single text in a single place (`systemPromptFileFor`, formerly
`projectContextFileFor`). Either half alone is a valid file — which fixed a
second thing on the way: a session under **no project** could previously be
given nothing at all, because the function returned `undefined` the moment there
was no project. The file name carries the switch, so a session with it on and a
session with it off cannot take turns overwriting one path.

**Every spawn, including a resume.** The appended prompt does not survive
`--resume` (measured, `test/smoke_project_context.mjs`), so the hook rides on
the same one line that already re-tells a resumed session about its project. A
card retaking its own seat is asked what it was started with — read a line
before that record is dropped — and a transcript coming off the shelf, which
carries no such memory, comes back at the agent's own default.

**The chip.** It sits on the project chip's line because they are two halves of
one invisible channel: what this session is told ABOUT, and how it is expected
to WORK. It shows the text **verbatim** on hover, the way the project chip does.
With a session selected it is a reading, not a control — a system prompt is
written once, at spawn. A folder that cannot supply the hook reads **⚡
Superpowers unavailable** with the missing file named, never as merely unticked:
an unticked box would be a lie about why nothing is being added.

**A default per agent** (`agentFarm.superpowersDefaults`, `developer` on and
everything else off until it is set). It is what the chip opens on, and it is
the only answer available where there is no chip: an unattended task, a terminal
launch, a resume. A mission delegation is excluded with the brief and for the
same reason — it arrives with an objective, not with a way of working to adopt.

**On an engine with no system-prompt channel** (Codex, Gemini, agy, OpenCode)
the hook rides inside the first prompt, exactly as the project brief already
does — otherwise the switch would look on and do nothing, which is worse than
not offering it.

Bridge: `console.start` takes `superpowers?` (omitted = the agent's default on a
fresh start, the card's own answer on a resume) and reports what really went in;
`superpowers.set { agent, on }` writes the default, onto the row already there
whatever case it is typed in; `superpowers.status` prints the map.

## 3.286.0 - X-132: the Superpowers skills sleep on disk, and the extension can produce the one page that wakes them (2026-08-26)

The engineering-discipline library (Obra superpowers v6.3.0 — TDD, systematic
debugging, planning, brainstorming, verification before completion) is fourteen
markdown skills. Putting them in front of a model would be a permanent bill on
every turn AND a procedure in front of work that does not need one, so they stay
files at **zero tokens** and only the library's own root hook is injected when a
session is switched on.

`agentFarm.superpowersPath` says where they are (portable variables expanded on
open, never written back — the wiki root's rule). `src/core/superpowers.ts`
reads the folder and builds the block: the hook's own words, its frontmatter
dropped, plus **an index of every skill with its absolute path**.

‼️ The index is the part that is easy to leave out and fatal to leave out. The
hook says "invoke the relevant skill" because it was written for a harness with
a skill REGISTRY behind it; here they are plain files, so a model given the hook
alone is told to invoke something it has no way to find — which looks like the
feature working right up until it matters. The index is read out of each skill's
own frontmatter, so a newer release dropped into the folder describes itself.

A folder that cannot supply a hook supplies **nothing**: half a hook sends a
model looking for skills that are not there. `superpowers.status` and
`superpowers.hook` are the two ops. Measured on the real folder: 14 skills,
6,660 characters of block.

Nothing is injected yet — that is the switch, and it is X-133.

## 3.285.0 - U-95: no compile starts unstated, the ticked rows are acted on together, and a compile that finishes says so (2026-08-26)

**Pressing 📚 started a real model over real transcripts and said nothing about
it.** Which agent writes the wiki, on which engine, with which model and at what
effort are four settings, none of them visible from the cockpit — so the one
button that spends quota and writes into the vault spent it unstated. Every
compile button now opens the same strip first: what it is about to read, what it
will run with (a setting nobody set reads as *default*, not as a choice), and
one press to start it. **⚙ Change…** goes to the Settings section that owns
those four rather than offering a second copy of them here; **Cancel** and Esc
start nothing.

**Three more ways to say which marks.** A waiting row compiles itself with **⚡**
without being ticked first. With the pool narrowed, **⚡ Compile these N** takes
exactly what the filters leave — it appears only when that is a different set
from *Compile All Pending*, so it is never the same button twice. And ticking
rows now brings **🚫 Drop** and **✕ Remove** for the selection, because ticking
five rows and then pressing 🚫 five times is the gesture the tick box was put
there to end. All of it goes through the bodies that already existed:
`wiki.candidates.edit` per id, `wiki.candidates.remove`, one
`wiki.compile.run`.

**A run that is out now looks like something happening.** `compiling` breathes
rather than sitting there in the same still blue as a state from yesterday —
off for a reader who asked for less motion.

**And a compile that finishes announces itself.** The run reports its marks back
one at a time, hours after the button was pressed and usually into a window
nobody is looking at; nothing else in the system observed that moment, so unless
the cockpit happened to be open you found out by going and looking. The marks
that close are collected and **one** notice is posted a few seconds after the
last of them — the pages written, what they were filed under, and the shape
check run at the only honest moment for it: after the pages exist. A mark whose
pages are corrected later is not a compile finishing and is not announced again.

## 3.284.0 - U-92: the wiki cockpit filters by one searchable menu instead of a stack of badges, and ✎ opens a picker rather than a comma-separated box (2026-08-26)

**A filter that could only offer what was already marked.**
The topic filter was built from the pool's topics alone, so a category you made
in Obsidian this morning was not on the list until something had been filed
under it — the one surface left disagreeing with the tagger U-90 built. It is
the same union now: the wiki's own folders AND the topics the pool uses, one row
per name however either side spells it, the waiting count on the row because
that is the number you filter by, and the pages on disk one hover away.

**And a long menu finds for itself.** Twelve options is where a list stops being
something you read and starts being something you scroll past what you wanted,
so at that length every picker in the extension — not just this one — draws its
own find box. Typing hides rows and changes nothing about what is ticked, so a
find typed and cleared leaves the selection exactly as it was; **Select all** and
**Clear** then act on what is SHOWN and the tools row says so, which with an
empty box is the same thing it always did. The fold is Turkish: `TARIM` finds
`Tarım`. Escape empties the box rather than closing the menu under the hand,
and closing the menu forgets the find — reopening onto a list silently cut down
to three rows is the invisible-filter trap the box was added to avoid.

**The state buttons carry their counts** (`All 6`, `⏳ Waiting 4`), and the
waiting hover breaks its own number down: how many have a run already out, how
many were left by a run that produced nothing.

**✎ was still a comma-separated text box**, on the one surface whose whole job
is fixing a mark — asking the reader to spell the taxonomy from memory, which is
precisely what U-90 exists to stop. It is the same picker now, in a row of its
own under the mark (three fields do not fit in a 180px cell, which is how the
comma box happened), and while it is open it also edits the two other things a
mark is wrong about: the note, and X-58's excluded turns as a strip of the
conversation's own turn numbers — everything is IN, a press takes one OUT and
strikes it through so it cannot read as "not reached yet". A category typed into
it is started by the host, single level, and an existing one in any spelling is
reported rather than duplicated. Emptying the topics keeps the editor open and
says why instead of sending a write the host would refuse.

**The source cell says what a compile will actually read**: how long the
conversation is, which turns are in scope and which were deliberately left out.
"Whole session" over a 40-turn conversation and over a 3-turn one are the same
three words and completely different amounts of work.

**And the vault strip is no longer a dead end.** It named the missing file and
offered nothing; **🛠 Start the wiki here** (X-57's scaffold, which only ever
creates) and **⚙ Choose the folder** now stand next to the sentence.

Also: `test/render_page.js --menu [id]` opens a filter menu in a rendered page,
so a picker can be photographed at all — everything worth looking at on one is
on the far side of a press.

## 3.283.0 - X-57: the wiki root is a section that reads the folder, and a path that survives another machine · X-58: a session no longer swallows the turns inside it, and a crashed compile no longer locks a turn out for ever (2026-08-26)

**X-57 — a path in a box cannot tell you whether the folder is a wiki.**
`agentFarm.wikiRoot` was one text field under *Reports & Digest*, and
`wiki.compile` refuses without `_KURALLAR_/-WIKI-ANAYASA-.md` — so a perfectly
spelled path to a folder that has never held that file looks exactly like a
working configuration and silently never compiles. Nothing on the page could
have told you, because a box shows a string and the question is "does a compile
work from here?".

So the wiki has its own section now, and it reads the folder: which of the three
files a compile needs are there, how many categories and pages, whether anything
is nested deeper than one level, and — loudly — that the law is the one absence
that stops every run. **🛠 Start the wiki here** writes the three starters, and
it only ever CREATES: a file already on disk is reported and left exactly as it
is, because the law is yours. Beside it: pick the folder, re-scan it (it is a
folder you edit in Obsidian while the page is open), reveal it, open the cockpit.
`wiki.health` and `wiki.init` are the same two acts on the bridge.

**And the path travels.** `settings.json` is synced between machines, so a
literal `C:\Users\<name>\…` is a wiki that exists on one computer. `%USERPROFILE%`,
`~`, `$HOME`, `${env:VAR}` and `${workspaceRoot}` are expanded when the folder is
OPENED and never written back into the setting — what you typed stays what you
typed, and the section shows both lines when they differ, which is also how a
variable that did not resolve is visibly a typo rather than a missing folder. A
variable nobody knows is left alone rather than blanked: `${nope}/wiki`
collapsing to `/wiki` would quietly name the drive root.

Who writes the wiki was already a setting; **what it writes with** now is too —
`agentFarm.wikiEngine`, `wikiModel`, `wikiEffort`. Synthesis is the expensive
half, and the cockpit's button, the palette command and the bridge op all resolve
the same three, so they cannot start three different runs.

**X-58 — marking a whole conversation used to delete the turns kept inside it.**
Two marks were "the same mark" when their ranges OVERLAPPED, and a
whole-conversation mark overlaps everything. So marking a session absorbed every
single turn already marked in it, topics and all: a session whose shape is
`Mimari` can perfectly well contain the one turn that is the best thing anybody
wrote about `Güvenlik`, and those are two pages compiled from two different
amounts of text. Identity is now the range, exactly — the same range marked again
is still one row (that is what keeps "mark it again to add a topic you thought of
later" working), and a different range is a different mark even when one contains
the other.

**"The whole session except the last two" is now a subtraction, not twelve
clicks.** Fourteen turns are the work and the last two are "commit this" and
"good night"; picking a span around them is a gesture nobody performs, so the
compile read the noise. Whole-session scope now draws the same turn strip
inverted — everything is IN, and a press takes one OUT, struck through so a turn
deliberately left out never reads as one merely not reached yet. The mark says so
wherever it is drawn (`whole session (except 13, 14)`), and the compile
instruction says it in a line that cannot be read as anything else.

**And the instruction itself is a block per mark instead of four dashes on one
line:** the transcript path, the scope, the turns as numbers, what each one opened
with, the note the person wrote, and the exclusion in capitals. A model reads past
a parenthesis at the end of a range.

**‼️ A crashed compile used to lock a turn out of the wiki for ever.** A run
stamps every mark it takes so two compiles cannot read the same turns twice —
and nothing took the stamp off. A rate limit, an expired sign-in, a cancelled
task or a VS Code restart all left the mark `pending` with a claim on it, and
every later compile refused it by name while the pool said "waiting". Now every
claim is checked against the run it names whenever the pool is read, and one
whose run is over is released with the reason written onto the mark: *the model
ran out of quota* · *it was cancelled* · *it is not on the task list any more*
· and the quiet one, ‼️ *it finished and reported no page* — silently the worst
of the four, because nothing is compiled until the run says so, and everything
looks healthy. The row reads ⚠ **failed** rather than *waiting*, carries the
sentence in its panel, and offers ↻ to hand it back clean.

**A mark whose transcript has been moved no longer takes the compile down with
it.** It is skipped by name, with the path that is not there, in the brief, in
the prompt, and on the mark itself; the other eleven are compiled. Only when NONE
of them can be read is there nothing to do, and then the refusal names the files
rather than the wiki root.

## 3.282.0 - U-90: the tagger asks what a turn is about with a searchable picker over the wiki's own folders · U-91: a category can be started without leaving for Obsidian (2026-08-26)

**U-90 — a taxonomy typed from memory is three taxonomies.** The tagger asked
what a turn was about with a free-text box, and free text is how `Ajanlar`,
`ajanlar` and `Ajanlar ` become three categories, three folders in the vault and
an index that agrees with none of them. Nobody spells consistently from memory
across weeks, so the list has to be in front of the person at the moment they
answer.

It is now a searchable multi-pick box (`media/afCombo.js`, shipped to every page
for the same reason the tagger is). What it offers is the union of two different
facts and it says which is which: the wiki's own folders — `00_WIKI/*`, where a
page would go, whether or not one has been written yet — and the topics the pool
already uses. A name in both lists is one row, with the figure that tells them
apart (pages on disk · marks in the pool). Pressing the empty box lists
everything; typing filters it, folding case the Turkish way, so `TARIM` finds
`Tarım`; the arrows and Enter reach every row without the mouse; what is picked
sits in the box as a chip with an ✕, and Backspace on an empty box takes the last
one back off. A word nobody has filed yet still counts — Enter keeps it as a
topic, exactly as the old box did.

Taking one puts the list away. It is drawn over the panel it sits in, and
leaving it down covered the "Keep it" button directly underneath — measured, in
the picture, before it shipped.

**U-91 — a folder in `00_WIKI` is a category the moment it exists.** Two things
were missing at once. A folder somebody had just made in Obsidian was invisible
until a page was written into it, because the only list was of pages; and a
category the extension needed did not exist until the user left for Obsidian to
make one. Both are closed from the same place: the picker reads the folders
themselves (empty ones included, with their page count) and offers `+ start the
category “X”` at the TOP of the list whenever what was typed matches nothing.

The category is a folder name, so it has to survive being one. The separators
and the characters Windows refuses are removed — `Ajanlar / Yol Haritası` would
otherwise have made a second level, which is exactly the deep hierarchy the
single-level rule exists to prevent — and a trailing dot goes, because Windows
would have dropped it silently and named the folder something else. A hyphen
survives on purpose: `Teknoloji - Tarım` is how a family is spelled here, at one
level. A leading `_` is the wiki's own prefix and is refused, as are the device
names Windows reserves.

‼️ And a category that already exists, in ANY spelling, is reported as that one
rather than duplicated: typing `ajanlar` beside an existing `Ajanlar` files the
mark under `Ajanlar` and says so. That is the duplicate this whole picker exists
to prevent, and it would have been the first one it created.

Two ops carry it, so an agent can do the same: `wiki.categories` (the folders,
the pool's topics, and the union — reported separately, because they are
different facts) and `wiki.category.add`.

## 3.281.0 - U-93: which turns to keep is a choice, not a number to type · U-94: keeping the whole conversation is a button on the surfaces that show one (2026-08-26)

**U-93 — the badge on every turn asked you which turn you meant.** Pressing the
🔖 on the turn you are reading opened a panel with a 62px box in it, and the
