scope was whatever you typed there. The turn number itself was already resolved
and filled in — but a box full of digits is not an answer, it is a form, and it
made the badge on each row pointless: you pressed the one you wanted and were
asked again.

The scope is now three answers on the panel, and the one you almost always want
is already chosen: **This turn (3)** · **Whole session** · **Range**. The whole
session says how much that is (`Turns 1–14 — the whole conversation`). Range
draws a chip per turn of the conversation and a span is two presses — the first
takes that turn, the second stretches to where you pressed, whichever side of it
that is, and the third starts over so the gesture has no mode to be stuck in.
The strip scrolls and opens on the turn that was pressed, so a reader on turn 140
is not looking at turn 1.

The box has not gone anywhere; it is the escape hatch for a conversation whose
turns could not be counted, and it stays authoritative — a span typed there is
the span the chips light up. A row the host could not place offers no "this
turn" at all rather than pretending to, and opens on the whole conversation.

**U-94 — keeping a whole conversation was only in the right-click menu.** A
session card and a session's own heading have no turns to hang a badge on, and
keeping the lot is the commonest thing to want from either — so on those two
surfaces the feature read as absent. Both now carry it: the session page's
heading has a labelled `🔖 Wiki` button in its action row, styled by the same
class as the buttons beside it so it cannot drift away from them, and every
Console session card carries the quiet badge in its header line, lit when the
conversation is kept.

The card badge needed a figure, not the marks: sending every mark of every
conversation on every repaint to draw one icon would be paying transcript prices
for a boolean. Each card is told the turn its marks start at, which is enough to
say "kept", "partly kept — 3 turns of it on their own", or "not kept", and the
tooltip says which. A whole-conversation ask is also answered without guessing a
turn: sending it through the resolver with no moment and no words would have
answered turn 1 flagged as something to check — a number nobody asked for,
presented as a doubt.

Measured against the item's own three surfaces: the transcript's turn bands and
the Console's prompt rows already carried the badge, and the Console's is on the
prompt deliberately — the backfill reads no result rows off a transcript, so a
badge hung at the end of a turn would be missing from exactly the scrollback a
reader goes back through.

## 3.280.0 - M-28: a setting VS Code refuses to register is written into settings.json by the extension itself, surgically (2026-08-26)

**M-28 — `agentFarm.budgetsUnlimited` could be read and could not be written.**
Exactly one of the settings this build contributes is missing from the running
window's configuration registry: reading it hands back `undefined` instead of the
declared default, and `update()` refuses it outright with "is not a registered
configuration". The manifest is not at fault and no extension can put the key
back from inside. The read side has fallen back to the user's own `settings.json`
for a while; the write side had nowhere to go and ended in a message telling the
user which line to paste by hand.

It now writes the line itself, into the same file the reader already falls back
to — so the value takes effect in that window with no reload.

What made this worth being careful about is the file: `settings.json` is JSONC.
The obvious completion — parse it, set the key, serialise it back — would have
handed the user their settings file stripped of every comment they had written
and reflowed to somebody else's indentation, which is a far bigger loss than the
switch was worth. So the write is SURGICAL: the text is scanned for that one
member's value span and only those characters are replaced. Comments, blank
lines, key order, indent width (spaces, tabs, whatever the file uses), trailing
commas, CRLF and a BOM are bytes the patcher never touches, and a new key is
appended in the file's own indentation with the comma placed BEFORE any comment
trailing the line above rather than inside it. A reset deletes the member and the
punctuation that was only holding it, and leaves any comment somebody wrote about
it. The nested `"agentFarm": { … }` spelling is patched where it lives instead of
being duplicated flat, and a key written twice is patched at the last spelling —
the one actually in force.

A file the scanner cannot understand is REFUSED rather than guessed at, and the
old paste-this-line message is what the user gets, now naming the reason. After
writing, the file is read back through the same door: a patcher that claims a
write it cannot see would be worse than the refusal it replaced. If the value is
also set in a workspace file that outranks the user file, that is reported rather
than reported as applied.

Measured on the 124 settings this build declares: every one of them writes into a
commented file and reads back, and the comments are still there afterwards.

## 3.279.0 - U-105: the session column is 250px of content whether or not it is scrolling · U-96: Check now is on every engine that has something to check, and the others say why (2026-08-26)

**U-105 — opening the Resume section at the bottom of the Console's left column
narrowed every card above it.** The Resume list lives inside that column, and the
column is the scroller: opening the section is what pushes it past the window, so
the scrollbar appeared and — on a classic, non-overlay scrollbar — was taken out
of the 250px the column is. Every card lost the gutter on a section being opened
underneath them and got it back when it closed. The width was never wrong; it was
being measured from a box that changed.

The gutter is now reserved permanently, so the first overflow moves nothing, and
the column is widened by exactly that gutter so its CONTENT stays at the 250px
everything on it is designed around — the width it had with the section closed,
which is the state being kept. The gutter is read off the column itself rather
than off a probe elsewhere on the page: measured on this machine, a probe answers
0 while the column really reserves 15. Where scrollbars are overlays the
measurement is 0 and the rule is exactly what it was. Verified on the rendered
page in this machine's own Chromium: 250px of content with the section closed and
with 3000px of content forced into it.

**U-96 — "Check now" was Claude's alone, and the reader could not tell a
technical limit from an oversight.** It was both. Codex's figures come off the
newest rollout file on this disk, so they can be re-read at any moment and there
was simply no way to ask — while Gemini is billed per token (there is no plan to
be a percentage of) and Antigravity writes its quota nowhere this machine can
read, so for those two there is genuinely nothing to press.

Check now is now offered wherever there is a source, and where there is not, the
panel says which of the two reasons it is, in the place the link would have been.
The rule is derived from what the engine's record already states rather than from
a list of ids, so an engine added later is covered by arriving. Only Claude's
re-read spends a request; every other engine is a disk read, and asking again on
one of them no longer touches the endpoint's budget. This also closes the last
place the hover still changed shape between engines, which is what U-40 was for.

## 3.278.0 - U-98: a filter you could not type a number into, because a number box has no caret to put back (2026-08-26)

**Typing into a min/max filter sent the caret to the far left after every
keystroke, so `120` came out `021`.** The filter boxes apply as you type, and
applying re-renders the page — which replaces the very box being typed into. The
component has always handled that: it saves the caret, lets the page repaint,
finds the new box and puts the caret back. On a numeric box none of that
happened. `<input type="number">` does not implement the selection API:
`selectionStart` answers `null` and `setSelectionRange` is refused with
`InvalidStateError` (measured, in this machine's own Chromium). Both calls sat
inside `try/catch` clauses that read like they were handling the case and were in
fact dropping it, so the caret was never saved and never restored — while the
focus still went back, and a freshly focused input starts at position 0.

The fix is at the root rather than at the six call sites that hit it: a box
handed to the live-filter component is by definition a box that will be
re-rendered under the reader's hand, so the component now makes sure it is one
whose caret can be read — on the way in, and again on the way back, because the
element it finds after the repaint is a new one built from the same markup.
`inputmode="numeric"` keeps the numeric keypad; what goes is the spinner, which
was never usable on a filter box this narrow, and every handler already parsed
the text because a filter box could always be empty.

That covers every live-filtered numeric box in the extension at once — the
Sessions and Turns range filters and their "Show" counts, the Missions run
filters, and the Dashboard compare count — and any added later. The one other
page that restores its own focus across a repaint (Search) now shares the same
guard, so it cannot grow a second blind spot beside the first.

## 3.277.0 - X-32 closes: the adaptive acceptance matrix is a table that breaks the build, and an un-pause that never travelled down is fixed (2026-08-26)

**X-46 — the gate X-32 had to pass is now an ADDRESS for every line it asks
for, not a claim that "it is all covered".** The item lists twenty-four
behaviours that must be proven — legacy records with no `mode`, every classic
verb and its bridge contract, revise and replan, serialized writers, nested
roll-up, independent review, hard ceilings, malformed planner output, reload at
every stage, cancel propagation, per-engine capability, the planner's honesty
about being Claude-only. Fourteen thousand green tests do not answer that: a
suite can be green with a matrix row nobody ever measured. The mapping is now
`docs/X-46-KABUL-MATRISI.md`, a table whose right-hand column is the exact test
file and the exact assertion that proves each row — and `test_x46_matrix.js`
reads that table back. A cited test renamed, deleted or reworded fails
`npm test`, so the document cannot go stale in silence. It deliberately does not
re-run the cited suites: the runner already proves they are green, and this
proves the citation points at something real.

**‼️ Filling the table found two things nobody had measured, and one of them was
a live defect.** A pause travels down to a mission's children — its own wave is
waiting on them, so a pause that stopped at the parent would leave the only
thing still spending money untouched. The un-pause did not: it descended from
the sidebar command and from nowhere else. Resume the parent from the Bridge
(`missions.resume`) or from the page's own button and it came back alive with
its children parked for ever — waiting on work that would never move again, a
deadlock wearing a green status. Both surfaces now descend, and
`test_mission_cascade.js` measures it **per call site**, so a new Pause/Resume
surface added without the cascade is refused rather than remembered.

The second was a hole in the record rather than in the behaviour: when the
planner could not be reached at all — the resumed session dead and the fresh one
dead too — nothing checked how the run ended. It ends `failed` with the engine's
own error quoted, never `cancelled` (which would claim a hand did it) and never
a verdict on work nobody planned; the round already paid for stays on the
ledger. That is now pinned.

**X-124 — "what it actually ran with" is now a fact about the turns a piece of
work occupied, not about everything its conversation ever did.** U-104 put the
engine's own testimony beside the request, and read it off the session: `models`
is every model the lane ever used and `permissionMode` is the last mode its
transcript mentions. A session is not a delegation. A lane that is resumed serves
several of them and a lead's lane can be older than the mission entirely, so
every step listed models from rounds it had nothing to do with — and the mismatch
check, which asks "is the model I requested among the ones that served me", found
the request in some unrelated turn and reported agreement. The one comparison the
feature exists for was being answered out of the wrong evidence, silently.

The reading is now bound to a window the caller owns: a delegation gets the
stretch its own task occupied, the orchestrator gets the run's own start and end.
A turn carries the permission mode in force while it ran — the last such event at
or before it opened, and a mode changed mid-turn governs the rest of that turn —
so a mode set on a later resume can no longer speak for work taken before it.

‼️ **And the three possible answers are kept apart rather than collapsed, because
collapsing them is the defect.** `turn` is evidence about this piece of work.
`session` is the old whole-lane reading, still shown when a step's task row has
been rolled out by retention and there is no window to bind — but labelled as the
lane's, out loud. `unattributed` is the honest silence: a window was known, no
turn of that session falls inside it, so none of its testimony is about this
work. **A ≠ verdict is only ever drawn on `turn`**; a disagreement computed from
the lane's aggregate is a claim about the wrong evidence. A permission mode that
changed inside the window has no single value and both are shown, because picking
one would be a coin toss on the fact somebody is reading the row to check.
`missions.status` carries `scope` and `permissionModes` on every `applied` block.

**A project document that grew past half a megabyte could no longer be written to
at all — including by the one operation that would have shrunk it.** Every
bridge write into a project's folder (`backlog.add`, `.check`, `.set`, `.move`,
`.promote`, `.archive`, `plan.check`, `decision.add`, `doc.write` with `append`)
reads the document, changes it and writes it back. That read used the ceiling
meant for a WEBVIEW: a file too big to paint comes back as its head and says so,
and the rewrite then — correctly — refuses, because writing the head over the
whole file deletes the tail. Sharing one number between painting and rewriting
turned the safety into a trap. A backlog at 525 KB refused every op it had, the
only remedy the system offers (archiving closed items out of it) was refused by
the same rule, and the way out was to hand-edit the file — which is the exact
work the bridge exists to spare the user.

The edit path now has a ceiling of its own, far above anything a person writes by
hand and still finite, so a folder pointed at something absurd refuses rather
than loading it into memory. The truncation guard stays exactly where it was; it
simply no longer fires on a document somebody actually wrote.

**M-29 — a finished run says what its orchestrator actually launched with, out of
its own record rather than out of today's files.** X-121 gave the preview a real
ladder; the run detail and `missions.status` still built the planner's profile
from `plannerModel`/`plannerEffort` alone and wrote "nobody set it, the CLI
decided" whenever those were empty — the same claim X-121 deleted, on the surface
a run is actually read from. Climbing the ladder again on the reading side would
have been the second mistake: a run started last week, and `agentFarm.taskExtraArgs`
and the lead folder's `.claude/settings*.json` are read as they are this morning,
so the answer would be an assertion about the past assembled out of the present.

So the launcher keeps the resolver's answer on the run and every reading surface
draws that record. The last planner call wins, exactly as a member's profile is
its last delegation — every round rebuilds the pair and a resume rebuilds it in a
new window, so "what is it running with" has one meaning for a run still going
and for one already finished. The detail panel names the rung that decided each
dimension, WHERE it was said (the settings file's path, or the flag verbatim) and
which `taskExtraArgs` flag the mission's own choice took off the command line.
`missions.status` gains `planner.launch` with the same four facts, beside the
`planner.model`/`planner.effort` that were always the mission's DECLARATION and
now say only that.

A run with no record — one that predates this, or one whose planner has not been
called yet — reads "not recorded" and explains why nothing will be worked out for
it now. That is the point of the item: the surface that cannot know stops
guessing, and the two fixed facts about the planner (it always runs on Claude
Code, in the lead agent's own folder, with no permission mode at all) survive the
missing record, because they were never a resolution in the first place.

**X-121 — the orchestrator's launch is resolved in one place, so the preview and
the run describe the same command.** The planner is a headless `claude` in the
LEAD AGENT'S folder with `agentFarm.taskExtraArgs` pasted onto its command line,
and two pieces of code described that line without reading it. The preview read
nothing: an empty planner-model box was reported as "nobody set it, the CLI
decided" while the extra args, or the lead folder's own `.claude/settings.json`,
were naming a model on that very line. The launch pasted the extra args down and
then appended its own `--model`, so a user whose extra args carry one got the
flag twice, with a precedence nobody here had measured.

There is one ladder now and both callers climb it: the mission's explicit
override, then the extra args' own flag (it is on the command line, so it beats
a file), then the settings chain the CLI itself reads in that folder — in the
CLI's own order, from the list measured once for X-84 rather than a second copy
of the same filenames — and only then `cli`, which finally means what it says.
The conflict is settled by REMOVAL rather than by a bet: when the mission
overrides a dimension, the extra-args flag comes off the line, so it appears
exactly once and the reported answer is the answer the CLI is given. The
displaced flag is named rather than dropped in silence. A value that came from a
settings file never becomes a flag — handing a file's own value back on the
command line is a second source of truth over a file the user edits by hand.
Effort has no settings rung at all, because Claude Code's settings.json has no
effort key, and saying so is part of the answer. And the resolver takes no "is
this a resume" flag: that absence is what keeps the first round and every later
one on the same launch.

**A-17 (second half) — the record is where the next mission is started, and a
delete means what it says.** The measurement had no surface: it existed, it was
correct, and the only way to read it was a bridge op — which is to say nobody
would have read it. It is now one strip above the run list on the Missions page
(no new dashboard: A-17 asked for exactly this), carrying the count, the most
common shape and its success rate, with the whole table in a hover panel. The
strip repeats every fence the core keeps rather than quietly relaxing one at
the last step: a group under the sample floor is drawn as a count and never as
a percentage; the classic-vs-adaptive pair is drawn only when the core computed
it, and its "which side is short" note is shown in its place otherwise; cost
appears in the panel as an observation, in the same line that says nothing acts
on it; and a store that could not be read says so instead of drawing a
confident zero. It also states why it can count more runs than the list shows —
run rows are evicted at 40, outcomes are kept to 2000 — so the discrepancy
reads as the feature it is.

And the open decision is settled: **an explicit delete forgets the outcome, the
store's own rollover does not.** Deleting a run (bridge, tree or panel — all
three funnel into one place) drops its outcome, so it stops moving averages the
person can no longer open or correct. Eviction at MAX_STORED_RUNS keeps it,
because a history that expired with the rows would be a second copy of the run
list rather than a memory. There is one call site and a test that says so.

**A-17 (first half) — orchestration keeps a record of what it has observed.**
A finished run knows something a run about to start does not: which SHAPE of
approach was taken and what came of it. That is now kept — and only that. Not
one prompt, artefact or message body is copied; what is stored is the sequence
of primitives the lead used (consecutive repeats collapsed, so the same
approach at two sizes is one group), the features of that approach, the
verdict, how many required criteria were actually met, the counts, the duration
and the money.

The fences are the feature. A group under the sample floor is reported but
never briefed to a lead — one run's accident read as a pattern is worse than
silence. The classic-vs-adaptive comparison refuses to draw a number while
either side lacks a denominator, and says which side is short instead of
implying they are equal. A project never sees another's runs, and "no project"
is its own scope rather than a wildcard. The same run recorded twice counts
once, while a rerun counts twice because it really is a second attempt. And
cost is recorded and decides nothing: there is no cheap-first, no model
escalation, no budget reserve and no expected-value stop anywhere in this
build, which is asserted against the source because it is a promise about what
the code does *not* do.

Readable through `missions.outcomes`, and on the Missions page itself (above).

**B-13 — an adaptive mission is drivable from the bridge, and two reads that
had no ceiling now have one.** The ops were all there — start, preview, status,
trace, guide, conversation, council, and the whole control set — and no second
`objectives.*` namespace was ever opened. What was missing was what they SAID.
A caller could start an adaptive run and not read back that it was one:
`missions.list` had no `mode`, so every adaptive-only field elsewhere was an
absence with two possible meanings. `missions.status` could not say the
strategy in force, whether a steer had actually been delivered, whether the
journal was sound, or what the run had started and not finished — the four
questions "what is it doing?" actually decomposes into. A step said it had run
a workflow or a nested mission and handed back no id to follow it with.

All of that is on the two read ops now: `mode`, `project`, `phase`,
`strategyVersion`, criterion and conversation counts and a `pending` object on
each list row; `strategy`, `guidance` with a real delivery state (pending /
inflight / applied), `trace` health and `resume` from the same reconciler the
reload uses, and `frontier` — the graph nodes started and not finished — on
`missions.status`, with `taskId` / `workflowRunId` / `missionRunId` /
`sessionId` on every step.

And the ceilings. `missions.list` returned every run the farm has ever made and
`missions.conversation` every message of a conversation, each one's body read
off disk; both are paged now through one shared contract (`bridgePage`) that
the whole bridge can use. It is KEYSET, not offset — these lists grow at the
end while a caller reads them — and an unknown cursor is refused rather than
silently answered from page one. `missions.trace` reads the journal FORWARDS
(it used to return the last n events, the wrong end of an audit record) with a
kind filter applied before the page is cut, so "show me every strategy change"
does not cost the whole file, and a misspelled kind is named back instead of
matching nothing in silence.

The journal itself is now read once per window through one memo, keyed on the
file's size and mtime rather than on the snapshot's `lastSeq` — the reload, the
Missions page, `missions.status` and `missions.trace` had been three separate
reads and one stale-prone cache, and a status call is what an agent polls with.
The catalog also says out loud what this layer is NOT: there is no cost
optimisation in a mission, the limits are mechanical ceilings, and nothing
decides anything from a price.

**X-94 — a mission is told what a project IS, not what is queued on it.** A
person ran an adaptive objective, read the planner's transcript, and found this
project's backlog in it: five unrelated items, the recent worklog, and an
instruction to record what it did in the worklog before it finished. None of
that is a mission's subject. A mission arrives with an objective, its
constraints and its success criteria — the project's standing work is the
question a SESSION opens with, and the write-back protocol is addressed to a
person's own conversation, not to a headless delegate that would then file
worklog lines about work nobody asked it to record.

The brief now has an audience. A mission's copy keeps the MAP — what the
project is, its people, its code roots and which document holds which role,
because a mission CAN be told to record something and then has to know where —
and drops the four standing lists (open plan items, top of backlog, recent
decisions, recent worklog) along with the session's write-back tail. Not merely
hidden: those documents are not read off disk at all on a mission spawn, so a
500 KB backlog is not parsed to be thrown away. The lead's briefing says the
omission out loud rather than leaving it to be discovered, because it used to
promise "what is open on it" and that promise is now deliberately false. The
two audiences are written to different files, since a mission's delegations are
spawns and they happen while somebody is starting a session.

And the second half of the same question — *is a mission even associated with a
project?* It was, invisibly. `MissionSpec.projectId` has existed since Faz 5 and
the Missions form drew no control for it, so a mission started while the window
sat on a project was filed under it, briefed with it, and had every delegation
filed under it, without the word "project" appearing anywhere on the form. There
is a Project box now, offering all three answers the host has always accepted:
this window's project (the visible default, named), a deliberate none, or one
you pick. `missions.preview` and the form both say which of the two it was —
`requested` or `window` — because "inherited while you were not looking" is the
answer to the question that opened this item.

**X-126 — the extension host is no longer frozen by the size of its own
history.** Agent Farm read every Claude transcript from byte zero,
synchronously, on the extension host's only thread: once at every window open,
and again in full every time a live session appended a line. Measured on this
machine on the day it became unusable — 328 transcripts, 703 MB, **7.5 s of
completely blocked host per scan**, plus 159–257 ms per write for each active
agent's own 12–37 MB file. With several agents running the host never got the
thread back; and since every extension in a window shares that thread, the
whole extension layer went unresponsive together, which is what "the New
Session button does nothing" actually was. This was not a new bug — it was the
architecture reaching the size of the user's history. VS Code's own profiler
had already named `muvusoft.agent-farm` in six of that day's unresponsive
events, at 42–59% of each profiled window.

The cost now follows what CHANGED, not what has ever been said, and three
things make that true. **The parser is resumable:** a transcript is
append-only, so its running total is kept and only the new bytes are fed into
it — an append costs about a millisecond however large the file has grown.
**Finished parses are written down** (`session-index.jsonl`, ~10 KB per session
against the ~2 MB it summarises), and a remembered parse is reused only while
its file still has the same size and mtime AND the arithmetic behind it —
prices, quota weights, the parser version — is unchanged; anything else is read
again, because the transcripts remain the only source of truth and this is a
cache that may never become one. **And nothing holds the event loop:** every
read is async, the walk breathes on a clock, and a large transcript is fed in
chunks, so no single parse can freeze the window by itself.

Measured after, same corpus: a first-ever scan 6.5 s with the longest single
freeze down from 7.5 s to **38 ms**, every scan after it **142 ms** (46×
faster), and an append to a 37.6 MB transcript **1 ms** instead of 159 ms.
Extrapolated to the sizes a tool kept for years has to survive, the old design
cost 68 s of frozen window at 3 000 sessions and 228 s at 10 000; the new one
reads a 31 MB index and re-parses only the day's work. The old parse stays the
definition of the right answer and is pinned as such: all 328 transcripts on
this machine come out byte-for-byte identical through the new path, and
`test_session_index.js` holds chunked feeding to the same standard at chunk
sizes chosen to split multi-byte characters — the one thing a byte-offset
resume can silently corrupt. Deleting `session-index.jsonl` is always safe: the
next scan simply rebuilds it from the transcripts.

**X-123 — "don't change" no longer means "profile everything against Claude".**
The bulk profile's Model and Effort lists were drawn from `claude`
unconditionally whenever the Engine box was left on `don't change`. So a user
who deliberately left the engine alone and wanted to set only a model was
offered Claude's catalogue and wrote the chosen value onto every included row —
the Codex row, the OpenCode row, and the rows that inherit a different engine
from the agent or the fleet. The lists now belong to the engine those rows
really resolve to: an explicit engine on the profile, or the one engine every
included row lands on. Over a mixed pool — or with the engine on `inherit`,
which hands each row back to a default only the launch can resolve — the value
lists close and the fold says why, naming the engines involved. `don't change`
and `inherit` stay offered on every dimension, because they are safe whatever
the rows are on, and Permissions stays open because no engine has an opinion
about it. And the press is atomic: what the apply would produce is checked on
every included row first, so one value that would not fit refuses the whole
press by name instead of half-profiling the pool and warning about it
afterwards.

**X-120 / X-122 — the model+effort pair is refused where it is promised, not
where it dies.** A mission row moved from one engine to another keeps its model,
and a model changed under a kept effort keeps that effort. The narrow strip
noticed and asked; press `Keep as they are` and its tooltip promised that the
draft's refusal list above Start would say so — and the list never looked. The
preview checked whether the machine could run the engine at all and whether the
engine had an effort flag, and nothing checked whether that engine's catalogue
had that model or whether that model takes that effort. So a Codex model on a
Claude row, or an effort belonging to a different model, went to a real
`--model`/`--effort` and was answered by the CLI hours later in a file nobody
reads. `capabilityRefusal` is now the one gate both questions go through, for
every worker AND for the planner (whose pair was validated for vocabulary only,
then handed to every planning call of the run). It states what the engine does
offer and what the model does take, so a fault is fixable in one pass. ‼️
Ignorance is not evidence: only a real catalogue (`engines.models` `source:
"catalog"`) can refuse a model — an alias-guess list and an engine that
publishes nothing refuse nothing — an engine with no effort flag at all is left
to the refusal that already owns that question, and an alias and the dated id it
resolves to are one model rather than one model and one stranger.

**X-119 — a draft the preview refuses can no longer be started.** `missions.preview`
resolved every participant and reported every refusal it would meet — an engine
this machine cannot run, an effort that engine has no flag for — and `create`
never ran a single one of those checks. Start and `missions.start` shared the
resolution and not the refusals, so the very draft the form was drawing `This
draft would be refused` for created a real spec, a real run and its tasks, and
the refusal arrived one delegation at a time after the planner had spent its
turns. Both doors go through one plan now: the same resolution AND the same
refusal set, in one structured answer. Looking still writes nothing; starting
refuses on a non-empty problem list, with the same sentences and all of them at
once, before anything reaches a store. Note the consequence on a whole-fleet
adaptive pool: if any agent in the fleet resolves onto an engine this machine
cannot run, the mission is refused up front rather than discovering it mid-run —
override that row's engine, or narrow the pool.

**X-118 — a preview answer belongs to the draft it was asked about.** The New
Mission form debounces its resolution request by 220ms, and the generation that
guards it was bumped when the REQUEST went out rather than when the draft
changed. So for the whole window between an edit and its own request, the answer
already in flight about the PREVIOUS draft still counted as current: it was
accepted, it painted the new draft's model and effort boxes and its refusal list
with the old resolution, and the repaint it caused cleared and re-armed the
debounce — pushing the new draft's own request another 220ms away every time it
happened. The generation now moves with the draft: it is the draft
fingerprint's generation, taken synchronously, so an answer whose token is
behind the draft is dropped before it can paint anything, and a repaint that
changed nothing (an arriving answer, a panel data refresh) no longer restarts
the clock on a request that is still waiting.

## 3.274.0 - Sessions has three honest switches; PowerShell cannot corrupt bridge text in transit (2026-08-24)

**You, Auto and Mission are three independent ON/OFF switches.** The Sessions
table no longer mixes a User/Auto/All radio with a separate mission exception.
Each row belongs to exactly one category: a mission stamp wins over its technical
automation origin, so Mission includes classic and adaptive missions, their
planners and every delegation without requiring Auto beside it. Pressing one
icon changes only that category; pressing it again reverses only that change.
The filled chip background is the whole state, the filter panel mirrors the same
three switches, and a particular-mission picker remains a narrower filter inside
Mission. Existing saved filters migrate once without changing which rows they
initially show, and the first Mission press after migration cannot inherit the
old empty-list sentinel and appear to do nothing.

**The bridge CLI has an ASCII-safe stdin route for Windows PowerShell 5.1.** That
shell can replace Turkish and other non-ASCII characters before Node receives a
piped JSON string, which was discovered while recording this audit's backlog
items. `--stdin-base64` (alias `--stdin-b64`) now accepts Base64-wrapped UTF-8
JSON, validates both the encoding and UTF-8 strictly, and preserves legitimate
replacement glyphs. Malformed transport is rejected before an operation can
write corrupted text.

## 3.273.0 - X-32 phase B complete: a mission's sessions are its own, and a run says what it really ran with (2026-08-24)

**X-95 — a mission's sessions are stamped, separated, and one click away.** A
mission opens a session for its planner and one for every delegation it hands
out. All of them landed in the one Sessions table, undivided, and on a farm that
runs missions they are the majority of it: the log of your own conversations
became unreadable and the other sessions could no longer be followed. Worse,
they did not even look alike — a delegation carried a launcher record and read as
🤖 automation, while the PLANNER has no task and runs in the lead agent's own
folder, so the orchestrator's own conversation was filed as 🧑 one of yours. Now
every session a mission opens carries the run's id: the planner's own lane, every
delegation, every conversation turn, and the stamp outlives the task rows that
retention removes. A mission row wears its own glyph — 🎯, never 🧑 and never 🤖
— and its hover names WHICH mission rather than saying "automation" and stopping.
They are left OUT of the Sessions page by default, with a permanent 🎯 chip
beside the origin switch that says so and counts what it is hiding; one click
lists them all (and widens the origin scope with it, or the chip would promise
rows the scope then threw away), and the filter panel picks particular missions
by name. A run's detail header has a `🎯 Sessions` button that opens the page on
THAT mission and nothing else. On the bridge: `sessions.page { mission }` and a
`sessions` block on `missions.status` — every lane the run opened, with its role,
its transcript and its own figures.

**U-104 — what was asked for, what was resolved, and what actually ran, side by
side.** Three different facts were being confused. What somebody CHOSE was
visible in the composer and nowhere afterwards. What the ladder RESOLVED was one
lossy line that dropped every dimension the CLI decided and the default engine —
so the commonest delegation of all, the one that took every default, was recorded
as nothing at all. And what the engine APPLIED was on no surface anywhere, so a
model override that had been refused looked exactly like one that had been
honoured. Every delegation now keeps the resolver's whole answer, every dimension
with the layer that decided it; what the CLI's own transcript says it served is
read back beside it; and a field the transcript does not state says "not
reported" rather than echoing the request, because that echo is how a mismatch
hides. The row carries a short mark — ⚙ some layer decided something, ≠ the
engine came back with something else, nothing when it all fell to the CLI — and
the panel behind it carries the table. An alias is not a substitution: `opus`
served by `claude-opus-5` is the CLI expanding a short name, not a disagreement.
The run header is now two summaries instead of one crowded line — Orchestrator
(the lead, its profile, its transcript) and Workers (each member: declared,
resolved, applied) — and the orchestrator's non-choices are said as non-choices:
its engine is Claude Code always, it has no permission mode at all, and it runs
in the lead agent's folder rather than the mission workdir.

**Found while building it.** The page-DOM test shim only dropped its element
cache on a whole-page repaint, so a component that owns one container re-wired
the same cached elements on every render and stacked a listener each time — a
control whose markup happened not to change then fired twice per click and looked
dead. Two visual fixtures had been shipping screenshots of a filter panel that
was never open, with every assertion about them passing.

## 3.272.0 - X-32 phase A complete: the composer says what it will do, and the rows are the answer (2026-08-23)

**U-101 — the member rows are the single source of truth, and the bulk profile
is an ACTION rather than a second hidden default.** The composer carried a
`Delegation engine` box that read as a bulk switch over the rows and was not
one: it wrote a mission-level FALLBACK, never touched an existing row override,
and had no model, effort or permission counterpart — so a user who set it and
then looked at the rows saw the rows disagreeing with it, and the same preference
could be recorded in two places at once. That box is gone from the form, and the
payload the UI posts no longer carries `engine` at all. In its place, in the
Team/Pool heading, `Apply profile to included workers` offers engine, model,
effort and permissions TOGETHER and writes what you choose onto the rows in
plain sight. Each dimension has three answers — `don't change`, `inherit — clear
the override`, or a value — which is why applying an engine can no longer wipe
the models beside it. Every cell now says whether it is an explicit override or
an inherit, with a left edge the AFTip explains. And a value is no longer taken
away without saying so: moving a row onto an engine that publishes neither its
model nor its effort used to narrow it on the spot, so something somebody had
typed vanished while their eyes were on a different control. The rows are named
once, in a strip that offers `Clear them` or `Keep as they are`, and a cleared
row afterwards says what went and why. `MissionSpec.engine` is untouched: the
bridge, every spec already on disk and child-mission inheritance still use it and
the resolver still reads it — this is the UI declining to write a second copy,
not the contract losing a field.

**U-100 — the orchestrator is one subject, so it is one block.** `Lead agent`
sat at the top of the New Mission form and `Planner model` eight rows below it,
with the team, the workdir, six ceilings and the delegation engine in between —
two halves of one answer separated by everything that is not it. They are now a
single Orchestrator block: the lead, the planner engine, a mission-only model
override and a new effort override on one line. The planner engine is drawn as a
FIXED value rather than offered as a picker, because the mission's control flow
parses Claude Code's JSON envelope — the decision object, the cost, the session
id that carries the lead from round to round — and a picker there would be a
control that cannot do what it looks like it does. `plannerEffort` is new on
`MissionSpec`, on `missions.start`, on child-mission inheritance and on
`missions.status`, validated by the same vocabulary a member's effort is and
carried onto the planner command line as a real `--effort` with the same
bare-word guard the model has; absent — which is every spec ever written — no
`--effort` reaches that call at all and today's behaviour is unchanged. An empty
override box no longer says "default": it says what the run would really use and
who decided, and `CLI chooses` when nobody did. There is still no permission
picker for the planner, and now the form says why: its write and spawn tools are
cut off by name (`--disallowedTools`), it keeps the read tools, and it is capped
at 15 turns and 10 minutes per decision — the whole fence is in one AFTip.
`missions.status` answers `planner` (agent, engine, model, effort, session) for
the first time: every dimension of every DELEGATE has been readable since M-18
while the participant that decides the whole run was invisible.

**U-103 — the mission form stopped guessing what it would launch.** It worked
the effective engine out for itself — the row's own, else the mission's, else
`claude` — while a delegation climbs a five-rung ladder (`resolveDelegateRun`):
member → mission → that agent's own default for that engine → `agentFarm.launchDefaults`
→ the CLI. Two of those rungs were not in the page's world at all, so a fleet
default sending the work to Gemini still drew a Claude model catalogue and
offered efforts that engine has no flag for. There is one resolver now and it
lives where the stores are: `resolveMissionInput` is the whole path from raw
validation to a startable mission, `createMission` starts what it returns and
`previewMission` describes it without starting anything — the same ceilings, the
same pool scope, the same deterministic lead, so a preview and a start cannot
answer differently. Each cast row comes back with `requested` beside `effective`
`{engine, model, effort, permissionMode, workDir}` and the ORIGIN of every field,
which is the answer to "why did that delegate run on a model nobody typed into
this mission?". A field nobody resolved stays absent and is drawn as `CLI
chooses` rather than filled in with something plausible. The form asks for this
on a debounce and drops any answer but the latest; every narrow control MIRRORs
it — the value it holds, where it came from and the chain that produced it, in
the tooltip the box is too small to carry. An engine this machine cannot run and
an effort the engine has no such flag for are now listed TOGETHER above Start
instead of one per press. `missions.preview` takes the exact arguments
`missions.start` takes, through one translator, so the page, the host and the
bridge give one answer. The planner is not described as a worker: it is a
headless Claude Code call whose engine cannot be chosen, which takes no effort
and no permission mode at all, and which runs in the LEAD AGENT's folder rather
than the mission workdir — the preview says so instead of implying five boxes it
does not have.

## 3.271.0 - X-32 phase A: the mission composer says what it will actually do (2026-08-23)

**U-97 — the worker row now reads in the order it resolves.** It was laid out
engine → permissions → effort → model, while the model depends on the engine and
the effort depends on the model: both stood to the LEFT of the thing that
decides what they may offer. The row is `Agent/role → Engine → Model → Effort →
Permissions`. The model box was free text over a `<datalist>`, which Chromium
anchors on the flex parent rather than the box — so the second press drew the
list at the far left of the row and a repaint collapsed it to one line. Model and
planner model are plain `<select>`s over the same `AFEngine` catalog every other
launch surface reads, and not one `<datalist>` is left on the form. Changing the
engine or the model narrows the row through `AFEngine.narrow`, the page-side
mirror of the rule the host applies at launch, so a member moved onto an engine
with `takesEffort:false` no longer carries a hidden `--effort` its CLI refuses.
An engine that publishes no catalog is not allowed to call a model wrong; a value
the catalog does not carry is kept as `⚠ <name>` with the sentence in its
tooltip. Four pickers at a fixed width overflowed a docked panel, so they shrink
together, the row wraps rather than clipping, and a hairline says where a member
starts.

**U-102 — an empty pool was two opposite answers in one picture.** Every box
empty posted `pool: []` and the host read it as the whole fleet, while the same
screen could as truthfully be read as "nobody is picked". The pool heading now
carries the answer: `Whole fleet` (the default, and what the old behaviour meant)
or `Selected agents`, where ticking nobody is REFUSED on both sides rather than
silently expanded to every agent on the machine. In whole-fleet scope every tick
is in and says so instead of offering a choice that would be ignored — the row
overrides stay live, because a whole-fleet pool is still a pool you may profile.

The contract is `poolScope: fleet | selected`, refused on the raw request if it
is anything else. **Omitting it is the old contract, untouched** — every stored
spec, template and bridge caller written before this sends no such key, and an
empty pool there still means the whole fleet. `missions.start` says all of that
in its own description.

Classic’s cast list and an objective’s pool shared one checkbox map, so choosing
a pool silently re-cast the mission; they are two answers and they are kept
apart. And the adaptive lead box, where leaving the field empty is legal, said
"— pick the lead —" and nothing else: it now names the agent the deterministic
rule would land on (`Automatic → <agent>`) and re-says it when the pool changes.
An explicit lead outside the pool is drawn as **planner only**; one inside it is
told that its row is about its worker delegations, not its planning calls.

**X-96 — a delegation’s evidence is one click from its row.** The step row
carried the archived output and nothing else, so "which session was this, and
what did it really do?" meant leaving the mission detail, opening Sessions and
matching by agent and clock. The session a delegate ran in has been recorded on
the step since M-19; the host resolves it to a transcript file the way it already
does for a speaking turn, and the row offers `session · output` under one
**Evidence** heading. The right-click menu offers the same two, gated on the same
facts. A step with neither says so rather than drawing a link that would do
nothing.

## 3.270.0 - X-69: a primitive is a contract, not a line in a menu (2026-08-23)

**What a mission's lead can do was a list that promised more than it kept.** The
registry built the planner's menu and the "unknown action" error, and that was
all it did: the parse of each primitive was an arm of one growing
`if (action === …)` chain, and the work it orders was an arm of another, in a
different function. Nothing tied the three together. So a name added to the list
was advertised to the lead and accepted by the lookup — and then, with the parse
arm forgotten, fell off the end of the chain and came back "unknown action" for
an action the lead had just been offered; or, with the executor arm forgotten,
parsed cleanly and ran nothing at all. Both were invisible until a real run
reached them, which for a rarely-picked primitive is a long time and somebody
else's money. It had already happened twice, to `message` and `council`.

**Both halves are on the row now.** Every primitive names its `parse`, and every
primitive that orders work names the `prepare` that builds it; the round loop
dispatches through the same table the menu is generated from, and there is no
action chain left to forget an arm in. A row without a parse does not compile.

**A handler reaches the engine only through what it is lent.** Work preparation
genuinely needs the run — only it knows what an id produced, how deep the run
sits, or which chains this window has — so the engine passes those in by name
instead of the handler reaching for it. A primitive's blast radius is that list,
and a new one that needs more has to say so in the open. Each handler narrows
the decision with a guard rather than a cast, so a row wired to its neighbour's
function refuses the round and says which action was misrouted, instead of
running the wrong preparation on it.

**The exception is declared rather than remembered.** `evaluate` orders work but
hands no tasks back: the verdict IS its round, so it runs its own wave and reads
the evaluation out of what came back. Its row says `ownRound`, and the gate
reads that instead of a name somebody has to keep in mind.

**And the gate is measured from both sides.** `primitiveHandlerParity()` fails
the build on a declared name with no parse, a work name with no way to build
work, a non-work name carrying work preparation, or a handler for a name nobody
declared — including for a row appended at runtime, which is the exact shape of
"somebody added a primitive and forgot the rest". Nothing about how a mission
behaves changes in this release: every one of the 13,700 checks that passed
before passes on the same words.

## 3.269.0 - Adaptive Mission user guide (2026-08-23)

The Adaptive Mission documentation now has two deliberately different books.
The existing architecture guide remains the source-verified reference for an
implementer and has moved to the `docs` root. Its new companion is a 26-chapter,
end-user teaching guide: it introduces every technical label only after its
plain-language meaning, then follows the user's journey from choosing the right
work type and filling the composer through watching a live run, intervening,
reading evidence, recovering from interruption and judging the final result.

The guide does not trade accuracy for simplicity. Its 14,000-plus words include
all fourteen leader actions as individual lessons, 135 callouts, six complete
mission examples, decision matrices, FAQs, a screen-language glossary and an
optional advanced appendix. It also marks today's contradictory composer
behaviour separately from the U-99 target interface, so a planned fix is never
mistaken for something the installed build already does.

## 3.268.0 - X-78/X-74: a council round is weighed whole, and a run is named before it is started (2026-08-23)

**A council's cap counted rounds, not turns.** Every speaker of one decision was
checked against the same before-the-round count, so a round that ordered three
speakers with one turn left read "one turn left" three times and all three ran.
The same held for the one exception that lets a council end: `close` is a
property of the decision, so a three-speaker round carried it on all three
turns — three closings past the cap, of which the record can honour exactly one
while the other two are paid for and said into a council that has already
closed. The round is now weighed whole, once, and an ending is one turn by one
speaker. A round that does not fit is refused with what would fit.

**The chair's call was cited, not addressed.** A turn by anybody other than the
chair had to name the chair's last message in `refs` — and that was the whole
test, so the lead could put any member up to answer a call the chair had put to
somebody else, and the transcript read as though the chair had chosen the
speaker. Who the chair called is already on the record; it is read now.

**An exit claimed things nobody checked.** `consensus` and `decision clear` say
the question was SETTLED, and a lead reading the record afterwards takes them at
their word. A council could be closed on `consensus` over a challenge nobody had
answered, or on `decision clear` by a turn that named nothing it rested on. Both
are refused, with the honest exits offered by name. Whether the participants
really agree is not a property of the record and is not guessed at; whether
anything is still unanswered is, and so is whether the closing turn points at
what it rests on.

**And the speaker was the last to know.** The close reached the order, the
record and every surface that reads them, and not the one agent whose message
has to make it true — so a turn was written as an ordinary one and then filed as
the message the conversation ended on. The closing turn is now told that it is
the last, on which stated reason, and in the council's own words for it. The
same for the chair's mandate: the speaker is told which message called it and
that where the chair's instruction and the lead's ask differ, the chair chairs.

**X-74 — a chain and a child objective were started before they were written
down.** `runWorkflow` and `startMission` started real work and returned the id
in one breath, so the parent's step ref, the child's parent bond and the
journal's "this began" all reached the disk strictly after money was being
spent. A window closing in that gap left a chain or a child working for nobody:
the parent read "interrupted — fate unknown" while the child finished perfectly
and charged for it. The order is now allocate → bond → journal → save → start,
the start is idempotent so the sequence can be replayed from wherever it broke,
and one run can never carry two engines.

**The reload could not repair it either**, because the one place that knew which
run belonged to which action was the journal — and the reconciliation that read
it dropped the ref. It is carried now and put back onto the step before anything
is decided about it. A subsystem that has no record of the id at all says
plainly that nothing ran, instead of frightening the lead with a fate it could
have known.

## 3.267.0 - Adaptive Mission architecture and operation guide (2026-08-23)

A new 37-section, source-verified handbook documents the Adaptive Mission
system from the user's outcome contract down to the processes and records that
run it. It covers Classic versus Adaptive semantics, the separate planner and
worker sessions, the exact engine/model/effort/permission resolution ladder,
all 14 primitives, real conversations and councils, evaluation staleness and
the success gate, limits, failure recovery, persistence, Bridge operations and
five end-to-end examples.

The guide explicitly separates today's engine contract, today's contradictory
composer, and the U-99 target interface. It also corrects three misleading
earlier descriptions: the primitive registry contains 14 distinct actions, the
current `Delegation engine` is a mission-level engine fallback rather than a
bulk row-editing switch, and Classic Mission is a shared planner lifecycle rather
than a pre-drawn workflow.

## 3.266.0 - X-77: a ref points at something that was said, and an answer is the addressee's (2026-08-23)

Four things about a speaking turn were checked too loosely to mean anything.

**A ref only had to EXIST.** An ordered turn has an id from the moment it is
ordered, so a pending, failed or cancelled turn's id satisfied the "this intent
must name what it answers" rule — and then the prompt builder, which materialises
only delivered messages, silently dropped it. The speaker was told to answer
something it was never shown, and the record said it had been given it. A ref now
has to name a message that was really said, and the refusal says which state the
one it named is in.

**Nothing tied the intent to the speaker's place in the exchange.** Any
participant could settle a question or a challenge that had been put to somebody
else, and the open-thread count would then show it answered by a turn nobody
asked for. A `response` and a `concede` are the addressee's to give now, and
nobody settles their own question. A question put to EVERYONE — the ordinary case
— is still anyone's to answer, and a `synthesis` is untouched by the rule: it
settles what it names but it is nobody's reply. Which intents are replies is
declared in the registry, not listed at the check.

**The lead could not choose how much a speaker sees.** A new lane always got the
whole delivered history and a resumed one everything after its own last turn,
with `refs` doing nothing but emphasis — so asking one participant about one
thing also handed it every position already taken, which is the opposite of an
independent opinion. `visibility` is now stated and kept: `all` · `refs-only` ·
`since`. It is on the RECORD, because "what did this turn actually see?" is
unanswerable afterwards otherwise, and the speaker is TOLD when the rest was held
back so it does not read a deliberate silence as an empty room. Omitting it keeps
exactly the behaviour that was always there.

**And the repeat guard read half the turn.** It skipped `to` entirely, so the
same question put to a different participant was refused as a duplicate; and it
compared refs in written order, so naming the same two messages the other way
round read as a new turn and was allowed. Both halves were wrong, in opposite
directions.

**U-65 follow-up: the room and the core now agree on what settles a thread.** The
Missions page carried its own copy of that list and it said `response | concede`,
while the registry has said `synthesis` and `vote` settle what they name since
M-20. One transcript therefore read as closed in the core and the bridge and as
unanswered in the room. The page reads the flags the registry ships.

## 3.265.0 - Shell-safe bridge arguments (2026-08-23)

The bridge helper's documented inline JSON example was not actually portable:
PowerShell can strip its inner quotes before Node receives it, turning valid JSON
into an invalid object-like string. Simple calls now accept repeated `key=value`
arguments and coerce booleans, numbers, and `null`, with no shell-specific escaping.
Complex or multi-line payloads continue to use the existing `@file.json` path.

## 3.264.0 - X-76: a turn that never happened does not hold a lane (2026-08-23)

A speaking turn's message was written onto the run BEFORE the planning-loop
guard and the task budget had had their say, and three exits from the round loop
returned above the line that settles messages. Both leave the same wreck: a
`pending` message nobody will ever settle — and pending is what holds a
participant's lane. That agent could then never speak in that conversation
again, and the lead was refused every time it tried without being told a real
reason.

A turn dropped before it ran is now settled as cancelled, on the record, saying
why. A conversation whose every turn was dropped is closed the same way: an open
room nobody ever spoke in is the same lock under another name. And the three
exits — a ceiling cut, a cancel, and a round the user refused — settle their
messages before they leave.

**And a conversation is closed by a turn that was really spoken.** The close was
applied from the ORDER, before anything checked whether the turn came back, so a
closer that failed or came back empty closed the conversation anyway: the record
said "consensus", the council said it had reached its verdict, and the message
that was to say so did not exist. The close now lands only alongside the
delivered message that carries it, and a failed closer says on its own record
that the conversation is still open.

## 3.263.0 - X-80: one reader for what a speaker actually said (2026-08-23)

A message stores a bounded excerpt plus a `contentRef` pointing at the archived
output the speaking turn produced. Three surfaces then called the excerpt "full
text" — the bridge in its field name, the conversation room in its own release
note — and both drew the same truncated paragraph, with nothing to say anything
was missing.

There is one reader now. It prefers the archive, read through the SPEAKER'S OWN
ENGINE (so an OpenCode run's JSONL event stream is the reply and not 4 KB of
transport), falls back to the stored excerpt when the archive is gone, and says
which of the two it handed back. The conversation room uses it too — and falls
back to the message's own `contentRef`, which outlives every task, instead of
losing both the link and the text the moment retention rolls the task row out.

**The resume message reads the archive with its task**, which it did not: an
OpenCode delegate's raw event stream went into the planner's resume prompt as
"what the delegate said". **And a lead coming back from a reload is told where
the talking had got to** — the live conversations, the open questions, the
council's mandate and the message ids, taken after the engine's catch-up pass
rather than from a snapshot written before it.

## 3.262.0 - X-71: a workflow run that has no rows is still an answer (2026-08-23)

`workflowRunState` began by filtering the task rows and returned `undefined` when
there were none. Two real chains produce none: one whose every step is skipped by
its `runIf`, and one whose first step names an agent that is gone. Both are OVER
— one done, one failed — and both came back `undefined`, which a parent mission
reads as "still working" and polls for ever.

A run is a record now: what it is, when it began, whose work it is, and how it
ended. Persisted, so the reason a chain stopped survives the window that knew it
— the loop guard's verdict and the step it died on used to be lost on reload,
leaving the reader "failed" and no answer to "where". A first step whose agent is
gone ends the run instead of returning in silence.

**And an abandoned attempt no longer outvotes the one that worked.** A failed step
resumed under the same run id leaves both rows behind, and asking "did anything
fail?" across all of them let the first attempt speak for a step the second one
had finished: after a reload, a chain that was resumed and completed cleanly
reported itself failed. Only the latest attempt speaks for its step; the earlier
ones stay on the record as history.

## 3.261.0 - X-72: money already spent is finished work, on every way out (2026-08-23)

The rollup that adds a round's spending to the run was a line in the MIDDLE of
the round loop, and two exits returned above it: the ceiling cut and the user's
cancel. So a wave that really ran, really settled and really cost something
closed a run that claimed it had spent only the planner's share — no reload
needed, the round simply returned over the line that counts it. The ledger line
for that round went with it, which is the only place the record says what the
round did.

Every way out of a round now books it first, through one method, and the round
carries a persisted mark saying it was booked — so calling it twice counts once.

**And the other half of the same failure: a window that closed between the wave
settling and the rollup.** Reconciliation restores what each step spent, but the
remaining budget reads the RUN totals and nothing recomputed those — the run came
back with expensive steps and an untouched budget, and the resume then started
fresh work on money that was already gone. Startup now books any round that is
entirely settled and was never counted, once, and says so in the ledger. A round
still holding live work is left to the engine that owns it.

## 3.260.0 - X-92: an undeclared writer takes the verdict with it (2026-08-23)

An evaluation went stale on two witnesses, and both of them were things the LEAD
chose to write down: a criteria label, or a lineage of sources. An ordinary
delegation may carry neither — that is legal and common — so work that rewrote
the very artefact a pass was recorded about left the pass CURRENT, and the
success gate opened on a judgement of a version that no longer existed. The test
suite had never caught it because it only ever measured a `revise`, which always
names its sources.

There is now a third witness, and it needs no label: whether the work could have
changed anything at all. The lead already marks every delegation reads-only or
not, for the parallel-write rule. A writer that declared NO reach stales the
verdict — not because it is known to have touched the artefact, but because
nothing in the run can say it did not, and between a review round spent for
nothing and a gate opened on a dead pass only one is recoverable.

Declaring reach is how a writer stays out of the way: work that names its
criteria stales only those, reading work stales nothing, and a record written
before the mark existed keeps the old two-witness rule rather than being staled
in bulk the day the extension updates.

## 3.259.0 - X-91: a cancel is an ending, and every ending is a result (2026-08-23)

Pressing stop left a run with `cancelled` and nothing else — no verdict, no
reason, no summary, and on an adaptive run no record of which criteria were
still open at the moment the hand came down. The reader got a run that ended for
no stated reason, from the same surface that explains every other ending in
full. There were two of these, and they disagreed: the engine's own mid-round
checks, and the host's path for a paused or unowned run.

Both go through the same door now. A cancelled run says it was a user stop, says
what had settled and what had not, and — when it had criteria — lists the ones
still open, exactly as an honest `partial` does.

**And the three parts of an ending must agree.** Action, verdict and reason were
each validated alone, so one terminal could give two opposite answers to "how did
this go?": an `abort` that claimed success, a ceiling that also reached its
objective, a failure that said its criteria were satisfied. Those are refused at
the parse boundary now, by name. `user-stop` is refused from the lead outright —
it is a fact about a person, and a lead that could pick it could dress a run it
gave up on as one that was stopped from outside.

## 3.258.0 - X-73: a chain's project is one binding, in three states (2026-08-23)

Which project a workflow run's work belongs to was a truthy in-memory map, and it
failed in three directions at once. An explicit "no project" was indistinguishable
from a caller who said nothing, so an automated chain quietly borrowed whatever
project the window happened to be showing. The memo died with the window, so
every step made after a reload fell back to the window again. And the four kinds
of step that mint their own task row — webhook, media, approval, select, plus a
blocked browser call — never asked for the binding at all, so one approval in the
middle of a chain filed itself under Unassigned while the agent steps around it
were the project's work.

The binding is decided once, when the run starts, and persisted: a project id, an
explicit `none`, or — only for a caller that says nothing — the window, resolved
then rather than whenever each step happens to be made. A run is one piece of
work, so the row made an hour later belongs where the first one did. Every step
kind goes through one factory, so the next one cannot forget. A trigger firing on
its own schedule now says `none` and means it, and `workflows.run` takes a
`project` argument.

## 3.257.0 - X-93: a reader's place belongs to one exchange of one run (2026-08-23)

`convThread` held a bare conversation id, and every run starts at `c1`. With two
run rows open, one click on `c1` opened BOTH of them, drew two elements carrying
the id `cv-scroll`, and `getElementById` then managed the scroll position and
unseen count of whichever came first. The key is the run and the conversation
together now, everywhere, and the transcript box is named for it — so it cannot
collide even if two were ever drawn at once.

The rest of the reading state was global too — the scroll offset, the "new
below" count, "show all" and the message the reader had jumped to — so opening a
second exchange silently handed it the first one's place. All of it is now per
exchange, and the "unanswered only" filter is per RUN, which is the scope of the
checkbox that sets it.

**And a ref link now reaches a target that was not on screen.** It set the mark
and redrew, and that was all: a message older than the compact window, or hidden
behind "unanswered only", or in a different exchange, was still not drawn — so
the link visibly went nowhere and the reader was left to work out why. The jump
opens the target's own thread, expands past the compact window, and lifts the
filter when (and only when) that filter is what is hiding it. A ref that names
nothing in the run is refused outright rather than redrawing to no effect.

## 3.256.0 - X-89: the journal's guidance, put back into the snapshot on reload (2026-08-23)

Two-phase delivery writes the journal FIRST and saves the snapshot second, in
both phases, on purpose: a record that exists only in memory does not survive
the thing it was written to survive. That leaves two crash windows, and startup
reconciliation was reading `answers` out of the projection and nothing else — so
both of them lost.

**The receipt was ahead.** The user's steer reached the journal and the window
closed before the save. The snapshot had no guidance at all, the journal had it,
and the run resumed as though nothing had ever been typed. The instruction was
gone and nothing said so — the worse of the two failures.

**The delivery was ahead.** The lead answered the call that carried the steer,
the `applied` line reached the journal, and the window closed before the save.
The snapshot still showed it in flight, so `reopenGuidance` re-sent an
instruction the journal already proved had landed — the double delivery the
whole mechanism exists to prevent.

Reconciliation now merges the projection's guidance into the run, by id, before
the engine reopens anything: a steer the journal alone knows about is restored
as pending, one the journal proves was delivered is settled and its in-flight
mark cleared. The journal may only ADD a fact here — a steer the snapshot has
and the journal does not is the snapshot-ahead case and stays the existing
refuse/degraded rule's. Both outcomes are said on the ledger rather than fixed
in silence, and the whole thing is idempotent across repeated reloads.

## 3.255.0 - X-83: an allocation already granted is not an overrun (2026-08-23)

X-46b made a ceiling reach a wave in flight, by asking the wave guard the same
question the planner boundary asks. They are not the same question, and the
reused wording got it wrong in both directions.

**A limit of one meant a limit of fifteen seconds.** `remainingBudget` answers
"is there room to START another round?" — and by the time a wave is running its
round is already in `run.rounds` and its steps are already in `spentTasks`. So
under `maxRounds: 1` or `maxTasks: 1` the remaining count was 0 while the one
legal, first, only wave was still working, and the guard cancelled it the moment
it outlived a guard interval. Rounds and tasks are ALLOCATIONS: the round in
flight has already been granted one, and refusing the NEXT round is the boundary
guard's job, which it does. The in-flight guard does not measure them at all.

**And cost and tokens did not "ride along for free".** The run's totals are only
advanced after the whole round, so the guard was reading a figure that could not
move and never cut on spending. What can honestly be read mid-flight is the
steps that have already settled — their own cost and tokens are filled in as
they come back — so the live figure is the run's booked total plus everything
settled and not yet booked, including earlier waves of the same round. A step
still running contributes nothing, which is the true answer: nobody knows what
it has spent until it says so.

The wall clock, which is why this guard exists, is unchanged. The two questions
now have two names (`inFlightGuardReason` beside `guardReason`) so the next
reader cannot reuse one for the other by accident.

## 3.254.0 - X-70: the planner call is not free, and the guard is asked after it (2026-08-23)

The registry-driven guard landed last round: a primitive whose shape is `work`
cannot begin once a ceiling is spent, and the next primitive is covered on the
day it is declared. The audit found the reading was taken at the wrong moment.

`guardReason` was computed BEFORE `runPlanner`, and the planner call is not
free: its own cost and tokens are added to the run the instant it returns, and
the clock has moved. So a call that spent the last of the budget still had the
work in its own reply started against a ceiling that was already gone — the
exact failure the guard exists to prevent, one round later. Every axis only ever
shrinks across a planner call (cost and tokens grow, time passes, rounds and
tasks are untouched), so the later reading is simply the true one, and it is now
the one that decides. When it newly bites, the prompt did not carry the
finish-only note, so the lead ordered work in good faith and gets its one nudge
before the structured hard-limit ending — which is what that nudge always meant.

And the permanent test now measures what it claims:

- **All ten work primitives, derived from the registry rather than listed.** It
  covered seven names typed into the file; `compare`, `message` and `council`
  were missing. The list is now checked against `PRIMITIVES` itself, so a
  primitive added tomorrow fails this file until somebody measures it.
- **All five ceilings.** It said "five" and tested four — `rounds` was not
  there at all.
- **Real handler counters.** Waves alone cannot tell "the handler was reached
  and unrelated validation stopped it" from "the handler was never reached", so
  every step that crosses into `delegateWave` is now counted by its kind — a
  workflow run, a child objective and a conversation turn all cross there.
- **One nudge, then the terminal.** A lead that keeps ordering work at a spent
  ceiling ends on `hard-limit` after exactly three planner calls, not by being
  fought to the planner-call cap.

The one-off proof scripts left in `.tmp/` by that round (`p_x70.js`,
`x70proof.js`, `x70proof2.js`) are out of the source tree.

## 3.253.0 - X-88: a verdict is a vertex, and a target is something you can read (2026-08-23)

Two holes on the same edge of the adaptive audit graph.

**An evaluation had no node.** `knownRefs` lets a later decision rest on an
evaluation id (`basedOn: ["e2-1"]`) and the engine accepts it as a real earlier
node — but the projection only ever updated the criterion summary from
`evaluation.recorded` and never built a vertex for `ev.actionId`. So the graph
carried an edge into something that was not drawn, which is precisely what M-16
exists to prevent. The verdict is now a node of its own kind: ONE node however
many criteria it judged (the engine writes a line per criterion under the same
id, and the projection is idempotent), settled the moment it was recorded, with
the results it looked at as its fan-in and the criteria it covered on its label.
It draws at the depth of the work it judged, because it is a reading of that
work rather than a decision of the lead's.

**And a failure that produced nothing could be evaluated.** The target allowlist
counted `failed` as settled and stopped there — so a delegation that came back
with nothing at all could be named as an evaluation target, and a
self-evaluation would record a `pass` against it. That is the success gate
opening on a verdict about an artefact that does not exist. X-67 asked for a
target that is real, settled AND readable, and the last of the three was
missing. A failure now qualifies only if it left something the canonical reader
can show: the conversation turn it spoke, the verdict sentence it handed back,
or a non-empty output archive. The line is at failures on purpose — a step that
came back `done` did the work that was ordered, and how thin its archive is, is
a judgement for the evaluation to make, not a reason to refuse to look.

`basedOn` is unchanged and stays wide: "we tried this and it came back with
nothing" is a real thing for a decision to rest on. The two lists were never the
same question.

## 3.252.0 - X-84: a setting the page shows applied and the engine ignores (2026-08-23)

VS Code can hand back `undefined` for a key its own manifest declares, so this
build reads the settings file back when it does. That fallback had grown into a
second settings engine with its own opinions, and it disagreed with the registry
in three ways at once.

**Which file.** The path was assembled from `process.platform` and hardcoded to
`Code/User/settings.json` — the DEFAULT profile of a normal install. A user on a
named profile, on Insiders, on a portable copy or in a remote window was having
a file read that VS Code does not write. It is now derived from
`context.globalStorageUri`, which the host hands us already inside the right
folder (`…/User/globalStorage/…` on the default profile,
`…/User/profiles/<id>/globalStorage/…` on a named one), so all four cases
resolve without a guess. The old platform path remains as the last resort.

**Which scope.** The fallback only ever read the user file, so a workspace
override of a dropped key was invisible. It now walks the same precedence VS
Code does — workspace folder `.vscode/settings.json`, then the
`.code-workspace` (whose settings live one level down, and are flat again
inside it), then the user file — and the scope that answered is named.

**Which shape.** The value was cast, not checked: a hand-typed `"false"` — five
characters, quotes included — is truthy, and `budgetsUnlimited` reading it as
"on" lifts every ceiling in the fleet. A value found in a file is now held to
the type the manifest declares and REFUSED if it does not fit, exactly as VS
Code refuses it. And the refusal is not private: the row on the Settings page
says the entry is being ignored and why, because a refusal nobody can see is a
second opinion held in secret.

**And every reader is behind the door.** The fallback was visible to the
Settings page and the bridge while ~200 feature readers went straight to
`getConfiguration('agentFarm')` — the page could show a value applied that the
engine never saw. `cfg()` is now the door itself (`core/settingsDoor.ts`), and
the direct reads in the panels and trees go through it too. Writes stay with the
