real configuration, which is the only thing that can perform them. A test walks
those files and fails the build on a reader that goes round it.

## 3.251.0 - X-79: a substring is not a vote, and a member is not two people (2026-08-23)

`readVoteChoice` looked for the longest option that appeared ANYWHERE in the
text as a substring. That answered confidently for three kinds of turn that had
chosen nothing: one that weighed BOTH options ("fragments read better, but the
single file is easier to ship"), one that named an option in order to REJECT it
("I would not pick fragments"), and one where the option was part of another
word (`file` inside `profile`). A tally built on any of those is the M-19
failure with numbers on it.

A vote is now read exactly or it is `unclear`. The structured line the brief
already asks for wins first (`Vote: X`, `I vote X`); failing that, whole-word
matches over the whole text, and the answer stands only when EXACTLY ONE option
is named and it is not being refused. A longer option still beats one contained
in it — `single file` and `file` on the same six words is one naming, not two.
Options are a SET: trimmed, blanks dropped, unique by casefold, at the parse
boundary, so a council cannot split its own vote between two spellings.

And a member is one ballot. Every vote message became another `CouncilVote`, so
the same member counted twice — on a three-member council, one agent
out-voting the other two by talking. A later vote is kept in the record and
marked `superseded`, out of the arithmetic; the first stands, because changing a
vote is a real thing a council might want and it needs a stated intent rather
than a second message that happens to look like one. ‼️ `tallyVotes` also
enforces it while READING, not only while writing: the in-memory planning-loop
guard blocks a repeat within one window, but it is gone after a reload and the
stored votes are re-tallied from disk.

## 3.250.0 - X-75: an unknown fate is not a licence to repeat (2026-08-23)

Two failure classes say, in their own words, that the work MAY HAVE RUN and
that nothing here can say which — and then advised the lead to order it again.
`record-lost`: "Order it again if the result still matters." `interrupted`:
"check the output file if there is one before re-ordering."

For a READ that is harmless. For a writer, a workflow or a child mission it is
how the same commit lands twice, a file is rewritten over somebody's edit, or a
second child run starts against work that was already done — with no record of
the first to compare against, which is the whole reason the class exists. And
the engine's own `seenWork` lock then refused the identical order, so a lead
that followed the advice literally hit "already delegated" and a small
paraphrase slipped past the lock straight into the duplicate.

The advice now depends on whether the action could have CHANGED anything, not
on the class alone. A step that said it only reads, and the `review`/`compare`
primitives that exist to read, keep `retry: same`. Everything else — including
any workflow or child mission, whatever the step claims — answers `inspect`: a
new advice that tells the lead to establish from the evidence what actually
landed, and to ask the user when that cannot settle it. The default is that
work writes, because a delegation whose prompt nobody here parsed can do
anything the agent can do.

The fact travels on the failure (`couldHaveWritten`), since the step is gone by
the time a reload or the bridge asks; `retryAdvice()` is the one resolver, so
`missions.status` can never answer `same` while the lead's own prompt says
`inspect` about the same step.

## 3.249.0 - X-81: ordered, spoken and silent are three facts (2026-08-23)

U-65 fixed the counter — a conversation's summary counts only turns whose
state is `delivered` — and left the row below it saying the opposite. The
transcript asked one question, `state === 'failed' || 'cancelled'`, and drew
everything else as an ordinary message: a `pending` turn got a real speaker, a
real intent and an empty body. One record, two answers, in the same box.

A turn is now drawn as what it is. `delivered` draws speech and is the only
state that ever does. `failed`/`cancelled` draw the ORDER and the reason it
produced none, as they already did. `pending` draws neither — it says it is
waiting, when it was ordered and what the lead asked for, wears its state as a
chip, and its speaker is dimmed rather than presented as somebody who spoke.

The summary counts three things instead of two: `4 spoken · 1 silent · 1
waiting`. A turn still in flight is neither said nor lost, and counting it as
either is exactly how the row and the transcript below it started disagreeing.

## 3.248.0 - X-85: who spoke is a fact about the past (2026-08-23)

M-19/M-20 added a name beside every id in a mission's cast, because an id on
this fleet is a folder path and `d:/zone/agent/ajanlar/asistan` is not an answer
to "who spoke". The resolver's own comment said an agent that has since left
the fleet is still who spoke — and then asked `agents.find(a => a.id === id)`,
the CURRENT fleet, and nothing else. So the moment an agent was removed, or its
id was written with a different case or slash than the folder scan produces,
the reader was handed the raw path again: the exact failure the name fields
were added to end, reproduced by the code that was supposed to end it.

A run already carries who its cast were AT THE TIME — the name stamped on each
message as it was said, the roles the lead bound on this run, and the spec's
lead, team and pool. Those are asked first, in that order; the live fleet is
only how the name is spelled TODAY and is asked second; the raw id is the last
resort it was always meant to be. Ids are compared as PATHS, so case and
slashes are not two different agents.

‼️ And the page no longer keeps its own answer. `media/missions.js` had a
second, independent `speakerName` that asked `fromName` then `DATA.agents`, so
`missions.status` could name a speaker the transcript beside it drew as a
folder path. Both resolvers now read the same sources in the same order, and
`test_mission_council.js` measures that they still do.

## 3.247.0 - X-87/X-86: a record that cannot lie about itself (2026-08-23)

Two doors into the same failure — a mission's history reading as whole when it
is not — one in the snapshot, one in the journal.

**X-87 · syntax is not schema.** X-62 taught the store that a missing file and
a corrupt one are different events, but it asked only whether the BYTES parsed.
Everything after that was a shrug: `Array.isArray(parsed.specs) ? parsed.specs
: []`. So `{"specs":"broken","runs":"broken"}`, a bare `[]`, `{}` and a list of
items that are not specs all opened as `health: 'ok'` with an empty list — and
the next `save()` wrote that emptiness over the fleet's whole history. The hole
X-62 closed on bad bytes was still wide open on bad shape.

`storeSchemaFault` now checks IDENTITY and only identity: the root is an
object, `specs`/`runs` are lists, and each item is an object that says which
spec or run it is. Anything else takes the X-62 path — the bytes are set aside
as evidence, the sentence names what was wrong with them, and a store that
cannot be set aside refuses to save at all. Everything else is a field an older
version may legitimately not have written, which is migration and not damage: a
pre-adaptive store still opens clean, with nothing lost and nothing invented.

**X-86 · the proven prefix is physical.** X-63 stops the projection at the first
break in the SEQUENCE. But a line that could not be read carries no seq for a
hole to show up in, so a chain assembled only out of the lines that parsed read
as unbroken straight across the damage: `seq1 · garbage · seq2` answered "two
events, up to seq 2" and handed the event AFTER the damage to the projection as
though nothing had happened — the exact guarantee X-63 was written to give.

The physical line position is now part of the prefix state: a break inside the
chain cuts it there, whatever the surviving numbers look like. (Junk sitting
ahead of every readable event is not a break — the event that follows it says
it is seq 1, and nothing comes before seq 1.)

And the file is closed to writing. A half-written TAIL is repairable precisely
because everything before it is intact; a break further up is not, and
appending past it buries the loss under history that looks continuous. Same
answer X-64 gives a future line: the bytes are left byte-identical, the run
carries on snapshot-only, and `degraded` says why.

## 3.246.0 - X-90: an explicit null is not silence (2026-08-23)

X-60 put a validator in front of `createMission` so a request is judged before
it is normalised. That validator asked one question — `!== undefined && !==
null` — and used the answer for three different facts: was the key GIVEN, is
what arrived the right SHAPE, and can the value be HONOURED.

So the faults walked past it. `mode: null`, `autonomy: ""` and `pool: null`
were read as "the caller said nothing" and went back into the lossy normaliser
that X-60 exists to stand in front of. An unknown `leadAgentId` fell through to
"the first of the pool", so an adaptive run was led by an agent the caller
never named. An unknown member of a CLASSIC team was FILTERED OUT, so a team of
five could start as a team of two — or as `Pick at least one team agent` for a
request that named five. And a list's ITEMS had no shape at all: `pool:
["coder"]`, the most natural thing a caller writes, read as one anonymous
member and then, resolving to nobody, as the whole fleet.

The three facts are now three tests. Presence is `hasOwnProperty`; an explicit
`null`, a blank enum, a wrong container type, a member that is a bare string or
a null, a constraint that is not text and a criterion that is not an object are
each refused with what actually arrived (`null` · `blank` · `a list` · `number`)
rather than with what it coerced to. Every identity in the request — lead, team
member, pool member — is checked against this window's real fleet, and the
adaptive run that names NO lead is still exactly the feature it was.

`test/test_mission_adaptive.js` measures omitted vs. explicit-empty on every
field, the unknown lead, mixed known+unknown team and pool, and
primitive/string/null list items — on the panel's path and on `missions.start`.

## 3.245.0 - X-82: a ceiling is lifted on purpose or not at all (2026-08-23)

`normalizeMissionLimits` asked `Number(v)` first and `n <= 0` second. Between
those two lines, `null`, `false`, `""`, a limit box the user had CLEARED and
every negative figure all became the word "unlimited" — the one word that
removes the cost, token, round, task, time and parallel ceilings of the run
being started. A typo did not fail; it handed out an unbounded budget.

Three states are now kept apart, on all six axes: an OMITTED field asks for the
documented default · an exact `0` (or the form's `"0"`) is the one spelling of
"no ceiling on this axis" · a positive figure is itself, floored as before.
Anything else is refused BY FIELD NAME at the raw boundary
(`validateMissionLimitsInput`, beside `validateMissionInput` — X-60's order:
judge the request before normalising it), and the normaliser falls back to the
default rather than to unlimited if it is ever reached another way.

The panel's `type="number" min="0"` is a convenience, never the guard: the
bridge reaches the same `createMission` with no HTML in front of it, so
`missions.start` and the form now refuse the identical payloads.
`test/test_mission_limits.js` measures all six axes against
null/false/blank/negative/NaN-string/list/object, both paths.

## 3.244.0 - X-70: a spent ceiling stops all work, not the one word (2026-08-23)

The budget guard asked `d.action === 'delegate'`. That was the whole vocabulary
when it was written and has not been since M-18.

Measured before the fix, with the cost budget fully spent: `parallel`, `review`,
`revise` and a reviewer-d `evaluate` each started a real wave and wrote a real
`action.created`. `compare`, `run_workflow` and `run_mission` take the identical
branch and were stopped, in that harness, only by unrelated validation. The
in-flight guard (X-46b) does catch them, but only AFTER the work has begun and
up to one guard interval of spending has happened.

The question is now answered by the PRIMITIVE REGISTRY - a primitive whose
`shape` is `work` orders work - rather than by a list of names somebody has to
remember to grow. One exemption, and it is not an oversight: an `evaluate` with
no reviewer orders nothing and is exactly what lets a run close honestly as
`partial` with real verdicts.

`test/test_mission_guard.js` measures every work primitive against every one of
the five ceilings the guard names.

## 3.243.0 — U-65: a live repaint does not take the reader's place (2026-08-23)

The Missions page redraws once a second while a mission runs, and the
conversation room is a READING surface. A transcript that jumped back to its
first line every second would not be a redraw, it would be an interruption —
the same failure `afTip` had to solve for its own panel.

‼️ There are two readers here and they want opposite things. One is FOLLOWING a
live exchange and wants each new turn as it lands; one is reading further up,
and their place must not be taken away. So the reading position is captured
before the markup that holds it is thrown away and put back after: a reader at
the bottom rides down with the new turn, a reader further up keeps the exact
line they were on and is TOLD what arrived — `N new below ↓`, sticky at the top
of the transcript. Pressing it is how they choose to go there, and the count is
spent. A reader who can already see the new turn is never shown a count for it.

Measured, not asserted: a scrolled-up reader's `scrollTop` survives a data
refresh with the accordion still open, a turn arriving while they are up there
produces the count and moves nothing, pressing the count lands at the end and
clears it, and a reader at the bottom follows the exchange down with no count
at all.

## 3.242.0 — U-65: the conversation is a room you can read (2026-08-23)

### The summary answered "did they talk"
A run that opened a council showed one line per exchange: an id, the question,
a message count. The question a reader actually has is what was **said**, by
whom, about which message, and where it ran — and none of that was reachable
from this page at all.

`Conversations` is now a room. Each exchange keeps its compact row (cast, chair,
spoken / silent counts, turns against the cap, the votes with who chose what,
and whether it is open, closed or ended for one of the council's seven stated
reasons) and opens into the real chronological transcript: speaker, intent in
SHORTHAND, the messages it is **about** as clickable refs, the lane it was
carried on, its timestamp, and deep links into the speaker's own session and
the archived output. The full text is drawn; the AFTip on the intent chip opens
with the long form, what the lead asked for, and how the lane was carried.

‼️ **No fake speaker.** A turn that was ordered and came back with nothing draws
no speech — it draws the order and the reason it produced none. A transcript
that filled that gap with a sentence nobody said would be the one defect this
surface cannot recover from.

A ref is a link: clicking `m3` marks and scrolls to the message it answers,
because "m3 answers m2" is what makes a transcript followable and a reader
scrolling for an id is a reader who has stopped following it. An `unanswered`
count and a filter show the questions and challenges nothing in the exchange has
answered. An exchange over 25 messages opens **compact** — the newest are what a
reader coming back wants and the rest are one click away.

### ‼️ And the reason the old summary looked right: the fixture was invented
The council pointed at its conversation through `conversation`; the record's
field is `conversationId`. A message's state was `'said'`; the record's states
are `pending` / `delivered` / `failed` / `cancelled`. A conversation carried
`messages` and `open` counts and a `closed` flag it has never had. Every string
test passed — and on a **real** run the council matched no conversation at all,
so the chair, the cap, the votes and the way out were silently missing from the
row, and `pending` turns were counted as spoken.

Both the page fixture and the webview test's payload are now the shapes
`MissionConversation` / `MissionCouncil` / `MissionMessage` really have, and the
exchange they draw is the one the item asks for: an independent opening round,
a challenge that names what it is about, a response, a concession, a one-to-many
synthesis over real refs, two votes (one of them naming no option), a turn that
failed, and a challenge nothing ever answered. A 200-message council fixture
covers the compact default.

A speaking turn's two deep links are resolved where the index is (`sessionId` →
the transcript file, `taskId` → the archived output). Resolving them in the page
would ship the session index to a surface with no other use for it; leaving them
unresolved would give the reader a link that silently does nothing.

## 3.241.0 — The briefing teaches what the parser now demands (2026-08-23)

X-65, X-67 and X-68 tightened what an adaptive lead may say; the briefing still
described the loose contract. A rule the model is refused on but never told is a
round spent on a correction that did not have to happen — and on a slower model,
two rounds and an ended run.

The decision schema now states that `targets` is REQUIRED for `evaluate` and for
`review` / `compare` / `revise`, with at least one result that has already
**settled**; that `stopReason` is REQUIRED on `finish` and `abort`; and that
`basedOn` takes real ids only — an empty list rather than an invented one. The
rules list carries the same three in the words the refusals themselves use,
including why an evaluation bound to nothing is a permanent pass, and that a
revise stales the verdict on what it replaced.

## 3.240.0 — A verdict names the version it judged, and dies with it (2026-08-23)

### X-67 — an evaluation bound to nothing was a permanent pass
The top of `missionEvaluation.ts` has said since M-17 that every evaluation
names what it looked at, and gave the reason in the same breath: *a verdict
bound to nothing can never go out of date, and one that can never go out of date
is a permanent pass* — exactly how a run revises its work and still finishes on
a judgement of the version it replaced.

Nothing enforced it. The type allowed `targets: []`, the engine accepted it, and
the tests for self and independent evaluation used it. An `evaluate` now needs
at least one target that really settled, refused with the settled ids in hand
and, before anything has run, told plainly that there is nothing to evaluate
yet. A reviewer's material is built only from the named targets — it used to
fall back to "the last six done steps", so a reviewer could be handed work the
verdict was never bound to.

Each verdict now pins `targetVersions`: the id **and the moment it settled**. A
step id is already immutable here (a step settles once and is never re-run under
the same id), but the moment is what lets a reader prove the verdict is about
the artefact that existed then rather than the one that exists now.

### X-67 — staleness had one witness, and it was optional
`isStale` asked only whether later work carried a **criteria label** the verdict
had judged. That label is optional on an adaptive delegation — so the artefact
could be rewritten by work that named no criteria at all, the old pass stayed
`current`, and the success gate opened on a judgement of a version nobody could
still produce.

Lineage is now the second witness: work that names one of a verdict's own
targets among its `sources` is that target's successor, label or no label, and
it ends the verdict. What still does **not** stale an evaluation is unrelated
work — neither aimed at a criterion it judged nor descended from anything it
looked at — because expiring on that would cost a review round every time
anything happened anywhere. `settledCriteriaWork` reports every settled step now
instead of filtering on the label itself: its job is to say what happened, and
`isStale`'s job is to judge it.

Acceptance measures both witnesses in isolation and the whole path in the
engine: a revise that carries no criteria label stales the pass on what it
replaced, and the run can no longer finish as `success` on it.

‼️ This closes **X-59** — all nine Adaptive Missions phase-2 corrections
(X-60 … X-68) are done.

## 3.239.0 — An ending that says why, and a request judged on what was sent (2026-08-23)

### X-68 — every adaptive ending says why it stopped, and what is still open
`stopReason` was optional. Most endings therefore carried no reason at all, so
the one question the field exists to answer — did this run reach its objective,
or run out of rope? — was answerable for some terminals and not for others, from
the same screen. It is now required on an adaptive `finish` or `abort`, refused
by name with the closed list in the error.

`unmet` was worse: it was filled in exactly **one** place — a lead claimed
"success", the gate refused, the lead insisted, and the verdict came down to
`partial`. Every other way a run can end short (an honest partial, an explicit
failure, an abort, a ceiling reached mid-wave) recorded no structured gaps at
all and left saying what was missing to whatever prose the model happened to
write. The same `partial` verdict sometimes showed the reader which criteria
were open and sometimes could not.

Every adaptive terminal now goes through one door. The criteria state is read
there, once, for anything that is not a stated success; the summary is
**deterministically completed** when the model's own words skipped the gaps; and
the engine's own terminals — the planner-call cap, an unreachable lead, a reply
that could not be read twice — carry a verdict and a reason like any other
ending instead of a bare note. A real success still carries no open list: an
empty one would read as a doubt.

### X-60 — a bad request became a different, valid-looking mission
`createMission` normalised the request into a valid spec and then asked
`validateObjective` to judge **its own output**. Every fault below was therefore
already gone by the time anything looked for it, and none of them produced an
error — each produced a different mission the caller was told was theirs:

- a misspelled `mode` ("adptive") started a **classic** mission;
- an unknown `autonomy` became `ask-when-unsure`;
- two criteria the caller gave the **same id** became `c1` and `c2`, so the run
  judged two things under names the caller never used;
- a `pool` naming three agents that do not exist expanded to the **whole fleet**,
  because "nothing resolved" and "nothing asked for" were one test;
- an unknown member `engine` was dropped and the member ran on the default;
- and `pool` / `team` / `constraints` / `successCriteria` sent as anything but a
  list were read as empty.

A raw-input validator now runs **first**, on the fields as they were sent, and
reports every fault at once. ‼️ An absent field is still not a bad one: a
classic Start sends no `mode` key at all (M-15), an objective with no `pool`
really does mean the whole fleet, and an omitted `autonomy` takes the documented
default. Only a field that was **given** and cannot be honoured is refused.

The unknown-engine case reverses an earlier deliberate drop. The reason is the
codebase's own, stated one line away in the `permissionMode` check: falling back
to a default is the exact silence a stated dimension exists to end. The runtime
fallback in `engineOf` is untouched — that is about a spec read off disk, not a
request somebody just made.

Acceptance measures the validator, the ORDER inside `createMission` (raw check
before the normaliser, before a single field is read), and the same broken
inputs dispatched through a `missions.start` handler shaped like the real one.

## 3.238.0 — An audit graph of what really happened, and a steer that cannot be lost (2026-08-23)

### X-65 — the graph may only point at work that really happened
`basedOn` and `evaluate.targets` are the audit graph's causality edges, and
both arrived as free strings that nothing checked. A lead could rest a decision
on an id no step or round ever had, on work that had not finished, or on the
round it was deciding — and the graph recorded that dependency as though it had
happened. A test approved exactly that. A graph you cannot trust to be real is
not evidence of anything, and it is the one thing a reader of it cannot detect
from the inside.

The engine now builds the allowlist from the run itself: **results** (steps that
have settled and left a record) and **nodes** (those plus the decisions and
evaluations already taken). The round being decided is deliberately not among
them, so a decision can never claim to rest on itself. An invented, future or
self-referential id is refused with the real ids in hand; a lead that insists a
second time has the *claim* dropped and keeps its decision, because the edge is
the provenance, not the work — and spinning the run to its call cap over a
footnote would cost more than the footnote is worth.

`evaluate` never checked its targets at all, so a verdict could be recorded
against an id no step ever had — a pass on nothing, which the success gate then
reads as met. And `review` / `compare` / `revise` asked only whether a step with
that id existed *anywhere* in the run, so a queued or still-running step could
be reviewed: reading an output that had not been written yet. Both now require
a target that has really settled.

### X-66 — a steer marked delivered before it was delivered
Guidance was marked **applied** — on the run and in the journal — immediately
before the planner call, on the reasoning that a crash mid-call must lose the
steer rather than repeat it. The reasoning was sound and the implementation was
not: a window that closed between the mark and the reply left a steer that had
**never reached the lead** recorded as delivered for ever. `buildResumeMessage`
does not carry applied guidance, and if the old planner session resumed
successfully the history fallback did not run either. The user typed it, it
never landed, and nothing said so.

Delivery is now two-phase: **pending → inflight → acknowledged**. Taking a steer
only puts it in flight; it becomes a fact — on the run and in the journal — once
the lead has actually answered a call that carried it. A crash in between leaves
it in flight, which is the honest middle state, and an engine taking the run
over re-opens it and sends it again **labelled as already in force, with its own
id**: a lead that did read it does not act twice, and a lead that never saw it
does not lose it. The ledger says why it came again.

The resume-fallback prompt now carries in-flight guidance too. It builds a
brand-new prompt, so a steer that lived only in the prompt that just failed was
being dropped on the floor by the retry that replaced it.

Acceptance covers the crash window itself (a planner call that never returns,
then a new engine over the same run), the session-resume fallback, normal single
delivery, and that no duplicate action is produced.

## 3.237.0 — An atomic save that is not undone by its own fallback (2026-08-23)

### X-62 — the snapshot keeps the guarantee it advertises
`MissionStore.save` swapped a temp file in atomically and then, if the swap
failed, answered by writing the body **directly over the target** — which is
exactly the truncation the atomic swap exists to prevent, reintroduced at the
one moment the machine is already in trouble.

A failed swap now leaves the target completely alone. The state that could not
land stays in the named temp file so a person can recover it, the failure comes
back as a structured `StorePersistence` verdict (`temp` · `rename` · `refused`),
and the next successful save renames the temp away by itself. A failed temp
write is the same answer one step earlier: the target is never opened.

### X-62 — missing and corrupt were read as one event, and one of them cost history
`load` caught a missing file and an unreadable one in the same `catch` and
started empty either way — and the very next `save` wrote that empty list over
the fleet's entire mission history. The only symptom was a Missions page that
looked like a fresh install.

The two are now separated. A store that was never there is `empty` and nothing
is reported. A store whose **bytes** went bad is evidence: it is set aside as
`missions.corrupt-<ts>.json` before anything can write in its place, and the
run list starts empty honestly. If the bytes cannot be set aside — the file is
locked, the disk is full — the store is `unreadable` and **refuses to save at
all** rather than overwrite what it could not preserve.

### X-62 — a journal append that fails is no longer silent
`MissionTraceWriter.append` swallows a write failure on purpose: a mission must
not die because its audit trail could not be written. Swallowing it and saying
nothing is a different decision, and it left surfaces drawing a live journal
off a file that had stopped. Failures are counted, and the writer states why the
run went snapshot-only; the run carries that sentence for Needs You to show.

### `missions.store`
‼️ An empty `missions.list` means one of two very different things — a fleet
that has run nothing, or a store that could not be read — and no caller could
tell them apart. The new op answers with the snapshot's own health,
`recoveryRequired`, the degraded sentence and where an unreadable copy was set
aside. A store that comes up damaged, or a save that fails, also says so to the
user directly (once per distinct failure, not on every state change).

Acceptance is fault-injected: a failing temp write, a failing rename, a failing
append, a corrupt store that can be set aside and one that cannot.

## 3.236.0 — A journal you can append to, and a hole you cannot step over (2026-08-23)

### X-61 — the half-written tail is repaired before anything appends to it
`readTrace` has always recognised a truncated last line and stepped over it,
which is the right answer for a reader. A writer stepping over it was a
different thing: the half line was still on disk with no newline after it, so
the next append landed flush against it and the two became **one unreadable
line** — the crash's damage and the new event lost together, and every later
read counting a bad line where there had only ever been a survivable tail.

`MissionTraceWriter.open` now repairs before it is usable. The tail is cut back
to the last complete line **byte-exactly** (a crash can stop in the middle of a
UTF-8 character, so this is never done on a string) and the removed bytes are
kept beside the journal as `<run>.jsonl.broken` rather than destroyed. A repair
that does not take blocks the writer instead of appending into the wreckage.

‼️ And cutting is only one of the two repairs. A crash can equally stop **on**
the newline byte, leaving a last line that is complete and simply unterminated:
the reader sees no damage at all, so nothing called it damage — and appending
after it glued the next event onto a good one and lost **both**. That case is
terminated, never cut. The line is evidence; the missing byte is the only thing
wrong with it.

### X-63 — a gap in the chain is loss, and order is evidence
The reader sorted the events it had parsed and then read the last element, so a
journal of seq 1 and seq 3 answered *"two events, up to seq 3"*: the hole was
invisible, and `snapshotBehind`, derived from that same maximum, promised the
snapshot a catch-up that could never arrive.

A journal is now read as the **proven prefix** — seq 1, 2, 3 … in the order the
lines physically sit in the file, stopping at the first break. Only that prefix
is projected, and `snapshotBehind` follows it. Gaps, backwards seq and a seq
that is not a positive whole number are each diagnosed by name and each make
the trace `damaged`; what was readable beyond the break is counted and reported,
never applied. A hole over work still in flight refuses a resume, because the
run cannot say what it already set in motion.

### X-64 — a journal from a newer build is read-only, full stop
The writer continued from the last seq **this** build could apply, so a line
written by a newer schema at seq 2 left the old build handing out seq 2 again;
and reconciliation answered `rebrief` whenever nothing was outstanding — and a
rebrief *runs* the mission. Two different truths then sat under one sequence
number and no later version could separate them.

The physical high-water mark is now kept apart from the applicable one, so a
number the file has spent is never handed out twice. A trace containing a
future line opens **blocked**: appends write nothing, the file stays
byte-identical, `lastSeq` does not move, and the run says it needs a newer
Agent Farm. A resume is refused outright, in-flight work or not.

### Also
`missions.trace` reports the four diagnoses it could not make before (`gaps`,
`outOfOrder`, `invalidSeq`, `beyondPrefix`) alongside `physicalLastSeq`. The
orphan sweep and `deleteTrace` know the `.jsonl.broken` suffix, so a quarantined
tail is culled with its run rather than kept for ever. A blocked writer sets the
run's degraded sentence, so a journal that has silently stopped growing says so.

‼️ And one fixture was green only after 05:20. `test_tasks_header_tips.js` asks
an absolute question ("since midnight") of a row pinned at a relative time (320
minutes ago); before 05:20 local the row fell into yesterday, the derived list
emptied and two assertions failed on the clock rather than on the code. Rows
whose today-ness a test relies on are now anchored with `todayMin`.

## 3.235.0 — A full Codex transcript cannot become nine loose replies (2026-08-23)

### Codex 0.149 changed the stored dialogue envelope
Codex did not lose the conversation: one reported session still held 10 MB / 671
JSONL lines, two human turns, nine agent messages and 101 tool calls. Agent Farm
lost the boundaries while reading it. Codex 0.149 stores a human turn as
`event_msg → item_completed → UserMessage`; both Codex transcript readers still
expected the legacy `event_msg → user_message`. With no recognised human line,
the viewer produced an empty title, zero turns and only the nine ungrouped agent
replies that its default Dialog filter could still see.

Both Codex-only readers now accept the measured 0.149 envelope while retaining
the legacy path. They deliberately do **not** treat every `response_item` whose
role is `user` as dialogue: Codex writes recommended plugins, AGENTS.md and the
environment through that same record, and one real session carried 23,758
characters of that host machinery before the person spoke. Paired
`AgentMessage` / assistant response records are deduplicated inside their turn.

The original session now parses as two titled turns, two user messages, nine
agent messages, 101 calls and 101 results, with no orphaned message. Captured
0.149 fixtures cover the session index, viewer and their turn-number agreement;
the legacy Codex tests and the Gemini, Antigravity and OpenCode acceptance paths
remain unchanged and green.

## 3.234.0 — A participant is a name, and the id travels beside it (2026-08-22)

### Three ops handed a reader a folder path where a person belonged
A cast is stored by agent id, which on a real fleet is a folder path
(`d:/zone/agent/ajanlar/asistan`). That is the right HANDLE — it survives a
rename and it is what the next call has to pass back — but it is not an answer to
"who spoke". Measured on a real run: `missions.status` reported a conversation's
`participants` and a council's `chair`/`members` as bare paths, and
`missions.conversation` named the speaker of every message and then said the
addressee in paths.

Both go out now, id **and** name, from ONE resolver — `missions.council` had the
only copy of that lookup and now shares it, because a second copy is how one op
quietly starts disagreeing with another about who was in the room. New fields:
`participantNames` (status + conversation), `chairName` and `memberNames`
(status; `missions.council` already had them), `toNames` on every message.
`lead` is a role rather than an agent and resolves through the spec; an id
nothing matches falls back to itself, because an agent that has since left the
fleet is still who spoke.

## 3.233.0 — A ceiling you can pass is not a ceiling (2026-08-22)

### The wall clock now binds a wave that stopped answering
Every mission limit was measured at the PLANNER boundary — the top of a round,
where the previous wave has settled. That is the one moment a hung wave never
reaches. Measured on a real run (`mt4gqn99mxam3`): one delegate sat 45+ minutes
without answering, the run went past its 50-minute ceiling, was still `running`
at minute 70, and had to be cancelled by hand. The figure said 50 and the run
took 70 — that is not a cap, it is the appearance of one.

The wave in flight is now measured on a coarse timer (15 s) against the SAME
`guardReason(remainingBudget(…))` the planner boundary runs, so cost and tokens
come along for free: a wave can spend both without ever returning either.

‼️ **It does not walk away from the wave.** A promise dropped on the floor leaves
real processes running that nothing will ever claim, so the guard asks for the
same cancel a person would — a new `cancelWave` dep that stops the wave's tasks,
child objectives and chains but NOT the engine — and then still waits for the
wave to settle. Each unsettled step carries "stopped by the mission ceiling — …",
and the run ends `hard-limit` with a `partial` verdict naming the ceiling rather
than the `cancelled` that would claim a hand did it.

## 3.232.0 — A setting that vanishes is not a setting (2026-08-22)

### The one key VS Code drops, and the file that answers for it
`agentFarm.budgetsUnlimited` — the documented switch that suspends every daily
budget without clearing the figures — could not be written (`settings.set` was
refused with "is not a registered configuration") and, worse, could not be READ:
`getConfiguration().get()` handed back `undefined` instead of the declared
default, so a user who ticked it by hand got no suspension and no explanation.

Measured before touching anything: **exactly one of the 124 settings this build
contributes is missing from the running window's configuration registry**, and it
is that one. The manifest is not at fault — the key occurs once, with a valid
boolean schema, in the installed folder's `package.json`, and the keys either
side of it in the same object both work. No extension can put a dropped key back
from inside.

So the READER stopped trusting the registry alone. Every Agent Farm value now
comes through one door that falls back to the user's own `settings.json` when the
registry has nothing to say — JSONC-aware, because that file legally carries
comments, trailing commas and a `//` inside every Windows path and URL in it.
The fallback is on the read side only: reading a file cannot corrupt it, and
hand-patching somebody's JSONC is not a risk worth taking for a switch. A write
VS Code refuses now answers with the file path and the exact line to paste, and
says the value will take effect without a reload because the reader will find it.

‼️ **And there was already a second way to lift a cap that nobody had written
down:** the brake tests `> 0`, so **a figure of `0` in `budgets` means NO CAP on
that name** — `{"*": 0}` lifts the fleet ceiling while every per-agent figure
stays in force. It is the same "0 = unlimited" word the mission ceilings speak,
and it goes through a setting that writes fine.

## 3.231.0 — The ceilings on a mission belong to whoever pays for it (2026-08-22)

### The arbitrary upper clamps are gone, and `0` means unlimited on every axis
`missions.start` used to clamp what the user typed — 24 hours of wall clock,
$500 of budget, 30 rounds, 60 tasks, 6 parallel — figures this extension invented
for somebody else's money and applied **silently**, so a run asked for a five-day
marathon ended on the second day for a reason nobody had written down. A command
centre hands out DEFAULTS; it does not hand out limits.

Nothing is capped from above any more, and **`0` on any of `maxRounds`,
`maxTasks`, `maxCostUSD`, `maxTokens`, `maxMinutes`, `maxParallel` means
UNLIMITED** on that axis — the one word `maxTokens` already spoke (X-19), now
spoken by all six. The FLOOR survives: a POSITIVE figure below the smallest
workable value is a typo rather than a request and is lifted to it.

‼️ **Two leashes were hiding behind the round ceiling.** `hardCallCap` read it as
a number (`maxRounds + 6`), so a mission asking for NO round ceiling would have
been cut off after six planner calls — the tightest limit in the file, produced
by the field that says "run as long as it takes". And the planner's budget line
would have told the lead it had "Infinity round(s)" left; every unlimited axis is
now said in words ("unlimited rounds", "no cost ceiling", "no time limit").
`maxParallel: 0` runs a whole round in one wave, and the one-writer rule still
splits it.

The rule left the caller and became `normalizeMissionLimits()` in
`src/core/missions.ts` — a rule inside a closure cannot be held by a test.
`test/test_mission_limits.js` holds it, and every surface that prints a ceiling
(the form, the spec summary, the budget bar, the runs table, the tree row, the
rerun prompt, the `missions.start` bridge description) says ∞ rather than 0.

## 3.230.0 — U-64: Classic and Adaptive in one Missions room, and a run that says what it is doing and why (2026-08-22)

### One form, two kinds of work

**The Missions page has asked for a recipe since the day it existed.** A lead, a team, rounds, limits — and an adaptive objective, which the core has been able to run since M-15, could only be started from the bridge. There is now a choice at the top of the form and nothing else moved: `Classic Mission` is pre-selected and its fields, its DOM and the message it posts are what they always were. ‼️ A classic Start sends **no `mode` key at all** — the host reads anything that is not the exact string `adaptive` as classic, so the absent key IS the answer and a payload that grew a field nobody reads would be the compatibility break this avoids.

**`Adaptive Objective` asks the three questions an outcome is made of** — what you want to end up with, what the run may NOT do, and how the result will be judged — and folds everything that already has a default under **Advanced**: the lead (leave it and the first of the pool leads), the pool, the workdir, the limits, the engines and the approval gate. A criterion is `required` by default, because an objective nobody can fail is not one, and each carries the stable id (`c1`, `c2`…) every later evaluation refers to for the life of the run. ‼️ Switching mode **reads the form first**: nothing typed in the other one is lost, it is hidden.

**And the model box finally knows which engine it is on.** Every other launch surface narrows the model and the effort to the engine the row is set to; this form offered four Claude aliases and six efforts to a member delegating on OpenCode, and the launch then refused the pair. Both questions now go to `afEngine.js` — the same helper the Console and the Task launcher read — per member row and live: change a member's engine, or the mission-wide one that members inherit, and its model box carries that engine's own catalog. ‼️ An engine with **no** effort setting draws the box dead and says which engine decided that, rather than offering five words that would be refused at spawn.

### A run detail that answers "what is it doing, and why"

An adaptive run now opens on seven sections a classic run does not grow, each with one subject and no fact repeated between them.

**Objective** — every criterion with the LATEST verdict that still speaks for the work as it stands, read by the same staleness rule the success gate uses, so the page can never show a pass the gate would refuse. Required and optional are visibly different, because the asymmetry is the whole point of the flag. **Strategy** — the approach in force with its version and phase, and ‼️ **every revision with the reason it was cut**, which is the half that exists only in the journal: the run record holds the strategy, the trace holds why it moved. A version is cut when the approach MOVED, so a run of eight rounds under one `v1` changed its mind never, and the round bands say which version each was decided under. **Guide next decision** — a one-off steer through the same door the command and the bridge use, and it says plainly WHERE it lands: the next planner boundary, never the delegation running now, because a task in flight has its prompt and cannot be renegotiated. **Cast** — the roles the lead BOUND at runtime, which is the only place an adaptive run's team is a fact, with who is working this moment and who in the pool is still unused. **Conversations** — one line per exchange and per council, counting only messages that were really spoken; the transcript is its own surface and a hollow one here would be a feature that does not exist. **Evaluations** — every verdict, stale ones kept, with who gave it and what it advised. **Runtime graph** — what actually happened, node by node, with each one's fan-in: nothing here was drawn in advance, which is the difference between this and a workflow.

‼️ **What is not drawn is the lead's hidden reasoning.** A round's stated thought, a strategy's own words and an evaluation's evidence are statements made for the record; there is no chain-of-thought here and the absence is deliberate. And an honest ending now names what it did NOT reach — the exact criterion ids the success gate refused on — instead of leaving that in a log.

**Two faults came out of drawing it.** A round's work was rendered only when the round was called `delegate`, so every `parallel`, `review`, `compare`, `revise`, `message` and `council` round — which is most of what an adaptive lead orders — showed its thought with its delegations invisible; the branch tested the round's NAME instead of its contents. And an adaptive run drew an empty `team ·` in its header, reading as a missing fact rather than as a cast that is bound at runtime.

### And a gate for the thing that shipped by accident

**A stray file in the repo root rides into the VSIX and nothing notices.** Measured while packaging this build: a 1.4 MB file a mistyped shell redirection had left in the root was packed, and every gate passed — each of them names a FOLDER, and the root matched none of them. `npm run verify` now refuses an artefact carrying any root file outside the short known list.

## 3.229.0 — X-46: what a real run found · M-20: a council is a chaired conversation (2026-08-22)

### The first real adaptive run, and the two things no unit test could have found

A real objective was run on the installed build: a Haiku planner, two OpenCode delegates on free models, `plan` permissions. The planner chose `message`, opened a conversation with the right cast and ordered a real speaking turn. Both faults below came out of that run.

**A delegate's archive was read as what the agent SAID, and on one engine it is not.** A headless OpenCode turn runs `run --format json`, so its archive is that engine's own JSONL event stream — `step_start`, `text`, `tool_use`, `step_finish`. An M-19 speaking turn takes its message text from the archived body, so the record held 4 KB of transport and the next speaker was going to be shown it as "what the other agent said". The same body is the material a `review`, `compare` or `revise` delegate is handed. M-14 had already met this in the workflow handoff and unwrapped it there, in two branches beside one caller; that is now `engineReplyText` in `core/tasks.ts` — one place, **keyed on the engine and never sniffed from the content**, because a bare `response` field in somebody's own output contract is their data and not a wrapper for us to unwrap. A mission reads a delegate's archive through it with that task's own engine. A stream that really carried no prose comes back empty, so the caller's own rule about an empty turn is the one that fires; a body the reader recognises nothing in is shown as itself, because a spawn error is not silence.

**A delegation a ceiling was holding reported nothing at all.** The run's one delegation was parked by the fleet's daily budget. The step read `running` on every surface while no process had been launched, the objective spent its entire wall clock waiting for it, and it then stopped with `hard-limit` — three true statements and not one of them the reason. The park's own sentence now travels to the step as `held`, is cleared the moment the task launches or settles, refreshes the surfaces while it lasts, and reaches any caller through `missions.status`. A ceiling is a thing the user can lift, and they can only lift the one they were told about.

### M-20 — Council

**A council is a conversation with a chair and a mandate, not a second engine.** The build this refuses is the obvious one: a council engine that runs round 1 = A, round 2 = B, round 3 = synthesis. That protocol is a guess about a debate nobody has had yet — the moment the second speaker concedes in its first sentence, rounds 2 and 3 are bought anyway, and the transcript reads like deliberation because the shape was printed before anyone spoke. So `council` adds no way of talking: it opens an ordinary M-19 conversation and orders its opening turns in the same decision, and every turn after that is an ordinary `message`. The participant lock, the ref check, the lane honesty, the repeat guard and the independent-round rule are the SAME ones, because there is only one set.

**What it adds is what the record cannot state for itself.** The **question** it settles, which is narrower than the objective. A **chair** — and ‼️ a chair that is not the lead really chairs: a turn by anybody else has to name the chair's latest message in `refs`, so the speaker reads what the chair actually wrote rather than the lead's account of it. A lead that wanted to invent an instruction would have to invent a message, and it cannot. The opening round is the one exception, because there is nothing to cite yet. A **turn cap**, which ends an endless debate mechanically — and ‼️ the cap stops the debate, not the ending: one turn is allowed past it and only if it closes, or every exit would be refused for being one turn too many, including the exit that exists for exactly this. And **seven stated ways out** (`consensus · sufficient evidence · no new information · decision clear · need execution · hard limit · chair abort`), because "the discussion finished" stands equally for "they agreed" and "we ran out of turns".

**A vote is optional, and its choice is the voter's own word for it.** Read out of the turn's real text against the options the council named; a turn that named none is recorded `unclear` rather than resolved into the likeliest one, and a tie is reported as a tie rather than handed to the lead as a leader. ‼️ **A council decides its own question and never the objective** — a majority is what the members think, and only an `evaluate` verdict judges a success criterion. `missions.council` returns one council's whole record: mandate, turns spent against the cap, what is still unanswered, which message the next turn has to cite, the votes and the tally, the synthesis's real refs, and the exit with what it means. `missions.status` carries one line per council and not the votes.

## 3.228.0 — M-19: a speaker knows who it is talking to, and the same turn cannot be bought twice (2026-08-22)

**A speaker was never told who else was in the room, or which of them the turn was for.** `to` is the record's own field — empty means everyone, and one-to-many is the ordinary case here rather than a mode — and it reached the transcript, the row and the journal but never the speaker itself. A turn the lead addressed to one participant was written to the room, and the row reading `Ada → Rev, Cy` was describing an address nobody had been given. Neither fact is inferable from the exchange on a first turn, because there is no exchange yet. Every speaking prompt now names the cast (with the speaker marked, so it does not address itself) and names who this turn is for, saying plainly that the others read it too because the record is shared.

**Ordering the identical turn again, with nothing said since, is now refused by name.** The planning-loop guard hashes agent + prompt, and a repeated speaking turn builds a *different* prompt — the second one carries a resumed lane's preamble and a record that has grown — so the strings never matched and a lead could re-order the same turn round after round, paying for each. What makes it a loop is a fact of the record rather than of the prompt, so it is refused where every other refusal already lives, naming the message that already is that turn and saying what to do instead. Once somebody else has spoken it is allowed again (the speaker now sees new words), and a retry after a **failed** turn was never a repeat at all — nothing was delivered.

**And a turn that came back clean with nothing in it now fails its step, not only its message.** The message was correctly marked `failed` and given a classified failure, but the step stayed `done` — one event with two answers, and the wrong one was on the surface that matters: the round message is built from step status, so a lead whose speaker said nothing was shown a successful round and never offered **retry · revise · replan · skip · ask_user · partial**. It would then have planned its next turn on a discussion that did not happen, which is the exact failure M-19 exists to refuse.

## 3.227.0 — M-19: an independent first round, a stated closing, and a lane a reload cannot lock shut (2026-08-22)

**An independent first round is one decision, not two rounds.** Asking two agents for their own position without either seeing the other cannot be done by ordering two turns in a row — by the second one the first message has been delivered and is in the record, which is the whole difference between a discussion and two people agreeing with a transcript. `from` now takes a list: every speaker in one decision is briefed from the record **as it stood before any of them answered**, they run in one wave (a speaking turn is readonly, so nothing serialises them), and each is told plainly that somebody else is writing on this at the same moment and neither will see the other. The ledger says `independent` for such a round, because "these two did not see each other" is only readable if the two are on one line. The same agent named twice in one decision is refused: that is a race over one record, not independence.

**A conversation is closed by a stated reason.** `close` ends it after the turn that closed it — so the closing message is in the record rather than lost to the shutting — and a closed conversation refuses further turns by name and reason. "Nothing has been said for a while" was never a closing; three months later a reader needs the sentence.

**And a turn a reload interrupted no longer holds its speaker's lane for ever.** A speaking turn is settled at the end of the round that ordered it, and a window that closes mid-round never reaches that line: the step was reconciled on the way back in, but the **message** stayed `pending` — and pending is exactly what holds a participant's lane. That agent could never have spoken in that conversation again, and the lead would have been refused every time it tried without ever being told a real reason. One catch-up pass now settles those messages from the steps that really finished, before anything else happens; work still genuinely in flight is left alone rather than given an invented outcome.

**A reload also no longer demotes a conversation to a handoff.** The session a step ran in now travels through reconciliation, so a participant's lane survives the window closing — without it the run would forget an id that was still perfectly good on disk, open a new session, and honestly label the loss `handoff`.

## 3.226.0 — M-19: agents can now actually talk to each other, and a discussion that did not happen cannot be reported (2026-08-22)

**The failure this closes.** A lead sends the same question to three agents, gets three independent answers, and writes "the three discussed it and converged on X". Nobody discussed anything: B never saw A's answer, and the convergence is the lead's own prose presented as the outcome of a debate. It reads exactly like the real thing, which is why it had to become structurally impossible rather than discouraged.

**A conversation is a record, not a rendering.** `message` is a new adaptive primitive: it opens a conversation with a stated purpose and a fixed cast, and every turn in it is a real speaking turn — the agent named in `from` runs as an ordinary headless delegation on the ordinary task path (same waves, same writer rule, same budget, same cancel; there is no message transport and no second engine). What it writes becomes the message.

**The next speaker is given the real words.** The lead names message ids in `refs` and the engine attaches the text those ids actually produced. There is deliberately no parameter through which a lead could describe what somebody said — the same rule M-18's typed intents already enforce for work, applied to speech. And a message that is *about* something somebody said (`challenge`, `response`, `concede`, `synthesis`, `vote`) is refused unless it names what it rests on, so a synthesis that cites nothing cannot enter the record at all.

**One participant at a time, and different ones at once.** Two turns of the same agent in flight on one conversation is a race, not parallelism — the second is briefed on a record the first is about to change, and on a resuming engine both would fight for the same session. Different participants speaking simultaneously is allowed and is exactly what an independent first round is: a speaking turn is readonly, so a wave can hold as many as the pool has.

**A resumed lane and a re-told one are different facts, and are labelled differently.** When the same participant speaks again its own session is picked back up, so it is still holding what it said and what it was shown — and it is then sent only what is NEW since its last turn rather than the conversation again. Where the delegate's engine has no resume vocabulary the speaker gets a fresh session with the exchange reproduced as a record, and the run calls that `handoff`. It is asked (`canResumeLane`) rather than assumed, because an engine handed a session id it has no flag for ignores it and quietly opens a new conversation — and the run would then be claiming a continuity it does not have.

**A turn that came back clean with nothing in it is a failure, not an empty message.** It matters because a settling intent CLOSES what it names: an empty "response" would mark a challenge answered by a turn that said nothing, and the conversation would read as resolved. What is unanswered is a fact of the record — `question` and `challenge` put something to somebody; a proposal nobody argued with is not a loose end.

**The lead gets a bounded digest, and readers get the transcript.** The planner session is resumed every round, so a whole transcript in front of it would be paid for once per round for the rest of the run and would grow while it did it. Between rounds the lead is given what is still unanswered, the last few turns in one line each, and the ids it may name. `missions.conversation` returns the real messages in full — speaker, addressee, intent, refs, text, and the task and session deep links — and `missions.status` carries a summary of each conversation with its open count.

**And a speaking turn survives a reload.** The step lookup read `kind !== 'task'` and would have repeated X-45's own bug one primitive later: a turn that finished while the window was closed would have come back "fate unknown", its message would never have been delivered, and the lead — told nothing happened — would have ordered the same turn again and paid for it twice. A conversation turn is a task and is now looked up as one.

## 3.225.0 — the bridge helper writes the file itself, and the encoding fixer survives a bad one (2026-08-22)

**Three traps that were being written down instead of removed.** Each had been met, understood, and passed on to the next session as a warning — which is the wrong artefact. A warning has to be read to work; a fix does not.

**`af.js` now has `--out <file>`.** Everything the gateway exists for was true in one direction only: arguments went in through `@file.json` and never met a shell, but the answer came back through **stdout**, and `node af.js farm.ops > catalog.json` hands those bytes to Windows PowerShell 5.1, which re-encodes them on the way out — UTF-16LE, the ANSI codepage, or UTF-8 with a BOM depending on the operator. A catalog dump taken that way was mojibake that the repo's own encoding gate then refused at the commit. `--out` writes the file from inside the helper, always UTF-8 without a BOM, creates missing folders, and prints a one-line summary instead of the payload — so a large result also stays out of the caller's context.

**`test/test_encoding.js --fix` no longer abandons the rest of the tree over one file.** Its refusal to write invalid JSON was a bare `JSON.parse` that threw straight out of the loop: every file after the damaged one went unrepaired, and the crash read as "the fixer is broken" rather than "this one file is". A refusal is now about the one file — named, counted, and the pass carries on. The scan still fails the build afterwards, so nothing is swept under the rug.

**And a leading BOM is now damage the gate can see.** It is exactly what a shell leaves behind when it re-encodes a file it was only asked to redirect, and in JSON it is not cosmetic: `JSON.parse` refuses it outright. Only position 0 counts — a U+FEFF *inside* a line is deliberate source here, written literally inside the nine regexes and fixtures that handle other people's BOMs, and flagging those would have made `--fix` delete the very code that deals with the damage. One real one was already in the tree, at the top of `src/core/projects.ts`, seen by nothing.

**`.gitignore` names the kind, not the file.** `.tmp/` holds both the session's scratch and the reusable tools that live there on purpose, and the rule listed two literal scratch names — so a session that called its commit message anything but `msg.txt` put it in the commit, and had to be warned about that by name. Everything under `.tmp/` is now scratch unless it is a `.js` tool.

## 3.224.0 — M-18: resuming a run settles every kind of round, not only a delegation (2026-08-22)

**A resumed mission was freezing its last round for ever.** The resume path asked `action === 'delegate'` — the whole vocabulary when it was written, and not any more. A round that was `parallel`, `review`, `compare`, `revise`, `run_workflow` or `run_mission` was skipped entirely: its steps stayed at "running" with nothing ever settling them, and the lead was re-briefed as though the round had never happened — which is the one way to make it order the same work a second time. Having steps is now the condition; the actions that produce none are excluded by that and need no list of their own.

**And a step is settled by the store that actually ran it.** Inside the loop, only the task store was consulted, so a chain or a child objective that had finished while the window was gone was written off as interrupted. Both reload paths — the one at startup and the one at resume — now go through one reader that knows which store a step belongs to, so the two cannot reach different conclusions about the same step. `stopped`, a chain's own word for what a task calls `cancelled`, is read as settled on both. A child hands back its verdict here too, from the same composer the live loop uses.

## 3.223.0 — M-18: the lead is told which project it is planning for (2026-08-22)

**Every delegation a mission makes has carried the project. The lead never did** — which is the wrong way round: a delegate does one prompt's worth of work and the lead decides what the whole run is for. It planned against the goal sentence alone, with no idea what the project is, what is already open on it, or which document holds which role.

The project's generated brief now reaches the planner through its **system prompt**, on the same file and the same flag every other Claude surface gets — one brief, one budget for it, and never a second copy pasted into the briefing text. It goes in on the **first call only**: every later round resumes that same session, so repeating it would pay for the same tokens once per round for the whole run.

**And the lead is told what its part in the project is**, which a brief cannot say. The planner has no write tools, deliberately — so if a run changes what is true of the project (something shipped, a plan item finished, a decision settled), **recording that is a delegation like any other**. Every delegate it sends already runs under the project and gets the same brief, so it can be told "update the plan" and will know where. A run that moved a project and recorded nothing leaves the next session blind.

## 3.222.0 — M-18 (X-45): a reload recovers a child objective and a chain, not only a task (2026-08-22)

**A window reload was throwing away two thirds of a nested run.** X-45 taught a mission to survive a reload — the journal says what was set in motion, the stores say whether it finished while we were gone, and nothing is ever silently restarted. Then the lead was given two primitives that start something other than a task, and the recovery was never measured against either: the lookup began by refusing every kind but `task`, so a workflow chain or a child objective that **finished perfectly** while the window was closed came back as "interrupted — fate unknown". Its cost vanished from the parent's ledger, its verdict was never read, and a lead told nothing happened orders it again — which for a child objective means paying for the whole run twice.

Each kind is now asked of the store that actually ran it, and `stopped` — a chain's own word for what a task calls `cancelled` — is a settled status by name rather than an unrecognised one treated as unfinished.

**Money already spent is finished work, even when the outcome is not.** A child caught mid-flight has a ledger of its own and it is not empty. The fate stays honestly unknown; the figures ride up to the parent, because on a deep unattended run the parent's ceiling is the only fence there is and a budget that forgets what it spent is not one.

**And a recovered child hands back its verdict, not just a status** — the same sentence it would have had if nobody had closed the window, from one function with two callers, so the recovered wording cannot drift from the live one. The same lookup now serves `missions.trace`, which had been answering from the journal alone: two surfaces were reporting different fates for one run.

## 3.221.0 — M-18: a failed primitive tells the lead what kind of failure it was (2026-08-22)

**"Failed" was the same word for four different situations.** An agent that is not in the fleet, a run this machine refused before a process existed, a person pressing Cancel, and a delegate that worked for four minutes and came back wrong all reached the lead as one status and a sentence of prose. A person reads prose fine; the lead gets one line inside a round message and has to decide from it whether to order the same thing again — so it guessed, and mostly it retried, and a delegation to an agent that does not exist failed identically for as many rounds as the ceiling allowed.

A failure is now a **shape**: which **class** of thing went wrong (from a closed set), **what was attempted**, the **ids of the evidence** — the task, the child run, the archived output — and, stated once and centrally rather than at each of the nine failure sites, **what to do about it**. The lead is told whether ordering the same thing again could ever work: `same` (the cause was outside the request), `different` (change the agent, engine or approach), `fix-request` (the request itself was rejected), `stop`. **The original sentence is not replaced** — classifying is an addition, and the prose survives as the failure's `detail`.

**And the two ways a task fails are different facts.** A run refused before it started spent nothing and wants another engine; a delegate that ran and returned failed wants its output read. One word for both is a lead that cannot tell them apart. A ceiling is recognised by its own block code, never by a sentence that happens to mention money.

On the page, the class rides next to the status in its short form and the hover carries the long form, what was attempted, the original words, the evidence and the advice — from the host's one registry, so the reader and the lead can never be told different things about the same failure. `missions.status` hands the same shape out, plus `ran`: the dimensions each delegation actually used and which layer decided them.

## 3.220.0 — M-18: a delegation is a launch, so it resolves its dimensions like one (2026-08-22)

**The same agent behaved differently depending on who asked.** Open agent `X` from Agent Farm and it runs on the model and effort you configured for it — its own default for that engine, then your fleet defaults. Hand the same agent the same work through a **mission** and none of that applied: a delegation read three fields off the team member and stopped there, so a member you left blank ran on the CLI's raw built-in default. That is the mystery the per-agent, per-engine defaults were built to end, restated one surface over. A delegate now climbs the whole ladder: **the member's row → the mission's engine and workdir → that agent's own default for the engine it lands on → `agentFarm.launchDefaults` → the CLI.** Claude's model and effort deliberately skip the per-agent layer, the same carve-out a launch makes: Claude Code reads that agent's `.claude/settings.local.json` itself, and passing the value back would be a second source of truth over a file you may have edited by hand.

**Effort is now per member** — it was the one run dimension a member could not state, so a reviewer that wanted `low` and a planner that wanted `xhigh` had to be the same. It sits on the member row next to the engine, the permissions and the model, and comes from the same one list every other launcher reads. A typo is refused when the mission is created rather than dropped; whether the *engine* has such a setting at all is answered at launch by the rule that already owns it.

**An adaptive run's pool was being ignored.** The delegation looked its member up in `spec.team`, which an adaptive mission does not have — so every dimension a pool member stated was silently dropped on exactly the runs the pool exists for. And nothing could write one in the first place: the pool was built from the fleet, which keeps an id, a name and a role. A pool member now takes the same five as a team member, from the panel and from `missions.start`.

**And each step says what it ran with and who decided it.** Four layers means three of them are settings written somewhere else, so "why did that delegate run on gpt-5?" had no answer on the run. The step's Agent cell now carries it, with each value labelled by the layer that supplied it.

## 3.219.2 — Bridge CLI helper (af.js): escape-free, self-provisioning gateway for agents (2026-08-22)

Calling the bridge from agents or external CLI scripts previously risked shell quote mangling in PowerShell and Bash when passing complex JSON strings, multi-line reports, or markdown content. Agent Farm now ships a standalone CLI helper (`af.js`) compiled from `src/service/af.ts` with zero external dependencies. On extension startup, it is automatically staged into `<globalStorage>/bridge/af.js`. It supports discovery (`node af.js farm.ops`), inline arguments, and `@file.json` payload loading for completely escaping-free calls.

## 3.219.1 — M-18: a workflow started by a mission is that mission's project's work (2026-08-22)

A chain inherited its project from **its own first task**, which for a chain nobody stamped meant the window's current project. That is right for a workflow somebody ran by hand and wrong for one a mission started: a wave fires whenever the planner decides to, possibly an hour after anybody looked at this window, and the work belongs to the project the mission is for — the same reason a mission's delegations already pass their own key rather than asking the window. `runWorkflow` now takes the project explicitly, and it lands on **step 1**, not from step 2 onwards. A chain nobody stamped is left exactly as it was.

## 3.219.0 — M-18 (X-32): an objective can hand a piece of itself to a child run (2026-08-22)

**`run_mission` is for work that needs its own planning.** A delegation is one prompt to one agent; some pieces of an objective are not that shape — they need a lead of their own, several rounds and a verdict at the end. The lead names an outcome and what would count as reaching it, and gets back a **verdict**, not an output. A child objective with no criteria is refused by name and told to delegate instead: the only reason to spend a whole run on something is that it comes back judged, and a verdict needs a subject.

**Everything that makes a child safe is INHERITED, not requested.** The lead states the goal, the criteria and any extra constraints. The pool it may draw on, the working folder, the engine and permissions, the approval mode, the autonomy and the project it is work for all come from the parent — a lead cannot give a child a wider reach than it has itself. The parent's constraints bind the child too: a limit somebody put on an objective is not escaped by delegating a piece of it.

**And it spends the parent's budget.** The child's ceilings are cut from what the parent has **left** rather than copied, so a chain of children cannot spend the parent's budget once each; what the child actually spends is charged upward **exactly once**, on the parent's step, because the parent counts its own steps and nothing else.

**‼️ Two things keep nesting from being a fork bomb, and both are checked where the run is — the only place that knows.** A **depth cap** of three, stated by number in the refusal along with the thing to do instead; and a **cycle refusal** — an objective whose goal is already an ancestor of this run is not started, because that is a run asking itself for the same thing, and each level would be convinced it had handed the problem on. The match is on the normalised goal, so re-punctuating it is not a new objective.

**A cancel travels down, and so does a pause.** A child is real work with its own lead and its own delegations; stopping the parent and leaving it running would spend a cancelled run's budget on an answer nobody is waiting for. The pause is the subtler one: a paused parent is waiting on its child's wave, so the one thing still costing money is exactly the thing the pause did not reach. Both walk descendants only — a child never stops work it did not order.

The child run records **who ordered it** (`parentRunId`, `sourceActionId`), **which tree it belongs to** (`rootRunId`, carried rather than walked, because a cancel is racing the same records it would have to follow) and **how deep it sits**. A step whose result is a sentence rather than a file now says so directly, so the lead reads the child's verdict, its stop reason and anything left unmet instead of an empty excerpt.

116 checks on the primitives; the full suite is 204 files and 12 350 checks.

## 3.218.0 — M-18 (X-32): a workflow run becomes something you can ask about, and an objective can run one (2026-08-22)

**`runWorkflow` returned `void` and announced its ending in a toast.** That is enough for a person watching the window and useless to everything else: a caller could start a chain and had no way to learn its id, whether it finished, where it stopped or what it produced. A mission that wanted a workflow as one of its steps therefore could not have one, and the only route left would have been a second workflow engine inside missions — the duplication this whole family refuses.

**So the run answers.** `runWorkflow` returns the **run id** (`undefined` when the chain has no steps — nothing started, rather than a run nobody can name), and `workflowRunState(runId)` reads it back: `running · done · failed · stopped`, the step it stopped at and why when it stopped short, every step with its task id and output file, the whole run's cost and tokens **added up once**, and the **final handoff** — the file and text the last completed step passed on, which is the run's actual result. On the bridge that is `workflows.run` (now returning `runId`) and the new **`workflows.status`**.

**The status is DERIVED from the tasks, not stored beside them.** A stored status is a second copy of a fact and disagrees with it on the first reload; the tasks are persisted, so the answer survives a window restart without anything having to be kept in step. The one thing genuinely remembered is *why* a run ended early — a chain stopped by the loop guard and one that simply ran out of steps leave rows that look identical — and after a reload that reason is honestly absent rather than invented. The rows always outrank the memo: a resumed chain reads as running again, whatever an earlier ending said.

**`run_workflow` is the sixth thing an objective's lead can do.** It names a chain that already exists — it cannot compose one and does not drive its steps — and gets back what the chain's last completed step produced. The chain has to really exist: a wrong name is refused with the list this window actually has, and the lead is shown that list in its briefing before it ever names one (inserted before the answer schema, because text after a JSON block gets read as part of it). A window with no workflows advertises none rather than an empty section to guess into.

**And it runs on the ordinary wave.** A workflow step goes out through the same path as a delegation — the same approval gate, the same one-writer serialisation, the same budget roll-up, the same cancel — because all of those are properties of that path, and a chain started anywhere else would quietly have none of them. The only difference is what gets started, and it is observed by its run id through the one reader the task manager exposes: the mission never walks the chain's tasks itself, or "did it finish" would have two answers.

Classic is untouched. 94 checks on the primitives, 29 on the run state, plus the bridge dispatch pair; the full suite is 204 files and 12 328 checks.

## 3.217.0 — M-18 (X-32): what a lead can do becomes a list, and three of them are typed intents (2026-08-22)

**Every primitive used to cost three edits in three places that had to agree** — a line in the prompt schema, an arm in the parser, a branch in the engine — and nothing checked that they did. A primitive advertised but unparsed, or parsed but never executed, looks exactly like a working one until a run reaches it. The set is now **data**: a primitive declares its scope (which kind of run may use it), its shape (`work` · `plan` · `human` · `terminal`), the graph kind it becomes and the line a person reads.
