The planner's menu is **generated** from that list, the parser dispatches through it, and the `unknown "action"` error names the same set the lead was offered. One side-effect of that alone: the adaptive error message had been listing five actions while the parser accepted six — `evaluate` was missing from it since M-17, and could not be now.

**`review`, `compare` and `revise` are typed task INTENTS, not executors.** Each becomes exactly one ordinary delegation on the ordinary wave path — same budget, same one-writer rule, same cancel — and the difference is that **the engine builds the prompt**. The lead names result *ids*, and the engine attaches what those results actually produced. It cannot hand a delegate a paraphrase of work that was never produced, which is the failure this whole family exists to prevent; an id that never existed is refused by name, with the ids that do exist listed, rather than a delegate being sent to work on an empty quotation. `review` and `compare` are read-only (weighing work does not modify it, and `compare` needs at least two things to weigh); `revise` writes, and needs the gap named — "fix it" is not a gap.

**‼️ A revise inherits the criteria of what it revises.** Otherwise correcting an artefact would leave the old pass looking current — a run could revise its work and still finish on a verdict about the version that no longer exists, which is the exact hole M-17's staleness rule was built to close. Charging the fix to the same criteria as the first attempt is what makes the pass expire, and it is derived from what the work says it serves rather than from anybody remembering to say so.

**`parallel` is a claim the engine may refuse, out loud.** It is `delegate` plus a statement that these tasks are independent. The one-writer-per-folder rule does not bend for it — two writers in one working folder is corruption, not speed — so the waves are planned exactly as before, and when the claim could not be honoured the lead is **told**: how many waves it really got, why, and what to do about it (`"readonly": true` on work that does not modify the folder). Silently serialising would leave a lead believing a timing it never had. When the claim *is* honourable, nothing is said.

**What a run records got one field richer.** A delegation carries the `intent` it was ordered as and the `sources` it was built from, so the runtime graph shows a revise hanging off the result it corrects — a fan-in on the step itself, which is the one place a typed intent's edge belongs. The ledger names the primitive (`R2 revise on s7 — …`) rather than flattening everything into "delegate", because a lead re-seeded from the ledger after a lost session has to see that round 2 was a correction, not a fresh order.

**Classic does not move by one character, and it is measured.** Its menu is the same four actions, its errors are the same strings, its ledger line is byte-identical, and none of the new primitives are offered to it or accepted from it. 75 new checks; the full suite is 203 files and 12 275 checks.

## 3.216.0 — M-17 (X-32): "the agent finished" stops meaning "the objective is met" (2026-08-22)

**Until now those were the same sentence.** An adaptive run ended because its last delegation exited zero — which answers a different question, *did the work run*, and answered it as if it were the one that had been asked. From this release **`finish` with `success` is a claim that has to be backed**, and what backs it is a current evaluation of every **required** criterion. A lead that claims success without one is refused, told exactly which criteria are open and why, and offered the two honest ways out.

**A verdict is a record, not a feeling.** `MissionEvaluation` carries what was looked at, who judged it (the lead itself, or an independent reviewer from the pool), a `pass` / `fail` / `unknown` per criterion **with the evidence behind it**, the gap where there is one, and advice from a closed list — `finish · revise · replan · explore · ask_user · partial · failed`. Three details are deliberate: **there is no mandatory score** (a criterion's nature decides how it is judged — "every op is documented" is countable, "the tone matches the guide" is not, and forcing the second into 0.0–1.0 invents precision nobody has; `confidence` is optional and nothing depends on it); **`unknown` is a real answer** (collapsing it into `fail` blames work that may be fine, collapsing it into `pass` is how a run declares success it never saw); and **`revise` and `replan` stay apart** — a revise is a targeted fix to the same artefact under the same approach, a replan says the approach was wrong and cuts a new strategy version.

**‼️ AN EVALUATION EXPIRES WHEN THE WORK IT JUDGED MOVES ON.** Not with age — an hour-old verdict on something nobody touched is still true. What ends it is a delegation for one of its criteria settling *after* it: the artefact it looked at is not the artefact that now exists. This is why a delegation now names the criterion ids it serves as a **field** rather than in prose. Without it, a run could revise its work and still finish on the old version's pass — which is exactly the shape of a green build that shipped a broken thing. Staleness is **derived** from the timeline, never stored: a stored flag is a second copy of a fact and would disagree with it on the first out-of-order replay. Stale verdicts are **kept**, and said to be stale — "we checked, then changed it" is the history, and deleting it leaves a run that looks as though it was never reviewed.

**`evaluate` is one primitive with two ways of running.** With no `reviewer`, the lead judges from the results already in its hands and the verdict is in the same reply — asking a model to re-read what it just read is a round spent on nothing. With a `reviewer`, the named pool agent runs as an **ordinary FarmTask**: same budget, same waves, same cancel, read-only, with a self-contained prompt carrying the objective, the criteria by id and the material. Both land on the identical parser and the identical record, because a gate that trusted self-review and independent review differently would be two gates. **A review that cannot be read says nothing about the work** — prose instead of JSON, a timeout, a crash — so it is recorded as `unknown` on every criterion *with the reason*: not `fail`, which would blame the delegate for the reviewer's problem, and not silence, which would let the run forget it ever asked.

**And it stops honestly.** `finish` and `abort` now carry a `stopReason` from a closed list — `criteria-satisfied · sufficient-evidence · no-new-information · execution-over-discussion · hard-limit · user-stop` — because "did this reach its objective or run out of rope?" cannot be answered from a summary's wording, and `no-new-information` gives a lead a way out of the "one more improvement" loop that has no natural end. A wrong value is refused by name rather than coerced. The hard limits still outrank everything: at the ceiling only an honest final is possible, and it says `hard-limit`. **A lead that insists on unbacked success is not fought to the call cap** — the refusal comes once, and the second attempt is taken as `partial` with the unmet criteria named in the record. `missions.status` returns `criteria` (each with its current verdict and evidence), `evaluations` (every one, `stale` flagged), `stopReason` and `unmet`.

**Classic is untouched and now measured to be.** It has no criteria, no gate and no evaluation; a classic lead that invents `evaluate` gets today's `unknown "action"` error to the character, and a `stopReason` on a classic reply is ignored exactly as it always was. All 91 classic mission checks pass unchanged; 67 new ones cover the acceptance list.

## 3.215.0 — M-16: "Guide an Objective…" — the user gets the same door the bridge has (2026-08-22)

`missions.guide` shipped with the previous release as an op, which left the mechanism reachable by an agent and not by the person watching the run. **`Agent Farm: Guide an Objective…`** closes that: it lists the adaptive runs that are actually open — each showing the strategy version and phase it is following, plus how many steers are already waiting — takes one sentence, and says when it lands.

**It is deliberately not a row action on the Missions tree.** Only an adaptive run can be steered, and a tree row's `contextValue` carries the run's *status*, not its mode. A row item would therefore either appear on classic runs and refuse when pressed — teaching the reader nothing — or force every other mission menu to be rewritten around a new value. A picker that lists exactly the runs the command can work on says the same thing and explains itself: a classic mission follows the recipe it was given and has no strategy to steer.

**Both doors run one function.** The command and the op call the same `guideMission`, so which runs may be steered, when the text lands and what the user is told about work already in flight are properties of the mechanism rather than of the door somebody walked through. They differ only in how they present the answer — a toast, or a JSON result.

## 3.214.0 — M-16 (X-32): the adaptive lead says what it is doing and why, and the run keeps the graph of what it actually did (2026-08-22)

**M-15 gave an adaptive run an objective instead of a recipe; X-45 gave it a journal. This release spends them.** An adaptive lead's reply is no longer just a decision: every call must also carry a `rationale` (one sentence, written to be **shown** — not the model's private deliberation), a `currentPhase` (its own label for where the run is, an observation nothing branches on) and its `strategy`, **restated in full every time**.

**‼️ A STRATEGY VERSION IS CUT WHEN THE APPROACH MOVED — NEVER ONCE PER ROUND.** The engine normalises the restated strategy and compares it: casing, spacing and a trailing full stop are not a change of mind. A lead that follows the same plan for five rounds has **one** strategy, and a version number that ticked per round would say the opposite while looking exactly as plausible on screen. Asking the model "has it changed?" would put that judgement in the one place it cannot be checked, so it is measured instead. Each revision records the reason the lead gave and the decision it came out of; the run carries the current one so a list can draw `v3 · verifying` without opening a JSONL file, and a run **resumed after a reload picks its strategy back up** rather than counting the restart as a change of mind.

**‼️ THE RUNTIME GRAPH IS NEVER DRAWN IN ADVANCE.** Nothing plans its shape. A node appears at the moment a decision is taken or a real primitive is set in motion, and the edges are whatever actually happened: a node per lead decision, per delegation, per question, per steer and one for the ending — each with `kind / status / actor / parentRefs / inputRefs / outputRefs / timestamps`. **Every delegation of one round hangs under the same decision**, which is what makes parallel work read as a branch rather than a chain; the decision that reads several results back carries them in its `inputRefs`, so a **fan-in is a fact of the graph rather than an inference from timestamps**. The lead may name what it built on (`basedOn`) and then that is the edge; when it does not, the results it was actually shown are. The graph does not drive the engine — deleting it would lose the view, never the run.

**A fifth action: `replan`.** A classic lead has a recipe and never needs to say "my approach has changed" as a move of its own; an adaptive one does, because burying a revision inside a delegation makes it invisible. It costs a round and a planner call like everything else — the ceilings are mechanical authority and nothing gets a free turn. A **classic** lead that invents `replan` still gets today's `unknown "action"` error, unchanged to the character.

**‼️ A FAILED DELEGATION IS EVIDENCE, NOT A VERDICT ON THE OBJECTIVE.** The classic round message states the results and asks for the next decision, which is right for a recipe: a step that failed failed. An objective has no recipe, and the same message read as "the plan broke" — a lead that treats one bad delegate as the answer has thrown away the only thing that made it adaptive. So when something fails the six options are named in the reply's own vocabulary — **retry · revise · replan · skip · ask_user · finish honestly as partial** — and it is said plainly that finishing now is one choice among them rather than the default. The lead says in its `rationale` which it took.

**‼️ `missions.guide` STEERS A RUN WITHOUT LYING ABOUT WHEN IT LANDS.** The text is recorded on the run and shown to the lead **exactly once, at the next planner boundary**. It is **not** delivered to work already in flight: a delegate's prompt is fixed when its task starts and cannot be renegotiated, and an answer that implied otherwise would be the lie noticed last. So the reply says `appliesAt` — `next-round` while the run is live, `on-resume` while it is paused — and a classic run (no strategy to steer) or a run that has already ended is refused by name. "Once" survives a window reload because it is written in two places that cannot disagree: the run records when it landed and the journal carries the pair of lines. When the planner session dies and has to be re-seeded from the briefing, steers already in force are replayed alongside the ledger and **labelled as in force, not as new instructions** — losing a steer for the rest of a run is not a promise worth making.

`missions.trace` now returns `phase`, `strategies` (every revision with its reason) and `graph` beside what it already had. The journal's schema moves to **2**; a file written by the old one reads exactly as before, and a mixed file is legal.

**Nothing classic moved.** The two modes still disagree about what the lead is told and what its reply is checked against, and about nothing else — the caps, the roster rule, the self-containment rule, the duplicate-work lock, the finish-only round and the hard planner-call cap are the same code and are now asserted word-for-word identical in both schemas. All 91 classic mission checks pass untouched; 85 new ones cover the acceptance list.

## 3.213.1 — the queue's two arrows and `tasks.move` stop being two implementations of "up" (2026-08-22)

**A named parity gap, closed rather than re-explained.** The tree's ↑/↓ arrows called `moveTask(task, ±1)`; the bridge's `tasks.move` resolved the queued siblings and the bounds a second time, inline, so it could say *which* end a task had already reached. Two pieces of code deciding what "up" means, kept in step by hand — the exact shape the parity gate exists to catch, and it was carrying the gap by name.

`moveTask` now RETURNS where the task landed, or `-1` when there was nowhere to go, and `tasks.move` calls it. The tree ignores that number (an arrow pressed at the top should do nothing, and does); the bridge turns it into the same sentence it always sent, because an agent that asked for a move and got silence cannot tell it from a move that worked. Behaviour is unchanged on both doors — what changed is that there is now one door frame. `parity.manifest.json` drops from 40 open gaps to 38, and `gapBudget` with it.

## 3.213.0 — U-88: "Choose only this" on a scope chip, and "only" finally means only (2026-08-22)

**Right-click any of Search's nine scope chips — You · Automation · Agent · Delegator · Handler · Tools · Results · Memory · Events — and choose "Choose only this".** It lights that one and puts every other one out. The gesture is not new: Ctrl-click (⌘ on Mac) has meant this since the chips became toggles, and it was discoverable only by reading the hint printed beside them. The menu is the door somebody looking for it will actually try, and both run the identical page function — a menu item and a button that can drift apart are two features pretending to be one.

**‼️ AND "ONLY" NOW REACHES ALL NINE CHIPS, WHICH IS THE PART THAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG.** Memory and Events are two booleans in the wire payload while the seven roles are an array — but on screen they are one row of chips a reader ticks, and the gesture used to stop silently at the array. So "only what a person wrote" also searched every memory note and every orphaned event: two sources the reader had just watched themselves not choose. One meaning, one row, both doors.

**Which needed the scope to be able to say "none".** An empty roles array used to be read as "the caller did not say" and quietly refilled with the conversation, so a memory-only search was not expressible at all. Absent and empty are now different answers: omit `roles` and you get the conversation, pass `[]` and you get no transcript roles — the same way `agents?` has always given `[]` its plain meaning. The Search page's own rule is unchanged in spirit and corrected in reach: **the scope never empties**, but the scope is all nine chips, so putting the last role out while Memory is lit is a legitimate memory-only search rather than a reason to switch the conversation back on. `search.transcripts` on the bridge takes the same `[]`, because a scope a person can point at and an agent cannot ask for is a hole.

The menu item hides itself on the chip that is already alone — an item that cannot change anything teaches the reader nothing when they click it.

## 3.212.0 — X-45 (X-32): the run keeps a journal, and the snapshot stops being the only copy (2026-08-22)

**`missions.json` was written whole, best-effort, on every state change.** That was survivable while a run was a handful of rounds. With strategy versions, a runtime graph, evaluations and real conversation on the way, three failures were waiting in that one line: the file grows without bound, a crash mid-write truncates the **only** copy, and a window reload silently loses everything the snapshot had not caught up to. This release splits the two jobs. The snapshot stays the fast list and the engine's current state, and is now written **atomically** — temp file, then rename — so a crash leaves the previous good store rather than half of one. Every adaptive run additionally keeps an **append-only journal**: one sequence-numbered, schema-versioned JSONL file per run under `mission-trace/`, carrying `strategy.changed`, `action.created/started/settled`, `evaluation.recorded`, `message.sent`, `human.asked/answered/guided` and `run.finished`.

**‼️ IT IS NOT A MESSAGE BROKER AND NOT A SECOND EXECUTION ENGINE.** The real work is still MissionEngine + TaskManager, and nothing reads the journal to decide what happens next. It is observation and audit — and it earns its keep exactly once, at reload, when the snapshot alone cannot say what is still in flight.

**‼️ THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE CONTRACT: APPEND FIRST, SNAPSHOT SECOND.** That way the only state a crash can produce is "the journal knows more than the snapshot", which is replayable. The reverse — a snapshot claiming work the journal never recorded — is unrecoverable, so it is made impossible, and when it is seen anyway the run is flagged rather than trusted. A half-written last line is a crash mid-append: it is dropped and reported as `truncated`. A broken line **anywhere else** is real loss and says `damaged`. A repeated sequence number is a replay and the first copy wins, because it is the one every earlier reader already saw — the projection is idempotent at its own level, not only in the reader.

**‼️ FINISHED WORK IS NEVER LOST AND UNFINISHED WORK IS NEVER ASSUMED.** On reload, an action the journal saw start but not settle is looked up in the store that actually ran it: a task that finished while the window was gone is recovered with its cost, its tokens and its output, and a task that is missing — or still claims to be running with nothing behind it — is marked `interrupted` and **says so**. Nothing is ever silently restarted; paying twice for work the user asked for once is the failure this whole item exists to prevent. An answer or an approval that reached the journal a moment before the crash is **the user's answer**, and they are not asked for it again. A run parked mid-question now shows the question itself in Needs You instead of "the window closed".

**And a resume is refused exactly when the run cannot say what it already set in motion.** Rubble on its own is survivable — the objective is in the snapshot, so the lead is briefed again from it (`rebrief`). Rubble **plus** work of unknown fate is not (`refuse`): continuing would either duplicate that work or build on a result that never arrived. Either way the run list opens, because a damaged trace must never hide a mission from the person who has to decide about it.

**Classic missions notice none of this.** No trace, no field, no behaviour change — a record written before this release loads, saves and reloads byte-for-value identical, which the test measures on a real file rather than asserting. Retention is unchanged in meaning: deleting a run takes its journal with it and leaves Task output archives alone, and orphan journals — from a delete that never reached its file, or a run culled by the history cap — are swept at startup, touching no file that is not ours by name. On the bridge, `missions.trace` reads a run's journal: the folded projection by default, raw events on request, with `health`, `resume` and how far behind the snapshot was. 102 checks in `test/test_mission_trace.js`.

## 3.211.0 — M-15 (X-32): a mission can be given an outcome instead of a recipe (2026-08-21)

**A classic mission is a RECIPE — here is the team, delegate round by round, finish. An adaptive one is an OBJECTIVE.** The user says what must be true at the end (`successCriteria`), what the run may not do to get there (`constraints`), who it may draw on (`pool`) and how much rope the lead has (`autonomy`) — and the lead works out the rest at runtime: how many rounds, which agents, in what order. This release is the CONTRACT for that, and nothing more. It writes no second engine, no second store and no parallel control plane: `mode` is one optional field on the spec Agent Farm already has, and it travels through the same `missions.json`, the same lifecycle and the same `missions.start`. The loop that spends it is M-16; the evaluation is M-17.

**‼️ AND ITS FIRST OBLIGATION IS TO EVERY MISSION THAT ALREADY EXISTS.** All of them are in the store with no `mode` field. Absent is read as `classic` **definitively** — there is no third "unknown" state and no heuristic, because a record that had to be guessed at is a run whose behaviour changes on upgrade. The migration touches a classic spec **not at all**: no field added, none defaulted in, nothing normalised, the same object handed back. Measured rather than asserted — the test writes a real old record to a real file, loads it, saves it, loads it again and compares the JSON.

**‼️ A CRITERION'S ID OUTLIVES ITS WORDING.** Evaluations refer to criteria across rounds, across a revise/replan and across a reload, so a criterion identified by its text would orphan every judgement already recorded about it the moment somebody fixed a typo. Each gets a stable `cN` at creation, is never renumbered, and a criterion added into a gap takes the first id **nothing else answers to** rather than the first that looks free. A criterion with no `required` flag is REQUIRED: an objective where everything is optional has nothing to decide "done" with, and that is refused by name.

**‼️ AND AN OBJECTIVE THAT CANNOT BE JUDGED NEVER STARTS.** No criteria · every criterion optional · two criteria sharing an id · an empty pool · no goal · a nameless lead · an unknown autonomy — each is a run that would otherwise call the planner and fail somewhere in the middle with the money gone. They are reported **all at once** before the mission exists, not one per attempt. The lead itself is never left to the engine: an adaptive user gives an outcome rather than a cast list, so if they named nobody the lead is resolved **deterministically** — the first of the pool, the first of the fleet if there is no pool — and the run is created with that name in it, where the person who wanted somebody else can see it.

**The split is a protocol, not an `if (adaptive)` growing through the loop.** The guards, the waves, pause, cancel, approval, the ledger, the store, the cost attribution and the reload recovery are ONE machine and stay that way — an adaptive run that could pause differently from a classic one is a run nobody can reason about. The two modes disagree about exactly two things: what the lead is TOLD and what its reply is CHECKED against. So that is the interface (`MissionProtocol`), the engine picks one at construction and never asks again, and both briefings end with the identical decision schema — the actions do not fork. What the adaptive lead is checked against is its **pool** rather than a team, and the first time it puts an agent to work that choice is recorded on the run as a **runtime role**: this agent, this brief, these dimensions. Bound once per agent, refreshed in wording, never re-stamped in time — nothing is written to disk and no agent folder is created, because the cast of one run is not a fact about the fleet.

On the bridge, `missions.start` takes `mode: "adaptive"` with `successCriteria`, `constraints?`, `pool?` and `autonomy?`; `lead` and `team` become optional there and only there. 76 checks in `test/test_mission_adaptive.js`.

## 3.210.0 — S-41: two axes, and the architecture that had only one (2026-08-21)

**A task started it, so it is 🤖 — and it opened a terminal, so it is not 🌙.** Agent Farm asks a session two questions and the Sessions page carries two filters for them: **who started it** (🧑 You / 🤖 Auto) and **where it ran** (🌙 headless, or a terminal somebody could type in). They are independent — which is the whole reason there are two chips rather than one — and the code had collapsed them into a single axis: everything headless was automation, everything else was you. A task launched in *interactive* mode is both automation and a terminal, and it came out 🧑 **You**, filed as one of your own conversations, invisible to the 🌙 chip and to every surface that scopes to automation.

**‼️ AND THE FAULT WAS NOT IN THE RULE, IT WAS IN THE DATA THE RULE NEVER GOT.** `publishLaunchBindings` opened with `if (t.mode !== 'headless') continue;` — an interactive run produced no launch binding at all, so it had no `launchedBy`, so the origin rule fell through to S-37's last clause ("an agent's own folder and no record of ours means it was not ours") and stamped it a person's. `publishLaunchers`, the map that puts a NAME in the origin hover, was keyed on `costSessionFile`, which only the headless cost matcher ever writes — so the run had no launcher name either. Both gates are gone: every task the farm starts gets a first-class binding whatever it runs in, and a run that KNOWS its session id at the spawn (a resume, or a Console-hosted task, whose panel hands the id straight back) is indexed on that id immediately rather than waiting for a transcript match. The surface needed no change — the fixture for this exact row, "a task, but in a real terminal", has been drawn and tested since 3.140.0 and had simply never been sent a session.

**‼️ AND THE SECOND AXIS NO LONGER ASKS THE FIRST.** `sessionHeadless` opened with `if (sessionOrigin(s) !== 'auto') { return false; }`, which does not narrow an answer — it defines one axis in terms of the other, and the state this release is about is precisely the one that definition forbids. It is read off the execution evidence alone now, in three clauses: the Console hosts a screen; a run we started states its own `mode`; otherwise the entrypoint is all there is (`cli` is a terminal, `sdk-*` is a program — except inside the fleet, where `sdk-cli` is also the Console's shape and its record can go missing). Every case answers exactly as it did; what is gone is the dependency, and a test walks all 48 combinations of the four facts to keep it gone.

**‼️ WIDENING THE BINDING DID NOT WIDEN WHAT IT MAY CLAIM.** A headless run starts, prints and exits; a terminal task opens **in the agent's own folder** — where your own conversations live — and stays open for as long as you keep typing, so it has no `endedAt` and its window runs "until now". Matched on lifespan the way a headless binding is, it would have claimed the next session you started there and stamped your own dialog 🤖: S-37's mislabelling, arriving from the other direction. An interactive run's prompt is on its command line, so its transcript begins at the spawn — it is claimed there (inside the same two-minute skew everything else allows) or not at all. A declared id is never subject to the clock.

**And the rule the two surfaces disagreed over is now a type.** `sessionOrigin`/`sessionHeadless` took `Pick<SessionInfo, …>`, every field of which is optional, so `sessionOrigin({ launchedBy })` compiled — and the Session Viewer, calling it that way, gave a different answer from the table reading the full record for the same session. They take `OriginFacts | SessionInfo` now: a surface holding the whole record passes that and cannot omit a field it does not know exists, while a page with only a transcript must write all four, `undefined` included. The third shape — two of the four facts, assembled by hand — no longer builds. 35 checks in `test/test_session_axes.js`.

## 3.209.0 — X-54: a shipped example is not a private note, and a cap you cannot suspend (2026-08-21)

**The budget example named a real agent of this installation, in Turkish.** `{"psikolog": 20, "*": 50}` sat in `package.json` — the file every user of this extension reads, in the Settings page and in VS Code's own settings UI. It is `{"agent_one": 20, "*": 50}` now; the dispatcher's routing example, which used Turkish match words and the same agent name, went with it. Both are the same fault, so the manifest is swept for it rather than fixed twice: a check in `test/test_settingsops.js` fails the build if any shipped description names one of this farm's agents or is written in the user's own language.

**`agentFarm.budgetsUnlimited` — suspend every daily budget without losing what you typed.** There was no way to lift a cap short of deleting the figures and typing them back in later, which is how a cap ends up permanently deleted. While the switch is on, no agent has a cap and nothing warns or blocks on spend, whatever `budgets` says; the figures stay in settings untouched and turning it off puts them back in force, unchanged. Off by default — a ceiling is never removed by an upgrade. It is drawn in Cost & Budgets, beside the setting it suspends.

**‼️ AND IT IS HONOURED EVERYWHERE OR IT IS NOT HONOURED AT ALL.** Seven places read the budgets — the health config, the task budget check, the fleet status card, the missions and messaging guards, the analysis page. A switch obeyed by six of them is worse than no switch: the ceiling appears to be off and something still refuses to run, with nothing on screen to explain it. So nobody reads the setting directly any more: `budgetsNow()` returns an empty map while the switch is on, which is already the shape every one of those readers treats as "no cap set". The rule is measured rather than remembered — the test counts raw reads of the setting and expects exactly one, the accessor's own.

**And the same fault, one layer out: the build was shipping the workshop's own scratch folder.** `.tmp/` holds the bridge recipes an agent writes its payloads with — including this installation's project id and half-written Turkish commit messages — and `.vscodeignore` never named it, so all seven files went into every VSIX. It is excluded now, and `tools/verify_vsix.js` reads the artefact for it (with `tools/` beside it) rather than trusting the pattern list: what ships is caught by the gate that reads what is actually inside, not by the list that was supposed to keep it out.

## 3.208.0 — S-43: the session nobody started, and the process above the one you can see (2026-08-21)

**A daemon's spare worker is not a session, and it is no longer drawn as one.** Claude Code v2.1+ keeps a daemon and one pre-warmed idle worker ready so a `claude` you type starts instantly. That worker registers itself in the CLI's own session registry exactly like a real session — `"kind":"bg","spare":true,"status":"idle"` — and fires the same SessionStart hook, so the Live Timeline drew a card for a session nobody had started and filed it under whichever agent's folder the worker happened to sit in.

**‼️ THE VERDICT IS RE-TAKEN ON EVERY READ, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — and that is the whole design.** The hook fires the instant the worker is born and the registry file for that pid may not be written yet, so the answer at SessionStart can honestly be *"I do not know"*. Deciding it there once is how you write a filter that passes its own test and leaks in production: read "I do not know" as *real* and the spare slips through on its first event; read it as *spare* and a session that has only just started is hidden for good. So nothing is held on a shrug — that is the old behaviour exactly, which is why Codex, Gemini, Antigravity and OpenCode cannot regress, none of them having a claude registry file at all — and the question is asked again whenever the list is read, by which time the file exists. The leak is self-healing (the card is gone by the next refresh) and no session the registry knows to be real is ever hidden. **A session that has ever submitted a prompt is released and never held again**: the daemon hands its spare over to a real conversation, and a rule that kept looking at `spare:true` would hide the conversation with it.

**☠ Force kill: stop the tree, not the leaf.** "End session" stops the process the registry names — the worker — and on Windows `taskkill /T` only ever walks DOWN from there. The daemon above it saw its worker die, started another under a new id, and the card came back: a loop the user could not get out of without leaving the editor. Force Kill climbs from the session's process to the top of the **claude** part of the tree and stops it there, then purges the card. The climb is bounded three ways and every one of them is a safety rule rather than a tidiness one: it never enters VS Code's own ancestry (the extension host has a parent too, and a rule that climbed far enough would aim `taskkill /T` at the editor), it only climbs *through* a process that is recognisably part of a claude tree (so a session started from a terminal stops at the topmost claude and never touches the shell that opened it), and it gives up after a fixed depth so a table with a reused pid in it cannot become an infinite loop. The confirmation names every process that will go, by name and pid, before anything is killed.

On the session card, in both right-click menus (`agentfarm.forceKillSession`) and on the bridge as `sessions.forceKill`. A Console-hosted session is refused by name: its tree runs under this window, and End session already closes it through the Console's own stdin + process tree.

The decision half is pure and lives in `src/core/processTree.ts` — the machine's process table goes in, a target comes out — because the only way to test a rule whose failure mode is *killing the wrong thing* is against a table written by hand. 45 checks in `test/test_spare_sessions.js`: the race, the hand-over, the four engines with no registry, an orphan with no parent left, a cycle, and the dangerous case where the leaf's grandparent is the editor.

## 3.207.0 — U-83: the Wiki is a destination, and the Toolbox gets a second row (2026-08-21)

**📚 Wiki is a global destination.** It sits in every page's toolbar but its own, between Studio and Toolbox — where the row turns from *what is being made* to *what it is made of*. Until now it was one click from the Toolbox and nowhere else: a page about the whole farm's knowledge, filed behind the page about Claude Code's extension model.

**‼️ A PAGE'S OWN DESTINATIONS MAY TAKE THEIR OWN ROW.** The Toolbox owns four — 🗄️ Airtable Engine · Capability Matrix · ⚖ Sync Constitution · 🔑 Secrets — and appending four to a twelve-button global row wrapped it under the cursor at any width a person actually works at; worse, *which* four fell to the second line was decided by pixels rather than by meaning. `relatedRow` on `AFHeader.html` sends the `related` cluster to a second row of its own, still flush right, so the two rows share an edge and read as one block. It is a full-width flex child of `.af-head` — inside the header box on purpose, because `wire()` scopes header actions to `.af-head [data-afact]` and a related ACTION lifted out of it would silently stop posting.

**⚖ Sync Constitution moved from the Dashboard to the Toolbox.** What it mirrors is the shared `CLAUDE.md` into the `AGENTS.md` files Codex and Antigravity read — a piece of the extension model that page is about. On a row of its own it has the width for its whole name rather than "Sync Cons.". The panel handler moved with it and the parity manifest with that (`toolboxPanel.ts#headerAction` → `constitution.sync`); the assertions moved into `test/test_constitution_sync.js`, where the feature they are about already lives.

`test/live_header.js` now draws the Toolbox's real header beside the interactive one and takes `--light`, so both rows were looked at in both themes before this shipped.

## 3.206.0 — X-51 (X-50): the chain walked end to end, and the build read rather than assumed (2026-08-21)

**X-51 — and then the chain, walked once from end to end.** B-14, K-26, M-23 and U-70 each had a suite, and every one of them passed against a world it built itself; what nothing covered was the **seam**. `test/test_wiki_e2e.js` (41 checks) walks it in order with nothing stubbed but the LLM: mark a turn → ask for the brief → read what the run would be told → start the run (claimed, still pending, second run refused by name) → **write exactly what the prompt instructs** → report back → ask both sides what happened → check the shape of what was written. Step five is *performed* rather than asserted: the synthesis is an LLM's and no test can check prose, but a compile whose pages land where nothing can find them is a failure a test can catch — and this one did, on its first run. **A `[[link]]` and the `index.md` line must use the page's FILENAME form** (`[[Aday_Havuzu]]`, not `[[Aday Havuzu]]`): Obsidian resolves a link against the filename and so does `wiki.lint`, so a spaced link to an underscored file is broken on both sides. The agent procedure (`_REF/wiki.md` §2, §4) now says so.

**‼️ And what is actually inside the build is now read, not assumed** — `npm run verify` (`tools/verify_vsix.js`, 12 checks). Every other gate in this repo runs BEFORE `vsce`, which makes `.vscodeignore` — a list of patterns — able to drop a new `media/*.js` or `out/panels/*.js` **silently**: the extension installs cleanly and the page is blank the first time somebody opens it, with no error anywhere. This reads the artefact's own zip central directory (no dependency, nothing decompressed) and checks that every compiled panel, every core module, every media asset and **every file `htmlShell` asks the webview for** is really in there — plus that `src/`, `test/`, the parity manifest and the render output are not, and that the build has not silently doubled in size.

## 3.205.0 — U-70 (X-50): the pool had four doors that write to it and none that read it (2026-08-21)

Marking a turn is one gesture and costs nothing, which is the point — and it is why the pool fills up faster than anybody empties it. Four doors wrote to it (the 🔖 badge, a session's right-click, the bridge, the palette) and **not one surface read it**: what was waiting, what a mark was about, which run was out for it and where a compile actually put the page were all invisible unless you called `wiki.candidates.list` by hand. **The Wiki page is that surface** — `Agent Farm: Open Wiki`, or Toolbox → 📚 Wiki.

**‼️ ITS TWO BUTTONS ARE `wiki.compile.run` AND NOTHING ELSE.** *Compile Selected* takes the ticked rows, *Compile All Pending* takes everything waiting, both as one run — and neither marks anything compiled. The run reports back with `wiki.candidates.edit {state:"compiled", pages:[…]}`, which is still the only thing that closes a mark (B-14). This is not a page that re-implements the ops beside them: `editCandidate`, `removeCandidates`, `startCompileRun` and `wikiStatus` moved into `core/wiki.ts` as the shared bodies, the ops became one line each, and the page calls the same four. A button and an op that disagree about what closes a mark is precisely what the parity gate is built to catch, so there is nothing for it to catch.

**‼️ A MARK WITH A RUN OUT FOR IT IS NOT OFFERED — AND THAT IS VISIBLE BEFORE THE PRESS.** `compiling` is not a state in the pool; it is a **pending** row whose claim is still alive. Such a row draws no tick box, is not in the "pending" count and cannot be sent, because reading the same turns twice files the same concept twice. The same rule at the other end: with the wiki root or `-WIKI-ANAYASA-.md` missing, **both compile buttons are dead and the reason is on the button** rather than in a refusal after the press. The vault strip across the top says which of the four files (root · law · index · log) is actually there, marks the missing ones ⚠, and opens any of them.

**DENSE, and the row is one line.** State · source (session + turn range) · topic chips (over three collapse to `+N`) · what was said · when · the pages written. Everything longer than the line is an AFTip: hovering the row gives the session, the agent, the engine, the range, the note and who marked it when — with **zero clicks**, which is the whole point of a page you use to decide what to compile. A compiled row carries its pages as a clickable `Category / Concept` breadcrumb, opened with your own `docOpen` preference — provenance, read backwards.

Filtering is a topic multi-select (each option carrying how many marks under it still wait), state toggles, and a search box speaking **the farm's shared query grammar** (`foo bar`, `-foo`, `"exact phrase"`) across a mark's topics, prompt, note, session and pages at once. ✎ edits topics inline — and an emptied list is never sent, because a mark with no topic has lost the pool's filing key. 🚫 drops a mark, ↺ reopens it, ✕ deletes it, and **none of the three touch a page already written in the vault**. 🩺 Lint reports `wiki.lint` into the page: orphans, broken `[[links]]`, unindexed pages — reported, never repaired.

41 checks in `test/test_wiki_page.js`, driven through the real page script; three fixture variants in `test/fixtures/wiki.js` (the pool with a run in flight · a wiki with no law · an empty pool).

## 3.204.0 — M-23 (X-50): the compile, done rather than described (2026-08-21)

B-14 drew a line the engine may not cross: `wiki.compile` hands back a **brief**, because an extension cannot synthesise and one that pretended to would produce exactly the mechanical summaries this whole idea exists to avoid. That left the second half of the system with no door — the pool filled up and emptying it meant calling the bridge by hand and doing the reading yourself. **`wiki.compile.run` is the honest way across:** it assembles the same brief and starts a **headless run** that carries out the synthesis under the vault's own law. **Agent Farm: Compile Wiki Candidates…** is the palette's door to it — everything waiting is ticked when the picker opens, so Enter compiles the lot and unticking is the exception.

**‼️ STARTING A RUN MARKS NOTHING COMPILED.** The only thing that closes a mark is the run reporting the pages back with `wiki.candidates.edit {state:"compiled", pages:[…]}` — the same contract B-14 wrote. A compile that marked its own work done would leave the pool claiming turns had been written into a wiki the first failure never reached.

**‼️ AND TWO RUNS OVER ONE MARK IS THE FAILURE THE POOL EXISTS TO PREVENT.** The same turns read twice file the same concept twice. So a run records its claim on every mark it took, a second compile over a claimed mark is **refused by name**, and the picker does not offer it. The claim is only real while the run is: a compile that crashed leaves a **stale** claim that is ignored, because a dead run must not lock a turn out of the wiki for ever. `wiki.status` counts them (`pool.compiling`) and they stay **pending**, which is what they are.

**The prompt is the product.** The run is told where the law is (and to read it first — it outranks the agent procedure), which transcript and which turns, what the wiki already holds (which is what decides create-vs-amend), and the three lines it does not cross: **one concept per page**, **nothing contradicted is deleted** (it is annotated with a dated line), **every fact carries where it came from**. The report-back is written out with the real candidate ids, so there is nothing to look up — and a mark it could not write a page for is told to stay pending and say why.

`agentFarm.wikiAgent` says who writes the wiki. The brief is **one assembly** shared by both doors, so the words an agent works from cannot drift from the words the op prints. 51 checks in `test/test_wiki_compile_run.js`, including the claim, the stale claim, and the three refusals that are not guesses: no root, no `-WIKI-ANAYASA-.md`, and "compile whatever is there".

## 3.203.0 — K-26 (X-50): the turn you are reading is one press from the wiki pool (2026-08-21)

S-38 put a whole conversation into the candidate pool from the row it is on. But a conversation is not what gets compiled — a **turn** is, and the moment worth keeping is the moment the answer lands, not an hour later when you would have to find it again. So every turn now carries a quiet **🔖** on the row that starts it: on the Console's prompt rows and on the transcript's turn bands, with the same item in the right-click menu on those bands and on every row of the Turns page.

**‼️ THE BADGE IS ON THE PROMPT, NOT ON THE LINE THAT CLOSES THE TURN.** The closing line is written by the panel and exists only for turns run in it: scroll back into a resumed conversation and the rows there came off the transcript, which carries no result lines at all. A badge hung there would have been missing from exactly the scrollback a reader goes back through. The prompt is also the row whose words say what the turn was about, which is the question being answered.

**‼️ AND THE TURN NUMBER IS THE TRANSCRIPT'S, RESOLVED FROM THE ROW'S OWN WORDS.** The pool files by turn number and a Console row does not carry one — the panel's counter restarts on every resume and the backfill numbers rows by their place in the file. Resolving it by the clock alone is wrong exactly where it looks right: the panel stamps a prompt when it sends it and the CLI stamps it when it writes it, and a queued message can start the next turn inside that gap, so "the last turn that had started by then" quietly files the **neighbouring** turn. The opening line, whitespace-flattened, matches one turn or none; the clock is only allowed to choose between turns that already said the same thing. When nothing matches — a transcript that has not caught up — the clock answers and **the popover shows that number as something to check**, in the row it is in, before anything is saved.

**A popover, not a window.** The saved-prompt picker takes the screen because choosing a prompt is what you stopped to do; this is pressed while an answer is still arriving behind it, so the panel opens against the badge, over a backdrop you can see through, and closes on Esc, on Save, or on a click anywhere else. It shows the turn range (editable — `4`, `3-7`, or empty for the whole conversation) against the conversation's length, the turn's opening line, the topics already in the pool as chips, a box for new ones and an optional note. Enter saves from any of the three boxes. **What you type counts whether or not you also ticked a chip** — the commonest way this will be used, and the one a naive picker throws away.

**A kept turn stays kept, and says so at paint time.** The marks travel with the page's own data rather than arriving after a round trip, so the badge is lit on the first paint of a panel that repaints on every step of a running turn. A turn inside a marked *range* is lit, and a whole-conversation mark (S-38) lights every turn in it. Pressing a lit badge opens with that mark's own topics already ticked, because the pool **merges** rather than adding a second row (B-14) — which is exactly how you add a topic you thought of later.

`media/afWiki.js` ships to every page from `htmlShell` and the host answers it in one place (`wikiMarkMessage`), so the next reading surface gets the badge by drawing it rather than by wiring it. 44 checks in `test/test_wiki_tagger.js`, including the neighbouring-turn case the clock gets wrong; `test/live_wiki.js` is the panel running in a browser, for the half a static render cannot photograph.

## 3.202.0 — S-38 (X-50): a conversation goes into the wiki pool from the row it is already on (2026-08-21)

The candidate pool only works if marking is **cheaper than deciding**, and until now the only way in was to call the bridge by hand — which is not a gesture anybody makes while reading. **Add to Wiki Candidates…** is on the session row, on the Console's own cards and on the Live Timeline: three surfaces, because which one you are on when a conversation turns out to be worth keeping is not predictable. It is filed with the other **marks** (label, pin, copy id) and never with the items that run something, because that is what it is — it writes nothing to the vault, and the compile stays a separate, deliberate act.

**‼️ It asks with a picker, not a box — for a reason, not to satisfy a rule.** A pool where one subject is spelled three ways files one concept three times, and nobody spells consistently from memory across weeks. So the topics **already in the pool are the list**, ticked in any combination and annotated with how many marks are waiting under each; a word that is not in the pool yet appears at the top of that same list as *new topic*, one keystroke further than an old one and no further. Typing still works exactly as it would in a box — and Enter on a fresh word with nothing ticked keeps that word, which is the commonest way this will be used and the one a naive picker would throw away.

Marking several selected conversations at once puts the same topics on each. A conversation already marked is not marked twice: the whole-session mark **merges** with whatever was pending for it (and swallows a single turn already marked inside it — the narrower mark was a subset), and the confirmation says how many merged and how many marks are now waiting to be compiled.

## 3.201.0 — B-14 (X-50): the wiki candidate pool, and the line its ops do not cross (2026-08-21)

*“Obsidian is the IDE, the LLM is the programmer, the wiki is the codebase.”* The user does not write `00_WIKI`; agents do. But a turn worth keeping goes past at conversation speed, and the moment marking one costs a decision about **where it belongs**, nobody marks anything. So the system is two halves, and this is the cheap one.

**Marking is free, reversible and touches no vault.** `wiki.candidates.add` takes a session, a turn (`4`, `"3-7"`, or nothing at all for the whole conversation) and the topics somebody typed in two seconds — the compiler’s filing key, and the only thing it insists on. It lands in `wiki_candidates.json` beside the other stores.

**‼️ Marking the same turn twice is not an error and is not a second row.** The console badge and the session menu both reach the same turn, so a double mark is certain — and two rows for one turn means the compile reads it twice and files the concept twice. An overlapping mark **merges its topics** into the pending one and widens the range, which is also how you add a topic you thought of later: mark it again.

**‼️ AND `wiki.compile` DOES NOT WRITE A WIKI PAGE.** An extension cannot synthesise, and an op that pretended to would produce exactly the mechanical summaries this whole idea exists to avoid. What it does is everything the extension is genuinely better at than the agent: gather the chosen candidates, resolve each one to a **transcript on disk and a turn range inside it**, find the vault’s own law, list what the wiki already holds (which is what decides create-vs-amend), and hand back a brief with the steps. The agent does the synthesis under `-WIKI-ANAYASA-.md` and reports back with `wiki.candidates.edit {state:"compiled", pages:[…]}`. **Asking for a brief marks nothing** — a compile that falls over halfway must not leave the pool claiming work that never happened.

**Two refusals rather than two guesses.** A missing wiki root, and a wiki with no law of its own: both stop the compile by name. The law outranks the agent procedure, so compiling without it would be a guess dressed as a result. And a `state` sweep on `remove` will not touch pending marks — they are the only thing in this file that cannot be reconstructed.

**`wiki.status` answers both sides at once** (pool: pending/compiled and every topic with its count · vault: root, rules, index, log, pages, categories, anything filed deeper than one category), and **`wiki.lint`** reports the wiki’s *shape* — orphans, broken `[[links]]`, unindexed pages — and repairs nothing. Whether two pages contradict each other is not a question a program can answer, and is not guessed at.

81 checks in `test/test_wiki_candidates.js`, against a real wiki on disk. `agentFarm.wikiRoot` is the folder; `_REF/wiki.md` §10 now says what these ops actually do rather than only their names.

## 3.200.0 — M-21 (part): the strip that summarises this page could not be asked anything (2026-08-21)

M-25 took the five design principles through this page’s two **tables** and stopped where the tables stop. The control strip above them is the first thing read on the page, and it answered almost nothing: **five of its eight figures had no hover at all**, three had a one-line `title` — which `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` names as a bug in its own right, not as a small tip — the shorthand durations `1h` / `8h` / `24h` had their long form written nowhere, and **the two tabs did not say what was behind them**, which is the one distinction this entire page is built on.

**Every figure now carries the derivation you would otherwise open another page for.** ⚙️ names both ceilings and lists what is under them right now · ⏳ says how the queue is ordered, how long the oldest has waited and who is in it · 🛡️ lists the things a person has to answer instead of only counting them · 📅 breaks the definitions down by kind, says why the fraction is not out of the total, and names what wakes next · 🏁 derives today’s success **rate** and names what failed · 💵 lists the top spenders, the per-run average and what the figure excludes · 🛡 says what share of the guarded wake-ups came to nothing · ⚠️ names the rows and their issues.

**ONE SUBJECT decides the split, and no figure explains another’s.** The ceiling is ⚙️’s subject, what is waiting is ⏳’s, and the two tab panels carry none of each other’s counts.

**SHORTHAND and MIRROR, where they actually apply.** `1h` is the right thing to write on a button four characters wide — the long form belongs in the panel, and there was no panel: *“Pause for one hour · automation starts itself again at 13:01 · 2 wake-ups fall inside that window and would be deferred.”* Every control that changes the gate opens with what the gate says **now**, and 🌙 Quiet states its current window as its first line.

**`test/test_tasks_header_tips.js` is the gate.** It walks the real span nesting to find any control on the strip that cannot be asked anything, refuses a panel of fewer than three lines **by name** (a one-liner is the bug this file exists for), and pins the derivations, the two principles and the tab split. `test_tasks_webview.js` reads the page **without its hover panels** now: “filtering narrowed the table” had been written as “that row appears nowhere on the page”, which stopped being the same question the moment the strip started deriving its figures from the same list — a filter narrows a table, it does not change what the farm is doing.

## 3.199.0 — M-21 (part): a run whose terminal outlived the window came back as a row nothing could ever launch (2026-08-21)

A VS Code reload is not a rare event — **installing a build is one**, and this project installs one every few minutes. Every task that is `running` at that moment has to be given a state by hand, because the process handle that would have answered went with the host. There are three different right answers, and the store cannot tell them apart by itself.

**‼️ The OS terminal one was wrong, and the code that would have made it right could never run.** A Windows Terminal window outlives the extension host *by design* — that is the whole reason M-26 gave that surface an exit file instead of a child-process handle. The constructor re-arms the watch on exactly that state (`running` + an exit file) — but the stale sweep that clears `running` rows lives inside `load()`, which is called from the constructor's **first line**. By the time the re-arm looked, there was no such task left. So an interactive run in its own terminal came back as `queued` **with `autoStart` already cleared by its own launch**, which means nothing on this earth relaunches it; the row sat there for ever while the terminal it belongs to finished the work minutes later into an exit file nobody was reading. Measured on a store written by hand, before and after.

**The Console is the opposite case, and had to stop being treated as the same one.** That session is a process *this* host spawned and read over a pipe: a reload starts with an empty session map, so `consoleTaskState` answers `undefined` for ever and a task left `running` would be followed by a timer that can never conclude. It goes back on the queue like any other cut run — and **its dead session id goes with the session**, so the row no longer offers a conversation nobody can open.

**And a run that was cut says so now.** Clearing `startedAt` on its own left a row that reads as though it had never run at all: the one fact the reader needs — that it was *cut*, not skipped — was written nowhere. Every one of the three paths writes its own line, and the `started` line above it keeps its own timestamp, so the two together tell the whole story.

**A new event kind, because "picked back up" is not "started".** A re-attached run — an OS terminal, or a media render still polling its URLs — has had nothing spawned for it, and drawing it as `started` would claim the one thing that did not happen. `resumed` is its own word on the timeline, and the media reattach (which crossed reloads in complete silence) writes one too.

**`test/test_task_reload.js` is the gate**: it opens a real `TaskManager` on a store written the way a window that died mid-run leaves one, once for each of the five shapes, and checks the vocabulary too — a kind the core can write but the page has no word for degrades silently to its raw identifier, so the two lists are compared rather than trusted.

## 3.198.0 — M-21 (part): the rule that every box records itself is measured now, and it caught one (2026-08-21)

The Tasks page redraws itself on every host push, and the redraw replaces the whole form. So **a field that lives only in the DOM is a field that a task finishing somewhere else silently empties, mid-sentence, with nobody watching.** M-21 named one victim — the continuation prompt, the longest text on the card and the one that only matters when nobody is looking — and the sweep that cleared the other 54 fields was done **by hand, once**. A rule found by hand once is a rule that rots.

**`test/test_composer_fields.js` is that comparison, derived rather than declared.** It reads the ids `readComposer()` and `readStep()` actually pull out of the page, reads the ids the wiring actually attaches an `input`/`change` listener to, and fails when the two sets disagree — so a field added tomorrow is checked tomorrow without anybody remembering the file exists. It runs **both ways**: a read with no listener loses what was typed, and a listener for something nothing reads is how a renamed field goes quietly dead. The one honest exemption (`nt-kind`, which reopens the composer instead of storing itself) is named, with its own check that it still reads the draft first.

**‼️ And the first thing it found was two days old.** M-26 shipped *Opens in* and *When it answers* on the interactive form; `readComposer()` reads both, and **nothing called it when either was changed** — they were in no wiring list at all. Pick “its own OS terminal window”, let any task anywhere finish, and the repaint drew the box back at the default. Silently, because the draft had never been told. Wired.

**The half nobody had audited is clean.** A workflow **step** is read through a different helper (`nt-st-` ids, list-driven), which is exactly why the hand sweep never covered it — and a step's prompt is the same kind of long text as the one that started this. All 31 of its fields are wired; measured, not assumed.

**And the third direction is closed too.** A box that is DRAWN and never read is a control whose answer is discarded — *“a box with no referent is a bug”* (`docs/CONVENTIONS.md`) — and the reader has no way of telling. All 78 boxes the form draws are read by one of the two readers; the only exception is the kind picker, which is the exemption already named. Asserted one-directionally (drawn ⊆ read), because a markup shape the scan cannot see must never turn into a false accusation.

## 3.197.0 — M-26: an interactive task says WHERE it opens and WHETHER it closes (2026-08-21)

*“An interactive task always opens in VS Code’s terminal and always stays open. I want to choose — the OS terminal or the Console — and I want a one-turn job to close itself when the answer is in.”* Two axes, on every surface that can install a run.

**`interactiveTarget` — where the run appears.** `vscode` (the integrated terminal, the default and what every interactive task did before this) · `external` (its own OS terminal window — Windows Terminal where there is one, which is the answer to xterm.js glitching on a long TUI session) · `console` (Agent Farm hosts the conversation in its own panel — the one surface where the extension can follow what a run is *doing* rather than only when it stopped).

**`interactiveClose` — what happens once the agent has replied.** `stay-open` (the default: the conversational CLI, and the task finishes when the surface is closed) · `auto-close` (one turn, then it ends).

**‼️ `auto-close` is not a TUI killed on a guess.** Nothing in a TUI says “the answer is over”, so a timer or a quiet-transcript heuristic would end a thinking agent mid-thought. The engine is asked in its **print-and-exit** form instead — the same `runArgs` / `claude -p` the headless path spawns — and the shell is told to leave when it returns. The surface is still a terminal you watch; what changed is that the run has an end.

**Two surfaces this extension does not own, and one honest way to follow each.** An OS window outlives the extension host by design and a Console conversation is the panel’s process, so neither can be followed by a child process exit. The window writes the CLI’s own exit code to a file and a 2-second watch reads it; the Console is followed through the panel’s own report, and `auto-close` ends the task the first time that session comes back to rest **with an answer behind it** (idle alone would end it before the agent had said anything). One timer drives both — an idle farm pays nothing.

### ‼️ What the first pass got wrong, measured rather than reasoned about

**The OS terminal surface never worked at all — not “mostly”, at all.** Three findings, each of which alone would have been enough:
- **`echo %ERRORLEVEL%> "f"` is not an echo.** A digit touching `>` is a **handle number**, so `echo 0> f` redirects STDIN, prints `ECHO is on.` to the console and leaves the file **empty**. Measured for codes 0, 1, 2 and 3 — every one wrote nothing. The watcher then read `""`, and `Number("")` is `0`, so **every external run reported success, a crashed CLI included**: the exact failure the exit file exists to prevent.
- **Parenthesising it fixes the redirection and not the answer.** `%ERRORLEVEL%` on a one-line `&` chain is expanded when the **line** is parsed — before the first command has run. Measured: a literal `0` whatever the CLI returned.
- **And the command never reached the shell.** node → `wt` → `cmd` is three parsers that do not agree about quoting: node escapes an inner `"` the C runtime’s way, which `cmd.exe` has never understood — and every command here has inner quotes, because the prompt is one. Measured: a launch carrying a quoted prompt opened a window that ran nothing, while the identical launch without inner quotes worked.

**So the command travels as a generated `.cmd` script now**, which crosses none of those parsers and is the only place the exit code can be read correctly at all — a batch file is parsed a line at a time, so `%ERRORLEVEL%` on the line *after* the command is that command’s own. Every `%` in the command is doubled (batch reads one as a variable); round-tripped against a prompt carrying `%`, `!`, `&`, `<`, `>` and quotes, intact. The script names its own window and deletes itself on its last line. The `start` fallback was broken too and by the same class of thing: it was handed an **unquoted** title, which `start` reads as a program name (`The system cannot find the file …`) — it passes an empty title now and lets the script do the naming.

**The bridge accepted the pair on a headless run.** The refusal read `mode === "headless"`, and `mode` is not a required argument: every door resolves it as `mode === "interactive" ? … : "headless"`, so an **omitted** mode is a headless run — and an omitted mode walked straight past the check. `tasks.add {interactiveTarget:"external"}` was accepted and stored on a background run nobody would ever see. It is `!== "interactive"` now, and the refusal says which of the two cases it is. Three doors legitimately know the mode without carrying it in those args — a trigger states it on the action while its dimensions sit outside it (or the reverse), a rerun and a template run inherit it — so they pass it in rather than being refused.

**A reloaded window followed its OS terminals and not its Console tasks.** One timer drives both followers and it was started on the external set alone, so the one surface that reports what a run is *doing* was the one surface whose task never finished after a reload.

**A half-written exit file read as a success.** The shell creates the file on the redirection and writes a moment later; a tick landing in between read `""` and finished a running task as `done`. An empty read is “not yet” now.

**And the contract is one sentence, not five.** `interactiveTarget` / `interactiveClose` are documented from a single shared string (`INTERACTIVE_NOTE`) on `tasks.add`, `schedules.add`, `triggers.add`, `templates.add` and `templates.run` — five hand-typed copies would have been five contracts.

**Measured:** `test/test_interactive_targets.js` (45 checks) pins the closed lists and their defaults, every bridge refusal including the omitted-mode one, the routing to all three surfaces, both follower fixes — and **runs the generated script for real**, for a success and for two different failures, plus a prompt round-trip. The live `wt.exe` path was smoke-tested end to end on this machine: codes `0` and `4`, both read back correctly.

**In the form:** *Opens in* and *When it answers* appear only while the mode is interactive (a box with no referent is a bug), the mode change repaints the form, and a half-written draft keeps both values across the repaint. `Create` sits in the corner with `Cancel` to its left.

## 3.196.0 — U-81 (part 2): the card’s panels stopped handing back the line you hovered (2026-08-21)

*“The whole reason we use an `AFTip` is that no text ever has to be cut — it takes any length and it scrolls. This one made it an AFTip and cut the text anyway. Then what was the point?”* There was none. Part 1 fixed how the panel was **painted**; nobody looked at what it was **carrying**.

**Both text lines on a session card now open WHOLE.**
- **The name / opening prompt.** A conversation’s name is the opening prompt cut to a line at the source (80 characters) — until somebody renames it, the transcript has no other name to give. The panel repeated that same cut, so hovering a clipped line returned the clipped line. It carries the opening prompt to its full stored length (`FIRST_PROMPT_MAX`, 4,000) and scrolls.
- **The last thing asked.** Same defect, worse cause: `lastPrompt` on the session record **is** 90 characters — a row’s worth, which is all a card or a strip can draw. There was no whole version of it anywhere for a panel to open. `LiveSession.lastPromptFull` now travels beside it, capped like the opening prompt, so both ends of a conversation are readable to the same depth.

**‼️ And the last-prompt panel stopped repeating the line above it.** It carried a `── How it opened ──` block holding the opening prompt — the fact the line **directly above it on the same card** already draws, and whose own panel now opens it whole. The same text twice on one card is ONE SUBJECT broken in the plainest way there is. Removed; each panel answers its own question and says how many characters it is holding.

**The two lines no longer read as one paragraph broken in half.** Same size, same grey, one under the other, both prose — so the name and the last prompt looked like the start and the end of a single sentence. The name takes the card’s own foreground and a little weight; the prompt stays quiet and italic behind a `↳ last` in the link colour, which says it is the **latest** thing said and not the rest of the line above it.

**Measured and looked at.** `test/test_timeline_card_tips.js` now pins the tail of each prompt inside the markup (a panel that cut the text would fail), that `How it opened` appears nowhere on a card, and that the two lines carry different classes; the fixture grew the long `lastPromptFull` that made the defect visible at all. Photographed with `render_page.js --tip card-open` and `--tip card-said`.

## 3.195.0 — U-81: the Live Timeline’s session cards answer when you point at them (2026-08-21)

*“The one AFTip there doesn’t draw right — it’s transparent, so everything it says mixes with the text behind it. Somebody tried to fix the CSS and clearly didn’t know how, because it’s still transparent.”* They were right about the diagnosis and right that the fix was in the wrong place.

**The panel was never the problem: `opacity` on the block above it was.** The panel lives inside `.card .sub`, which was dimmed with `opacity: .7` — and opacity is applied to the whole **subtree** after it is painted. So the panel was drawn at 70% too, whatever it declared about its own background; `background: … !important` is painted at the ancestor’s alpha like everything else, which is why two rounds of fixing the background changed nothing. The same rule opens a stacking context, so the panel’s `z-index` was trapped inside the dimmed block and the next line of the card painted over it. **The dimming is kept — the same grey, applied as a colour** (`tip-host` in `common.css`), which inherits into the text and stops at the panel’s own.

**And it was the wrong shape of panel.** It used `tip-block`, which measures the panel against the block it sits in — right for a wide table row, wrong for a 260px card: it produced a panel narrower than any other panel in the extension. Anchored to its trigger it is a classic AFTip again, at its own width, with afTip’s edge flip keeping it on the page.

**The panel also answered a different question from the one asked.** The card draws the **last** prompt; the panel opened the **first** one, under a head that named neither — hover a cut line to read the rest of it and you got a different prompt entirely. It now carries both, labelled, in the order a reader asks: *the last thing asked*, then *how it opened*.

**Then every other element on the card, one at a time.** A card is a row of the Sessions table stood up, so each figure is answered the way that table answers its column — same shape, same order, same words.
- **The name** — the conversation: agent, whether the name is resolved, folder, how long it has been running, transcript, and whether this engine reports the full hook stream or only open-and-close.
- **The id chip** — the id: the full string, everywhere else it appears, what owns the process, and which YOUR-TURN alerts this session has set. (The engine badge **stopped repeating it** — that is the chip’s subject, and a fact in two panels is ONE SUBJECT broken. The badge answers what the engine decides instead: model, cost reported, tokens, transcript.)
- **The status badge** — SHORTHAND, so all seven states are now one hover from their meaning: what `PERMISSION?` and `YOUR TURN` actually mean, the tool in flight, how long it has been silent against the stuck threshold, whether a process still owns it, and whether there is anything to interrupt.
- **Money** — figures, not the paragraph it used to carry: cost per turn, per hour, per 1M tokens · raw and plan-weighted tokens with the ratio · context now and its share · the model of the last reply, and where the figures were read from.
- **Work** — prompts, tool calls, **tools per prompt**, files, errors with their share, compactions, sub-agents, and what the count is based on.
- **Time** — both clocks and the machine’s own offset, like every other time in the extension, for the start and the last event, plus how long it has run, how long it has been silent, and minutes per turn.
- **The pid** — what a headless entrypoint means, and that the claim comes from the CLI’s own registry rather than from a hook.
- **The folder** — the path whole, and that clicking reveals it.
- **All five buttons** — what pressing each one does, what it does *not* touch, and whether it asks first, instead of the sentence-long native tooltips they carried.

**Looked at, not asserted.** `render_page.js` grew a `--tip <class>[:n]` flag that opens a panel using the component’s own stay-open class, so a hover panel can finally be photographed — opaque, at its real width, in its real place, in both themes. `test/test_timeline_card_tips.js` pins the rules the picture cannot: every block that carries a panel is exempt from the opacity dimming, no card panel uses `tip-block`, and every pressable trigger says it can be pressed. Swim lanes untouched.

## 3.194.0 — U-82: “Copy ▸” copies again — everywhere, not just in the backlog (2026-08-21)

*“There are Copy options — the code, the words, code and words — and I have never once seen any of them put anything on the clipboard.”* They were not putting anything on it. **Every Copy ▸ in the extension was broken, on every page, for the same reason.**

**The root cause: the page was writing a clipboard it is not allowed to touch.** `navigator.clipboard.writeText` requires the document to be **focused**, and every one of these copies arrives from a menu pick — the right-click hands focus to VS Code’s own menu, the command relays back, and the page runs the one clipboard call it cannot satisfy. The write was rejected each time. The session viewer’s ⧉ button had already hit this and quietly moved its write to the host; nothing generalised that, so the other ~40 copy items kept failing together.

**The host holds the clipboard now, for every page at once.** `media/afCtx.js` — the single door behind every Copy ▸ — asks the extension host, which writes with `vscode.env.clipboard` and answers. **The “Copied: …” line is only drawn once the host says the write happened**, and a refusal or a door that never answers is reported instead of swallowed. Wired from the same mint-once path `htmlShell` runs for every page, so no panel opts in and the next panel cannot forget.

**The first line said it did something it does not do.** “The code — *quote it at an agent*” reads as a second action, and left the reader unsure whether a plain “copy just the code” existed at all. Quoting an item **at** something is what the two entries above it do (the work queue, the agent) and they say so. The three copy lines are now **The code, on its own · The words · Code and words** — what lands on the clipboard, not what it is for.

**Measured, so it cannot rot back:** `test/test_clipboard_host.js` drives the whole round trip (asks the host · claims nothing early · reports a refusal · hands the acquired API on to the page script that loads after it) and fails the build if any page in `media/` grows its own `navigator.clipboard` write again; `test/test_backlog_page.js` pins what each of the three lines actually copies.

## 3.193.0 — U-80: Live sessions cards prompt truncation restored (2026-08-21)

**Live session cards on the Live Timeline page are compact and proportional again.**
- **90-char row limit restored:** `s.lastPrompt` on the session record is truncated to 90 characters, preventing raw 4,000-character prompts from blowing out the card height and breaking the grid layout.
- **Full prompt on hover:** The card prompt line carries the complete opening/last prompt in its tooltip (`title="“...”"`), keeping the full context instantly readable on hover without cluttering the card face.
- **Swim lanes untouched:** All swimlane drawing, markers, segments, and toolbars remain completely unaffected.

## 3.192.0 — in-webview task & retry architecture guide popup (2026-08-20)

**The New-task form now carries its own architectural guide directly inside the webview.** A mini `?` button is placed on the action bar next to the submit buttons.

**One click opens the complete architectural guide in a floating modal popover.** It details:
- **Conversation & Session Continuity (S-19):** Fresh vs resumed session models, context inheritance, and cost isolation (`resumeCostBefore`).
- **Timing & Quota Resolution (M-3, M-10):** Limit reset (`resetAware`) timing against 5-hour rolling windows, 1st/2nd/3rd wait intervals, and backoff growth curves & AST formulas.
- **Failure Phases & 3-Prompt Routing (M-10, M-12):** `not-started` vs `interrupted` vs `unknown`, `Simple` vs `Smart` recovery, and Initial vs Retry vs Continuation prompts.
- **Safety Brakes:** "If it cannot tell" resolution choices (`park`, `simple`, `ask`, `stop`).
- **Quick Decision Matrix:** Rules of thumb for overnight heavy tasks, fresh alternative prompts, and resumed console sessions.

**Dismissible without losing your draft:** Clicking outside on the backdrop, clicking the `✕` close button, or pressing `Escape` dismisses the guide immediately while keeping all half-written fields intact. Pure UI addition — zero functional backend logic touched.

## 3.191.0 — M-25: the Plan table answers when you hover it (2026-08-20)

*“The tooltips in the tables don’t give anywhere near enough detail — they don’t follow our design principles.”* M-8 answered that for the **Runs** table. The **Plan** table beside it never got the same pass, and this is it, against the five names (`docs/CONVENTIONS.md`).

**Every column is defined, once, on its heading.** *What runs · Agent · Guard · Cost 7d · Last run · On* each say what they mean on the `<th>`; four of them said nothing at all, and one heading’s whole tooltip was the word `sort`.
