**The Guard’s hover was a copy of the Guard.** A native `title` holding the same words the cell had just drawn — the purest wasted hover on the page. It is an `AFTip` now (a guard is text and grows to a path plus a window), and it carries the only question a guard raises: **how many wake-ups it has actually saved**, out of how many, at what rate, and the runs and cost that got through.

**Three cells had no hover at all.**
- **Agent** — now says what this page already knows about that agent: how many definitions on the page run as it, how many of those are switched on, its runs and its cost over 7 days with **this row’s share** beside each, and the working folder when the row sets one. Every figure summed off rows already on screen — no second query.
- **Cost 7d** — the total, the runs, and the figure the reader was being left to work out: **per run**. Plus the skipped wake-ups, and the sentence that has to be there when a row has runs and no money behind it: the engine bills a plan and publishes no price, which is not the same claim as “free”.
- **Last run** — the exact moment in both clocks (local and UTC, like every other time in the extension), what happened that time, and the 7-day run count. A row that has **never** run now says what “never” means for *that* row — due at a time, already overdue, or simply never launched.

**MIRROR, where it was most missing.** The on/off switch is a bare coloured square: its hover now opens on **what it currently is**, then when it fires next, then what pressing it would do. A row with no switch says why it has none. And the ▸ triangle says which way it is pointing and **what is behind it** — how many setup fields, how many steps, whether there is a prompt — instead of the word “details”.

**Launch stopped repeating itself.** The cell was carrying a two-line explanation under *every* row; the explanation lives on the heading, so the cell now carries figures — engine, model, **effort and permissions**, each naming the launcher’s default where the definition sets nothing.

**Two real defects found on the way:**

- **`Started: undefined` in the Runs table’s *Took* panel.** `'Started: ' + x || '—'` reads as `('Started: ' + x) || '—'`, which is never falsy — so a run with no matching event drew the word `undefined` rather than an em dash. Both lines fixed.
- **The Runs table’s Cost cell had no hover at all** when a price *was* published — the last bare cell in that table. It now carries the cost, the tokens, the effective rate per million tokens and the cost per minute, and says plainly that it is an API-equivalent at your `agentFarm.pricing` rates, never a bill.

**A derived rate is no longer rounded to `$0.00`.** The column formatter is two decimals wide, which is right for a column and wrong for anything divided: cost per run of a cheap schedule, cost per minute. Those print to as many places as it takes to be a real figure — the page spends enough effort elsewhere refusing to let a zero read as “free”.

## 3.190.0 — M-24: the prompts you saved, in the form that writes prompts (2026-08-20)

**The Console has had this since S-11: right-click a send button and the phrases you keep get pasted at the caret.** The New-task form asks the same question in four more boxes — the task’s own prompt, the retry prompt, the continuation prompt and a workflow step’s prompt — and had none of it. Those are the prompts nobody is sitting in front of when they run, so a wording that was got right once and then retyped from memory costs more here, not less.

**Right-click any of those four boxes and the same window opens.** Same list, same filter, same *✎ Edit the file* and *📁 Change file…*, same rule that a pick is **pasted** and never sent. Left-click is untouched everywhere.

**It is the SAME window, not a second one** (`media/afSnippets.js`). The picker was lifted out of `media/console.js` whole and the Console now uses the component; the three messages behind it are answered in one place too (`promptSnippetMessage` in `src/panels/base.ts`), so the file dialog’s rules cannot drift between two surfaces. It ships to every page, like the hover panel and the query grammar do — a component a page has to opt into is the component the next prompt box does without.

**The window hangs off the body rather than off the page.** Every page redraws its own `#app`, and this page repaints on every host push: a picker living inside the form would be taken away by a task finishing somewhere else.

**And the paste is recorded the way a keystroke is.** It fires the same `input` event, so the composer’s own listener writes it into the draft — no page needs a callback to stay in step with itself.

**‼️ M-21 (part) — one box on this form was never doing that.** Every field records itself as it is touched, because the page repaints on every host push and a form that lived only in the DOM would lose a half-written prompt to a task somewhere else finishing. **The continuation prompt was read at submit time and nowhere else**: type one, wait for any push, and it was silently gone — the longest text on the card, and the one that only matters when nobody is watching. It is wired now.

**The filter box in the picker offers the query grammar**, which it never did on the Console either — the sweep that requires it was passing at file level because the page around it had other boxes that did.

## 3.189.0 — M-21 (part): the Tasks page — where “New task” lives, and what a run burned (2026-08-20)

**“New task” was on the wrong bar, and invisible from the tab you think on.** It sat in the **Runs** filter row next to `Cancel queued` and `Clear finished` — things you do TO a list of runs — while the form it opens is a planning act. Worse: from the **Plan** tab, the one page you are on while deciding what to set up, there was no way to start one. It is now on the page’s own bar beside 📊 Analytics, reachable from either tab; the composer already moves the tab under itself, so pressing it from Plan lands on the form.

**The Runs table could tell you a run took four minutes and not what those four minutes burned.** Tokens are the figure EVERY engine publishes and the only spend figure three of the four have — and they were on no surface of this page: the Cost column borrowed them for the plan-billed engines and hid them for Claude. **Tokens is a column now**, sortable, beside Cost. Each answers one question (ONE SUBJECT): this one what was spent, Cost what it was worth. A plan-billed engine’s Cost is an honest empty rather than `$0.00`, which reads as “free”, and its heading says where the tokens went instead.

**The rate moved with them.** “… tokens a minute” was in the *Took* panel; how fast something spent is a fact about the spending, and one fact belongs in one panel.

**‼️ This is part of M-21, not the whole of it.** The item asks for the entire Tasks page to be swept, functionally and in its UI, and the rest of what it names is filed as its own work: saved prompts on right-click in every composer prompt box (M-24), the page’s tooltips brought up to the five design principles (M-25), and the sweep itself — placements, state mismatches, stuck states, edge cases — which stays on M-21.

## 3.188.0 — K-28: resuming an OpenCode session stops inventing a model change (2026-08-20)

**A red line on every resume, for a change nobody asked for:** *error OpenCode refused the model change — session/set_config_option: Invalid params: model not found: big-pickle — {"providerId":"big-pickle","modelId":"big-pickle"}*.

**Two spellings of one model, and the Console compared them raw.** OpenCode names a model `provider/model` and `session/load` reports `opencode/big-pickle`. Its own **export** does not: `info.model` is `{ id: "big-pickle", providerID: "opencode", variant: "default" }` — measured on this machine’s cached exports — so an indexed transcript carries the bare id. A resumed card therefore asked for `big-pickle`, the live connection said `opencode/big-pickle`, the two did not match, and `applyOpencodeConfig` read that as “the user changed the model” and sent the bare id. The engine had never published that name, so it refused it — every time.

**The wanted value is now resolved against the engine’s OWN option list before anything is compared or sent.** Already published → itself. The tail of exactly one published value → that one, which is the completion the export made necessary. The tail of several → refused, never guessed: two providers offering the same model is a real shape and picking one by luck would quietly answer with a different engine’s model. Not offered at all → refused here, with a line naming what was asked and what the session is actually on, instead of a round trip that could only come back “model not found”.

**So a resume on the model it is already on sends nothing at all** — and the card takes the engine’s spelling, so the model picker has a selected row instead of a name that is in no list.

## 3.187.0 — K-27: “last turn interrupted” after turns nobody interrupted (2026-08-20)

**The strip above the composer said `⎋ last turn interrupted` on turns the agent had finished normally.** No Stop was pressed, the reply was complete, and the Console called it an interruption anyway — on Antigravity most visibly, and on three other engines for the same reason.

**`error_during_execution` is CLAUDE CODE’s word, and its one meaning there is “a person stopped it.”** Every translator that needed to report a failure of its own had reached for the nearest-looking Claude subtype, and inherited a verdict it never meant: Antigravity’s adaptor mapped *any* not-`SUCCESS` run to it, Codex’s `turn.failed` did, Gemini’s error result did, and so did OpenCode’s refusal and its two ceilings.

**Measured on this machine’s own Antigravity conversations before changing anything:** 25 of 67 turns ended not-`SUCCESS`, and every single one carried a **tool’s** complaint — 14× `exec: "grep": executable file not found in %PATH%`, 9× a schedule-task conflict, 2× a task that had already finished — with the agent’s reply already written. (That schedule-conflict line is the one seen in the console flow and wondered about: it is this, not a transcript problem.)

**A translator now SAYS which it is, and is believed.** `interrupted` is stated on the result rather than guessed from a subtype; only an event that does not answer falls back to Claude’s word, which is the engine that owns it. OpenCode’s `cancelled` says `true` — it is the one ending in the fleet that really is a Stop — and refusals, ceilings, engine faults and tool faults say `false`.

**And an Antigravity turn is now closed by what it PRODUCED.** It answered → the turn is done, and the engine’s complaint rides on the closing line as the warning it is, in the engine’s own words, exactly where it was drawn before. It produced nothing → the turn really did fail, and says so.

**The other half of the pair, which had never worked:** a real Stop on a per-turn engine kills the process, so no `result` line is ever read — `lastTurn` kept whatever the turn **before** it had put there and the strip described a turn two turns old. A turn that ends that way now records its own outcome, and the caller passes the word rather than the code guessing it.

## 3.186.0 — U-75: resuming an Antigravity conversation stops eating its own transcript (2026-08-20)

**A transcript whose “turn 1” was a turn from the middle.** Reopening a resumed Antigravity session showed a page that began with a stray paragraph under no turn heading, then “Tur 1” — a turn that had a couple of dozen turns before it. Resume it once more and most of what was left went too.

**It was not the engine and it was not the viewer: the record was being overwritten with a window onto itself.** `external-console-transcripts/<id>.json` is the only transcript in the farm written as a whole file out of memory — every other engine appends to a log it owns — and it is written from the Console card’s own message list. A resume rebuilds that list from the **last ~150 messages** of the very same file (`historyWindowIndices`), the next turn writes the card back over the file, and everything above the window is gone. Measured on the reported conversation: 292 rows on record starting at `xh221`, under a head row still saying “↑ 221 older message(s) are in the transcript” — they were not; that row **was** the stray paragraph at the top, and the message under it was the false “Tur 1”.

**A write MERGES now.** The record is kept whole and stays first; the card contributes only rows the record does not have, matched by message id, so the merge is safe to run on every write and on a card that took over a seat. Rows the card **read back** out of the record are dropped — the record already holds them, in the form they were written in — unless there is no record to merge into, in which case they are all the history there is and they are kept. Sentences **about** a read (“↑ 412 older message(s)…”, “— read back from the transcript · resumed here —”) are true of one reading of one file at one moment and are never written down at all. `startedAt` comes off the record too: a conversation that began on Tuesday is no longer filed as having started when somebody reopened it.

**Only Antigravity could have this bug**, and the answer is structural rather than a guess: `farmConsoleTranscript` is `agy`-only, and Claude, Codex, Gemini and OpenCode are read from append-only logs their own engines write, which a Console card cannot shorten.

**What was already lost is still on disk and is not restored by this.** Antigravity’s own step log for that conversation holds 35 user turns against the record’s 17, so the head can be recovered — as its own piece of work, because joining two differently-shaped sources is not something to bolt onto the write path.

## 3.185.0 — U-73: the Live Timeline's tooltips stop flickering (2026-08-20)

**A tooltip that opens and closes while the pointer sits perfectly still.** The Live Timeline rewrites `#app` whole on every data event **and** every five seconds, so the wrapper under the pointer is destroyed and rebuilt — and a browser does not put `:hover` back on the node that replaced the one you were on until you move again.

**The component already had a bridge for exactly this, and it only knew about one kind of panel.** It watches the ordinary path's state (`af-on`), while every trigger on the Live Timeline is `tip-free` — a panel that is taken out of the flow and placed by its own placer. So a free panel's wrapper went, `openW` became an orphan, the panel closed, nothing reopened it, and the next redraw did it again. **A `tip-free` panel is now re-opened on the node that replaced its trigger, re-placed from real measurements, and put back at the line the reader had scrolled to.**

**‼️ And the other half of the same bug, which was the ordinary bridge being too eager:** `af-on` shows a panel with **no delay at all**, and it was being applied to free wrappers too — so a redraw that landed while the pointer was still inside a free trigger's opening wait **flashed the panel open**, unplaced, in the corner of the window. Each kind of panel is now put back by its own bridge and by nothing else.

**Deferring the page's own redraws was the other way out, and it is worse:** a live page that stops telling the truth while you rest a pointer on it is a page that lies. The panel is what has to survive, and it survives in the component rather than in each page.

## 3.184.0 — U-76: Copy Corpus — what that point said, in one click (2026-08-20)

**The gesture that existed was four steps long.** Left-click a dot on the Live Timeline, the viewer opens on that exact moment, find the step's copy button, press it — two clicks and a lost place, for one line of text somebody wanted to paste into a message.

**Right-click a dot or a tool bar and the menu opens with `Copy Corpus`.** It copies what that step's own copy button copies: a tool step's payload is its **input**, everything else says what it has to say in its **text** — the same rule as the viewer, stated once, so a shortcut cannot become a second and quieter answer to the same question.

**It reads the TRANSCRIPT, not the chart.** The event store shortens what it keeps and flattens its newlines, so copying that would have handed over a clipped one-line version of a prompt while looking like the whole thing. The file has the whole thing. The entry is absent — rather than present and unable to answer — on a lane with no transcript behind it, and the receipt says what was copied and how big it was.

**On the bridge as `timeline.corpus`** (`file`, `ts`), which is the same question an agent asks without a clipboard to ask it through. Both doors go through one function; nobody re-parses a transcript of their own.

## 3.183.0 — U-78: the Live Timeline shows both sides of the conversation (2026-08-20)

**A transcript with one speaker in it.** Every point on the page could say what was ASKED and none of them what came back. The page had known how to draw a reply since U-67 — the body is quoted as speech, the legend is derived from the same table — but the text never arrived: `Stop` was pushed with no detail at all, and an agent's reply had no event kind to arrive as, so it was dropped or fell into the `notify` box.

**`say` is a first-class event now, and there are two sources because there are two kinds of session:**
- **A hosted conversation is Agent Farm's own**, so each reply is mirrored in as it arrives, and the turn's last one rides on its `Stop` — a turn end says what the turn ANSWERED, not only how long it took.
- **Claude fires its own hooks and none of them carries the assistant's text.** So at a turn end the reply is read from the **tail** of the transcript the hook already names — a quarter of a megabyte, which is comfortably more than the last lines of any turn and a cost nobody notices. A sidechain line is a subagent talking to itself and is skipped; a `text` block from before the last real user prompt belongs to a previous turn and is not claimed.

**Nothing is invented.** A reply with no text draws no point, and a turn end with nothing to quote is exactly what it was before: its duration and its tool count.

**‼️ And the reply is no longer drawn in the tool's colour.** Green is what a TOOL is on this page — the bars above the axis, the badge, the running segment — so a green dot for a reply put two subjects in one colour and gave the legend two entries nobody could tell apart. A tenth hue was not the answer either (the theme publishes eight chart colours and all eight are spoken for; a literal reads on one theme and not the other). **A reply is the other side of a prompt, so it is the same blue and the opposite fill:** a filled dot is what you said, a hollow ring is what came back.

## 3.182.0 — U-74: a hover panel yields to the hand (2026-08-20)

**A tooltip was standing in front of a control and the control could not be used.** `Console` in the toolbar is one button that drops a two-item menu **under itself**, in exactly the place its own hover panel opens. Reach for the button and the panel is already there; press it and the panel **stays** — the pointer never left the trigger, so `:hover` never ended — with the menu behind it.

**A panel answers a question the reader has while they are LOOKING.** The moment they stop looking and start WORKING it has nothing left to say and everything to be in the way of. So `media/afTip.js` now does this for every hover surface in the extension, with nothing asked of the page:

- **A press mutes the trigger under it**, with no fade and no box, until the pointer **leaves that wrapper**. Coming back is a new hover and waits the full delay again — a panel that reopens under a hand mid-gesture is the bug, not the fix.
- **A press INSIDE the panel is exempt.** Selecting a line of a prompt is reading, not leaving.
- **A key does the same** — Escape, or typing anywhere: the pointer is only resting.
- **A trigger you can press opens slower** (.6s against the ordinary .25s; 700ms against 420ms on `tip-free`), so aiming at a control and pressing it never sees a panel at all. Written from what the pointer is actually on — a `button`, an `a[href]`, a menu item, or anything carrying `data-aftipact`.
- **A control whose own list is open has nothing to explain**: `data-aftip-mute` is now honoured on the ordinary panel as well as on `tip-free`, and the claimed nav button uses it, so coming back to `Console` while its menu is down stays silent.

**And the menu itself was broken, which nothing had noticed.** Wrapping the button in a hover panel made the menu the WRAPPER's sibling rather than the button's, and the handler still looked at `parentElement` — so `Console ▾` opened nothing at all. It opens now, and says so in `aria-expanded`.

**‼️ This is a design principle, not a fix to one button:** `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` → "Hover" now opens with it, and it is the first question when a new hover surface is designed — *what will the reader press under this, and will the panel be gone before their hand arrives?*

New: `node test/live_header.js [--check]` — the real header running in a real browser, because `:hover` needs a pointer no string test has. It is what caught this release's own second defect: the mute rule lost the cascade to `:not(.tip-free)` (which counts as a class) while every string assertion passed.

## 3.181.0 — U-67: Live Timeline tooltips streamlined per Design Principles (2026-08-20)

**The lane header and timeline points each answer for their own role (ONE SUBJECT & DENSITY):**
- **Lane Header (Gutter) as Session Overview:** Displays the comprehensive session identity card — including the **opening prompt (purpose)** whole and quoted, agent, engine, model, session ID, project, folder (`cwd`), totals (tokens, cost, duration, turns, tools), and live PID/status.
- **Dialogue / Turn Points:** Focus purely on the conversation text without repeating duplicate session identity headers on every dot. Shows what was sent/requested whole, the turn number, clock time, and interval.
- **Tool Spans:** Kept short, concise, and clean. Displays the tool name, run duration, target (file/command), and explicit failure/error if any, without bloated multi-paragraph JSON/stdout dumps.

## 3.180.0 — X-49: a queued item can say who should take it — engine, model, effort (2026-08-20)

**The queue was written when there was one engine.** `target` answers "which repo or which agent", and with five engines the question an item could not answer was *which engine, on which model, at what effort* — so a task could only ever be told "do the queue", never "do the work meant for me and leave the rest".

**Three optional axes now sit beside `target`: `engine` · `model` · `effort`.** They are set when the item is captured, changed later from the row or with `queue.route`, and filtered on in `queue.list`. Each axis moves **on its own** — filling one in from a row never wipes what somebody set from the other surface — and `""` unclaims one.

**‼️ AN EMPTY AXIS IS A REAL ANSWER, NOT A MISSING ONE:** the item does not care. That is why nothing is defaulted at capture: a value invented here would be indistinguishable from one the user chose. So "the work for me, and the work nobody claimed" is **two** questions and two calls (`engine:"codex"`, then `engine:"(none)"`), while omitting the axis is a third thing — every item, claimed or not.

**Nothing is dispatched from a route.** The queue does not start work and this does not make it start any; it is a hint the task prompt reads to pick its own share out of the pile.

On the page: three placeholder selects that ask for nothing — `— engine —`, `— model —`, `— effort —`, in the row and in the capture box, in the manner of the Backlog capture box's own `— area —`. **They narrow each other**, because the engine decides what the other two can mean: no engine means no model box (a model without an engine names nothing), an engine with no effort setting draws no effort box rather than an empty one, and the choices come from the same `launch` contract the Tasks form reads — two surfaces disagreeing about what `codex` can run is the bug S-20 was filed for. A claimed item wears the engine's own badge with its model and effort beside it; an unclaimed one says so in the row's hover. The filter strip gains **Engines**, with "(none)" in the list as a first-class choice.

## 3.179.0 — U-67: every point on the Live Timeline says what happened there (2026-08-20)

**The page's whole subject is which conversation is doing what, and it could only ever be asked about the ROW.** A dot was a native `<title>` reading `prompt — p1 (14:23)`: a kind, ninety characters and a clock. What a person hovers a dot for is the moment itself — which conversation, what was actually said, what came back, where in the talk it fell — and that is TEXT, so it is an `AFTip`.

**Every dot and every tool bar is now a panel of its own**, and they all answer the same four questions in the same order, so the eye learns the shape once: **who** (the conversation's own name, the agent, the engine, the model), **what was said** (the prompt whole and quoted, the command a tool was given, what it answered), **where in the talk** (the clock, the turn number, and the gap back to the previous point on that session), and **what pressing it does** (click opens the transcript at that moment; right-click gives the session's actions). The point that closes a turn says what the turn cost: how long it ran and how many tool calls it made.

**‼️ AND THERE IS SOMETHING TO READ, because the store now keeps it.** An event kept ninety characters of what was said, which is a row's worth and not a panel's; prompts, permission messages and tool inputs keep 1,200 now. `PostToolUse` carries the tool's **response**, which was thrown away entirely — a bar could say that a tool ran and never what it answered, and "it ran" and "it worked" are different facts. A failure says so first. The session's own `lastPrompt` stays short: it is drawn on cards, where the row is the whole space there is. Points recorded before this build have no answer to show and say so rather than showing an empty heading.

**The panels are blocks, not a list of lines.** A panel that answers four questions and runs them together into one paragraph is a wall, which is what this item was reopened for; each block is its own subject with a blank line between, and a block with nothing in it is dropped whole rather than left as a heading over silence. The row's own panel no longer repeats the name that is already its head, and it carries figures only — what was said at a moment belongs to the point it was said at (ONE SUBJECT).

Under it: the drawing carries no data and no hover at all any more. Each trigger is a transparent HTML box laid over the SVG — `.chartbox svg` is `width:100%; height:auto` on a viewBox, so a percentage of the wrapper **is** the SVG's own coordinate — and that one box is the hover, the click and the right-click together, so a dot cannot disagree with its own panel about which session it means. A dot's box is wider than the dot is drawn and lights up as a circle.
## 3.177.0 — K-9: the writing box stays where it was dragged, and stops growing (2026-08-19)

**This was closed once and came back, so the fault was in the arrangement, not the wording.** The height a drag sets is an INLINE style on the textarea, and both pages that have one rewrite their whole markup — so the height had to be *put back by hand* after every rebuild, and whatever ran between the two won instead. That is why it looked random: whether it survived depended on what happened to repaint next, and on the Console only some things repaint.

**The height is `--af-boxh` on the document root now** — the one element no rebuild reaches — so a new box is already the right size the moment it exists. There is nothing to restore and therefore nothing to lose. The fallback is `auto`, so a box that was never dragged still takes its height from the layout exactly as before.

**‼️ AND THE CEILING IS ENFORCED WHERE THE NUMBER IS STORED.** That is the half that was missing, and the reason the box crept: the figure goes back into storage, so one value let through above `max-height` is read back as the new normal — the box snapped back a little taller every time, until it could cover the page. It is clamped on the way in and on the way out, against the same 70% of the window the stylesheet states. A ceiling only the stylesheet knows is not a ceiling.

Two smaller pieces of the same fault: the observer watching for a drag is **stopped** when its box is replaced (one left alive holds the height *its* box had and writes it into the same slot), and the value is stored as a **number** rather than a css string, so there is one thing to compare and clamp. A narrower window lowers the box with it and gives the dragged height back when it widens.

It is one mechanism for both boxes — `AFTextTools.keepHeight`, beside the four text tools they already share. These were the same eight lines twice; the Backlog tab's capture box, which repaints on a filter chip, a tab, an area, a queue position and every host push, had the identical defect waiting.

## 3.176.0 — U-67: a swim lane finally says which CONVERSATION it is (2026-08-19)

**The row's hover opened with the agent and never named the session.** "developer · 3f8a1c2b · working", on the one page whose entire subject is which conversation is doing what. It was also a native `<title>` — the wrong surface for what a lane has to say, since a prompt, a name and a path are TEXT and a platform tooltip repeats what is already drawn and then stops wherever it likes.

**It is an `AFTip` now**, and the panel's head is the **conversation's own name**, in full: the row is cut to thirteen characters, so the long form belongs in the hover (SHORTHAND). A packed track says so there too — "+2 earlier sessions on this row" — rather than naming one of them and implying the row is it. Under the head, per session: the agent, the id and status, **the prompt it is on right now** (a different fact from the name it was given, and on a long session they stop agreeing after turn one), its money, its work, its clock, its pid and its folder. A session with no title yet says *that*, in those words — an absent line reads as an absent session.

**‼️ HOW HTML GOT ONTO AN SVG.** An `AFTip` is HTML and an `<svg>` cannot hold HTML, so the trigger is a transparent HTML box laid over the gutter: `.chartbox svg` is `width:100%; height:auto` on a viewBox, so the drawing scales with no letterboxing and a percentage of the wrapper **is** the SVG's own coordinate. That box carries the row's **click and right-click** as well — one element answering for the label instead of two that can disagree about which session they mean — and it wears the hover highlight the SVG's own `:hover` used to give.

One thing this found on the way: `statLines` builds the weighted-token figure as a `<span>` with a hover of its own, which is right on a card and is a wall of escaped markup inside a panel whose body is text. It takes `plain` and returns the existing plain-text twin — not a stripped copy, which would have been a second answer to "how many tokens".

## 3.175.0 — X-47: no spawn of this extension's can flash a console window any more, and it is measured (2026-08-19)

**The extension host is a windowless process, so every console program it starts gets a console of its own** — a black rectangle that appears and disappears over whatever the user was looking at — unless the spawn asks for `windowsHide`. Three calls did not ask: the two `taskkill`s that end a task's process tree and the one that ends a session, all written as `exec`, which is a `cmd.exe` with a console around the thing being run. They are `execFile` with `windowsHide` now, killing exactly the same tree with the same `/T /F`.

**‼️ And the rule is now measured rather than remembered.** `test_no_console_flash.js` reads every child-process call in `src/` — through the source with comments and string literals stripped, and matching each call's OWN argument list by balanced parentheses rather than "the next few hundred characters" — and fails the build if one does not pass `windowsHide`. Three files are exempted by name, each with the reason a window is the POINT of it: the external terminal, revealing a file in Explorer, and launching the app the user chose to open a document with.

**What this does not fix, stated plainly:** the two paths that actually run Antigravity — the model-catalog fetch at startup and the per-turn spawn — were already hidden, and still are. If a window still flashes when `agy` starts, it belongs to a process `agy.exe` starts for itself, which nothing on this side can suppress.

## 3.174.0 — X-48: two more orderings for the backlog, and the widening has a way back (2026-08-19)

**A backlog line carries no clock.** What it says, when it was written down and when it was last worked on are three different questions and the document answers none of them — the **track ledger** does, because every add, touch, state change and reopen is stamped there to the second. So the page can now order by:

- **opened** — what was written down last. The first thing the ledger ever recorded about that code.
- **last touched** — what was worked on last. The most recent record of any kind.

They are deliberately two orderings and not one: an item written down in June and worked on yesterday sits at opposite ends of them, and that is the fact worth seeing. Both obey the rule `closed` already obeys — an item the ledger cannot date stays **behind** the dated ones in either direction, because "never recorded" is not "recorded long ago". The **date deciding the order is drawn on the row** (🌱 opened · ✎ touched) and nowhere else: an order nobody can check is a list taken on trust, and three date marks on every row of a two-hundred-line backlog is the opposite mistake. The hover carries both figures whichever is showing.

**‼️ `touched` is honestly "last worked on".** Rewording a line in Obsidian without moving its checkbox is not an event the ledger sees, and the hover says so rather than promising a per-item file-modification time nothing measures.

**The ordering box was also reordered.** The three that answer a question about TIME now sit together under the user's own queue order — that is what a long backlog is asked after "what is next" — and the two that are pure lookup, **alphabetical** then **code**, are last.

**And the widening that "closed" does now has a way back.** Choosing `closed` opens the state axis so the answer is not an empty list; returning to queue order with it still open leaves finished work sitting in the list that answers "what is next", which is the one thing that ordering is for. Queue order restores **Active** (open + doing) and says so on the page — a filter the reader cannot see change is one they cannot undo.

On the bridge, `projects.backlog` takes `sort: file|closed|opened|touched` and every item carries `openedAt` / `touchedAt`.

## 3.173.0 — S-40: the Turns page is the whole farm, not the two engines that happened to build turns (2026-08-19)

**The page said "every user turn across the farm" and listed two engines.** Not because it filtered the others out — because they were never in the data. `buildTurnRows` maps over `SessionInfo.turns`, and three of the five adaptors left that array empty, which does not produce a thin row: it produces **no row**. And the engine picker's options are derived from the rows present, so the missing engines were missing from the filter for exactly the same reason. Measured on this machine after the fix: **48 Antigravity conversations, 15 hosted Antigravity sessions and 122 OpenCode conversations** now unroll into turns that were on disk the whole time.

Each adaptor opens a turn on the boundary its own format states, and bills into it only what that format actually says:

| engine | what opens a turn | what the turn can prove |
|---|---|---|
| Gemini | a `user` record with text | its own reply's tokens, weighted tokens, price and model; `apiCalls` per reply |
| Antigravity (brain log) | `USER_INPUT` | tool calls, planner prose, failures, duration — **no tokens and no price, because the engine publishes none** |
| Antigravity (hosted here) | a `user` line that is not `steer` | the Console's own `result` row: that turn's tokens, dollars and milliseconds |
| OpenCode | a message with text, or an attachment-only one named by its file | the assistant message's own spend, `step-finish` as the round trip, `reasoning` counted apart, and the window it ended holding |

**‼️ The number has to be the SAME number.** A row folds open by asking the *viewer* for `turn === n`. Index and viewer therefore have to count the same file the same way or a fold quietly shows somebody else's prompt — so what opens a Gemini turn is now one exported function both of them call, and `test_engine_turns.js` parses every fixture **both ways** and holds the two together.

Two rules the new figures obey and one trap they avoid: a figure the format does not carry stays at an **honest zero** rather than being split out of the session total; `reasoning` is added to output on OpenCode exactly as the session total does it, because it is not inside `output` on that engine; and a **steering line does not move the turn's clock** — it sits inside the open turn, but it arrives after the engine has already said how long that turn took.

## 3.172.0 — U-72: the OpenCode badge is the blue the user chose (2026-08-19)

**A hue picked by hand is written down as itself.** OpenCode's engine badge is now `rgb(60, 135, 255)` — a literal, not a `--vscode-charts-*` variable, because the point of a value somebody chose is that a theme cannot move it. Every other engine still reads its hue from VS Code's own chart palette.

The palette test required that *every* engine resolve a VS Code variable, which is a real rule and would have refused this. It now names the exception: the ids allowed to hold a literal are listed, and each is checked against the exact value that was picked — so a sixth engine cannot arrive with a colour of its own without somebody saying whose decision that was.

## 3.171.0 — U-69: the Turns table is a table again, and Turns is reached from Sessions (2026-08-19)

**Turns leaves the global toolbar for the place it is actually about.** It is the same subject as Sessions one level down — a session unrolled into the turns it is made of — so it is reached from beside **⤢ Open Sessions page**, as **⤢ Open Turns page**, where somebody is already looking at sessions.

**And the table itself was doing the one thing this codebase's own conventions forbid.**

| | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| widths | `table-layout: auto` — every boundary a function of whichever rows happened to be listed | declared shares + a `<colgroup>`, so the table is the same table after every filter |
| Steps | the widest numeric column, holding whitespace | 6.6% — `31api·84steps` is already the short form |
| Tokens | narrower than its own value, so `412.9k ⚖ 168.3k` wrapped and the row grew a line | 8.2%, and it fits |
| rows | as tall as the worst wrap | one line, cut at the column's own edge |
| a cell's hover | the SAME twenty-line readout of the whole turn, pasted onto twelve cells | that cell's own value in full on the first line, then the figures it implies |
| a heading's hover | a paragraph in a native `title`, cut wherever the platform liked | an `AFTip`: the column's full name, then its definition |

**‼️ The first line of a cell's panel is that cell, spelled out.** That is what makes cutting safe: a number the column could not finish is one hover from being read in full, and it is drawn at reading size rather than as a faded caption. Under it, after a rule, are the figures that value already implies — Steps now says its API calls, its steps per call and the share of them that was **reasoning**, which is the dearest step there is and was nowhere on this page.

The two columns that hold WORDS keep the shape text needs: the caption names the column and the body opens with the whole prompt, then the figures. And the row lost its own `title` — with every cell opening a panel, a native tooltip underneath was a second hover on top of the first; the hint lives once in the caption, exactly as the sessions table already keeps it.

Two things this cost, both now guarded: a cell that clips its own overflow clips the hover panel inside it (the cut moved to an inner block), and a backtick inside a CSS template literal is a syntax error no text-reading test can see (`test_turns.js` now parses the page).

## 3.170.0 — U-68: the row that is on every page finally says what it opens (2026-08-19)

**A dozen destinations, most of them one word, and not one of them said where it went.** The global toolbar was the one control shared by every page and the one control with no hovers at all — and it had also run out of width, so it wrapped onto a second line and moved under the pointer. Both halves are the same fix.

**Every button in the row now carries an `AFTip` whose FIRST line is its own full name**, then one sentence saying what that page is for — the row where text gets cut is the row that must state its long form (SHORTHAND + MIRROR). A `tip` is now part of a nav entry's definition; a destination added without one is an unfinished one, and the test says so by name.

**Five of them are drawn as their icon alone**, at a fixed 24px so the cluster's right edge stops moving from page to page: **🧪 Evals · ⌕ Search · ⚙ Settings · ⟳ Refresh · ? Guide**. They are identical on every page and in the same order, so nobody reads them — they are aimed at. Each keeps an `aria-label`, because a name that is not on screen has to be in the accessibility tree and not only in a hover.

A **related** button pointing at a page the row already knows inherits that page's sentence rather than restating it, and one that carries a shortened label (`⚖ Sync Cons.`) states its long form on the panel's first line. A **claimed** nav button — where a page has made "Console" mean *talk to THIS agent* — says its own name, then what this page made it mean, then that it is still a menu with the plain destination under it.

Measured on the dashboard at 1400px: the cluster was on two rows and is now on one.

## 3.169.0 — U-71: pressing a backlog code on the Track tab stays in the extension (2026-08-19)

**The cheap answer was behind a right-click and the expensive one was the default.** Pressing a code on Track left for Obsidian; "Show it in the Backlog tab" — the same item, on the next tab of the page already open, where it can be edited, moved and closed — was a menu entry most readers never saw. The two have swapped:

| | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| left click on the code | opens the document | **shows it on the Backlog tab**, narrowed to that code |
| ↗ beside the code | opens the document | unchanged |
| right-click | *Open the backlog at this item* · *Show it in the Backlog tab* | *Open the backlog document at this item's line*, in the slot the other line held |

The narrowing is written into the Backlog's own **search box** rather than a hidden focus variable, so the reader can see why they are being shown one item and can clear it in one press; `states` is cleared with it, because an item whose whole history somebody was just reading is very often closed, and landing them on an empty list would be the worst possible answer. The small code chips in **No history at all** behave the same way — a code is a code on every view of this page.

## 3.168.0 — X-52: OpenCode's model box stops waiting for somebody to open a session (2026-08-19)

**Choosing OpenCode offered `haiku / sonnet / opus / fable` — four names its CLI can only reject.** The same shape of bug U-31 fixed on Antigravity, arrived at from the opposite direction: OpenCode's catalogue is genuinely free, because `session/new` answers with every model this machine can reach AND their display names. That made the handshake the cheapest source, so it was made the ONLY source — and every surface that draws a model box *without* opening a session was left on the alias fallback for ever. Writing tomorrow's task, saving a preset, looking at Settings: none of them start a conversation, and "start a session first" is not an answer a picker can give.

**The list now has two sources and neither waits for the other.**

| | source | when | carries |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `opencode models`, spawned in the background | 8 s after the window settles, then at most once per 6 h | ids only (`opencode/big-pickle`) |
| 2 | the `session/new` handshake | whenever a Console card opens | ids **and** display names |

A handshake list replaces a CLI one, because it knows the names; a CLI list that agrees with a handshake list only refreshes its age rather than flattening the labels. Either way a **changed** list redraws every open picker and an identical one redraws nothing.

**‼️ AND IT IS REMEMBERED ACROSS WINDOWS.** The point of the item is that the box is right *the moment it is drawn* — a fresh window draws its first picker long before an 8-second warm-up returns, so the catalogue is kept in `globalState` and is there at activation. The user's own case is the ordinary one: open VS Code, write a task for tomorrow, pick its model, close the window.

The picker also says which of the two it is reading, and how old that read is; with neither answered yet it still says it is the alias list and that this is almost certainly wrong for this engine. `{ "op": "engines.models", "args": { "refresh": true } }` now re-asks **both** `agy` and `opencode`, awaited, so the caller gets the new list rather than the one it was refreshing away from.

Measured on this machine: `opencode models` answers in 3.6 s with 7 models, exit 0 — and only with its stdin closed, the same handshake trap `agy models` taught us.

## 3.167.0 — X-40: the fifth engine's acceptance set is a file that RUNS, and it ran (2026-08-19)

**‼️ EVERY OpenCode FIXTURE IN THIS REPO IS WRITTEN AGAINST A TRANSCRIPT SOMEBODY ONCE CAPTURED.** Three and a half thousand lines of them pass on a translation layer that could still produce an empty Console against the binary that actually shipped — that is the exact failure X-15 wrote its Codex smoke to prevent, and OpenCode had no equivalent. `test/smoke_opencode_console.mjs` drives the REAL `ConsoleHost` with the REAL `opencode acp` process, and it proves the seven things X-40 names, in order:

| | proved on the live binary |
|---|---|
| 1 | a fresh turn carries a nonce the model could not have known — and a real `ses_…` id comes back |
| 2 | a SECOND turn on the SAME id recalls it: one conversation, not two runs |
| 3 | a second card in a different folder gets its own conversation under the SAME process |
| 4 | `session/cancel` mid-turn closes the turn and leaves the card usable and the conversation intact |
| 5 | a session created OUTSIDE, by `opencode run`, loads through ACP and is continued — it recalled a token said before Agent Farm ever saw it |
| 6 | the shared runtime is killed under the cards and they come back **on the same conversation** |
| 7 | none of it spends a cent |

**‼️ A SMOKE SET THAT QUIETLY BILLS THE USER IS A SMOKE SET NOBODY RUNS TWICE.** The model is chosen at run time from the connected provider's `*-free` list, the way the Engines page's Test button already does; with no free model on offer the set **refuses to run and says so** (`exit 2`) rather than falling back to a priced one.

**‼️ AND IT NEVER KILLS A PROCESS BY NAME.** "The runtime crashed" is produced by restarting the runtime **the host owns** — because `opencode.exe` on this machine may well be the user's own TUI, and killing that is the one thing this set must never do. Sessions live in a disposable folder under TEMP, only the `ses_` ids this run created are closed, and the user's own sessions, auth/config/provider files and open TUI are never read, written or killed.

**Two faults the set found in its first minute, which is the whole argument for having it.** A `ConsoleHost` built without the shared-ACP io answers every OpenCode card with *"this build was not given a way to start `opencode acp`"* — correct, and it would have made a smoke set prove nothing while looking like it ran; the set now wires the io exactly as `extension.ts` does. And a fresh card is `starting`, not `idle`: on this engine alone that status means real work (a handshake plus `session/new` over a shared connection), so the set waits for it instead of sending into a socket that is not open yet.

**The SOP now points at files, not at a list.** Its general closing matrix is unchanged; what was added is the rule that each engine's own acceptance set is a **runnable file** — `smoke_codex_console.mjs`, `smoke_agy_console.mjs`, `smoke_opencode_console.mjs` — with the three rules above stated once for whatever ships next.

README, both BLUEPRINTs and the cross-engine section were brought level: three engines in the sync table, the duty command lane, the third MCP suggestion, why skills are deliberately not copied, and the sentence about the walk stopping at the git worktree.

## 3.166.0 — X-39: the constitution reaches a fifth engine, and where it does not is now a thing you can read (2026-08-19)

**‼️ OpenCode's instruction walk STOPS AT THE GIT WORKTREE, and nothing in this build knew that.** The rule was read out of the shipped `opencode.exe` 1.18.18 — `Instruction.systemPaths` and `Filesystem.findUp`, verbatim — and then confirmed against the running binary: the names `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTEXT.md` are tried in that order, the first name that matches ANYWHERE wins outright, and for that name every file from the cwd up to the **worktree** is merged. So the shared constitution at the nest root arrives for free in the normal layout, and is **invisible** in exactly one case: an agent folder that is its own git repository. Every file present, every sync saying "in sync", and the rule simply not in the prompt. Measured on the real folders: all eight of this machine's agents reach it, and the lane writes nothing.

**Measured, in a live turn, with a free model, on the real `developer` folder:** asked which language it must use and what ZEN is, OpenCode answered *"(a) Türkçe — (b) Chrome Web Store'da yayınlanmış bir Chrome uzantısı"*. The shared constitution's rule and the agent's own identity, both applied, in one turn, from one file each.

**And where the walk cannot reach, the repair is one line and it is not written into a file that would carry this machine's paths.** `instructions: ["../AGENTS.md"]` goes into the agent's own `opencode.json` — **relative**, because that file travels with the repo — and the same fragment goes to the processes Agent Farm starts through `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` with an **absolute** path, because the environment never leaves the machine and a task may run with a `workDir` somewhere else entirely. Both forms were measured escaping the worktree; without either, the same tree answered "None".

**A config with comments in it is never rewritten.** `JSON.parse` drops comments and writing back would delete the user's own notes from the user's own file. Such a file is left byte-for-byte alone, and the note says what is still uncovered rather than implying it is handled.

**‼️ AND THE ONE THING IT DOES NOT COVER IS SAID OUT LOUD.** The Console's ACP runtime is ONE process for every card (X-38's 383 MB decision), so a process-wide variable cannot say something different per agent. The Console is covered by the file, not the environment — and when the file could not be written, the note says `Console cards are NOT covered` instead of letting a reader assume otherwise. A manual `opencode` started outside Agent Farm is outside all of it, and is named.

**`AGENTS.md` shadows `CLAUDE.md` on this engine, which means the Codex lane's file CHANGES what OpenCode reads.** That is the intended outcome; it stopped being a silent one.

**OpenCode is also loading a file nobody configured.** With no `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, its global slot falls back to the user's personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` — a file written for a different engine, in every OpenCode turn on this machine. `agents.sync` reports it (`globalInstruction`); Agent Farm does not write there.

**Duties get the engine's own equivalent, and skills get nothing on purpose.** A standing duty becomes `.opencode/command/<slug>.md`, invocable as `/slug` — with the body as the template, because OpenCode rejects a `template:` key in the frontmatter. Skills are **not** copied: OpenCode auto-loads `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, which is where these already live, and a copy would be a second set to keep in step for no gain.

**MCP is translated, not copied — the shapes genuinely differ.** `command` is an ARRAY (executable first), `type` is required (`local`/`remote`), and the env map is called `environment`. The result is a merge-ready `.opencode/mcp.suggested.json`; the live config is never edited. **No credential value leaves through a note, a toast or a bridge reply** — the note counts the servers that carry values instead of showing them, and a test asserts it.

**Insights reports the blind case**, because a rule nothing checks is not a rule: an agent whose OpenCode lane cannot see the constitution gets a line saying which worktree the walk stopped at.

**‼️ A free model's own token figures are not a measuring instrument, and this is recorded so nobody spends the afternoon again.** In one tree `tokens.input` read 615, 8526 and 13710 across three runs; four *different* trees returned the identical total 13671. Adding "if you cannot find one, answer NOTGIVEN" to a prompt made the model take the escape while it was demonstrably holding the file. The findings above stand on the decompiled source plus single-question live runs with no escape hatch — not on counters.

The two sync commands stop naming a subset of engines (`Sync Agent with the Other Engines…`): a static list is the thing that goes stale, and this one already had.

## 3.165.0 — S-39 is closed: twenty failures, one number, and none of them OpenCode's fault (2026-08-19)

**‼️ `failed: 20 · exported: 0` was a count with four possible causes and no way to tell which.** `session list` that would not run, `export` that would not run, an export whose output could not be found, and a write that threw — every one of them incremented the same integer, and none of them kept the reason. So the diagnosis had to be done by hand, outside the extension, because the extension had thrown away the only thing worth reading. Measured through the bridge on the running build first: **`roots 24 · listed 63 · exported 0 · failed 20 · inTable 2`**.

**‼️ Nine of this machine's roots were folders that no longer exist.** `learned` grows from the `directory` of every conversation a listing names, and **a conversation outlives its folder**: nine of them were `%TEMP%\af-oc-contract-*` directories a previous *measuring* run had created and deleted the moment it finished. Each one cost a two-second spawn that could only fail — and because the walk stops at `HARVEST_MAX_ROOTS`, a dead folder near the front was pushing a live one off the end of the list. They are dropped by a `stat` before anything spawns, and counted as `skippedRoots`, which is **not** a failure: it is a machine that has moved on, not an engine that is broken.

**‼️ And every export was being handed one of those dead folders as its working directory — which is the whole of `exported: 0`.** Measured against the real binary: OpenCode's store is machine-wide, and `opencode export <id>` run from an unrelated **live** folder returns a conversation whose own directory was deleted, in full — exit 0, valid JSON. The cwd only has to *exist*. It uses the conversation's own folder when that folder is still there, and a live root otherwise.

**The result, on the same machine, same roots, same conversations:**

| | roots | skipped | listed | exported | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 24 | — | 63 | **0** | **20** |
| after | 13 | 1 | 63 | **12** (the per-pass ceiling) | **0** |

A second pass exported twelve more; the cache went from 22 conversations to 46.

**A failure that is only ever counted cannot be fixed, so it is not only counted any more.** `failures[]` carries `{stage: list|export|read|write, where, reason}`, capped at eight — enough to see that the twentieth is the same sentence as the fourth without turning a background errand into a log file. Both surfaces report it: `sessions.opencodeSync` returns it, and the **Refresh OpenCode History** toast quotes one reason instead of saying `20 call(s) failed` and stopping there.

## 3.164.0 — B-12: closing a card promised a file on the one engine that keeps none (2026-08-19)

**‼️ `console.close` said "its transcript stays on disk and stays resumable" — and the first half is false on exactly the engine a reader would go hunting for a file on.** OpenCode keeps its conversations in SQLite and publishes no transcript; what it publishes is `session list` and `export`, so the history really is readable, through the CLI. Promising a path that does not exist is worse than saying nothing, and `noTranscriptNote` — the sentence the Console already prints — knew this. The contract asks it now, so the panel and the catalogue cannot disagree about one engine.

**And "resumable" without an id is not an answer.** The reply carries the engine, the `ses_…`/thread id, the exact `console.start { resume: … }` call that takes the conversation up again in its own seat, and where its history lives — a file this build can open, or the engine's own export command.

## 3.163.0 — B-12: three answers where the contract offered two, and a flag name that fails if you type it (2026-08-19)

**‼️ `engines.test` had a third answer since U-59 and the bridge contract described two.** Agent Farm will not pick a *billed* model for a health check, so on an engine whose cheapest turn depends on which providers are connected the check can come back `refused: true` — nothing spent, nothing proved. The page was taught that in 3.159.0 and given its own `⊘`; the contract still said "returns ok, how long it took, and the engine's own words when it failed", so an agent reading `ok:false` off a refusal reports a **working engine as broken**. That is the fault the page was fixed for, surviving on the surface agents actually read. Three states are now named, and a test asserts the function really returns the flag rather than the contract describing a wish.

**‼️ The fallback model list captioned every row with Claude's flag name — found by RUNNING the op, not by reading it.** `engines.models { id: "opencode" }` against the live bridge answered `haiku / sonnet / opus / fable`, each one *"passed as `--model`"*. The list itself is honest — OpenCode publishes its catalogue on the connection and no session had opened, which the note says out loud — but the caption was wrong on the three engines U-59 measured taking `-m`. The one moment a reader is told least about an engine was also the moment they were handed a flag that fails if they type it. The caption comes from `engineFlagFor` now: Claude `--model`, Codex `-m`, Gemini `-m`, Antigravity `--model`, OpenCode `-m`, each read back out of that engine's own argument builder.

**`sessions.end` said "the claude process" about an op that ends a session on any engine**, and `reports.cost` explained its Claude-only scope with the wrong reason — *"because a plan-billed engine states no price"*, which stopped being a rule the day a second engine started stating one. The scope is unchanged and real: that series is defined against Claude's transcript format and would read zero or read wrong on a foreign one. Saying the true reason keeps the sentence honest when the false one has expired.

**The stale-enum scan now covers every file that registers an op**, not the three that happened to be wrong — a subset typed into a contract is invisible until somebody reads that contract, so proving the fixed places stayed fixed proves nothing about the catalogue.

**Looked at with the real bridge.** `engine: "opencode"` was written and read back through `schedules.add/list/edit`, `templates.add/list`, `triggers.add/list/edit` and `workflows.add/step.add` on the running build: the engine and a provider-qualified model id (`opencode/big-pickle`) survive every trip, an effort is refused on all four write paths, and `engine: "opencodee"` is refused rather than quietly run on Claude. The same run is what caught the two faults above — and confirmed the one 3.162.0 fixes: `schedules.edit { permissionMode: "sudo" }` was accepted and stored by the build that was running.

## 3.162.0 — B-12: the catalogue an agent reads before it calls, brought level with the engine that already shipped (2026-08-19)

**‼️ `farm.ops` IS the contract, so a stale one is not cosmetic — it is an engine that cannot be reached.** Fourteen `describe` lines still spelt `claude|codex|gemini|agy` by hand long after the fifth engine had run end to end. A caller with a real OpenCode job reads the catalogue, concludes the engine is unsupported and never tries it — while `bridgeRunDimensions` would have accepted it and run it. The list is now `ENGINE_ENUM`, built off the registry, and a test refuses any contract that spells a SUBSET of the ids by hand.

**‼️ `console.send` promised steering on four engines that cannot be steered.** *"While a turn is running this goes INTO that turn"* is a persistent engine's answer; a per-turn run has its stdin closed and a shared-ACP run declares no mid-turn channel, so on both the message is HELD. The host had always done the right thing — the contract described a third of it, and a caller reading it waited for a redirect that could never arrive. The reply now says which happened and **why** (`heldBecause`), so "you asked me to hold it" and "this engine is deaf mid-turn" stop looking alike. `console.queue` says the same thing about releasing one.

**‼️ Stopping a turn is three different acts and the contract described one.** A persistent engine is interrupted over its control channel; a per-turn engine's turn IS its process, so the process ends; a shared-ACP engine is **asked** (`session/cancel`) because its process is shared with every other card and killing it would end their turns too. `console.interrupt` returns `how`.

**‼️ Claude's own permission sentence was Codex's.** `engineModeNote` routed `claude` to `codexModeNote`, so asking what a Claude session's mode meant answered *"Codex cannot stop and ask"* — the wrong engine's name on the wrong claim about the one engine that can. Nothing had reached that branch: every caller guarded it with `shape !== 'persistent'` first, and it surfaced the moment a contract asked every engine the same question.

**‼️ Real money was being dropped out of every project total.** `measured: !s.source` asked *"is this a Claude transcript"*, which was the same question as *"did the engine quote this price"* until OpenCode arrived publishing `cost` on the wire and in its headless JSONL. `engineQuotesPrice` asks the second one — and deliberately NOT via `engineOf(...).reportsCost`, which falls back to Claude for a name it has never heard of and would count a custom CLI profile's derived dollars as measured ones.

**A permission mode is now refused where it is written down, not at 3 a.m.** X-35 moved the engine-name check to write time and left the effort and permission VALUES behind, because `tasks.add` happens to call `validateLaunch` afterwards and a schedule, a trigger, a template and a workflow step do not: `schedules.add { permissionMode: "sudo" }` was stored happily and failed hours later with nobody watching. Same list, same words, asked earlier.

**And the engine `schedules.add` has always accepted is finally named in its contract** — the handler read it through `bridgeRunDimensions`, `schedules.edit` named it, and this one listed every other dimension. Every read-back (`tasks.get`, `schedules.list`, `triggers.list`, `templates.list`) now carries the engine's capabilities beside the dimensions — `engineLabel`, `turnShape`, `reportsCost`, `costSource`, `takesEffort` — answered once in `bridgeDimsOut` so a sixth engine describes itself on all of them at once. `console.sessions` carries the same five per row, plus `steerable`, with the warning that `false` does not mean the controls are dead: on a shared-ACP engine they reach a LIVE connection at the next turn boundary.

**The security decision is unchanged and is now said out loud.** OpenCode's Console permission card is user-triggerable, so the SOP asks whether it belongs on the bridge. The STANDING rule does — it is a session dimension like model and effort. The ONE-OFF answer to a question the engine has stopped to ask does **not**: that is an agent granting itself the tool it was just refused. It stays with the user in the panel, and the pending request is READABLE (`console.sessions` → `asking`, `pendingPermission`) so an agent can report what it is stuck on without settling it. A test asserts no credential value leaves through `engines.status` or the matrix behind it.

## 3.161.0 — U-59 is closed: the sentence that called a stopping engine a sandbox, and a row missing from five surfaces at once (2026-08-19)

**‼️ The Console told the user OpenCode cannot stop and ask, on the panel where its permission card appears.** The permission tooltip branched on one boolean — `steerable`, which answers *can this change while a turn is RUNNING* — and a shared-ACP engine says **no** to that while saying **yes** to the question the reader is actually asking. So it fell into the per-turn sentence: *"This engine cannot stop and ask, so the mode becomes a SANDBOX chosen up front."* Both halves false. It stops and asks over ACP with its own `once / always / reject` card, and it has no sandbox at all — the exact promise-that-is-not-kept this panel already refuses to make about Antigravity, made about the one engine that keeps it. Three shapes now answer separately, and the shared-ACP branch says the thing that actually bites: **unattended there is nobody to answer, so the same request comes back refused rather than waiting.** The Tasks form's Engine and Permissions boxes say it too, from the engine's `shape` rather than from a sentence about "any engine that is not Claude".

**‼️ Two engines were handed an empty dropdown to stare at.** Gemini has no reasoning-effort setting and OpenCode has none either (ACP declares only `model` and `mode`; no reachable model publishes a variant). The Tasks form already dropped the box; the Console drew it anyway, at a fixed 82px, on both of its rows. The question is now the **engine's** — `engineTakesEffort`, the same answer the bridge refuses on — and not the catalogue's silence, which only arrives after a handshake. And `(--model)` `(--effort)` `(--permission-mode)` were Claude's flag names printed over every engine: they come from `engineFlagFor` now, or there is no parenthesis.

**‼️ OpenCode was missing from the plan-usage matrix, which is three surfaces at once** — the status-bar hover, the Dashboard's Plan usage card and `usage.engines`. An engine simply absent from a list cannot be told from an engine this build has never heard of, which is the distinction that whole module exists to keep. Its row is `no plan` and **not** `not published`: nothing is being withheld — each model runs against its own provider, and it is the one engine besides Claude that states a real price per turn. It gets its own two words for that (`priced per turn`), because `per-token` was Gemini's reason and read as *your tokens are being billed* on the engine whose free models cost nothing.

**‼️ "The check did not run" wore the same red ✗ as "the engine failed".** Pressing Test on OpenCode with no free model on offer produced a refusal — correctly, since Agent Farm will not pick a billed model for a health check — and the page drew it as a failure, directly under a green row saying the engine was ready. A refusal is now its own state (`⊘`, in the palette's "your move" colour), and its hover says the engine was never asked instead of timing a call that never happened.

**Roll calls are asked for, not typed.** `Which CLI ran the session: Claude · Codex · Gemini · Antigravity` and its twin on the Turns page were hand-written lists that a fifth engine shipped straight past; both ask `AFEngine.names()` now. Farm Status said `0/4 engines ready` and recommended installing a list OpenCode was not on. The mission form's two budget fields claimed **only Claude Code** states a per-turn price — on a *budget* control, which is the worst place to be describing the farm as it was. The Cost columns on Turns, Sessions and Tasks called every figure an "API-equivalent"; they state the rule instead, so it stays true whatever ships next. The marketplace description, the walkthrough and three settings descriptions say five.

**Looked at.** New fixture variants draw the Console on OpenCode (five boxes become four), the Live Timeline and the Turns table with every engine on them, and the Plan usage card with five tabs on one line. Checked in dark and light.

## 3.160.0 — U-59: two surfaces disagreeing about one engine, and a flag name that was wrong on three (2026-08-19)

**‼️ Farm Settings still called OpenCode broken after the Engines page had been taught otherwise.** 3.159.0 gave the badge its fifth state; the picture then showed Settings drawing the row the old way — amber `not signed in`, and `Sign in with a plan` offered as the repair. Two pages drew the same badge from **two copies of the same rule**, so teaching one taught only one. The decision now lives once, in `media/afEngine.js` — the component that already owned how an engine is named and coloured — and both pages ask it. `builtin` and `none` are opposite answers and can no longer share a badge in one place while differing in another.

**‼️ And the per-agent default sentence named a flag three engines out of four do not take.** It read *"kept by Agent Farm and passed as `--model`/`--effort`"* for every engine that is not Claude. Measured by asking each engine's own argument builder:

| engine | model | effort |
|---|---|---|
| Codex | `-m` | *(none — it is a config assignment, `-c model_reasoning_effort=…`)* |
| Gemini | `-m` | *(none — this engine has no effort setting at all)* |
| Antigravity | `--model` | *(not carried on its own flag)* |
| OpenCode | `-m` | `--variant` |

So the sentence was right for one engine and wrong for the rest — and wrong in a way the user could **check**, by typing the flag and watching it fail. `engineFlagFor` now runs the engine's own builder with a sentinel and reads back which token ended up in front of it. Nothing knows a flag name any more, which is the point: an engine that renames one renames it here too. **An engine that carries the value some other way gets a sentence that names no flag at all** — printing `model_reasoning_effort=` as if it were one would be worse than saying nothing.

**Also in this pass:** the per-agent engine list had a hand-typed fallback (`['claude','codex','gemini','agy']`) that was complete the day it was written and silently short of OpenCode ever after — a defaults box the user was simply never offered. It comes off `SPECS` now (`ENGINE_IDS`). The Settings fixture gained the OpenCode row, the per-agent boxes and the model catalogue, including the **long-label** case U-59 asks for: every other engine names a model in a word or two, OpenCode's are `provider/model` and run past thirty characters. Checked in dark and light.

## 3.159.0 — U-59: OpenCode had no health check, and its row called itself broken (2026-08-18)

**‼️ The Engines page showed an engine that could never be tested.** Pressing Test on OpenCode answered *"No health check is defined for this engine."* — measured through the bridge, not guessed. Four engines had a spec and the fifth did not, so the one control on that page that proves a call really gets through was permanently unavailable for it.

It could not simply be added like the others, because the others are constants: a flag set and the smallest model on the plan, both true for as long as the CLI keeps its vocabulary. **OpenCode's cheapest turn is a free model from whichever providers happen to be connected on this machine**, and a name pinned in the source would become a *paid* turn the day that model is retired — on the very engine whose own provider gives free ones away. So a spec may now work its call out at press time:

- The catalogue is read first (`opencode models` — a listing, not a turn, so it costs nothing) and a `*-free` model is taken from it. The naming convention is the **engine's** signal, not ours: nothing here decides what is free, it reads what the provider called free. Sorted, so two runs of the check test the same thing and a flaky result cannot be blamed on the choice.
- The turn runs on **`--agent plan`**, which M-14 measured as calling *no tool at all* — a stronger read-only guarantee than a permission mode, because it is the engine's own behaviour rather than a setting a user's `opencode.json` could have overridden.
- The prompt goes on **stdin**, the channel this engine's run really uses. `EngineRunner` gained that parameter for the same reason it already carried `shell`: a health check that speaks a channel production does not is a check of a path nothing uses. Stdin is now closed on every engine, so nothing can sit waiting for input that will never come.
- **With no free model on offer, it refuses.** "This check would spend money on a paid turn — connect the provider, or pick a model and run one turn by hand" is worth more than a silent bill. Verified against the real binary outside VS Code: **ok in 12.2s**.

**And the row itself was calling a working engine broken.** `AuthMode` used `none` for two opposite answers to "is there a credential?" — *nobody has signed in, so this cannot run* and *this engine asks for nothing*. Every reader with only the mode to go on drew the second as the first: the badge said **`not signed in` in the warning colour, directly above a sentence saying the engine was ready**, and the row offered **"Sign in with a plan"** as the fix for a fault it did not have. `builtin` is now its own state — a state rather than a flag beside the mode, because the mode is what the exhaustiveness tables switch on, so a new reader is made to answer for this case instead of falling into the failure branch by default. The badge reads *no sign-in needed* in the ready colour, and the button says *Add paid providers*, which is what pressing it actually buys.

**Found by looking at it.** The Engines fixture had four engines and had never drawn this one; both faults were plain in the first picture and invisible to every string test, because each string was correct on its own. Checked in dark and light.

## 3.158.0 — M-14 is closed: every surface, on the real engine, verified twice (2026-08-18)

The last two fixes were run through their own paths on the live build, which closes M-14's acceptance matrix.

- **Agent Farm can now find the conversations it causes.** `sessions.opencodeSync` went from `roots 15 · listed 11 · inTable 0` to `roots 24 · listed 62 · inTable 2` — the run folders the farm itself chose are scan roots now.
- **‼️ Explicit resume works from a surface, which was the last open row.** `tasks.add { resume: "ses_feac8a864ffe…" }` was accepted, came back on the **same** session id rather than a new one, and answered `ZARFIL-M14` to a prompt that said *don't look at the file again* — so the only way it could know was the conversation carrying. `resumeCostBefore: 0` and 8 572 tokens for the turn, not the conversation's total.
- **Antigravity's handoff verified on a real two-step chain.** Step 2 received the answer alone: no `conversation_id`, no `status`, no timings.

**M-14's acceptance matrix is complete:** fresh **and** explicit resume on every surface · tool success · tokens / cache / `cost: 0` on a free model · cancel · retry · restart binding · attachment · a readable refusal, before anything starts, for a model the engine cannot take.

**What the item actually cost, and what it bought.** Running the six surfaces for the first time found **five** bugs — an empty prompt on every bridge retry, a schedule that could not be given an engine model at all, two handoffs that carried a transcript instead of an answer, and a farm that could not index the conversation it had just created. Every one of them passed all 10 700+ tests that existed at the time. The shared root is one assumption — *what is true on Claude is true on every engine* — and the only thing that exposed it was running the real binary through the real surface.

*One thing is now visible that was not before, and it is not M-14's:* the harvest reports `failed: 20`. Fixing the roots means far more conversations are seen, and a fifth of them fail to export. The cause was not measured; it is filed as its own item rather than guessed at here.

## 3.157.0 — verifying the three fixes found two more (2026-08-18)

3.156.0's three fixes were run again through the same paths on the live build, because a passing test is not a working feature. All three held: `tasks.rerun` with no `prompt` now **inherits** the original's; `schedules.add` **accepts** `opencode/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free` while still refusing `opencode/x; rm -rf /` and `opencode/$(whoami)` — the guard was not loosened, a missing character was added to its class; and a two-step chain's second step received `… : ZARFIL-M14`, the answer rather than the transcript. The reload also closed an acceptance row that only a restart can answer: **the launch binding survived it** — every pre-reload run still knows its engine, its `ses_…`, its tokens and its cost.

Verifying them turned up two more.

**‼️ Agent Farm could not find a conversation it had caused itself.** `opencode session list` is cwd-scoped, so a conversation is only ever found from the folder it was created in — and the harvest roots were the open workspace plus the agent directories. A task's own `workDir` is neither. So the farm would send a run to a folder **it chose**, write that folder onto the task, and then be unable to index the conversation it had just created: `tasks.add { resume: <ses_…> }` refused every such id. The refusal was right — continuing a conversation it cannot find would silently open a new one — but there was no way for it to ever succeed. Roots now include the `workDir` of tasks that ran on OpenCode. Found by trying to resume a run this farm had made ten minutes earlier.

**Antigravity had the same handoff fault as OpenCode.** Found by reading every archive on this machine rather than by running the engine again — a cheaper measurement, and one that answers the question 3.156.0 left open. `agy --output-format json` prints **one envelope** and the answer is `response`; the generic unwrap knows only `result`, which is Claude's word, so an Antigravity step handed the next one the whole envelope — conversation id, status and timings included. Keyed on the engine, like the OpenCode branch: a `response` field in somebody's own JSON output contract is their data, not a wrapper for us to unwrap. *(Codex and Gemini have left no archives on this machine, so they remain unmeasured.)*
